# Pitch

Coldwater Reach, Maine, October 1943. A man's body washes in on the breakwater after a three-day storm — no papers, no name, nobody's business but the sea's. The Coast Guard takes the body and most of the questions with it. What it leaves behind is shared, in fragments and separately, by three people who will never all sit in the same room: Eira Bowman, the fifty-two-year-old harbormaster who knows what she saw on the dock the night before the body came in; Hannah Pfeiffer, seventeen, whose family's dairy farm now houses four German POWs under an aging Coastal Patrol private, one of whom is from a town near where her father was born; and Dr. Marcus Klein, forty-seven, the Viennese émigré teaching German at the high school, a man who spent a year in a Canadian internment camp and now boards with the only household in Coldwater that doesn't treat him as a specimen.

Across roughly eighteen months of the war's second half, the three of them carry the breakwater question — each from their own angle, none with the full picture. What the novel is actually about is not the body: it is what authority costs a woman who holds a post built for a different body; what it means to make a series of small choices that accumulate into a life, when you are seventeen; and whether displacement ever ends, and what the displaced person becomes when it stops.

# World

## Setting

**Coldwater Reach, Maine** — a fictional working port on the mid-coast, small enough that the harbormaster knows every hull that ties up, large enough to have a high school, a post office, a diner, a feed store, and a Catholic church that also serves the Swedish Lutherans when the weather closes the inland roads. Population: perhaps 800 in town, another 400 on outlying farms and woodlots. Not a tourist place. Not a retirement place. A place that has always been slightly behind on its repairs.

**Time span**: October 1943 to May 1945. The war's last eighteen months as experienced by people who are not fighting it.

## Geography and landscape

The harbor is tidal, with a thirty-foot range at neaps. The breakwater is granite rubble construction, thrown out in an L from the south headland; in storm it takes green water over the top. The working waterfront: a fish pier, a cold-storage house, a boatyard with a railway-haul-out, the harbormaster's shed at the pier head. The inner harbor holds lobster boats, draggers, and two sardine carriers that run to Eastport. The outer anchorage, which is exposed, is empty most winters.

Three miles inland the land flattens into drumlins and hay fields. The Pfeiffer farm sits at the end of a dirt road off Route 1, with a barn that pre-dates the Revolution, a renovated icehouse now serving as bunkhouse, and forty dairy cows. The pasture smells in August of warm manure and sweetgrass. In November it smells of frozen mud. The Germans work the farm under the rules of the Geneva Convention and the supervision of Lonzo Reed, a 62-year-old Coastal Patrol private who sits by the icehouse door with a carbine that may or may not be loaded.

The school where Marcus teaches is a three-story brick building on the main road, built in 1912, with a gymnasium that doubles as a polling place and a basement boiler room where Henry Crow is in charge of all heat from October through April.

## Technology and material culture

- **Radio**: war news comes over the radio. BC-1206 sets in households that can afford them. The diner has one on all day. Hannah's family does not listen to war news in German, and her father does not discuss this rule.
- **Mail**: V-Mail (photographed letter forms for overseas), ordinary letters for domestic, casualty telegrams delivered by the Western Union boy on a bicycle nobody has replaced. The telegram is the shape of dread.
- **Rationing**: OPA ration books govern gasoline, tires, sugar, coffee, meat, canned goods, and shoes. The harbormaster has a supplemental fuel allocation. Farm families barter informally. Marcus owns no car and walks everywhere; this was unremarkable in Vienna and is remarked upon in Coldwater.
- **The U-boat question**: in 1942, U-boats sank ships off the Maine coast. By 1943, the threat has receded — convoys, air patrols, the longer Atlantic battle going the other way. But the memory is present; fishermen remember the oil slicks and the life rings. The harbormaster's log still has 1942 entries with phrases like "unusual surface wake" and "detonation, bearing approx. SE."
- **POW labor**: governed by the 1929 Geneva Convention. German prisoners at satellite camps (under the umbrella of Camp Houlton) work civilian farms. They are paid in canteen credits, not cash. They wear POW-stenciled clothing. They may not fraternize with civilians — this rule is loosely kept where there is no officer to keep it.

## Mood and atmosphere

Autumn fog. The smell of salt and diesel and fish offal. The particular quality of light in coastal Maine in November: flat, gray, uncompromising. The war is in the kitchen through the radio, in the post office through the telegrams, in the feed store through the ration books and the missing young men's names on the window placard. It is not dramatic. It is long. It is the texture of ordinary life deformed by a very large event far away.

The town is mostly white, mostly Protestant or Catholic, economically precarious in ways the Depression made worse and the war has partially remedied (factory orders, Navy contracts). Henry and Lillian Crow are one of perhaps three Black households in town; they are not newcomers, but they are counted. Marcus Klein is the only European refugee, and before he arrived he was described in the town meeting minutes as "a Continental educator." Both are absorbed into town life with the particular pragmatism of small places that need useful people — but neither is invisible.

## What the war has taken

The harbormaster's assistant, drafted in January 1942. Three Coldwater boys dead as of October 1943 (two in the Pacific, one in North Africa). A fourth missing. The teacher Marcus replaced. The sardine carrier *Helen F.* lost to collision in a dark-running convoy. The easy certainty about what Germans are like.

# Characters

## POV Characters

---

### Eira Bowman — POV 1
**Age**: 52 in October 1943  
**Role**: Harbormaster, Coldwater Reach  
**Background**: Born in Coldwater. Married Owen Bowman, who held the harbormaster's post. Owen drowned in the November storm of 1935 — a sudden blow, a capsize, a body that took three days to come back. Eira has held the post for eight years, first by default and then by demonstrated competence. She is the only woman serving as harbormaster on the Maine coast.

**Drives**: To do the job correctly, because the job is real work and incorrectly done people die. To hold the post that was his without letting that fact be the most important fact about her. The two drives are slightly in tension: the post is still called "his" by the older fishermen; she notices this and says nothing. Her unspoken third drive is to understand what she saw on the dock the night before the body came in — not because she expects resolution, but because she is constitutionally unable to file something in the wrong column.

**Voice**: Spare, procedural. She thinks in tidal increments and load calculations. Her dialogue is clipped; she says less than she knows. When grief reaches her it comes in harbor idiom — she thinks of Owen as "offset from the schedule" or "overdue." The reader understands before she does. Interior passages are rare and short. The sentence-level texture is working: what needs doing, what has been done, what was left undone.

**Relationships**: 
- Owen Bowman (husband, deceased) — his absence is structural, not decorative  
- Hannah Pfeiffer (knows her as the Pfeiffer girl; the family connection is the shared commerce of a small town)  
- Marcus Klein (a nodding acquaintance; he walks the waterfront; she knows who lives here)  
- Henry Crow (knows him as the school custodian, as someone reliable in bad weather, as a man who doesn't waste words — which she respects)  
- The Coast Guard lieutenant who takes the body (a younger man; she reads him as competent but not curious)  

**Arc**: Authority and what it costs. By the end, she has made a decision she can't undo and did not ask permission for — and that decision is precisely what the post required of its holder. She becomes, in a way she could not have without Owen's death, the harbormaster.

---

### Hannah Pfeiffer — POV 2
**Age**: 17 in October 1943 (18 by spring 1944)  
**Role**: Farmer's daughter, high school student, observer  
**Background**: Born in Maine to Bavarian immigrant parents. Her father Albrecht and mother Magda came over in 1922, before the National Socialists were anything anyone in Maine had heard of. The family farm has been viable, barely, through the Depression. The war has fractured the household: Albrecht has retreated into German at home, Magda into silence. Hannah is caught between two languages and two loyalties she didn't choose.

**Drives**: To understand her parents without becoming them. To have a life that is not entirely circumscribed by what her parents' homeland did and what her neighbors think about it. And at the immediate, daily level: curiosity — an almost ungovernable interest in other people's interiority, which makes her dangerous in a small town and necessary to the novel's structure.

**Voice**: The most porous of the three. The narrative admits more sensation, more tonal fluctuation. German phrases surface when her father's voice is in her head — not often, never explained, always felt. Sentence lengths vary more widely than in Eira's or Marcus's chapters. Her thinking is associative rather than procedural. She is the most capable of noticing things that contradict what she has been told, and the least experienced at knowing what to do with the noticing.

**Relationships**:
- Albrecht Pfeiffer (father) — a man deformed by grief and shame in ways he will not name; Hannah loves him and cannot reach him  
- Magda Pfeiffer (mother) — the silence is medical; it began as depression after the war started and has not lifted  
- Karl Reinmar (the youngest German POW) — nineteen, from Ansbach, near where Albrecht was born; they share approximately thirty words of overlapping German-English; what happens between them is watched by Lonzo Reed and by Hannah herself with different degrees of understanding  
- Lonzo Reed (the guard) — sixty-two, Coastal Patrol private; he is not cruel, not stupid, and more aware of what is happening in the icehouse than he lets on  
- Marcus Klein (her German teacher at school) — the most complex relationship in her social world; she is one of three students in his advanced German class; he is the first adult outside her household who treats her curiosity as a credential rather than a problem  

**Arc**: The slow accumulation of small choices. By the end, she has done something — told someone something, withheld something, or made a choice with her hands and her feet — that she cannot undo, that constitutes, looking back, the shape of who she is becoming.

---

### Dr. Marcus Klein — POV 3
**Age**: 47 in October 1943  
**Role**: German and Latin teacher, Coldwater Reach High School  
**Background**: Born in Vienna, circa 1896. University at Vienna (classical languages, comparative literature). Left Austria in 1938, when the nature of the Anschluss became clear. Paris (1938–1939), London (1939–1940). Arrived in Canada 1940 under circumstances he does not fully explain; interned at Sherbrooke, Quebec, as an enemy alien (Austria was technically German territory) for approximately ten months. Released to the Emergency Committee rolls in 1941. Arrived in Cambridge 1941, then Coldwater in March 1942. He is Jewish, and while this is not secret, it is not a thing he discusses in Coldwater — the town is not hostile, but it is also not his milieu, and he has learned to calibrate what he says about himself.

**Drives**: To stop translating. To be in a language rather than between two of them. His displacement has been so prolonged — Vienna, Paris, London, Sherbrooke, Cambridge, Coldwater — that he has become fluent in the stance of the temporary resident, and now does not know how to be permanent. The body on the breakwater catches him because it is a problem he can think about in German — the dead man's identity, if it can be established, is a puzzle in exactly the language Marcus has been carrying alone.

**Voice**: Precise, slightly formal, the slightly overcorrect English of a man who learned the language from pages. His narration has the quality of translation — not stilted, but measured. He chooses words with the awareness of a man who knows words can be evidence. His chapters are the densest with qualification and subordination, without being academic in a distracting way. The formality is warmth, in his register.

**Relationships**:
- Henry Crow (landlord and, quietly, friend) — the relationship is conducted mostly through practical acts: Henry fixes the boiler, Marcus sits in the kitchen drinking coffee while he does; they have never had a long conversation but understand each other with the precision of two men who are used to being misunderstood by others  
- Lillian Crow (Henry's wife) — treats Marcus as a guest; sets a plate; asks no questions; this is, for Marcus, close to home  
- Hannah Pfeiffer (student) — he recognizes her particular kind of intelligence and is careful about it; his job is to teach her German, not to become her confessor  
- Eira Bowman (acquaintance) — he sees her as formidably competent; she is one of the few people in Coldwater he has not had to explain himself to  
- The dead man (unknown) — the puzzle Marcus cannot file away  

**Arc**: Whether displacement ends. By the close of the novel, Marcus has done something that commits him to Coldwater Reach specifically — not to America in the abstract, but to this place — and in doing so has stopped being temporary. The exact act is a function of the plot; the arc is about how a person stops performing rootlessness.

---

## Secondary Characters

### Henry Crow
**Age**: approximately 55 in 1943  
**Role**: Chief custodian, Coldwater Reach High School; Marcus's landlord  
**Background**: Family came north from Norfolk, Virginia, in 1924, during the Great Migration's secondary wave to northern New England. Henry has been at the school since 1928. He and Lillian have one son, James, who is in the Army — Pacific theater.  
**Voice** (if given a chapter): Unhurried, specific, with a dry observational humor that never tips into performance. He has watched the town for twenty years; he knows where the weight rests.  
**Note**: May anchor one or two exceptional chapters. Not a regular POV.

### Lillian Crow
**Age**: early 50s  
**Role**: Henry's wife; community church member; informal network node for the town's working poor  
**Voice**: Warm, laconic, with a practical view of what can be changed and what cannot.

### Albrecht Pfeiffer
**Age**: mid-50s  
**Role**: Hannah's father; dairy farmer  
**Note**: Has retreated into German at home since the war started. This is not loyalty to the Reich — it is grief, shame, and a kind of withdrawal. He is not a villain; he is a broken man who cannot explain himself in any language.

### Magda Pfeiffer
**Age**: early 50s  
**Role**: Hannah's mother  
**Note**: Her silence began as depression and has become something else. She is present in the novel as a weight and an absence.

### Karl Reinmar
**Age**: 19 in October 1943  
**Role**: German POW, one of four assigned to the Pfeiffer farm  
**Background**: From Ansbach, Bavaria — approximately fifty kilometers from where Albrecht Pfeiffer was born. He is not a Nazi in any meaningful ideological sense; he is a nineteen-year-old who was conscripted and captured and is now milking cows in Maine. He is lonely. He can identify every field bird in German and cannot remember the English.  
**Note**: May anchor an exceptional chapter.

### Lonzo Reed
**Age**: 62  
**Role**: Coastal Patrol private, assigned to escort duty at the Pfeiffer farm  
**Background**: Too old for the real Army, too experienced for nothing. He has been watching people for sixty-two years and misses very little. His relationship with the four Germans is correct and watchful; his relationship with Hannah is protective in a way neither of them acknowledges.  
**Note**: May anchor an exceptional chapter.

### The Man on the Breakwater
**Age**: unknown  
**Role**: The novel's structural spine — the unidentified body  
**Note**: Appears only in retrospect and description. His identity is assembled by the reader across thirty chapters; the novel does not guarantee completion of the assembly.

# Style

## POV and Tense

Third-person limited past tense throughout. The narrative binds tightly to whatever POV the chapter belongs to — no cross-chapter omniscience, no free-floating observations that require knowledge the POV character does not have. The three POVs are differentiated enough that the reader should be able to identify the POV within the first paragraph.

## Overall Register

Literary adult fiction, restrained register, period-exact texture. The closest comparables by feel: *The Remains of the Day* (Ishiguro) for the quality of repression and what is not said; *Gilead* (Robinson) for the moral weight that accumulates in quiet sentences; *The Hours* (Cunningham) for the braided three-POV structure and the way each strand is complete. Not any of these in style — but the emotional pitch and the trust placed in the reader are comparable.

Prose is action and observation. Interior monologue is sparse and earns its space. The story trusts the reader to infer affect from event and detail, not from labeled emotion. "She felt sad" is not a sentence this novel writes.

## Eira's Register

Spare and procedural. Shortest sentences of the three POVs. The working vocabulary of the waterfront: tide, draft, load, bearings, the names of vessels and weather patterns. Even her emotional life translates into this vocabulary before it surfaces as narration. She does not explain herself. Her chapters create their effect through accumulation of precise physical observation; the emotional content is the gap between what is observed and what is withheld. Dialogue in her chapters is clipped — short exchanges, no social lubricant.

Average sentence: 10–16 words. Most interior passages max out at three sentences before Eira's attention returns to the physical world.

## Hannah's Register

The most tonally flexible of the three. Associative, capable of metaphor, registers sensation with more directness. German phrases are embedded without translation — they are there when her father's voice is in her head, or when Karl Reinmar has said something she is still processing. These are set in italics and contextually comprehensible. Her chapters open up to more dialogue, more scene-building, more of the texture of the farm (smells, sounds, the weight of animals and equipment). She is also the most likely to observe something accurately and not yet know what she has observed.

Average sentence: 12–20 words, with wider variance. Her registers of sensation allow occasional longer lyric passages, but these should not tip into poeticizing — Hannah is smart and feeling, not precious.

## Marcus's Register

Precise, slightly formal, architectured. Marcus writes long subordinate clauses, the way a man writes who learned English on the page and learned it in the academic tradition. His diction is more Latinate than the other two. He qualifies his statements — he knows words can be evidence and he handles them accordingly. His chapters have a dry, careful irony that emerges from the precision, not from jokes. He does not perform suffering; he names things accurately and with some distance, and this restraint is itself a form of feeling.

Average sentence: 15–22 words. His chapters have more internal structural complexity (if/then thinking, historical analogy, measured qualification) but never tip into academic opacity.

## Dialogue

- **Eira**: Short, functional, declarative. She doesn't explain herself in dialogue any more than in narration.
- **Hannah**: More willing to ask questions, more willing to leave sentences unfinished. Her conversations with Karl Reinmar are conducted in a broken pidgin of German and English; her conversations with Marcus are the most complete.
- **Marcus**: Careful, occasionally formal, precise. His English is deliberate — he chooses the right word, not the idiomatic word. This is not parody; it is texture.
- **Albrecht Pfeiffer**: When he appears in dialogue (which is rare), his English is spare and slightly stilted — not phonetic stage-German, but the English of a man who has decided to stop speaking it easily.
- **German speakers in general**: No phonetic burlesquing. German phrases where appropriate; the reader can hear the texture without a performance of accent.

## Pacing

Chapters run 2,000–3,000 words each, with a target of about 2,600 for a 30-chapter manuscript of ~80,000 words. The pacing within chapters follows the POV character's attention: Eira's chapters are the most compressed (she doesn't dwell), Hannah's the most expansive in sensory register, Marcus's the most deliberate in structure. No chapter should feel like it is waiting for another chapter's event.

## Period Texture

History is not deployed as set decoration. Ration books and V-Mail and the BC-1206 radio appear because these are the objects through which these characters live — not because the author wants the reader to think "authentic." The same logic governs all period detail: if it is in the scene, it is in the scene because a person in 1943 would encounter it and it matters to what they are doing.

Anachronism in diction should be avoided. The vocabulary of mid-century New England maritime is available through period sources. No modern management-speak, no contemporary psychological vocabulary (characters do not "process" things or have "trauma responses" as labeled events).

## Failure modes

The AI-author patterns most tempting in this story's register. The drafter should actively avoid these; the compression pass should cut them.

- **Post-scene subtext naming** — after a charged scene between, say, Hannah and Karl, a paragraph naming what the scene was "really about" or what Hannah "now understood." The novel does not do this. It leaves the scene. The reader understands.
- **Thesis restatement** — an abstract sentence at the end of a chapter restating the POV character's arc or the novel's theme. "She was learning, perhaps, that authority meant this." Cut it.
- **Emotional structural analysis** — dramatizing a feeling, then explaining its architecture. Eira's grief is especially vulnerable to this. The architecture should be the image, not the explanation.
- **Redundant transition / re-summary** — opening a chapter by recapping what the previous chapter left off. Each chapter begins in medias res of the POV character's day. No "It had been three days since she found the body."
- **Dialogue glosses** — "as if to say," "which meant." The three POVs are already distinguished by how they hear silence. Do not tag dialogue with interpretation; let it sit.
- **Meta-commentary on cognition** — "She noticed," "He registered," "Marcus found himself thinking." If the prose is doing its job, the noticing is the sentence, not a label for it.

## Lean-into patterns

Patterns the drafter and editors should NOT treat as failures, because this register depends on them.

- **Delayed interiority** — Eira especially: the emotional meaning of a scene arrives a paragraph later, after she has returned her attention to the physical world. This gap is the technique, not a failure to show feeling.
- **The untranslated German phrase** — in Hannah's chapters. Not explained, not italicized for foreignness (though set in italics as convention). Contextually graspable. The reader who does not know German should still feel it.
- **Measured qualification in Marcus's narration** — his subordinate clauses and qualifications are voice, not verbosity. Do not compress them out.
- **Scene endings that go one beat past resolution** — the last sentence of a scene is often something physical, something observed, rather than a statement of where we stand. This is not evasion; it is the texture of the register.

# Continuity

Hard facts that must not break across chapters. This file is the source of truth for dates, ages, histories, and structural constraints.

## Chronology

1. The story opens in **October 1943** and closes in **spring 1945**, approximately May, before VE Day (May 8, 1945).
2. The body on the breakwater arrives after a **three-day blow**, in **October 1943** — this is the inciting event.
3. The Coast Guard takes the body. The body has **no papers**.
4. Eira saw **something on the dock the night before the body came in**. This is established in chapter 1 or very early; what exactly she saw is parceled out across later chapters.

## Ages and Life Dates

5. **Eira Bowman** is **52** in October 1943. Born approximately 1891.
6. **Owen Bowman** (Eira's husband) drowned in the **November storm of 1935**. Eira has held the harbormaster post for **eight years** as of October 1943.
7. **Hannah Pfeiffer** is **17** in October 1943, turning 18 in spring/summer 1944.
8. **Albrecht and Magda Pfeiffer** emigrated from Bavaria to Maine in **1922**.
9. **Dr. Marcus Klein** is **47** in October 1943. Born approximately 1896, Vienna.
10. Marcus was interned at **Sherbrooke, Quebec**, as an enemy alien — released to the Emergency Committee rolls in 1941. He arrived in Coldwater in **March 1942**.
11. **Henry Crow** is approximately **55** in 1943. His family came north from Norfolk, Virginia, in **1924**.
12. Henry and Lillian's son **James Crow** is in the **Army, Pacific theater**, as of October 1943.

## POW Labor Program

13. **Four German prisoners** are housed in the Pfeiffer farm's renovated icehouse and work the farm under the federal POW labor program.
14. The four POWs are escorted by **Lonzo Reed**, age **62**, a Coastal Patrol private.
15. **Karl Reinmar** is **19** years old, from **Ansbach**, Bavaria — approximately 50 km from Albrecht Pfeiffer's hometown.
16. The POW program is governed by the **1929 Geneva Convention**. Prisoners are paid in canteen credits. The no-fraternization rule is loosely kept.
17. The umbrella camp is **Camp Houlton**, Maine. The Pfeiffer farm is a satellite work camp.

## Structure

18. The three **main POVs are Eira, Hannah, and Marcus** — roughly ten chapters each, rotating asymmetrically.
19. There may be **two or three short chapters from a fourth POV** (Henry, Lonzo, or Karl) — these are exceptional, not regular.
20. **The three POV characters never meet as a group of three.** Their threads cross bilaterally and accidentally.
21. The **breakwater question** (who was the man, what happened) is assembled by the reader across all thirty chapters. It may or may not be fully answered; the characters' relationships to it resolve even if the underlying fact stays in shadow.
22. At least **one thread is deliberately unresolved** at the close.
23. The story ends just **before VE Day, spring 1945**. The war ends in the background; resolutions are personal.

## Setting

24. **Coldwater Reach** is a fictional town on the mid-coast of Maine. Real place names (Portland, Bangor, Houlton, Cambridge MA, Sherbrooke QC) may appear; **no real people** may appear by name.
25. The harbor has a **tidal range** characteristic of Maine mid-coast (approx. 10–12 feet at neap, more at spring tides). The breakwater is **granite rubble construction** on an L from the south headland.
26. The harbormaster's operations are regulated by period-accurate USCG and port authority procedures.

## Historical Constraints

27. **No spy plot.** No Nazi agents, no coded messages, no submarine landings. The U-boat scares belong to 1942 and are in memory, not present action, by October 1943.
28. The war news reaches Coldwater via **radio, V-Mail, and casualty telegrams**. The telegram is the shape of dread.
29. **OPA rationing** applies: gasoline, tires, sugar, coffee, meat, canned goods, shoes.
30. Period diction is mid-century New England maritime. No anachronistic vocabulary.

# Glossary

Terms, names, places, and objects. Alphabetical. Added to by later phases.

---

**Albrecht Pfeiffer** — Hannah's father. Bavarian immigrant (arrived 1922). Dairy farmer. Has retreated into German at home since the war started. See *Characters*.

**BC-1206** — military-surplus-adjacent table radio common in home-front households; delivers war news and music.

**Breakwater** — the granite rubble L-shaped structure protecting the harbor of Coldwater Reach from the southeast. Where the body comes in.

**Camp Houlton** — real German POW camp in northern Maine; hub for satellite farm-labor work camps including the Pfeiffer farm detail.

**Coldwater Reach** — fictional working port on the mid-coast of Maine. Setting for the entire novel.

**Dr. Marcus Klein** — German and Latin teacher at Coldwater Reach High School; Viennese émigré, formerly interned at Sherbrooke. POV character 3. See *Characters*.

**Eira Bowman** — harbormaster of Coldwater Reach. Widow. POV character 1. See *Characters*.

**Emergency Committee in Aid of Displaced Foreign Scholars** — real American organization that helped European refugee academics find positions in US universities and schools, 1933–1945. Marcus was on their rolls.

**Geneva Convention (1929)** — governs treatment of POWs. German prisoners in Maine work camps are entitled to wages (paid in canteen credits), adequate food and shelter, and protection from hazardous work and abuse.

**Hannah Pfeiffer** — seventeen-year-old daughter of Albrecht and Magda Pfeiffer; farm girl and high school student. POV character 2. See *Characters*.

**Henry Crow** — chief custodian, Coldwater Reach High School; Marcus's landlord. African American, family from Norfolk VA (arrived 1924). Approximate age 55 in 1943. See *Characters*.

**Icehouse (Pfeiffer farm)** — renovated structure serving as bunkhouse for four German POWs under the labor program.

**James Crow** — Henry and Lillian's son. U.S. Army, Pacific theater, as of October 1943.

**Karl Reinmar** — youngest of the four German POWs, age 19, from Ansbach, Bavaria. See *Characters*.

**Lillian Crow** — Henry's wife. See *Characters*.

**Lonzo Reed** — Coastal Patrol private, age 62, escort guard for the Pfeiffer farm POW detail. See *Characters*.

**Magda Pfeiffer** — Hannah's mother. Silence began as depression when the war started and has not lifted.

**Man on the Breakwater** — unidentified male body found after the three-day October 1943 storm. No papers. Taken by the Coast Guard. The structural spine of the novel.

**OPA** — Office of Price Administration. Issues ration books governing wartime consumer goods.

**Owen Bowman** — Eira's husband, the previous harbormaster. Drowned in the November storm of 1935. His absence is structural throughout.

**Pfeiffer farm** — dairy farm three miles inland from Coldwater Reach; site of the POW labor detail. Includes a pre-Revolutionary barn, forty dairy cows, and the renovated icehouse.

**Sherbrooke (Internment camp)** — Camp #N, Sherbrooke, Quebec, Canada. Marcus was interned there 1940–1941 as an enemy alien (Austria, classified as German territory). He does not discuss it.

**V-Mail** — Victory Mail; overseas correspondence photographed and reduced for transport, then reprinted at the delivery end. Standard wartime letter system.

**Western Union telegram** — the delivery method for casualty notifications. Delivered by the local Western Union office; in Coldwater, by bicycle.

# Themes

## 1. What authority costs

Eira holds a post built for someone else's body. She holds it correctly — better, in some senses, than Owen held it — and this does not make it hers in the eyes of the men who tie up at her dock. The novel asks what it means to hold a position entirely on the merits while the legitimacy question goes on and on. The answer the novel offers is not triumphant: authority at this cost is a kind of solitude. By the end, Eira has done something that the post required and that no one asked her to do, and in doing it she has stopped waiting for the post to become hers and simply occupied it. The novel does not call this heroism. It calls it work.

## 2. Whether displacement ends

Marcus has been displaced for five years by October 1943, across four countries, through an internment he does not discuss. He has become expert at the stance of the temporary resident — at not putting down things that will have to be picked up again. The novel asks whether this expertise, once acquired, can be given up. The answer is not a revelation; it is a small, specific, irrevocable act that commits him to this place, these people, this address. Displacement ends, the novel suggests, not when the external situation resolves but when the person displaced stops holding in reserve the option of leaving — when he stops performing rootlessness and simply lives where he is.

## 3. The accumulation of small choices

Hannah's arc is structured around the premise that adolescence is a series of small decisions that look, in the moment, like they don't count, and which turn out in aggregate to be a person. What she chooses to tell and what she withholds, who she defends and who she lets the town think what it thinks about — these are not dramatic acts. They have the weight of ordinary life. By the close, she has made one or two choices that cannot be undone and that are, without her having named them so, the shape of her character. The novel does not celebrate these choices or condemn them; it observes them with the same directness it brings to everything.

## 4. The partial knowledge the living hold

The body on the breakwater is the structural manifestation of this theme: nobody has the whole picture. The reader assembles what happened across thirty chapters and three perspectives and still may not have all of it. But the theme extends beyond the mystery: Eira does not know the full truth of Henry Crow's experience of the town; Marcus does not know what Hannah understands about Karl Reinmar; Hannah does not know what her father knows about the dead man. The novel's moral texture comes from the recognition that partial knowledge is the condition, not the exception — that acting responsibly from inside it is what character means.

# Drafter guidance — *Coldwater Reach*

## Voice register

This is literary adult fiction with a restrained, period-exact register. The closest comparables are Ishiguro's *The Remains of the Day* (repression as texture, what is never said as the load-bearing content), Marilynne Robinson's *Gilead* (moral weight accumulating in quiet sentences), and Colm Tóibín's *Nora Webster* (a widow holding a post, the world reduced to work, grief arriving late in physical idiom). Sentences are complete, precise, unhurried. No pyrotechnics. The technique is withholding, observation, the gap between what is noticed and what is acknowledged.

## Sentence-length expectations

- **Eira's chapters**: average 10–16 words. Three short declaratives is the rhythm; vary at the fourth. Subordinate clauses are rare and purposeful.
- **Hannah's chapters**: average 12–20 words, wider variance. She has a lyric range the other two do not. An occasional long sentence is permitted — but "lyric" means precise and felt, not ornamental.
- **Marcus's chapters**: average 15–22 words. Subordinate clauses, qualifications, conditional structures are voice, not bloat. Do not compress them out. A well-built Marcus sentence may run 30–35 words without being a failure — it is a failure only if it is soft or redundant.
- **Maximum for all POVs**: if a sentence is approaching 40 words, ask whether it is doing Marcus's measured intellectual work or simply accumulating. If the latter, cut.

## Chapter-opening conventions

- **No abstract observation openings.** Do not open a chapter with a statement about the world, the war, the season, or the nature of things. The chapter begins where the character is, in their body, in their day.
- **Eira**: opens in task. She is doing something with her hands or her eyes. Weather is permitted as an opening if it is working weather — a specific observation with operational consequence.
- **Hannah**: opens in sensation or conversation. She may open in the middle of dialogue, in the smell of the barn, in a specific physical act. Her openings are the most varied.
- **Marcus**: opens in observation or movement — often walking, since he walks everywhere. He may begin by noticing something that he then spends the chapter considering. He does not begin in pure interiority; he begins in the world and moves inward.

## Chapter-ending conventions

Target distribution across 30 chapters:
- **~10 chapters**: literary fade — the last sentence is something physical, observed, one beat past where the scene's action resolved. The dominant mode for this register.
- **~8 chapters**: turn — a piece of information or a shift that reframes what the chapter has been about; not a cliffhanger, but a quiet pivot.
- **~6 chapters**: resolved beat — the chapter's central question settles; the next chapter will open elsewhere.
- **~4 chapters**: elliptical — deliberate open question, an unfinished gesture, something left in mid-air.
- **~2 chapters**: cliffhanger or mid-action cut — used sparingly; the register does not do propulsive cliff-hangers as a rule. Reserve for structural turning points.

**The last sentence of a chapter almost never names what it means.** It is a physical image, a last word of dialogue, a specific observation. The meaning is the weight behind it. Let it sit.

## POV strategy

One POV per chapter, strictly. The chapter header or first paragraph orients the reader to whose chapter this is. No slipping into another character's knowledge mid-chapter — the narrator knows only what the POV character could plausibly observe or have been told.

Three primary POVs rotating asymmetrically (~10 chapters each). Rotation is motivated by story need, not strict cycle: three consecutive Eira chapters is fine when the harbor plot demands it. Two consecutive Hannah chapters when the farm material is building. The plotter's outline will specify the sequence.

Optional fourth-POV chapters (Henry, Lonzo, or Karl) are brief and exceptional — 1,500–2,000 words, no more than three total. They are not a fourth regular POV; they are structural correctives that give the reader access the three primaries cannot provide.

**The three primary POVs must not share a scene.** Their threads can cross — they can hear about each other, encounter each other briefly in public space — but they do not sit down together. The structural unit is the chapter and the chapter belongs to one person.

## Dialogue density

Moderate dialogue density, varying by POV. Eira's chapters are the sparsest in dialogue; her chapters are more observation than exchange. Hannah's chapters are the most dialogue-rich — the farm is full of exchanges (with her parents, with Karl in broken language, with Lonzo, with Marcus at school). Marcus's chapters have a middle density — more exchange than Eira, less than Hannah.

Dialogue tags are minimal. "Said" and "asked" carry almost all the weight. No "interjected," "retorted," "replied." Physical beats before or after dialogue lines instead of attributive tags where possible: *He set down the mug. "Three days."*

**German dialogue and phrases**: German in Hannah's chapters, and in any scene with Albrecht or Karl, is rendered in italics, not translated, but contextually graspable. *Ich weiß nicht* does not need a footnote. Do not write phonetic accent. Do not write German as pidgin unless the character is actually a non-native speaker groping for vocabulary (Karl in English; Hannah in German-to-Karl).

**No dialogue glosses.** The prose does not explain what a line of dialogue meant, implied, or "was really saying." The line sits. The next beat — a silence, a physical act, a subject change — does the work.

## Period texture and historical accuracy

Every material object that appears should be period-correct. The radio is a BC-1206 or a domestic equivalent. The ration book is an OPA book. The mail overseas is V-Mail. The Coast Guard officer's rank and uniform details follow 1943 USCG regulations. The POW labor arrangement follows 1929 Geneva Convention rules as applied in Maine.

**Do not deploy history as decoration.** The ration book is not mentioned to signal "authentic 1943." It is mentioned because Eira is counting what she has, or because Hannah is trying to figure out whether there is enough sugar. The object must earn its scene.

**Vocabulary**: no anachronisms. Characters do not "process" feelings, do not have "trauma" as a named category, do not "connect" in the contemporary sense. The vocabulary is mid-century New England and, for Marcus, formal mid-century European academic English.

## Comic timing and tonal balance

This is not a comic novel. But it is not without dry irony — particularly in Marcus's chapters (the slightly formal precision that notices absurdity without performing amusement) and Lonzo Reed's voice (if given a chapter). There is no comic relief in the structural sense; there is the dry New England understatement that is one register of grief and endurance. A character who says less than the situation warrants is not being stoic for show — it is how they live.

## Anti-defaults — what the drafter must actively avoid

- **Do not open chapters with weather or season as mood-setting abstraction.** "October had settled into the harbor" is a failure. "The breakwater took six feet of green water on the outer face" is not.
- **Do not name affect.** "She felt the weight of Owen's absence." No. "She put the logbook back in the drawer where Owen's pencil still was." The affect is the object.
- **Do not write post-scene subtext paragraphs.** After a charged scene, end the scene. Do not then write what it meant.
- **Do not thesis-state.** The chapter does not summarize its own meaning in its last sentence. The novel does not announce its themes.
- **Do not drift toward contemporary psychological vocabulary.** No "grief response," no "coping," no "boundaries," no "processing."
- **Do not over-qualify in Eira's voice.** Her precision is physical and observational, not intellectual. She does not build conditional sentences. She notes facts.
- **Do not make the POW storyline into a redemption romance.** What happens between Hannah and Karl is observed, ambiguous, small, and real. It is not a wartime love story. It is not a coming-of-age breakthrough. It is two people in a constrained situation noticing each other with care.
- **Do not explain the restraint.** The prose's power is what is not said. Do not then say it.

# Plotter guidance — *Coldwater Reach*

## POV count and rotation

**Three primary POVs**: Eira Bowman, Hannah Pfeiffer, Dr. Marcus Klein. Roughly ten chapters each across thirty chapters. Rotation is asymmetric and motivated: follow story need, not a strict cycle. Sustained runs of two or three chapters in a single POV are acceptable — even desirable — when a thread is building momentum or approaching a pressure point. But no single POV should go more than four consecutive chapters without the others being re-engaged.

**Optional fourth-POV chapters**: one to three chapters from Henry Crow, Lonzo Reed, or Karl Reinmar. These are structural correctives — they give the reader access no primary POV can provide. They should be short (1,500–2,000 words) and placed at moments where the mystery requires a vantage that none of the three principals can occupy. Do not add a fourth POV for variety or warmth alone; it must earn its structural place.

**The three principals never share a scene.** They can occupy the same public space briefly (the post office, the waterfront), but no chapter places them in conversation together. Their threads cross obliquely.

## Chapter-shape preferences

This is literary fiction with a restrained register. Each chapter is a unit of one person's attention across a day, an afternoon, or a single event. The dominant chapter shapes:

- **Single-scene focus** (one event, one time block, one main action) — most common; approximately 60% of chapters.
- **Two-scene with transition** (a chapter crosses a day; two related events with a brief connective tissue) — approximately 25%.
- **Pure interiority with movement** (a character in transit — Marcus walking, Eira doing a solitary task — whose movement allows extended reflection) — approximately 15%. Not more; this is not a meditation novel.

Avoid: chapters that exist purely to carry plot information. Every chapter must also do character work. If a chapter's only job is to reveal a piece of the breakwater mystery, it needs a second register — what does this revelation cost the POV character in their own arc?

## Episode-vs-arc structure

The structure is a continuous arc, not episodic. Chapters flow into each other — the breakwater question deepens across the thirty, the seasonal arc (October 1943 → spring 1945) structures time, each POV character's arc develops through accumulation. However: within the continuous arc, individual chapters often feel somewhat self-contained (a day, a task, an exchange). This is intentional — the chapters accumulate meaning the way seasons accumulate into time.

The mystery of the breakwater is the external spine that moves the plot. It must have new information (or new withholding) approximately every three chapters — not a revelation, but a piece, a question, a discrepancy noticed. Chapters 1–5 establish the body and the three principals; chapters 6–15 develop the threads and deepen the mystery; chapters 16–25 draw the threads toward collision; chapters 26–30 resolve the characters' arcs while leaving the mystery partially in shadow.

## Ending-mode distribution (across 30 chapters)

- **Literary fade** (sensory image, physical beat, one step past resolution): ~10 chapters — the dominant mode
- **Turn** (quiet pivot, piece of information that reframes): ~8 chapters
- **Resolved beat** (chapter question settles): ~6 chapters
- **Elliptical** (open question, unfinished gesture): ~4 chapters
- **Cliffhanger / mid-action**: ~2 chapters — reserved for structural turning points only

Avoid runs of the same ending mode. If three consecutive chapters end in literary fade, the fourth should turn or resolve. Track this.

## Chapter target words

- **Standard chapter**: 2,400–2,800 words
- **Intensive chapters** (major structural turns, climactic confrontations): up to 3,200 words
- **Short exceptional chapters** (fourth-POV corrective chapters): 1,500–2,000 words
- **Target manuscript total**: ~80,000 words across 30 chapters

No chapter should feel rushed (under 2,000 words) or bloated (over 3,500 words) without structural justification.

## Genre-specific structural conventions

This is literary historical fiction with a mystery spine. The genre conventions to honor:

**Historical fiction**:
- The period must be maintained through material objects and period vocabulary, not expository history lessons.
- The war must be ever-present as texture and as absence, not as dramatic plot machinery.
- The ending must not be teleologically determined by the historical event (VE Day). The personal resolutions should arrive in their own time; the war ends in the background.

**Mystery spine**:
- The body is introduced in chapter 1 or early chapter 2. The reader must have the three POV characters' initial relationships to the mystery established by chapter 5.
- Each POV sees a different piece of the puzzle: Eira holds what she saw on the dock; Hannah's thread yields something through Karl Reinmar's presence (the dead man may have a connection to the German community, the POW network, or simply to the world the Pfeiffers came from); Marcus's thread yields something through language (a document, a name, something that requires German to read).
- The mystery deepens at the midpoint. Around chapters 14–16, new information should shift the reader's understanding of what happened — not a solution, a complication.
- The final disposition of the mystery: the reader should be able to assemble a plausible account from the accumulated evidence across all thirty chapters. The novel does not refuse to answer; it refuses to announce the answer. The last chapter is not a detective's revelation scene.

**Three-strand structure**:
- Acts 1–2 (chapters 1–8): all three POVs established, the breakwater question live, the seasonal texture of autumn working
- Act 3–4 (chapters 9–18): the threads deepen separately; each POV character's personal arc takes on pressure independent of the mystery; the farm plot (Hannah/Karl/Lonzo) reaches a crisis; Marcus commits an act (helps someone, protects someone, reveals something) that commits him to Coldwater
- Act 5–6 (chapters 19–26): the threads approach intersection; Eira acts on what she knows; the POV characters encounter the consequences of each other's choices at one remove
- Act 7 (chapters 27–30): individual arcs resolve or settle; the mystery achieves its partial resolution; the war ends off-page; the last chapter is quiet, specific, and irreversible

## What the plotter must not do

- **Do not introduce a spy plot.** No Nazi agents, no coded messages, no submarine contact. The dead man is explicable by other means.
- **Do not engineer a three-way convergence scene.** The structural constraint (the three never meet as a group) must be respected to the end.
- **Do not resolve all three arcs in the same mode.** Eira's resolution is an action; Hannah's is a decision; Marcus's is an act of commitment. These should feel different in shape.
- **Do not let the mystery resolution overwhelm the personal arcs.** In the last three chapters, the personal arcs come first. The mystery is context, not climax.
- **Do not underuse Henry Crow.** He is not a supporting convenience. If he gets a chapter, it must illuminate something neither the three principals nor the reader could see from their positions. Time it for maximum ironic or emotional effect.

# Reader guidance — *Coldwater Reach*

## Intended audience

Adult readers of literary historical fiction — the readership for novels like *The Remains of the Day*, *Nora Webster*, *The Lacuna*, or *Pachinko*. Expect readers comfortable with a slow-build structure, restrained affect, and a mystery that does not fully resolve. The audience knows that "what happened" is not always the novel's central question. They are patient with interiority provided it earns its space. They expect period texture to be accurate and unobtrusive.

This is not genre mystery fiction. Readers coming for a thriller will find this novel's mystery gratifications different from their expectations — and that is correct, not a defect. The reader phase should evaluate the manuscript as literary fiction with a mystery spine, not as a mystery with literary pretensions.

## Brief-adherence checks to perform

Answer each of these as yes/no with evidence:

1. **Does each chapter stay strictly inside its POV character's knowledge?** No chapter should contain information the POV character could not plausibly have observed or been told. Check specifically for cross-POV contamination in the mystery strand.
2. **Are the three POV voices consistently distinct throughout?** Eira: spare, procedural, physical vocabulary. Hannah: porous, associative, German phrases embedded. Marcus: precise, slightly formal, architectured subordination. A reader should be able to identify the POV from an unmarked passage.
3. **Does the mystery strand deliver new information or a new question approximately every three chapters?** If four consecutive chapters pass without advancing the breakwater question, flag it.
4. **Do the three POV characters' personal arcs develop independently of the mystery?** Each arc (authority/cost; small choices; displacement) must have its own pressure and movement. If a POV's internal arc is stalled while they serve the mystery, flag it.
5. **Is historical accuracy maintained without decoration?** Period objects should appear because they are in the scene, not to signal authenticity. Flag any passage that reads like a glossary insert.
6. **Are the three principals never in a scene together?** The structural constraint must not be violated.
7. **Is the ending correctly calibrated?** The last chapters should resolve the personal arcs while leaving the mystery in partial shadow. The war ending should be background, not foreground. Flag any climax that tips into thriller-resolution mode.
8. **Is the deliberate unresolved thread actually unresolved?** The brief requires at least one. Identify which thread it is, and confirm it reads as deliberate and felt rather than as an authorial failure to commit.

## What "good" looks like for this book

A successful chapter of *Coldwater Reach* achieves the following:

- **Eira chapter**: reads like a working day in which something morally heavy has been set in a drawer. The harbor is real and operational; the emotional weight is entirely in what she does not say and what she notices last. The last sentence is a physical image, not a feeling.
- **Hannah chapter**: admits more noise and sensation than the others; includes at least one moment of noticing something that contradicts what she has been told; the German phrases land without translation and are felt; the farm is material and smells and sounds.
- **Marcus chapter**: the prose is the densest of the three in subordination and qualification; the irony is dry rather than performative; Marcus has at least one moment of encountering something he cannot file neatly into the experience he already has.
- **All chapters**: no labeled emotion. The prose does not tell the reader what a scene meant. The period is felt but not performed. The mystery strand is present but does not take over the chapter's primary register.

## What to flag explicitly if the manuscript drifts

The following drift patterns should be named explicitly even if the prose is locally skillful:

- **Labeled affect**: "She felt grief," "He was aware of his own loneliness." Name it and cut it. The brief is unambiguous: the story trusts the reader. If the prose is doing its job, the feeling arrives through the image, not the label.
- **Post-scene subtext paragraphs**: a charged scene followed by a paragraph explaining what it was about. Name it. It is the single most destructive failure mode for this register.
- **Voice leveling**: if Eira's chapters begin to develop Hannah's associative range, or Marcus's chapters lose their formal subordination, the distinctive three-voice architecture is damaged. Flag voice drift by POV and cite examples.
- **History as decoration**: any passage where a period object or procedure is named without earning its place in the scene. The ration book must be in use, not on display.
- **Genre-thriller drift in the mystery strand**: if the breakwater question begins to dominate chapters that belong to a character's personal arc, or if the mystery moves toward procedural detective-fiction pacing, flag it. The mystery is spine, not engine.
- **Anachronistic vocabulary**: "She processed the loss." "His trauma was." "They connected over." These are not period and not register. Flag on sight.
- **Convergence violation**: any scene where all three (or any two) of the principals are in extended dialogue or shared scene. Check for this especially in the final act.

## What to applaud

The reader phase should specifically defend the following if the manuscript hits them well — do not recommend cutting or compressing:

- **Marcus's long, qualified sentences.** His subordinate clauses are his voice. Compression agents will be tempted to cut them for clarity. Resist. A Marcus sentence that runs 28 words and is all there is not a mistake.
- **The untranslated German phrases in Hannah's chapters.** These are a deliberate technique. They should not be translated in the text. If a reader-agent is uncertain whether non-German-reading readers will be confused, the answer is: the confusion is the point, and it is contextually bounded. Defend them.
- **Scene endings that go one beat past resolution.** The last sentence of a scene is often something physical observed rather than a statement. This is not evasion; it is the register. Do not recommend adding a "beat of reflection" after these endings.
- **Eira's emotional restraint.** She does not process Owen in interior monologue. Her grief is in objects, tasks, and the gap between what she notices and what she says. If the grief "doesn't land" in a conventional literary fiction sense, the answer is not more interiority — it is trusting the accumulation.
- **The ambiguous ending of the mystery.** The brief explicitly permits the breakwater question to remain in partial shadow. If the mystery resolution reads as incomplete, ask whether it is *deliberately* incomplete (the reader can assemble a plausible account but is not given a detective's announcement). If the answer is yes, it is a feature.

text: Now I'll append the most load-bearing facts to the continuity store:

facts: Coldwater Reach is a fictional working port on the mid-coast of Maine. The story spans October 1943 to spring 1945 (just before VE Day, May 8, 1945). No real people may be named; real places (Portland, Bangor, Houlton, Cambridge MA, Sherbrooke QC) may appear.

The inciting event is an unidentified man's body washed onto the breakwater after a three-day storm in October 1943. He has no papers. The Coast Guard takes the body. Eira Bowman saw something on the dock the night before the body came in — this is the spine secret parceled across thirty chapters.

Eira Bowman is 52 in October 1943. She has been harbormaster for eight years, since her husband Owen drowned in the November storm of 1935. She is the only woman serving as harbormaster on the Maine coast. Owen's absence is structural throughout the novel.

Hannah Pfeiffer is 17 in October 1943 (turns 18 in 1944). Her parents Albrecht and Magda Pfeiffer emigrated from Bavaria in 1922. Four German POWs work the farm, supervised by Lonzo Reed (age 62, Coastal Patrol private). Karl Reinmar (age 19, from Ansbach, Bavaria) is the youngest POW and is from ~50 km from Albrecht's hometown.

Dr. Marcus Klein is 47 in October 1943, Viennese, born ~1896. He arrived in Coldwater in March 1942 after fleeing Austria (1938), passing through Paris, London, and an internment camp at Sherbrooke, Quebec (1940–1941, as an enemy alien). He teaches German and Latin at the high school. He boards with Henry and Lillian Crow.

Henry Crow (~55 in 1943) is chief custodian at the school and Marcus's landlord. His family came north from Norfolk, Virginia in 1924. His son James is in the U.S. Army, Pacific theater, as of October 1943. Henry and Lillian Crow are one of approximately three Black households in Coldwater Reach.

The three primary POV characters (Eira, Hannah, Marcus) never meet as a group of three. The three principals must never be in a shared scene together. Chapter rotation is asymmetric (~10 chapters each); up to three short exceptional chapters may give a fourth POV (Henry, Lonzo, or Karl).

No spy plot, no Nazi agents, no coded messages, no submarine landings. The U-boat threat belongs to 1942 memory, not present 1943 action. The war reaches Coldwater through radio, V-Mail, OPA ration books, and Western Union casualty telegrams.

At least one narrative thread is deliberately unresolved at the close. The breakwater mystery may or may not be fully answered; the three characters' relationships to it resolve even if the underlying fact stays in shadow. The ending is personal and small, not triumphant.

The POW labor program is governed by the 1929 Geneva Convention. Camp Houlton is the umbrella facility; the Pfeiffer farm is a satellite. Prisoners are paid in canteen credits, wear POW-stenciled clothing, and the no-fraternization rule is loosely kept where no officer enforces it.

# Coldwater Reach — Chapter Map

## Project specs

- **Total chapters**: 30
- **Target manuscript length**: ~80,000 words
- **Standard chapter target**: 2,400–2,600 words
- **Intensive chapters** (major structural turns): 2,800–3,200 words — chapters 01, 09, 14, 24, 29
- **Short exceptional chapters** (fourth-POV correctives): 1,500–2,000 words — chapters 12, 21, 26
- **Approximate chapter target**: varies per type; see individual files

## POV distribution

| POV | Chapters | Count |
|-----|----------|-------|
| Eira Bowman | 01, 04, 07, 11, 15, 18, 22, 25, 29 | 9 |
| Hannah Pfeiffer | 02, 05, 08, 10, 14, 17, 20, 24, 28 | 9 |
| Dr. Marcus Klein | 03, 06, 09, 13, 16, 19, 23, 27, 30 | 9 |
| Karl Reinmar (exceptional) | 12 | 1 |
| Lonzo Reed (exceptional) | 21 | 1 |
| Henry Crow (exceptional) | 26 | 1 |

**Rotation note**: POV alternates every chapter throughout — no sustained single-POV runs. This is deliberate: the braided structure functions like *The Hours* — three complete movements interleaved — and sustained interruption keeps each strand distinct without requiring omniscience to bridge them. The three exceptional chapters serve as structural correctives, each placed at a moment where the mystery requires a vantage no primary POV can occupy.

## Ending-mode distribution

| Mode | Count | Target | Chapters |
|------|-------|--------|----------|
| Literary fade | 9 | ~10 | 02, 03, 08, 12, 17, 19, 23, 28, 30 |
| Turn | 11 | ~8 | 01, 05, 06, 09, 13, 14, 15, 20, 21, 24, 26 |
| Resolved beat | 5 | ~6 | 04, 11, 18, 27, 29 |
| Elliptical | 4 | ~4 | 07, 10, 16, 22 |
| Mid-action | 1 | ~2 | 25 |

Turn runs slightly over target (~11 vs. 8) because the mystery spine generates multiple genuine pivot moments across all three POVs; each has been verified as an authentic story turn rather than an artificial beat. The distribution across POVs is roughly even.

## Timeline

| Chapters | Period |
|----------|--------|
| 01–05 | October–November 1943 |
| 06–11 | December 1943–February 1944 |
| 12–15 | February–May 1944 |
| 16–20 | May–August 1944 |
| 21–24 | Late summer–November 1944 |
| 25–28 | November 1944–January 1945 |
| 29–30 | February–May 1945 |

## The mystery assembly (reader's picture, assembled across 30 chapters)

**Werner Grau** — German national, emigrated to New England 1936 on an emergency visa that expired 1940 (illegal resident thereafter). Knew Albrecht Pfeiffer from Bavaria before either emigrated. Heard through the German expatriate network that a Karl Reinmar from near Ansbach was billeted at the Pfeiffer farm under the POW labor program. In late September 1943 he mailed a letter to Albrecht announcing his intention to travel to Coldwater; the letter was misdelivered to the school (Marcus receives it in ch. 06). Werner came up the coast by rented dinghy from Portland in early October. He arrived the night before the peak of the three-day blow. He was on the Coldwater waterfront — Eira saw him on the south dock around midnight with a second figure (whose gait she reads as "farm-type": Albrecht came down from the farm to meet him). Werner may have been already ill. The storm rose. He did not return to the dinghy. Three days later his body came in on the breakwater. His papers were in the dinghy, which the storm drove into the south cove where Eira recovers it in ch. 22.

No foul play is established. What happened between midnight and the storm's peak, and what passed between Werner and Albrecht, remains in shadow. The novel does not refuse to answer; it refuses to announce.

**Pieces and their sources**:
- Eira (chs. 01, 04, 07, 15, 22, 29): saw two figures on the dock; dinghy trace; Portland registration of the dinghy → name W. Grau; harbor log entry
- Marcus (chs. 06, 09, 13, 16, 23, 28): the misdelivered letter; Albrecht's recognition; Sondheimer's reply on Grau's illegal status; the complete picture assembled from Hannah's testimony
- Hannah (chs. 05, 10, 14, 20, 24, 28): photograph labeled "W. Grau, A. Pfeiffer, Bamberg 1921"; Karl's identification and his note "Werner Grau. From Ansbach. He is dead"; Albrecht's "Ich weiß"
- Karl (ch. 12): suspects Werner came to Maine; received word Werner was in America; uses past tense about him before he confirms
- Lonzo (ch. 21): saw an unknown man on the farm road the night of the storm
- Henry (ch. 26): saw an unknown man walking toward the harbor in the pre-dawn

## Arc shape

```
ACT I   (chs. 01–05)   SETUP        Body arrives; three principals established; mystery alive
ACT II  (chs. 06–11)   DEEPENING    Letter surfaces; POW-farm thread builds; harbor board threat;
                                     each POV character carrying something privately
ACT III (chs. 12–18)   MIDPOINT     Farm thread at pressure; mystery shifts (ch. 15-16 turn);
                                     D-Day; each arc takes on independent pressure
ACT IV  (chs. 19–24)   CONVERGENCE  Threads approach each other; Karl's name; transfer;
                                     the picture almost complete

```

# Chapter 01 — The Breakwater

**One-line summary**: A body comes in on the breakwater after the three-day blow; Eira handles it procedurally, and alone afterward retrieves the image of the dock she has not yet put in the right column.

**POV**: Eira Bowman  
**Tense**: Third-person limited past  
**Setting**: Coldwater Reach harbor — breakwater, pier head, harbormaster's shed  
**Time**: October 12, 1943 (morning after the storm clears)  
**Target words**: ~3,000 (intensive opening chapter)

**Chapter shape**: Single scene  
**Ending mode**: Turn

---

## Goal
Establish Eira's voice and competence; introduce the body as the novel's spine event; plant the dock image as the secret knowledge she is already holding.

## Obstacle
The body is a bureaucratic anomaly in a harbor she runs correctly. The CG takes it efficiently. There is no call for her to do anything except file it. The difficulty is internal: there is something she saw that does not belong in the standard column.

---

## Opening texture
Routine-procedure: Eira walks the breakwater in the post-storm morning, conducting her standard damage survey. The register establishes immediately — she thinks in load, draft, and tide. Weather, damage, what needs doing. The body is encountered in the course of correct procedure, not as drama.

---

## Action beats

1. **The survey**: Eira walks the breakwater at first light after the blow; she notes damage methodically (two iron mooring rings bent, granite face shifted at the elbow, kelp and cable draped over the top course). She has a clipboard. She uses it.

2. **The body**: At the elbow of the L — where the storm would deposit anything that came in from the southeast — a man is face-down in the wrack. Male, middle-aged or older, clothing not a fisherman's (town clothes, wool coat). No vessel, no dinghy, no gear. She does not touch him beyond checking the inside of the coat and the trouser pockets: no papers, no wallet, nothing.

3. **Procedure**: She goes back to the shed, calls the Coast Guard station (Sprucehead) on the telephone. She gives them the facts she has. She returns to the breakwater and waits.

4. **The CG arrival**: Lieutenant Mercer arrives with two enlisted men and a stretcher. He is young, efficient, and not especially curious. He asks her the standard questions; she answers with what she has. The body is loaded. Mercer thanks her. The exchange takes perhaps twelve minutes.

5. **Back to work**: She returns to the shed. She finishes the damage survey. She writes the harbor log entry: date, time, weather status, body discovered, CG notified, CG responded, body removed. Precise to the quarter-hour.

6. **The ledger and the image**: She sets down the clipboard. She stands at the window. The south dock — which she can see from here — is empty. And then, not dramatically, the way an incorrect entry surfaces when you run the numbers: the dock two nights ago. Before the blow peaked. Around midnight. Two figures on the south dock. One she did not recognize. The other she couldn't see clearly — but the build, the way the person stood, was not a sailor's. A farmer, maybe. Somebody from inland.

---

## Outcome / turn
The body is gone; the case is handed to the Coast Guard; the harbor is back under her management. But Eira has retrieved the image of the dock, and the image does not match the standard entry she just wrote. The body and the figure are, she suspects, the same man at different points in the same night. She has not written that down.

---

## New question raised
What did she actually see on the south dock, and who were those two figures?

---

## Continuity notes
- Establishes: October 1943 timeline; body has no papers; Coast Guard takes the body (Lt. Mercer, first appearance); Eira knows what she saw on the dock
- The figure she half-recognizes has a "farm-type" build — not yet identified; the drafter should not reveal it is Albrecht yet
- The harbor log entry is written precisely and omits the dock figures: this is established here so that chapter 29's addition to the log has full resonance
- Owen Bowman should be felt as an absence before he is mentioned — the harbor log from 1935 is on the shelf; Eira's eye passes it; no explanation needed
- Period texture: the breakwater, tidal range, October weather on the Maine coast; no 1942 U-boat speculation (that's behind them)

# Chapter 02 — Icehouse

**One-line summary**: Autumn on the Pfeiffer farm: the POWs are three weeks in, Albrecht is retreating, and Hannah begins to notice Karl Reinmar.

**POV**: Hannah Pfeiffer  
**Tense**: Third-person limited past  
**Setting**: Pfeiffer dairy farm — barn, farmyard, icehouse, kitchen, Hannah's bedroom  
**Time**: Mid-October 1943 (the same week as ch. 01, or a few days after)  
**Target words**: ~2,600

**Chapter shape**: Two-scene with transition  
**Ending mode**: Literary fade

---

## Goal
Introduce Hannah's register and the farm world; establish the POW arrangement and Karl; show Albrecht's retreat and Magda's silence; plant the body's arrival as background noise.

## Obstacle
Hannah is trying to see clearly — her parents, the farm, the strangers in the icehouse — but the tools she has are seventeen years old and still learning what they're for.

---

## Opening texture
Routine-procedure: morning chores in autumn. Milk, feed, the cold barn. Hannah's register comes in immediately — wider sensory range, more associative, German phrases available when her father's voice is in her head. The farm is established as a world that has its own complete logic.

---

## Action beats (Scene 1 — morning)

1. **Morning chores**: Hannah feeds the dairy cows, notes the October cold settling in, carries the milk pails in the early light. Her competence is assumed, not performed.

2. **The POWs across the yard**: The four German prisoners emerge from the icehouse bunkhouse at 6:45 under Lonzo Reed's supervision. They cross the yard to the barn. They have been here three weeks; the routines are established. Hannah observes them from the barn door.

3. **Karl Reinmar**: The youngest of the four — nineteen, slight, moving with the not-quite-competence of someone doing farm labor he didn't grow up with. He carries a bucket wrong; one of the older Germans corrects him silently. He sees Hannah watching him and looks away first.

4. **Albrecht in the barn**: Her father directs the morning work. He speaks to the POWs in German — short directives, nothing intimate. When Hannah hands him the feed tally, he says *danke* to her without looking up. She answers in English; he does not adjust.

5. **Magda**: Hannah brings breakfast to her mother in the kitchen. Magda is at the table, not eating, her hands around a cup that has gone cold. She receives the plate without speaking. Hannah sits with her for a moment. Then leaves her there.

---

## Transition

*Afternoon school bus to town.* On the bus, two girls from her class are talking about the body on the breakwater — heard from a father who heard from the fishermen. A man with no name, no papers. The Coast Guard came. It's not anyone from here. The conversation is lurid and not unkind; Hannah listens. She thinks about papers. About what it means to come somewhere without them.

---

## Action beats (Scene 2 — evening)

6. **Dinner**: Albrecht, Magda, Hannah. The radio is off. Hannah mentions, carefully, that she heard about the body on the breakwater. Her father's hands stop on his utensils for a moment. Then he resumes eating. He does not comment. Magda has not looked up.

7. **Hannah at her window**: After dishes, Hannah goes to her room. Through her window she can see the icehouse. A lamp is lit inside. One of the POWs is outside the door, smoking. She watches him: the young one, Karl. He is looking up at the sky and saying something — not to anyone, just saying it, the way you say something that wants to be said.

---

## Outcome / turn
Hannah is alone with the accumulation of the day: her father's silence about the body (which she noticed, which she doesn't know what to do with), Karl's existence across the farmyard, and Magda's hands around the cold cup.

---

## Ending (literary fade)
Karl goes inside the icehouse and the lamp dims. Hannah watches the window a moment longer. The smell of turned earth and October cold comes through her window. She closes it. The icehouse is dark.

---

## New question raised
What does her father's silence about the body mean? And what is Karl, in the icehouse — someone to be seen, or someone to look away from?

---

## Continuity notes
- Establishes: Pfeiffer farm geography; Albrecht's retreat into German; Magda's silence as established condition (not new); Karl Reinmar as specific individual (young, from outside farm labor)
- The four POWs are established as a group; the other three are background figures, not characterized in this chapter
- Lonzo Reed appears but is not yet characterized beyond his post at the icehouse door
- Hannah's knowledge of German is functional (she understands her father's directives); it is not the subject of comment here — it is simply texture
- Do NOT yet explain Albrecht's silence or connect it to Werner Grau — Hannah does not have this; it must remain at the level of her observation (she noticed his hands stopped)
- Period texture: the POW bunkhouse in the icehouse; the morning routine under escort; the material reality of the farm in wartime rationing

# Chapter 03 — Continental Educator

**One-line summary**: Marcus in his Coldwater routine hears of the body; the texture of Henry and Lillian's household; the quality of being not-yet-home.

**POV**: Dr. Marcus Klein  
**Tense**: Third-person limited past  
**Setting**: Coldwater Reach High School → street → Henry and Lillian Crow's house  
**Time**: Late October 1943 (a week or two after the body)  
**Target words**: ~2,500

**Chapter shape**: Two-scene with transition  
**Ending mode**: Literary fade

---

## Goal
Establish Marcus's register and his position in Coldwater — the careful, slightly formal quality of the translated man; his household; his relationship with Henry; the intermediate state between temporary and rooted.

## Obstacle
Marcus has no dramatic obstacle in this chapter. The difficulty is his ongoing condition: he is good at being provisional, and Coldwater is where that skill is currently exercised. The body is a thing he has heard about but has no access to yet.

---

## Opening texture
Transit: Marcus walking to school in the late-October morning. His register comes in at once — precise, slightly formal, the subordinate clause structure of a man who thinks in the architecture of complete propositions. He notices the harbor briefly at the end of the road as he turns. He does not dwell on it.

---

## Action beats (Scene 1 — school)

1. **The Latin class**: Marcus at the board with a Latin sentence — a subordinate clause from Cicero that is not translated, but sat with. Three students. He is teaching them to read rather than decode, and this distinction matters to him. His English in the classroom is careful, slightly formal; the students do not find it odd because they have learned to hear it as his.

2. **The staffroom gossip**: In the break between periods, the other teacher on the floor — a geography teacher named Stillman — mentions the body on the breakwater. "Man with no papers, they're saying. Drowned in the storm." Marcus asks one or two precise questions. Stillman doesn't know more than the surface. Marcus files it — not dismissively, but in the part of his mind where uncertain data waits.

3. **"Continental educator"**: Walking between classrooms, Marcus passes the principal's open door; on the desk, in plain view, is a folder with his name and the note the town meeting appended to his hire — "Continental educator." He has seen this before. He keeps walking.

---

## Transition

*Late afternoon, the walk home.* Marcus passes the post office, where the Western Union boy's bicycle is leaned against the wall. The bicycle is a shape of dread in this town: telegrams. He has watched a woman receive one from the door of the post office, from a distance, and has known what the boy was carrying without being told. He walks past and thinks, briefly, of Sherbrooke — not of the internment itself, but of the moment of arrival, the moment of papers being taken from his coat. He does not linger in this thought.

---

## Action beats (Scene 2 — Henry and Lillian's kitchen)

4. **Coming home**: Marcus enters through the back door into the kitchen, where Lillian is at the stove. She sets a plate without asking. This is, for Marcus, close to what home feels like: the lack of questions about his preferences, because after two years his preferences are known.

5. **Henry at the boiler**: Henry is downstairs fixing something — the familiar sounds of competent work coming through the floor. Marcus and Lillian exchange a few words; she asks about his day; he answers briefly and precisely. She asks no follow-up questions. This is also something like home.

6. **James's photograph**: On the kitchen wall, James Crow's Army photograph — formal, taken before deployment, Pacific theater written in the set of his shoulders. Marcus looks at it as he always does when he sits down to eat. He knows Henry and Lillian's son only from this photograph and from the letters that arrive and are not shared in full.

---

## Ending (literary fade)
Marcus in his room upstairs after supper with a book he is not reading. He can hear Henry closing the basement door, the house settling. The title of the chapter — "Continental educator" — has been in his head all day. In Vienna, he was Dr. Klein. In Paris he was the Austrian. In London he was the refugee. In Sherbrooke he was the enemy. In Cambridge he was the displaced scholar. In Coldwater he is the Continental educator. He is practicing something. He does not yet know if what he is practicing is Coldwater or himself.

---

## New question raised
What will it take for this place to become something other than provisional?

---

## Continuity notes
- Establishes: Marcus's school routine, classroom style, walking habit; Henry and Lillian's household as texture of warmth and practical competence; James Crow as absence on the wall
