# Chapter Eleven — Load Calculations

She was three entries into the December fuel receipts when the door opened. The man said his name — Tarbell, Amos Tarbell — and the county harbor authority, and that he was here for the routine inspection.

Eira put down her pen. "Harbormaster Bowman," she said. "I've been expecting someone from the county."

He had a clipboard with a county authority form already clipped to the board and a brown wool overcoat that had been brushed clean. Mid-thirties. His politeness had the quality of a specific instruction carefully followed.

"How long have you held this position?" he asked.

"Eight years."

"Prior experience in harbor operations?"

"Assistant harbormaster. Under the previous harbormaster." She let him write. "Owen Bowman. My husband."

He looked up once. Then he looked back at his clipboard.

"How long as assistant?"

"Four years."

"You currently have no assistant of your own."

"Since January 1942. He enlisted." She kept her voice even. "The county authority hasn't authorized a replacement. I've managed without one."

He wrote something on his form. She could not read it from across the desk.

She had laid the winter documents out on the table before he came: the mooring registry open to the current page, the fuel allocation ledger beside it, the vessel registration file beneath. The safety inspection folder was on the shelf; she would take it down when they reached it.

She walked him through the mooring registry. Each vessel currently on a winter mooring in the inner harbor: the lobster boats Ida May, Sadie H., and Clara B., and three others on the west float; the dragger East Wind; the cold storage skiff; the Ellsworth against the east float on her winter berth. Seventeen vessels in total. She named each one, its registration status, its current mooring position. He checked them against his form. He did not find a discrepancy, because there was not one.

The fuel allocation ledger was next. Wartime supplemental allocation for harbor operations: every vessel drawing against the harbor's quarterly allotment from the Department of the Interior was entered by vessel name, date, and quantity in gallons, each entry initialed. The column balanced to the gallon.

"The authorization document?" Tarbell asked.

She took it from the folder beneath the ledger. He read through it. He handed it back without comment.

They went outside.

February cold, flat gray sky, the harbor on an ebbing tide. The dragger that worked the offshore grounds had gone out at first light and would not be back until afternoon. The Ellsworth sat against the east float with her forward lines gone slack in the ebb. The compressor at the cold storage house ran in a steady cycle. The inner harbor water was undisturbed except where the tide drew over the submerged ledge at the harbor mouth.

Tarbell walked the length of the pier to the breakwater end. She walked beside him. He asked about the depth at the elbow at mean low water, the height of the inner float at mean high water, the fuel storage configuration. He asked whether the tank was inside the hundred-foot setback from the waterline.

"Inside," she said. "By eight feet. The wartime exception was filed in June of 1942."

"Section four."

"Subsection B."

He wrote it down. At the pier head he stopped and looked at the harbor for a moment without writing anything. She stood beside him and looked at the same water. The sky was low and the gray ran without break from the cloud to the harbor surface.

"Everything here appears to be in order," he said.

"Yes," she said.

They went back inside.

The vessel registration file came next, then the safety inspection folder. Forty-two active vessel registrations, all current, no lapses, no outstanding renewals. The safety inspections for the winter-berthed vessels complete; the summer boats scheduled for spring before the season opened, the schedule printed on the folder's back page. He read the schedule. He made a note. His form was nearly full.

Tarbell sat down across the desk. He set his pencil on the clipboard.

"I want to ask you about the formal basis of your appointment," he said. "The — transitional nature of it."

She opened the bottom drawer and took out a folder she had kept there since 1935. Inside was a single typed letter on county authority letterhead. She set it on the table in front of him.

"November 21, 1935," she said. "Signed by Director Pearce. It appoints me harbormaster of Coldwater Reach pending formal review by the county harbor authority board."

Tarbell picked up the letter. He read it. He had the look of a man reading something he had already been briefed on — the eyes moving at the speed of confirmation.

"This review," he said. "It was scheduled?"

"December 1935. Then rescheduled. Then not rescheduled again."

"You never pressed for it."

"I did the work," she said. "The review would have confirmed what the work showed. I took it to be the board's matter to pursue."

He turned the letter over. The back was blank. He set it face up.

"You might have requested formal appointment on your own initiative," he said. Not accusatory. The tone of a man filling in a form.

"I might have," she said. "What I did instead was manage the harbor."

She let that sit. Outside, the compressor cycled off and ran. The last of the ebb moved through the pilings.

"There is one more thing I'd like to show you," she said.

She went to the north shelf and took down the harbor log for 1935. Green board cover, the year inked on the spine in Owen's hand — a forward-leaning cursive with compressed vowels and the particular t-crossings that ran slightly below the stalk. The log she had opened more times than she had ever counted, for reasons she did not examine. She set it on the desk and opened it to November.

November 7. *Barometer 29.4, NE backing N, Beaufort 5 outer harbor. Doubled all moorings afternoon watch. Advised small craft haul 1600. E. Anderson dory on A-ring 1645. Harbor secure 1800.* Owen's entries were that way: terse, accurate, complete. She had been reading them for eight years and could still hear his attention in the abbreviations — the way a man writes when he is doing the actual work and the writing is the record of the work, not a separate act.

November 8 was blank.

November 9 was hers. *Barometer 29.2, NW 8, seas 4–6 outer harbor, abating. O. Bowman, harbormaster, missing evening 7 November. Search conducted CG Sprucehead and harbor tender. Body not yet recovered. Harbor open. All moorings secure.* Her own hand, smaller and more vertical than his. The change on the page was visible without requiring comment.

"A continuity of record," she said. "Unbroken."

Tarbell looked at both entries for longer than he had looked at anything else in the shed. He read November 7 and then November 9. He looked at the blank November 8 in between them. He set his pencil down flat on the clipboard.

"November 7 to November 9," he said.

"Forty hours."

He picked up the pencil and wrote something on his form. It was the longest entry he had made all morning. She did not try to read it.

There was a pause. The cold storage compressor ran outside. The harbor was quiet the way it was always quiet in February — the boats that were left had already found their winter arrangement; the pier held only the sounds of the tide.

"I want to tell you," Tarbell said, "that there are some parties on the county board who have expressed concerns. About the long-term stability of the arrangement."

"Stability," she said.

"The formal basis of your appointment." He stopped. He started again. "They believe the matter of formal confirmation should be addressed."

"What would constitute a satisfactory confirmation?" she asked. "In the board's view."

He turned the pencil between his fingers. He was choosing words. He chose them and they did not constitute a direct answer.

"The board's preference," he said, "is that the appointment be placed on a formally established footing."

"What process would satisfy the board?"

He looked at the county authority letter on the desk. He looked at his clipboard. He looked at the window.

He did not answer.

She gave him one more moment. He did not fill it.

"I see," she said.

That was what she had come here to know. Not whether the numbers were right — she had known the numbers were right before he came through the door. The numbers had never been the question. She had needed him not to answer, and she had needed to hear him not answer, and now she had. The inspection had been irrelevant before Tarbell arrived. The question it was meant to address was not the kind that dies of a clean ledger.

Tarbell gathered his clipboard and reached for the county authority letter. He asked whether he could take it to copy for his file; she said yes, and asked him to return it when he was done. He put it in his briefcase. He stood. He said he would file his report with the county authority office by the end of the week. He thanked her for her time.

"Thank you for coming," she said.

She walked him to the door. She stood in the doorway and watched him cross the pier and turn up the road toward town. The tide had turned; the Ellsworth's forward lines had gone taut again. She noted the time: twenty past eleven.

Inside, she put the 1935 harbor log back on the north shelf. She returned the fuel ledger and the vessel registration file and the safety inspection folder to their places. She straightened the table.

Then she put the kettle on.

The harbor lay in February quiet: the dragger out, the Ellsworth cold at the east float, the lobster boats on their moorings with their bow lines leading east into the turned current. Ice on the float cleats, thin enough to break with a boot. The cold storage house ran steady. The sky was flat and would not change before dark.

She looked at the north shelf. The harbor logs ran left to right across it — the years in Owen's hand, then the 1935 volume with both their hands in it, then hers from 1936 on. Eight spines in a row, identical green board. The column ran unbroken.

The water came to the boil. She poured her cup and went back to the December fuel receipts.

# Chapter Twelve — Ansbach

The fourth cow on his row was the old one, the one that would kick if you came at her from the left. He came from the right, settled on the three-legged stool, and began. The milk came down in the rhythm he had learned. This had surprised him — that his hands could learn a new herd. His father kept Simmental on the farm in Ansbach, brown and cream, and these were Holstein, black and white, and the cold here was a different cold, harder at its edge, without the softness the Franconian hills put into winter. But the hands had learned without needing to be told.

Four months. He held the number the way you hold a stone: not warm yet, not simply part of the weight you carry, but manageable.

He did not count toward an end. There was no end to count toward. The war would end when it ended. Until then there was this row of cows and the pail going heavier and the barn smelling of hay and dung and animal-warm, which smelled the same in Maine as in Bavaria. This sameness was not comfort. It was a kind of information: some things do not change with the country.

The bakery on Karolinenstraße opened at five. By six the smell reached the kitchen window — the sweetness of *Hefegebäck* in morning cold — and his mother would call from the back of the house. Not urgently. Just the daily calling of his name from a known direction, which meant: you are here, it is morning, this is still the place.

He held this for a moment. Then he set it down.

Not buried. Set down at his side. He had learned the difference over the past two years, and the learning of it was more useful than almost anything else he had learned.

---

Through the barn door he could see across the farmyard. The sky had begun to lighten at its far edge — not sunrise yet, but what comes before it: the sky deciding. Hannah Pfeiffer crossed from the henhouse toward the feed shed, her coat buttoned to the collar, her breath a white cloud, a pail in each hand.

He watched.

He had thought about what made her different from the others here, and what he had arrived at was this: she did not look through him. Fischer and Bauer and Hentschel were present — men in the same difficulty, which was a kind of presence — and Reed the guard was present as a watcher: noting him, accounting for him, not seeing him. Old Pfeiffer moved between barn and house with the quality of a man who had placed himself somewhere by accident and had found no procedure for revising it. The Army men who came each month with the supply truck were a form, a function, a category.

Hannah looked at him like a person at a specific person.

There had been the bird — *Seidenschwanz* — and she had said the English back, and after that she had said his name. *Karl.* As if she had tested the word before using it, to be sure it meant what she intended. He had been called many things. That word, said that way, was not common.

He did not have German or English for what this was. He knew it was not nothing.

---

The waxwing arrived at the fence post at the barn door without any announcement, the way they always arrived: already there when you looked. Black mask, yellow tail-tip, the small red wax of the secondary feathers.

"*Seidenschwanz*," he said. Quietly, so as not to startle it.

He kept a count. Forty-one birds since October, each given its German name and held in some interior list he had not meant to start keeping. It had begun with this one — the waxwing in the autumn, the first bird he had recognized at a distance in a country where none of the field-names matched anything he carried. And then the others, one by one: *Meisen* for the chickadees, black cap and white cheek, the same birds you found in any German woodlot; *Graureiher* for the great blue heron that came to the drainage ditch at the low end of the east field; *Bussard* for the red-tailed hawk that worked the north stone wall in the afternoon light. The small brown ones that moved through the meadow in January flocks he had not been able to name with certainty — he thought *Ammern*, something in the bunting family, but he was not sure.

It was not nostalgia. It was more like this: the world was still nameable, even here, in the language that was his. Naming it was a way of asserting this — quietly, to himself, to each bird in turn. The waxwing on the fence post was not an English bird or an American bird. It was *Seidenschwanz*, and the name was his and the bird's together, regardless of the geography.

The waxwing turned its head and looked at nothing in particular.

---

Fischer had said it last Tuesday, quietly, in the icehouse after supper. Not to Karl specifically — Fischer's way was to make announcements to the air and leave the air to distribute them. He had been a *Feldwebel*, a sergeant, and he kept his accounts.

*"Der Mann, der dich besuchen sollte. Er ist nicht gekommen."*

The man who was supposed to visit you. He didn't come.

Karl had known this already. He had known it since November, though in November he had been calling it something else — delay, the slowness of wartime mail. By December he had stopped calling it anything. It had become a shape: a gap in a fence line where the rail is missing. You know the gap when you reach it.

In September, a scrap of paper had come folded inside his mother's monthly letter. Three sentences in German, no name signed. Werner Grau, who had known Karl's father from the years on Karolinenstraße, was now in America. Werner hoped, if circumstances allowed, to arrange some contact. If it was possible.

He had read those three sentences until he could say them in his sleep.

October: nothing. November: nothing. December: nothing. January, and Fischer's voice in the icehouse, making the accounting that Fischer always made.

Karl had nodded at the air and returned to his bread. There was nothing to say in return. Fischer had not known Werner or Karl's father and had only heard something through whatever channel Fischer used for such things.

---

What he turned in his mind now — he moved to the next cow in the row and sat and set his hands to the work and let the thought run alongside it — was not the absence of contact itself. Men in wartime did not keep appointments. Men in wartime died or were arrested or crossed a border at the wrong moment and went into some process that had no window in it. He had been away long enough to know this; he had seen the gap in the fence from both sides.

The thing he kept turning was this: Werner Grau had come all this way. *Amerika.* Not by accident. He had made a plan and the plan had included Maine and had been close enough to completion that the three sentences could be sent, that the unsigned note could travel inside his mother's letter to this barn, to this farm, to a boy milking cows who was also from Karolinenstraße and would understand who Werner Grau was.

And then the October storm. Karl had watched it from the icehouse window: three days of wind and rain from the northeast, beginning the night of the eleventh or the twelfth, the lower field going to mud, the hay bent flat along the ground. He had watched it and not thought anything particular about it at the time — it had been weather, the weather of this place, harder than what he knew.

He did not think Werner had simply been lost in it. He thought Werner had found something, or come close to finding it, and that the storm had been the last thing in a sequence Karl could not see from inside the icehouse. He thought the gap in the fence was Werner — Werner who had crossed the Atlantic when crossing the Atlantic was not a small thing, who had found his way to Maine, who had known where the farm was and who was on it, and who had not come.

Karl did not know what had happened. He knew the shape. He knew the shape and he knew he was not going to learn the rest of it from here, in this barn, in a language of twelve words.

He set the pail down and moved to the last cow on his row.

---

The waxwing lifted from the fence post. It crossed the farmyard in a low arc, unhurried, and disappeared into the woodlot at the far edge of the field.

He watched the treeline for a moment. The woodlot held the bird — inside and invisible, already become a sound among sounds, which was not the same as gone.

The barn was warm with the bodies of cows. Not the warmth a stove makes, arriving from one direction and weakening with distance, but the warmth of animals: patient, surrounding, the same in any country. His breath still showed. Outside the cold had not changed. But inside the warmth the work continued and the cold was only a fact about the air beyond the door, and he could hold that.

He heard Hannah cross the farmyard again. The empty pail swung from her hand and caught the fence post with a small sound. She did not look toward the barn.

*Seidenschwanz.* Gone.

He set his hands back to the work.

1. **The barn and the hands** — Karl milking the fourth cow, his hands having learned the Holsteins despite growing up with Simmental; four months in, he does not count toward an end he cannot see.

2. **Ansbach in memory** — Karolinenstraße, the bakery at five, *Hefegebäck* in morning cold, his mother's voice. Held briefly, then set down. *Not buried. Set down at his side.*

4. **The bird / Werner Grau** — a cedar waxwing arrives, *Seidenschwanz*, part of Karl's private taxonomy of 41 Maine birds named in German. Then Fischer's statement from last Tuesday surfaces: *Der Mann, der dich besuchen sollte. Er ist nicht gekommen.* The September scrap of paper, the three sentences, the months of nothing afterward. Karl infers Werner came close to completing his plan and the October storm was the last thing in a sequence he cannot see from inside the icehouse. He knows the shape, not the facts.

# Chapter Thirteen — Displaced Scholars

The translation papers were in alphabetical order, as Marcus had trained himself to keep them, and the name at the top was Pfeiffer.

He had six students in the advanced German section. Two were seniors who had enrolled to satisfy a modern-language requirement and who wrote translations that were technically correct in the manner of things produced under mild compulsion. Three were juniors of varying ability; a boy named Graves had a natural ear for German syntax but lacked the patience for the long clause, which was a correctable problem Marcus had been correcting since September. The sixth was Hannah Pfeiffer, who was also a junior and whose work Marcus graded first not because she required more attention — she required less than any other student in the section — but because her translations tended to establish the ceiling for the evening's task, and the ceiling, once identified, made everything below it easier to assess.

Tonight's passage was from Schiller. Five lines from *Die Bürgschaft*, short and subordinate-heavy, with two dependent clauses that required the student to decide where the sentence's weight fell. The predictable failure with such constructions — the one he had spent half the autumn correcting in the intermediate section — was to flatten them: to take the weight of a dependent structure and distribute it evenly across the sentence, producing translations that were accurate and empty. In the advanced section Marcus was marking for something a Vienna professor he had once admired called *die Entscheidung der Unterordnung*, the decision of subordination — not whether the student could identify the clause but whether they understood what its dependence was doing to everything around it.

He read Hannah Pfeiffer's rendering:

*Though he who asks is master of the hour, the thing asked for lives in a different grammar.*

The original was more compressed; she had given herself room. The word *grammar* was her own interpolation, absent from Schiller's German, which had *Zeit*, time. As a rendering it was less accurate than Schiller's word. As a reading of the construction — of what the subordination was for, of why the clause held its position in the sentence rather than dissolving into the main verb — it was more precise than anything Marcus could have specified in the assignment.

He took up his pencil and wrote in the margin: *The grammar of the subordinate clause is not decoration — it is the shape of what is being withheld.* He considered the sentence for a moment, then left it. She would understand what the note was about, or she would ask him on Friday, and either would serve the instruction.

He moved through the remaining five papers in forty minutes. The classroom was empty; Henry had come through with the push broom at half past three and not returned. The afternoon light through the south-facing windows had thinned — March, longer now than February and not warm, the late light catching the dust on the glass at a low angle. The heating pipes ticked in the wall behind the blackboard. Forty minutes, and he set the graded stack to his left and uncapped his pen.

He had been composing the letter to Sondheimer in his head for nine days. The content required no composition — a name, a description, a question. What had taken nine days was the framing. In twenty years of letters written under circumstances where the wrong word could establish the wrong thing, Marcus had learned that the architecture of a request carried as much weight as its substance.

Dr. Heinrich Sondheimer's position at Columbia was nominally in the German department, but his actual function — as Marcus had understood since his own time on the Emergency Committee rolls, in the autumn of 1941 — was closer to that of an archivist of displacement. He had been on the intake end of the rescue network that the Committee had assembled as the war made rescue necessary: the person who matched names to placements, who held the files, who knew which scholars and artists had passed through the system and which had simply vanished somewhere in the gap between one country's border and another's paperwork. It was not an official position. It was a position constituted entirely by memory, by the particular willingness to keep track of people because someone ought to. In Marcus's experience, such positions were more reliable than official ones.

He wrote:

*Dear Dr. Sondheimer,*

*I hope you are well. I write on a matter of administrative record that falls, I believe, within the range of your particular knowledge. I am trying to establish the history of a Werner Grau — German national, painter or laborer by occupation, last known address Portland, Maine — specifically whether he appears on any Emergency Committee roll or affiliated rescue register, and whether his immigration status in the United States was ever formalized. I ask as a matter of private inquiry, not on behalf of any institution or authority. I have reason to believe Mr. Grau may have been in the Boston area around 1936, and that he has been in the United States since approximately that time.*

*Any record you hold, or any channel you might pursue on my behalf, would be of genuine assistance.*

He read the letter back once. The phrase *a matter of private inquiry* was accurate and included what it did not state. The phrase *any channel you might pursue* communicated that this was a question for informal handling — through the network of people who held such things in filing cabinets and memory rather than in any official record. The formality of the register established his distance from the question: an academic making a historical inquiry. Not a man with personal stakes in the answer.

This was approximately true.

He was addressing the envelope when the thought arrived, in the quiet way thoughts arrive when the hands are occupied with a mechanical task: what he had described was Marcus Klein in 1940.

A man without the correct documentation in a country not constructed for him. A man whose standing depended on a committee's willingness and a series of telephone calls between people who had been, at least, willing to make them. A man who could be required, at any moment, to demonstrate what he was doing here and whether anyone official had approved it.

He had been, in the autumn of that year and the winter that followed it, a Werner Grau.

He did not write this in the letter to Sondheimer. He did not write it anywhere. He pressed the envelope flap closed and set it on the right side of the desk where he kept things requiring the post. Then he sat for a moment in the quiet of the classroom — the graded papers on his left, the thin March light leaving the window glass, the heating pipes gone still — and held the thought in the way he had learned, at Sherbrooke, to hold thoughts that had nowhere to go. Not suppressed. Held in parallel, alongside everything else, and carried forward.

---

The road from the school to Henry and Lillian's house was three blocks toward the harbor and then one block west. He had walked it for two years in every condition this section of the Maine coast offered, and he had come to know it with the intimacy that daily repetition produces: not attachment, exactly, but familiarity so complete it had become spatial memory, each crack in the pavement belonging to its season. The spring thaw was at its worst this week — the road heaved, the edges soft, the ground giving back what it had been holding since December. He knew the smell of it. He had not expected, when he first walked this road, to come to know its smell by season as a fact of his own life, the way he knew the smell of the Ringstraße in December or the particular damp of the Paris sixth in autumn. He knew it. He walked through it.

He came in at the side door, as Lillian had told him to in his first week.

She was at the table with her cup and a length of white fabric, a piece of church sewing Marcus had seen in various states of progress for the past three weeks. Henry was across from her, and between them lay a V-Mail letter — the small photographed form, reduced by the postal process, that was what arrived when something arrived from the Pacific. The letter had the position of a thing already read and placed back with care: not put away, not left carelessly, but replaced as if putting it elsewhere had not yet been decided.

"James," Lillian said. She had not looked up.

He set his coat on the hook. "Good news?"

"He's well." She smoothed the edge of the envelope. "Somewhere he can't say."

Henry did not add anything. He drank his coffee.

Lillian read a portion of it aloud. The part she chose: James had received a meal that had given him a new and firmly held position on the subject of Army provisioning, which he had committed to paper — he noted it was the most cogent military document of the current conflict — and sent up the chain. Two weeks later, on a separate ship, a crate of canned peaches had arrived. He took this as the official reply. He asked whether the school boiler was behaving. He asked whether Mr. Marcus had been informed about the spring mud, and if not, whether someone could see to it before the term was too far gone.

Marcus said he had been informed.

Henry smiled briefly — reserving, as he always did, the full extent of it.

They sat. Lillian returned to her sewing. The kitchen was warm from the stove and from the radiator Henry had bled last week, which now ran without the complaint it had been making since January. The smell of the kitchen — coffee from the morning and something from supper that Marcus had missed, and beneath both of these the particular smell of the house itself, which Marcus had stopped noticing as foreign sometime around November — was familiar in the way the road was familiar. A fact. A specific fact belonging to a specific place.

Henry stood and rinsed his cup at the sink. He crossed to the small shelf above the kitchen radiator — the shelf that held the clock, the accumulated mail, and the one or two objects a household gathers over twenty years without deliberate selection — and placed James's letter under the clock. He had done this with every letter from James since the first one, in the spring of 1942. The clock held the paper flat. The letter did not go anywhere else.

He stood for a moment and looked at the photograph on the wall.

James in his uniform, taken at Camp Upton before he shipped — standing before some building Marcus did not recognize, shoulders squared, the expression of a man being photographed: present, composed, held slightly in reserve. The photograph had been on that wall for eighteen months.

Henry looked at it for perhaps half a minute. He did not say anything. Then he went through to the back of the house, where a pipe had been making a small complaint since the previous week.

Lillian said nothing. Marcus drank his coffee.

He thought: this is the shape of family at distance — the maintenance of the ordinary against what cannot be named. He had written letters like James's letters, from Paris, from London, from Sherbrooke in the months when letters were permitted, and the letters had been full of meals and small complaints and inquiries about things at home that were not the things he was thinking about. He knew what James's letter contained that was not in the portion Lillian had read. He did not say this. He sat with his cup and listened to the pipe being attended to in the back of the house, and when Lillian refilled his cup he said thank you and meant it precisely.

---

Sondheimer's reply came on a Friday, nine days after Marcus had posted the letter.

He found it in his school mailbox before the first class — addressed in Sondheimer's direct hand, the handwriting of someone for whom a letter is a professional instrument. Marcus read it standing at the mailboxes, then took it to his classroom and read it again at his desk, with the deliberate attention the contents required.

Sondheimer had made a telephone call to a contact in the Boston office. That contact had made another. The answer: Werner Grau, German national. Entered the United States at Boston in March 1936, on a one-year visa sponsored by the Boston Alliance for the Arts, which had brought over a small group of painters and printmakers under a cultural exchange program that ended when its funding was redirected in 1937. The visa had been renewed once, in March of 1937. It had expired in March of 1940. After that: no renewal application on record, no deportation proceeding initiated, no departure recorded.

He had been in the country without legal standing for nearly four years. From the spring of 1940 to October 1943, Werner Grau had been in the United States in the way that many men in those years had been in countries not their own: by the extension of circumstances originally intended as temporary, prolonged by a war that had made the simplest crossings impossible, sustained by the patience of whoever around him had chosen not to ask.

Marcus placed the letter beside the folder in the bottom drawer of his classroom desk: the letter Werner had written to Albrecht Pfeiffer, now in its original envelope; the two pages of careful handwriting Marcus had made for himself in December, his private account of what he knew and the chain by which he had come to know it. Three documents. They occupied the space where a Latin dictionary usually rested. He looked at them briefly, then closed the drawer.

Werner Grau had been, by the classification the relevant governments applied, an enemy alien without formal standing. As had Marcus Klein, at Sherbrooke, in 1940: held for ten months under a warrant whose precise language Marcus had never been shown, released to the Committee rolls in a country that had not yet settled what to do with him. The form of Werner's situation was different. The underlying condition was the same: a man whose right to be where he was could not be demonstrated to any authority that chose to examine it.

If the body on the breakwater had been identified — if the file at Sprucehead bore a name rather than a blank — Werner Grau's four years without papers would have become the first fact of the official record. A German national, undocumented, found drowned on the Maine coast in October 1943. The sentences organized themselves cleanly. They were not false. They were simply not an account of anything that mattered about Werner Grau.

He sat with the drawer closed and the translation papers on his left, marked, ready for return in the morning. On top: Hannah Pfeiffer's Schiller, the word *grammar* in the third line, the note in his own hand in the margin. The March light had gone off the roofline of the building opposite. The heating pipes had been quiet for an hour.

He was not going to report Werner Grau's status to any authority that could act on it. He had not reasoned his way to this. His hands had made the decision when they placed the letter in the drawer, and in the seconds after his mind had confirmed it, and there was nothing further to deliberate on that count.

Whether this constituted his doing something, or his failing to do something, or simply the act of a man who understood that what mattered about Werner Grau was not the state of his papers — that question remained open, in the drawer, alongside everything else he was holding.

# Chapter Fourteen — The Photograph

The tin box lived on the shelf in her parents' room, above the folded shirts — had lived there, as far as Hannah could trace, since before she was old enough to notice things on shelves. Small and dark, the paint worn through at the corners to bright metal, a small dent near the clasp that she had pressed her thumbnail into many times without ever asking how it got there. She had moved the box dozens of times to reach the shirts. She had never opened it.

Her mother was downstairs. The room had the particular cold of upstairs rooms in April, heated only by what rose from the kitchen below, which in April was not much. The smell: cedar from the blocks Magda kept in the bottom drawer with the wool things, and beneath that something fainter — her father's shaving soap, or the wood of the floor still releasing winter, or simply the close particular smell of a room where two people have slept for twenty years. The bureau along the north wall had a painted border she had traced with her finger since she was four. The quilt on the bed was one her mother had made the winter before Hannah was born, eighteen years old and not looking it.

She set the laundry basket on the bed and began to sort.

Her mother's room, her mother's order. She moved with the particular care of a person who has learned to take up only the space she has been given. Her mother's blouses, her father's good shirts, the household linens. When she lifted the stack of folded shirts to place them on the shelf, the tin box came forward against her hands.

She set it on the bedspread.

The same as it had always been. The bright corners, the dent near the clasp. She held it a moment, the weight of it in both hands — lighter than it looked — and then she lifted the clasp and opened it.

Letters, folded to fit the box. She could see without reading them that they were in German — her father's hand, the cramped vertical script, the particular way he formed his capital *S* that she had known before she learned to write herself. She didn't unfold them. They were her parents' letters; that was enough. There were papers beneath, creased many times over, that might have been documents; she touched the edge of one and let it go. At the bottom, held together with a rubber band that had gone dry and left a faint brown mark on the photograph on top, a small stack of pictures.

She looked.

The first was a woman she didn't know — older, perhaps a grandmother, seated before a painted studio backdrop wearing the expression of someone enduring a long exposure. No name on the back. The second was a group of men outside a building she couldn't place, European, with a low-pitched slate roof. Nobody she recognized.

She came to the third photograph and stopped.

Two men before a stone doorway. A carved lintel above them, heavy and deliberate — civic, she thought, or a church entrance, the kind of archwork that had been standing for two or three centuries and didn't expect to stop. Both men in their thirties. Wool coats, hats held in their hands: they had taken the hats off for the photograph, which was what men did when they wanted the photograph to count. Both squinting. The shadows on the paving were short, the light full and direct, a summer afternoon or early autumn with the summer still in it. A quality to the light she couldn't name exactly, except that it was not the light here — not the flat particular grey of coastal Maine but something more direct, more central, a light that knew where it was from.

One of the men was her father.

She knew him by the jaw and the set of his shoulders and the way he held the hat brim, which hadn't changed. He looked younger than she had ever seen him — not happy exactly, but present. Unguarded. His face was simply a face, open to the bright day, not yet arranged into whatever it had since become arranged into.

The other man she looked at for a long time.

Heavy in the shoulders. A laborer's build, the neck thicker than her father's, the coat a little tight across the chest. She guessed he was her father's age in the photograph, early thirties. His face was ordinary — she looked at it and found nothing to catch on. Not unkind, not cold, not worried or proud or marked by any particular feeling. Just the face of a man who happened to be standing in front of a stone doorway on a bright day. The kind of face that comes up ahead of you in a line somewhere and by the time he's gone you couldn't say whether his eyes were light or dark. She kept looking, trying to fix it in memory, and the harder she looked the more it seemed to come apart, until what she was seeing was features in a rough vicinity of each other rather than a person. The squinting might have been concentration. It might have been the sun.

She turned the photograph over.

Her father's pencil. His vertical German hand.

*A. Pfeiffer. W. Grau. Bamberg, 1921.*

She stood at the edge of the bed and held the photograph and thought about Bamberg. Bavaria — she was fairly sure. Somewhere in the middle of the country, north of Munich. Not where her father's family was from; they had been from south of there, nearer the Austrian border. But not far from Ansbach either, she thought, and the thought came and went before she decided whether to catch it. The photograph was from 1921. The year before her parents came to Maine.

*W. Grau.* She had never heard the name. *Grau*: in German, grey. A man named Grey, standing beside her father in the afternoon light of a stone doorway, twenty-three years ago.

She put the photograph back with the others. Replaced the rubber band. Closed the box and latched it. Set it on the shelf above the shirts where it had always been.

She picked up the laundry basket and went back to her work.

---

The afternoon was farm work, which it had been every April of her life.

She filled the near trough and opened the gate to the far pasture, which had been closed since November. The mud on the track between the barn and the gate was deep and cold and smelled of the earth beginning to come back — different from summer mud, more mineral than animal, with something green underneath it. Two cows came out and stood in the new grass looking at it with their usual expression, which was the expression they had for everything. She worked the pump handle and let the water run. In the north field she could hear the four Germans — the sound of tools in turned ground, a word or two carried on the wind, Lonzo Reed's voice in its usual even register and then quiet. She didn't look that way.

She split kindling. The axe came down and the cedar split clean, the smell sharp in the cold air. She stacked it under the overhang and worked until her shoulders told her to stop.

*W. Grau.*

The name was there through all of it, not urgently. The way a half-heard phrase stays with you during repetitive work — you think about something else and there it is again, unchanged. She tried to hold the face from the photograph and it kept going. Her father's face stayed because her father was here and she saw the same face every day. But the man beside him dissolved each time she turned her attention away, until what came back was only the shape of the shoulders and the squinting and the stone archway behind them, and not the face itself.

He had written both names on the back in pencil — in his own vertical German hand, a name for each face so neither would slip without the other. He had wanted to remember.

October arrived in her, the way it kept arriving: dinner, three weeks or so after the storm, her saying *they found a body on the breakwater* in the same tone she carried any news home from school, and her father's hands going still on his utensils. She had noticed. She had said something about the milking instead, because not asking had felt like the right thing, the careful thing, the choice that maintained the particular equilibrium of silence her household ran on.

She wasn't sure anymore that it had been.

She went inside.

Her mother was at the kitchen window, standing with her arms at her sides, looking out at the east field. Hannah had learned, over the better part of a year, not to try to read those stillnesses. She measured flour. She put the kettle on. Magda moved to the table and sat down, and neither of them spoke, which was the usual arrangement and worked well enough.

She kneaded the dough longer than she needed to and covered it with a cloth and sat at the table with her library book and read two pages three times without them settling into anything.

*A. Pfeiffer. W. Grau. Bamberg, 1921.*

Her father had written both names because he wanted to keep them. That was all she could say for certain. He had wanted the name alongside the face so the face wouldn't go when the memory of it tried to go. The letters in the tin box were in German; she hadn't read them. The papers she hadn't unfolded. Whatever her parents had kept from before — before Maine, before she was born, before whatever the before was that had become this household — it was in that box on the shelf in their room, and she had opened it today for the first time, and she was seventeen years old and had found a name she had never heard.

She took the loaves out when the kitchen smelled right and went to set the table.

---

Her father came in from the fields at half past five, which was when he always came in. His boots on the porch step, the pump, the towel on its nail. He sat down. Magda brought the soup. Hannah set the bread on the board, the pickles, the salt.

The lamp was on the table between them. The ceiling wiring had been unreliable since the spring rain two nights ago and her father didn't trust it after wet weather, so the oil lamp, which made the kitchen smaller and closer, the corners going to warm shadow, the window above the sink dark and reflecting the room back at itself.

Her father bowed his head.

*Komm, Herr Jesu, sei unser Gast.* The same four lines he had always said, always in German, at every meal, since before she was old enough to know what grace was. She moved her lips with the words without making sound — habit, and also she didn't want to forget them entirely. Her mother was still. Then her father raised his head and picked up his spoon.

The soup: potatoes, the last of the winter's dried beans, a hamhock stretched to its limit. There was bread. The lamp flame shifted in a brief draft from the hallway and stilled. Her father broke bread. Her mother moved her spoon through the broth.

She had not planned to say it. She set her spoon down.

"Papa." Not carefully, not carelessly. A normal tone of voice, the tone she would use to ask about the fields or the feed. "Who is W. Grau?"

Her father's hands stopped.

She watched them. His fork was raised, and the piece of bread he had broken in his other hand, and both stopped where they were — two or three inches above the plate, suspended. The lamp flame moved again in the same draft. One second. Two. The flame stilled. Three. Then her father's hands came down. He set the bread on the side of his plate and picked up his spoon.

He said nothing.

She looked at her mother.

Magda had looked up.

Magda, who for months had kept her eyes to the table or the window or the interior distance she had been moving toward since the start of the war — Magda had looked up. Quickly. Her eyes found Hannah's across the lamp and the table.

What was in them was not alarm. Not the particular flatness of the depression that had been Magda's face for the better part of a year. Something older than that, something worn smooth by being held a long time — not bitterness, not grief exactly, though grief was somewhere underneath it. The look of a woman who has been sitting beside a door for a long time without knowing when it will open, and has now heard the latch.

Two seconds. Then Magda's eyes went back to her bowl.

Her father said nothing. He ate. He drank from his water glass. He broke the bread and ate the bread and did not look at Hannah and did not answer.

Nobody spoke for the rest of dinner.

---

Hannah washed the dishes. Magda dried, her hands moving from bowl to towel to shelf with the efficiency of someone for whom the task has long since stopped requiring thought. Through the window above the sink the farmyard had gone dark. The barn roof flat against the sky. At the base of the icehouse door, a thin line of yellow light showed, steady and faint.

She handed the last plate to her mother and dried her own hands.

Her father had moved to the accounts book. The table was as it always was at this hour: book open to the usual page, his pen in his hand, the bread plate at the side, the salt beside it, the lamp moved to give him light on the columns. His pen made its small sounds. He did not look up when she passed.

She went upstairs.

Her room was dark. She sat on the edge of the bed without lighting the lamp and listened to the house — the pen, faintly; her mother's chair; outside, the April wind working at the window frame, still with winter in it at this hour. Down the hall, through the wall, the shelf above the shirts.

She tried once more to hold the face from the photograph. The shoulders, the squinting, the ordinary arrangement of features she had looked at and looked at and couldn't keep. She held it for a moment. Then it was gone, the same as it had gone every time.

But her father's hands had stopped.

She lay down in her coat. Downstairs, the pen moved in its columns. Outside the window, the wind worked at the frame.

input.summary: April 1944. Hannah's chapter. Doing laundry in her parents' bedroom, Hannah finds a tin box she has never opened. Inside: letters in German she doesn't read, documents she doesn't unfold, and a small stack of photographs. The third photograph stops her — two men before a European stone doorway, Bamberg, 1921. One is her father, younger and unguarded. The other has a laborer's build and an ordinary face she cannot hold in memory no matter how long she looks. Penciled on the back in her father's vertical German hand: A. Pfeiffer. W. Grau. She has never heard the name. She puts everything back and carries W. Grau through the afternoon farm work — splitting kindling, filling troughs — and into dinner, where she says the name aloud before she has decided to. Her father's hands stop on his fork and bread, suspended for two or three seconds, then come down. He says nothing. Magda — who has not looked up from her plate in months — looks up. Her eyes find Hannah's across the lamp. The look in them: not alarm, not grief exactly; something older, worn smooth, the look of a woman who has been sitting beside a door for a long time and has heard the latch. Then her eyes go back to her bowl. Nobody speaks for the rest of dinner. Hannah washes the dishes, passes the table, goes upstairs alone in the dark. The tin box is on its shelf down the hall. Her father's pen moves in its columns below.

input.content:
# Chapter Fifteen — What Grandy Soule Saw

The registration table went up at the pier head the last week of April the way it had gone up every spring Eira could remember: the clipboard, the fee box, the carbon forms weighted at the left with the big shackle she kept for this purpose, because the wind off the harbor had no patience for paperwork in April.

She had the table set before seven. The harbor lay in front of her with the particular quality of spring — the light longer now, working into the east faces of the pilings and under the boathouse eaves where the winter sun hadn't reached, the water still cold enough to raise a thin steam at the harbor entrance in the early morning air. The mud at the basin head had softened. Dark fronds of weed were coming off the south rocks. A pair of eiders worked the current beside the fish house float and did not look up.

The first boat in was the *Bertha L.* at half past, Pete Alley at the wheel with his boy in the stern. She had the hull in the card file and wrote it up while he tied off: tonnage, engine, mooring assignment. He'd put fresh paint on her over the winter and the hull had that new brightness to it that wouldn't last but was good while it lasted. She collected the fee and the signature and filed the carbon.

By noon she had seven: *Bertha L.*, *Perseverance*, *Sea Star*, *Laura K.*, *Edna C.*, and two others whose documentation was in order and whose owners had nothing more to say to her than the minimum. She wrote each entry in the column and checked it against the card file and wrote the total at the bottom of the page.

Seven. Last spring there had been nine.

*Crestview* was still in the cradle at the railway yard. Harold Oakes had gone into the Navy in January of 1942 and the boat had been on the railway since that June. She had sent two letters about the cradle fee; neither had been answered, which was not Oakes's fault. The mooring pen sat empty. *Walter D.* had been sold south to Tenants Harbor in February when the Withams made the decision they had been putting off since autumn — Lyle had taken sick and there was no one left to run the boat. She had given that mooring pen to the *Laura K.* when Ed Croft's hip made the row from the inner float a problem for him.

Two fewer boats. The column said so.

*Sea Star* was Ray Coffin's — Fred Coffin's younger boy, who had come home from the Pacific in November with two fingers gone from the right hand and had been on the water again by April, which was not a surprise to anyone who knew the family. He signed the registration form left-handed. He wanted the mooring lines inspected before he started hauling and she made a note.

Wendell Talbot on the *Edna C.* had a new inboard he was willing to explain at length. She let him explain it, asked for the documentation twice, received it the second time. New tonnage in the column. She signed the carbon.

The rest of the afternoon went the way it went: boat by boat, fee by fee, the spring talk running alongside the transactions the way it always did. Ice-out dates, trap losses from the winter, whether the herring were moving early or late, the price at the pound. Asa Parker's gear had fouled on the north ledge in January and he had things to say about it. She heard about the Gifford boy's medical discharge from Portsmouth Shipyard, about trouble with the mooring chain at the north buoy, about a rumor of striped bass in the outer bay. She listened and wrote and handed over receipts.

By two o'clock the registration table was packed and she was at the fuel dock going over the morning log when the *Maud L.* came in.

---

Grandy Soule brought her alongside the fuel dock without ceremony — no wasted motion, the boat coming against the fender the way something comes to rest in the hands of a man who has set it down in the same place for more years than he has counted. The *Maud L.* was a thirty-two-foot lobster boat with a dull red hull that had been brighter once; Soule had bought her in 1928 and she had been working this harbor since. He was perhaps seventy, perhaps past it. His age was a harbor fact she had stopped trying to fix, the same way you stop sounding every ledge you already know is there.

He paid for his fuel in exact change from his coat pocket, signed the carbon, and stood at the dock while the tank filled. The harbor went on around them: the sound of the pump, the water working the pilings, a dragger coming in from the outer harbor and taking its mooring. Soule had his eyes on the south end of the inner pier — the double-planked float at the fish house end, the one that had needed new decking since before the war and was not going to get it this spring either.

She was finishing the log entry for the *Laura K.*

He said nothing for a while and she did not expect him to.

Then, without turning: "Saw a strange dinghy at the south pier. That October night. Before your blow."

She looked up. She kept her face. "Which pier," she said.

"South end. That last float." He moved his chin toward it. "Late. After midnight. I was driving back from Owls Head."

"What night."

"Night the weather came on, or near enough. I've thought about it." He watched the harbor. "Numbers on the transom weren't Coldwater. I didn't know them."

"Could you read them?"

"Not properly. Too dark, and I didn't stop. Might have been Portland — I couldn't say for certain. Small boat, fiberglass tender, not large." A pause. "One man come off her. He walked up toward the main pier."

"Did you see him come back to the dinghy?"

"No." He held the mooring line, not working it yet. "I drove on. Figured whoever it was had put in because the weather was turning — thought nothing of it." He looked at the float. "Dinghy was gone when the blow cleared. I don't know when it went. Could have gone in the storm."

She looked at the fuel gauge. Her pen was in her hand. She had written nothing since he started speaking.

"One man," she said. "That's all you saw."

"One." He began working the mooring line loose. "I heard you were still asking about that October business. Thought maybe you'd want to know."

"I would," she said. "Thank you, Grandy."

He untied the *Maud L.* and backed her out with the same economy he'd brought her in with, turned toward the harbor mouth, and was gone past the outer breakwater. The wake spread into the basin and went flat. She stood at the dock end and watched the boat go.

---

She stood at the end of the fuel pier with the harbor in front of her.

She laid what she had against what she had been carrying, the way she would lay a vessel's log against the tide tables: columns together, the matches showing you what you could confirm, the gaps showing you what you hadn't accounted for yet.

Soule's column: a dinghy at the south pier, the night the storm came on or the night before. Not Coldwater registration — possibly Portland. One man came off her. He walked toward the main waterfront. He did not return to the dinghy before Soule left. The dinghy was gone when the blow cleared.

Her column: two figures on the south dock, same night, past midnight. One coming from the direction of the main pier — heavyset, town coat, moving from some distance. A second figure near the fish house end, further back, that she had taken at the time for a dock worker.

The columns met at the south pier. The man who came off the dinghy and the man she had seen from her window were the same man, or she had to explain why they weren't, and she could not.

The second figure was not in Soule's column. One man, he had said. She had seen two. Which meant the second figure had come on foot, not by water — had come separately, or had come after Soule drove on.

Two days later, with the storm in between, the body was at the breakwater elbow.

Not proof. But it had a shape.

She picked up her clipboard and walked back to the shed.

---

The harbor log was on its stand. The tide tables were pinned to the board behind the door. She hung her coat and sat at the desk. The window gave onto the inner basin — three boats still at their moorings, the outer harbor going pewter in the late-afternoon light.

She opened the middle drawer.

The letter was between the duplicate mooring assignments and the east anchorage survey notes, where she had put it in November. Coast Guard, Sprucehead station. Dated November 14, 1943. Lt. A. Mercer's signature at the bottom, the same neat hand from the October paperwork. *Should any information come to light bearing on the identity of the deceased or the circumstances of his presence in Coldwater Reach, the station would be grateful for its communication at the address above.*

She had read that sentence a dozen times since November. It said what it said.

Below it: male, fifty or older, no identifying papers, recovered at the breakwater elbow, morning of October 12, 1943. Navy wool coat with lapels, wool trousers. Probable cardiac event — no water in the lungs. No next of kin identified, no missing persons report in any register that matched. Case status: open.

She set the letter on the desk.

What the letter did not have: a dinghy at the south pier, possibly Portland registration, the night the storm came on. One man off her, walking toward the main waterfront. That was not her private information. Soule had told her at the fuel dock this afternoon in plain daylight and would confirm it if asked. She could write it in the reply, cite the source, send the letter.

What else: two figures on the south dock, past midnight, October 10 going into the eleventh. One from the direction of the main pier — heavyset, town coat. One near the fish house end, further back, a shape in the dark she had taken for a dock worker. Her own observation, from the shed window, two hundred feet of dark harbor between the glass and the south float. She had been watching the barometric trend. She had seen what she had seen.

She had held the reason for not writing it. The reason was sound: what she had seen from the window was two shapes in the dark at a distance through glass, and two shapes in the dark at a distance through glass was not what the harbor log was for. An entry that couldn't hold on its own was not an entry. She had told herself this in October and in November and in February. The column had stayed blank.

Eight years in this post and she had kept the log accurate. Every entry had something under it: a document, a witness, a measurement, a recorded time. She had not been wrong to wait for more.

What Soule had given her today changed the calculation. Not because he had seen the same things she had — he hadn't stayed long enough for that. Because he had put a transport under the man she had seen. The man coming from the direction of the main pier had not walked in from the road. He had come off a dinghy at the south float, a boat with out-of-town registration, and he had not gone back to it. The storm had come on. Two days later the body was at the elbow of the breakwater, no water in his lungs — a man who had died on land or at the dock edge, and the storm had done the rest.

Together — Soule's piece and her piece — they had a shape that neither piece had alone. A man came to Coldwater from outside, by water, at night. Someone else was on the dock the same night who had not come by water. The man from the dinghy did not return to his boat. The body was at the breakwater in the morning.

She had been holding this alone for six months.

The envelope was in the right-hand drawer. She had put it there in January when the winter had seemed like enough reason to wait.

She reached for her pen.

# Chapter Fifteen — What Grandy Soule Saw

The registration table went up at the pier head the last week of April the way it had gone up every spring Eira could remember: the clipboard, the fee box, the carbon forms weighted at the left with the big shackle she kept for this purpose, because the wind off the harbor had no patience for paperwork in April.

She had the table set before seven. The harbor lay in front of her with the particular quality of spring — the light longer now, working into the east faces of the pilings and under the boathouse eaves where the winter sun hadn't reached, the water still cold enough to raise a thin steam at the harbor entrance in the early morning air. The mud at the basin head had softened. Dark fronds of weed were coming off the south rocks. A pair of eiders worked the current beside the fish house float and did not look up.

The first boat in was the *Bertha L.* at half past, Pete Alley at the wheel with his boy in the stern. She had the hull in the card file and wrote it up while he tied off: tonnage, engine, mooring assignment. He'd put fresh paint on her over the winter and the hull had that new brightness to it that wouldn't last but was good while it lasted. She collected the fee and the signature and filed the carbon.

By noon she had seven: *Bertha L.*, *Perseverance*, *Sea Star*, *Laura K.*, *Edna C.*, and two others whose documentation was in order and whose owners had nothing more to say to her than the minimum. She wrote each entry in the column and checked it against the card file and wrote the total at the bottom of the page.

Seven. Last spring there had been nine.

*Crestview* was still in the cradle at the railway yard. Harold Oakes had gone into the Navy in January of 1942 and the boat had been on the railway since that June. She had sent two letters about the cradle fee; neither had been answered, which was not Oakes's fault. The mooring pen sat empty. *Walter D.* had been sold south to Tenants Harbor in February when the Withams made the decision they had been putting off since autumn — Lyle had taken sick and there was no one left to take the boat over. She had given that mooring pen to the *Laura K.* when Ed Croft's hip made the row from the inner float a problem for him.

Two fewer boats. The column said so.

*Sea Star* was Ray Coffin's — Fred Coffin's younger boy, who had come home from the Pacific in November with two fingers gone from the right hand and had been on the water again by April, which was not a surprise to anyone who knew the family. He signed the registration form left-handed. He wanted the mooring lines inspected before he started hauling and she made a note.

Burton Talbot on the *Edna C.* had a new inboard he was willing to explain at length. She let him explain it, asked for the documentation twice, received it the second time. New tonnage in the column. She signed the carbon.

The rest of the afternoon went the way it went: boat by boat, fee by fee, the spring talk running alongside the transactions the way it always did. Ice-out dates, trap losses from the winter, whether the herring were moving early or late, the price at the pound. Asa Parker's gear had fouled on the north ledge in January and he had things to say about it. She heard about the Gifford boy's medical discharge from Portsmouth Shipyard, about trouble with the mooring chain at the north buoy, about a rumor of striped bass in the outer bay. She listened and wrote and handed over receipts.

By two o'clock the registration table was packed and she was at the fuel dock going over the morning log when the *Maud L.* came in.

---

Grandy Soule brought her alongside the fuel dock without ceremony — no wasted motion, the boat coming against the fender the way something comes to rest in the hands of a man who has set it down in the same place for more years than he has counted. The *Maud L.* was a thirty-two-foot lobster boat with a dull red hull that had been brighter once; Soule had bought her in 1928 and she had been working this harbor since. He was perhaps seventy, perhaps past it. His age was a harbor fact she had stopped trying to fix, the same way you stop sounding every ledge you already know is there.

He paid for his fuel in exact change from his coat pocket, signed the carbon, and stood at the dock while the tank filled. The harbor went on around them: the sound of the pump, the water working the pilings, a dragger coming in from the outer harbor and taking its mooring. Soule had his eyes on the south end of the inner pier — the double-planked float at the fish house end, the one that had needed new decking since before the war and was not going to get it this spring either.

She was finishing the log entry for the *Laura K.*

He said nothing for a while and she did not expect him to.

Then, without turning: "Saw a strange dinghy at the south pier. That October night. Before your blow."

She looked up. She kept her face. "Which pier," she said.

"South end. That last float." He moved his chin toward it. "Late. After midnight. I was driving back from Owls Head."

"What night."

"Night the weather came on, or near enough. I've thought about it." He watched the harbor. "Numbers on the transom weren't Coldwater. I didn't know them."

"Could you read them?"

"Not properly. Too dark, and I didn't stop. Might have been Portland — I couldn't say for certain. Small boat, fiberglass tender, not large." A pause. "One man come off her. He walked up toward the main pier."

"Did you see him come back to the dinghy?"

"No." He held the mooring line, not working it yet. "I drove on. Figured whoever it was had put in because the weather was turning — thought nothing of it." He looked at the float. "Dinghy was gone when the blow cleared. I don't know when it went. Could have gone in the storm."

She looked at the fuel gauge. Her pen was in her hand. She had written nothing since he started speaking.

"One man," she said. "That's all you saw."

"One." He began working the mooring line loose. "I heard you were still asking about that October business. Thought maybe you'd want to know."

"I would," she said. "Thank you, Grandy."

He untied the *Maud L.* and backed her out with the same economy he'd brought her in with, turned toward the harbor mouth, and was gone past the outer breakwater. The wake spread into the basin and went flat. She stood at the dock end and watched the boat go.

---

She stood at the end of the fuel pier with the harbor in front of her.

She laid what she had against what she had been carrying, the way she would lay a vessel's log against the tide tables: columns together, the matches showing you what you could confirm, the gaps showing you what you hadn't accounted for yet.

Soule's column: a dinghy at the south pier, the night the storm came on or the night before. Not Coldwater registration — possibly Portland. One man came off her. He walked toward the main waterfront. He did not return to the dinghy before Soule left. The dinghy was gone when the blow cleared.

Her column: two figures on the south dock, same night, past midnight. One coming from the direction of the main pier — heavyset, town coat, moving from some distance. A second figure near the fish house end, further back, that she had taken at the time for a dock worker.

The columns met at the south pier. The man who came off the dinghy and the man she had seen from her window were the same man, or she had to explain why they weren't, and she could not.

The second figure was not in Soule's column. One man, he had said. She had seen two. Which meant the second figure had come on foot, not by water — had come separately, or had come after Soule drove on.

Two days later, with the storm in between, the body was at the breakwater elbow.

Not proof. But it had a shape.

She picked up her clipboard and walked back to the shed.

---

The harbor log was on its stand. The tide tables were pinned to the board behind the door. She hung her coat and sat at the desk. The window gave onto the inner basin — three boats still at their moorings, the outer harbor going pewter in the late-afternoon light.

She opened the middle drawer.

The letter was between the duplicate mooring assignments and the east anchorage survey notes, where she had put it in November. Coast Guard, Sprucehead station. Dated November 14, 1943. Lt. A. Mercer's signature at the bottom, the same neat hand from the October paperwork. *Should any information come to light bearing on the identity of the deceased or the circumstances of his presence in Coldwater Reach, the station would be grateful for its communication at the address above.*

She had read that sentence a dozen times since November. It said what it said.

Below it: male, fifty or older, no identifying papers, recovered at the breakwater elbow, morning of October 12, 1943. Navy wool coat with lapels, wool trousers. Probable cardiac event — no water in the lungs. No next of kin identified, no missing persons report in any register that matched. Case status: open.

She set the letter on the desk.

What the letter did not have: a dinghy at the south pier, possibly Portland registration, the night the storm came on. One man off her, walking toward the main waterfront. That was not her private information. Soule had told her at the fuel dock this afternoon in plain daylight and would confirm it if asked. She could write it in the reply, cite the source, send the letter.

What else: two figures on the south dock, past midnight, October 10 going into the eleventh. One from the direction of the main pier — heavyset, town coat. One near the fish house end, further back, a shape in the dark she had taken for a dock worker. Her own observation, from the shed window, two hundred feet of dark harbor between the glass and the south float. She had been watching the barometric trend. She had seen what she had seen.

She had held the reason for not writing it. The reason was sound: what she had seen from the window was two shapes in the dark at a distance through glass, and two shapes in the dark at a distance through glass was not what the harbor log was for. An entry that couldn't hold on its own was not an entry. She had told herself this in October and in November and in February. The column had stayed blank.

Eight years in this post and she had kept the log accurate. Every entry had something under it: a document, a witness, a measurement, a recorded time. She had not been wrong to wait for more.

What Soule had given her today changed the calculation. Not because he had seen the same things she had — he hadn't stayed long enough for that. Because he had put a transport under the man she had seen. The man coming from the direction of the main pier had not walked in from the road. He had come off a dinghy at the south float, a boat with out-of-town registration, and he had not gone back to it. The storm had come on. Two days later the body was at the elbow of the breakwater, no water in his lungs — a man who had died on land or at the dock edge, and the storm had done the rest.

Together — Soule's piece and her piece — they had a shape that neither piece had alone. A man came to Coldwater from outside, by water, at night. Someone else was on the dock the same night who had not come by water. The man from the dinghy did not return to his boat. The body was at the breakwater in the morning.

She had been holding this alone for six months.

The envelope was in the right-hand drawer. She had put it there in January when the winter had seemed like enough reason to wait.

She reached for her pen.
