# The Cove

The survey ran north to south: Heron Point first, then Seal Neck, then the two unnamed pockets between the outer heads, then the south cove behind the headland. She did this every September before the season closed. The work was not difficult. She had run the same route for eight years and the harbor launch knew the shape of it.

She went out at the morning ebb. The ebb pulled the water off the rock and showed what the season had deposited — pots and hawsers and storm-blown floats, the gear that accumulated where the harbor's circulation said it would accumulate. The pattern was reliable. Drifted things moved in a direction that could be predicted given the prevailing set of the tides and the shape of the headlands. She had mapped the pattern in her first years by noting what turned up where, and the map had held.

Heron Point: two lobster pots with the surface buoys worn blank. She logged the positions and the condition and went on. The gannet working the tide rip off the point was nothing to log; she logged it anyway, a habit from her early years when she was still learning what went into the record and what did not, a habit she had since decided to keep.

Seal Neck: a length of commercial hawser above the tide line, fifty feet or better, flagged for the boatyard to collect at their convenience. The small pocket east of Seal Neck: a mooring float she had been carrying in the spring records since the line parted in April. She hooked it with the boat hook and brought it aboard and wrote the return in the log. The second unnamed pocket: a section of fish net from some farm operation, three seasons old if she was reading the growth right, too far gone to save.

The light in September was flat and honest. Not the glare of August that showed the water's surface and pressed everything into a shimmer, and not the November light that compressed the whole harbor into gray distance. September put things at their actual size. She could see what was there.

She came around the south headland at half-ebb.

---

The cove behind the south headland was a hundred yards end to end. Its entrance faced east, which set it across the prevailing swell; what came in on the northeast blow came in, and what drifted on the tidal circulation from around the headland came in and stayed. She had learned the cove's habits in her second year and added it to the survey route in her third. In eight years she had found in it, among other things, a salmon net from a farm forty miles up the bay, a fuel drum still three-quarters full, and two sections of the old outer marker that the Navy had replaced and apparently lost track of. She expected gear.

The dinghy was not gear.

She saw it before she was within fifty yards: a white hull, discolored, the shape unfamiliar. She brought the launch down to drift and worked in toward the cove's north end. The dinghy had come to rest bow-on to the granite, the bow caught on a ledge a foot above the current waterline with the stern swung around on the ebb. Its freeboard on the port side was low — the hull was down amidships where something had gone wrong with it. She put the launch alongside the rock and looked.

Twelve feet, twelve and a half at most. A pulling boat with a flat bottom, the kind built for a sheltered harbor and nothing past the heads. The damage was to the port side amidships: planking crushed inward, the frames behind it broken, the seam at the garboard open on both sides of the break. The hull had taken a hard blow or had been ground hard against something with weight behind it. Below the damaged section, the boat had shipped water enough to settle it. Above the damage, the hull cleared the surface, held up by the bow on its ledge.

She put her hand on the rock and steadied the launch against it and looked at the waterline.

The weed was the record. It grew at a predictable rate on a hull left in one place; it stopped at the surface; it did not lie about the time elapsed. The line of growth on this hull ran six inches above the cove's present waterline, which meant the hull had come to rest here when the tide was running six inches higher than today's ebb — a normal tidal variation, nothing unusual. The barnacle growth started below the weed line and went down into the murk. She estimated ten months. Maybe eleven. Late autumn or early winter, which put the arrival somewhere in the months after the October blow.

She shipped the oars and stepped onto the rock.

---

The bow ring was brass, tarnished to near-black, but solid. She got both hands through it and pulled back, working her grip down toward the waterline, bracing her feet against a lower ledge. The hull was heavy — waterlogged through and through, the planking saturated, the broken section adding to the weight by holding water in the bilge. She set her weight against it and worked it up the rock in stages until the transom lifted clear of the water.

She held it there and looked at the transom.

The paint was gone. Where it had been heaviest it had left a primer stain on the wood; where it had been thin it was down to bare grain. There had been a name painted on the board, centered, in large letters and a dark color. Most of it was unreadable. The middle section — the heart of the letters, where the wood had worked most through the wetting and drying of eleven months — had come down to bare board. What remained was at the right end of the painted surface: four characters at the edge of where the name had ended. *STEN,* in the trace of a pigment that had held on a little better than the rest.

That was all the name had left.

She held the bow up with one hand and got the log out of her coat pocket with the other. Below the remnant of the name, set into the lower edge of the transom on a rectangular plate, was the registration. The bronze had gone green at the edges but the center was still readable: the Portland Harbor Authority's district and vessel number, stamped in standard format, the registration year clear at the right. She wrote the number in the log against the date and the position.

She let the bow down. The dinghy swung back on its ledge.

She spent another minute on the hull: looking at the damage, reading the angles of the broken frames. A rock in the cove could have done it, or a dock edge, or a piling in a blow. She could not say what had made the wound or when, except that it was at least as old as the growth on the waterline, which meant it had happened before the hull came to rest here or at the same time. She could not say more than that.

She stepped back to the launch and rowed out of the cove.

---

She wrote up the outer cove survey in the afternoon. Six items: the two Heron Point pots, the Seal Neck hawser, the recovered mooring float, the old fish net, and the dinghy. For the dinghy she noted the position, the condition, the estimated time the hull had been in place, and the registration number, and flagged the entry for a Portland inquiry.

The inquiry form was standard. She had submitted three in eight years, all for vessels that had come adrift and ended up where they did not belong. Registration number, found position, condition on discovery, date. She was the reporting officer; she signed her name. She addressed the envelope to the Portland Harbor Authority, Commercial Street, and put it in the outgoing tray.

Portland kept good records. She would have a reply within the week.

---

She did not think much about the dinghy in the three days between sending the letter and receiving the reply. The survey's other items wanted attention: the mooring float needed a return notation against the spring record; the boatyard needed the authorization for the autumn railway haul-out, which she had been building since August and could finalize now that the season's last draggers had scheduled their maintenance dates; the winter mooring allocation list wanted revision now that two of the summer vessels had declared they were laying up in Portland rather than Coldwater. The harbor did not stop.

The reply came Thursday. One page, the Portland Harbor Authority heading, a brief paragraph below it.

She read it.

The registration number submitted belonged to a chandlery on Commercial Street, Portland, operating a rental service for small harbor craft — dinghies and similar vessels, civilian use. The registered vessel had last been carried in the active rental fleet as of late September 1943. At that time it had been rented and not returned. The chandlery's record listed the matter as unresolved. The last rental entry showed the vessel released on the twenty-eighth of September, 1943.

The customer at time of rental had provided a name and an address.

*W. Grau, 114 Franklin Street, Portland, Maine.*

---

She read it twice.

W. Grau. She turned the paper over as if the back would offer something, which it did not. The initial was nothing by itself. The last name was nothing she recognized: not a Coldwater name, not a harbor name, not a name from any registration or manifest she had handled in eight years at this post. Portland was sixty miles south. Portland men worked the outer grounds; they had business everywhere on the coast.

But a rental dinghy out of Portland on the twenty-eighth of September, 1943.

She did not need to calculate. The sequence was there: the dinghy goes out from Portland at the end of September; the three-day blow runs the ninth through the eleventh of October; the body arrives on the breakwater on the morning of the twelfth; the dinghy comes to rest in the south cove in the months after. The middle was not visible. The two ends were visible and they pointed toward each other.

She did not write any of this in the log. She was not ready to write it.

She opened the middle desk drawer.

The CG form was as she had left it: Mercer's case number at the top, the date October 1943, the blank for identifying information still blank, the blank for additional observations below her final logged entry still empty. In April she had reached for this form after Soule mentioned the dinghy at the south pier. She had picked up her pen and then set it back down. She had not been ready in April either.

She set the Portland letter on top of the CG form and looked at them together.

W. Grau, 114 Franklin Street, Portland. The name on the rental form was not necessarily the name of the man who had used the boat; a man could give any name at a chandler's counter, and a man with a reason for one name had a reason for another. But a man with a reason gave the name he gave, and the name he gave went into the record, and the record was in her desk drawer now alongside the unanswered form.

There was also what she had seen on the south float on the night of October tenth going into the eleventh: two figures, one with something under his arm, one in a pale coat, at a time she had fixed in the log as 0055. She had carried that entry without a column for eleven months. In April Soule's account had brought her part of the way, had put the dinghy at the south pier and one figure alongside it, and she had reached for the pen and found she did not yet have enough. She was looking at the question of what enough meant, and whether she was closer to it or only holding more pieces that did not yet make a shape.

The column without a label had more in it now.

---

She closed the drawer.

The harbor was quiet in September. The offshore fleet had been coming in since the first of the month — the season declaring itself over in the way it always did, gradually and then at once. The boatyard was on maintenance schedule. The cold-storage house was running reduced hours. The summer traffic was done and the winter's rhythm had not yet started, and between those two states the harbor had its annual brief stillness, a week or two when the pier held fewer boats than at any other time of year and the water in the channel was flat and clear.

She looked at the desk: the open log, the fuel ledger, the stacked forms in the outgoing tray for the mail boat. The middle drawer was closed.

She had a name. The name had an address. The address was in Portland, which was a city with a post office and a record of residents, and a harbormaster who knew what a harbormaster knew. She was not certain what any of that made possible. She was not certain it made anything possible except what she was already doing, which was holding pieces and waiting for them to accumulate into something that could be entered in the correct column.

She turned back to the log.

The channel held the September light. The mooring chains ran straight down to their blocks with no motion in them — full slack at this hour, the fleet riding easy. The two outer buoys were in their positions at the harbor mouth, the red to port and the green to starboard, visible from the pier head window where she had watched them through eight years of whatever the harbor had brought.

She wrote the afternoon's log. She wrote it correctly.

The drawer stayed closed.

# One Year

He took the harbor road from the foot of Schoolhouse Hill, as he had taken it on most afternoons in two and a half years. The road ran three-quarters of a mile to the pier head, crushed stone with the grass coming through the middle where the wheels did not run; the smell of the harbor moved against him as he came down — cold salt water and diesel, and under both the smell of wet granite that he had absorbed, over the course of his time here, into what he thought of as the working inventory of the place.

It was the fourteenth of October.

One year since the harbormaster's log had carried its first entry on the matter. Two and a half years since he had set his suitcase on the floor of the spare room at the top of Henry Crow's stairs. Six years since Vienna. He held these intervals as he held all precise dates: accurately, as a matter of discipline, not to be confused with what the accumulation of them was for.

The harbor came into view past the cold-storage house.

---

The cold in October had a different quality than the summer cold, which was still a marine cold, the cold of fog and damp and the offshore breeze moderated by the season's remaining warmth. October had given up on moderation. The air off the harbor at the foot of the hill was the air of what was coming rather than what had been, and it carried, mixed with the salt and the diesel, the low-tide smell of October flats: cold mud and rockweed, the harbor floor exposed an extra foot by the autumn tidal range. He had added this smell to the inventory in his second October here, filed under the heading of *this place in this particular week of autumn*, which was as specific as any entry in the inventory was required to be.

Most of the offshore fleet was hauled or preparing to haul. Three draggers were already up on the boatyard railway, their hulls in the pale wood of fresh bottom paint, their shapes oddly elevated without the sea to hold them level. The sardine carrier at the fish pier was loading its last run of the season. The lobster boats were down from their summer counts — he had been counting the mooring buoys in the inner harbor since his first October here without having decided to count them, in the way you come to know the dimensions of a room by crossing it often enough before you think to measure its walls.

The inner harbor was quiet in the way of the brief interval between the end of the season's work and the beginning of what winter made of the harbor — a week or two of stillness, the mooring chains running straight down in the slack water without motion. The water in the channel moved between what was still there without urgency. The cold was steady and without argument.

He turned at the boatyard fence toward the pier head.

---

The breakwater extended from the south headland in an L, the outer arm turning at its elbow toward open water. He had looked at it many times — from the pier head, from the harbor road in its various weathers, from the harbormaster's shed window as he passed on his afternoon walks. He had not walked it.

There was no reason he could have stated precisely for walking it today. The afternoon's marking was done; the stack of translation exercises on his desk was not going anywhere. The light was still adequate. He walked toward the breakwater's landward end and went over the low seawall step and onto the granite without having told himself he was going to.

The surface was irregular — rubble construction, the stones fitted without mortar, the faces worn smooth between the courses. His shoes found the flat planes between the higher stones and moved along them with some care. To his left the outer face dropped to the October sea: twelve or fifteen feet of granite to the water, which was the gray-green here of deep water without a bottom to lighten it. The swell was working in on a long period, lifting and falling against the outer face without violence, the sound at the base of the rock a low continuous suck and drain that was not the sound of the inner harbor but the sound of open water doing what it did against fixed stone, without particular regard for what the stone was there for.

He walked to the elbow.

---

At the elbow the cap widened where the construction doubled back, and there was a section of flat stone large enough to stand on without having to pick between the irregular courses. He stood on it.

The wind from the east had no land behind it, coming off open water without the headland's modification. It carried the cold of unobstructed distance, which was a different quality than the harbor cold — less interested in compromise. The bell buoy at the channel entrance was audible from here in a different way than from the pier head or from his room at night: not muffled by the headland's bulk, closer to its actual sound on the water, which was a lower note and longer interval than the version that arrived through walls and granite.

He looked at the October water.

He had been carrying Werner Grau for a year in the way one carries an assembled account: as a set of documented and plausible facts, each uncertainty marked, the limits of the account defined. The letter addressed to Albrecht Pfeiffer, opened in October 1943 because no one else in Coldwater could read it. The inference from Albrecht's face when Marcus had placed the letter in his hands — not surprise, which would have meant the news was new, but recognition, which meant only that the confirmation had arrived from outside the household rather than being formed within it, from pieces Albrecht had been assembling on his own. The dinghy from Portland, rented on the twenty-eighth of September under the name given at a chandler's counter. The three-day blow. The body on the morning of the twelfth. He had put this on a sheet of school paper in March of 1944, had drawn a circle around the phrase *by some combination*, and had locked everything in the bottom desk drawer, where it had remained since.

For a year Werner Grau had existed in that drawer. The classified account. The provisional conclusions.

What Marcus had not done — what the year had apparently required without his noticing that it was requiring it — was consider Werner in the other way. Not as a set of established facts with their limits marked, but as a person who had made a set of choices, each following from the one before in the way that a person's life follows from the conditions it has been given and the decisions it makes within those conditions.

A man from Ansbach, in Bavaria, which was a market town in a region Marcus could place precisely on any map and had no personal experience of. A man who had left Germany in 1938 or 1939, when leaving had still been possible for a person who moved with some decisiveness, and who had then managed five years in a country not his own on papers whose legitimacy had become, by 1943, a matter of administrative interpretation. Who had managed this for five years and had then decided — for reasons the letter had given Marcus only obliquely, the Pfeiffer name and the Reinmar name and the implication of a message that had waited long enough — that the time had come to come to Maine.

Marcus had made a version of this calculation himself, in Paris in the autumn of 1939, standing at his desk with a newspaper that clarified what the summer had still held in suspension. The calculation was not complicated. It had a correct answer and an incorrect answer, and the correct answer required leaving. He had the address of a colleague in London; he had money enough; he had the competence of a man who had left one country already and knew the mechanics of leaving a second. He had left in October and been in London by November.

Werner had made the same calculation. Werner had made it with less institutional support and onto a harbor dinghy on the coast of Maine at the end of September with the blow coming on. These were the variables of Werner's version, not Marcus's, and Marcus had stopped, at some point in the past year, placing them in the same column. They were two different men who had both been required to calculate. Werner's calculation had taken him farther and had cost him more.

He had been carrying — according to what the letter implied, between the lines of a letter composed by a man who had learned to say only what needed saying and trusted the recipient to supply the rest — something in the category of message that a person carries when they have held it alone long enough that the holding itself has become part of what it is. Here is where Karl Reinmar is; here is what you should know. More than twenty years since Bamberg, where a photograph had been taken and two young men had been in the same place at the same time without any knowledge of what the next twenty years would require of either of them. Werner had come from wherever five years of managed displacement had taken him to put something directly into another man's hands, because some things could not be trusted to a letter, and Werner understood this, having trusted too many things to letters and official channels for too many years to believe in their reliability for what mattered.

He had made it to Maine. He had made it most of the way.

Marcus stood at the elbow of the breakwater for some time. The October water moved below him without hurry. The bell buoy rang its interval at the channel entrance, and then rang again.

---

He looked down.

One of the breakwater stones had broken from its course — roughly fist-sized, the fracture face still comparatively sharp, the outer surface worn smooth to the same gray-green as the cap stone around it. It had settled into the joint between two larger stones, held in place by its neighbors on three sides.

He picked it up.

Cold, in the way of granite that has been sitting in October air near October water. Heavier than its size suggested — the specific density of granite, which was what made it the material of choice for anything meant to hold its position against what the sea brought. He turned it once in his palm, looked at the rough fracture face and the worn outer surface, the gray-green that was the color of this harbor in this season.

He put it in his coat pocket.

He had learned, in six years of sustained displacement, that certain acts arrived before the account that would justify them, and that pressing for the account before it had formed was one reliable way to lose the act. He had the stone. He would carry it home. The account could form at whatever pace it chose.

---

He walked back along the breakwater.

The inner harbor opened ahead of him as he came toward the landward end: the anchorage, the boatyard with the hauled hulls on their jack stands, the cold-storage house, the pier head with the harbormaster's shed at its end and the window lit against the October dusk. Above the roofline the town held its standard configuration — the Congregational steeple the highest point, the school chimney beginning to smoke now that Henry had the boiler running again this week.

At the seawall step he paused. The bell buoy rang from the channel entrance — the same sound that came to his room on certain nights with the wind out of the east, the sound that had been part of the specific air of that room since his first week here, already filed in the inventory under the heading of *this place, this particular channel entrance, this buoy*. He heard it now without modification, from its actual position, with nothing between.

He went over the seawall step and walked back along the harbor road.

---

Henry was at the kitchen table when Marcus came in the back. A boiler fitting lay in a rag in front of him, two wrenches beside it; his hands were moving with the unhurried attention of a man who has understood the problem fully and is in no hurry about the solution. He looked up at Marcus in the way he always looked up — taking note, not requiring commentary — and then looked back at the fitting.

Marcus hung his coat on the peg by the door — the coat with the stone in its pocket, which he would carry upstairs after supper — and washed his hands at the kitchen sink. Lillian had left a covered plate in the warming oven, as she did on evenings when the household schedules did not align in time for a shared meal. The arrangement of the house was as it had been for two and a half years: three people managing their separate schedules with a minimum of friction, the arrangement working because it had been worked out before Marcus arrived and had been adjusted, over time, to account for his particular shape in it. He poured coffee from the pot on the stove and sat at the kitchen table, not in Henry's way, and Henry went on working the fitting.

After supper he went upstairs.

The room was as he had left it: the window over the back garden, the desk with the exercise papers stacked and waiting, the bookshelf with its two rows of German and Latin and the three English titles he had bought in Cambridge and never returned. The chair by the window where he read on Sunday mornings when the light came in at the right angle. He took the stone from his coat pocket.

He set it on the windowsill.

It sat there as granite sits — its weight absorbed into the surface below it without demonstration or comment, without either offering or withholding. Gray-green, fist-sized, one face rough where it had broken from the course and the rest worn smooth by whatever number of years it had spent at the breakwater's elbow before this afternoon. A piece of the breakwater in the room where he slept, which was a fact of the same kind as the other facts in the room: accurate, present, making no claim about what it meant. He looked at it for a moment.

He went downstairs.

---

Through the dining room window the October dark was completing itself over the town. The streetlight at the corner came on — one of the town's fixed intervals, reliable and without reference to whether anyone was watching. The Congregational steeple held its position against what remained of the western light, which was diminishing in the way of October evenings, steadily and without drama.

Lillian passed the bread.

He took a piece. Henry was explaining the boiler fitting — whether the thread wanted redressing or whether a new washer would resolve it, a practical question with a knowable answer, the kind the evening ran on. Marcus ate. Outside the window the October dark settled over the street in the way it had settled over it in every October he had watched it from this table.

He keeps these intervals as inventory facts. The October harbor: fleet hauling, the season's end showing everywhere. At the pier head, for no reason he can precisely name, he walks out onto the breakwater for the first time. At the elbow, standing on the cap stone, he thinks about Werner Grau — not as an assembled account in a desk drawer, but as a person: a man who made the same calculation Marcus made (leaving while leaving was possible), who came a considerable distance carrying something that mattered, who made it most of the way. He picks up a piece of granite from the breakwater's cap, cold and heavy, and puts it in his coat pocket without examining the gesture. On the walk back, the bell buoy at the channel entrance is audible from its actual position. Henry is in the kitchen working on a boiler fitting; Marcus hangs his coat (stone in the pocket) and eats supper. Upstairs, he sets the granite stone on his windowsill — gray-green, fist-sized, one rough face, the rest worn smooth — without examination. He goes back down to dinner. Through the dining room window the October dark completes itself over the town. Lillian passes the bread; Marcus eats; outside, the October dark settles as it has in every October he has watched it from this table.

input.content:
# Transfer

The truck came down the farm road at nine and she heard it before she saw it — the engine note through the bare tree line at the gate, the particular sound of a loaded vehicle finding its way over the ruts her father had not had time to fill. November had come fully in the week since the transfer order arrived; the cold was in the ground now, in the flattened grass, in the particular quality of morning air off the back fields that was not yet winter-cold but had given up on anything else. She had been in the farmyard since a quarter past eight.

There was no more milking to do. She had done it before five, moving cow to cow in the dark with the kerosene lamp hanging from its nail, doing the work thoroughly because it was something she could do thoroughly. She had fed afterward and swept and split a week's worth of kindling from the pile behind the barn, in the dark, by feel, until the kindling pile was stacked and there was nothing left to do with her hands. Then she had come out to the farmyard and stood.

The four Germans had come out of the icehouse at ten minutes to nine.

Each carried a kit bag — not much in any of them; she knew the shape of these bags by now, the rough khaki canvas with the stenciled letters, the few things that had accumulated over thirteen months: issued clothes, extra socks, whatever photographs or letters had made their way in. Dieter and Rolf stood near the gate with their bags over their shoulders, talking low about something she could not hear. Hans was squatting over his bag adjusting the clasp. Karl was standing at the fence corner.

He had something folded in his hand. She looked at it once, noted the columns — a list, parallel lines, two across — and then looked at the gate.

Lonzo was at the icehouse door without the carbine. He had left it inside on its rack, or she assumed he had; it was not at his side and not in his hands. He stood with his arms loosely folded and watched the top of the gatepost.

The truck came through.

---

Two MPs in the cab, a younger one driving and an older one with a clipboard. The older one got out and stood by the truck door and read four names from the list in the carrying voice of a man who has done this enough times that he no longer hears the names as names: *Reinmar. Steinbach. Huber. Bauer.* Each man answered. The MP made his marks. That was all of the official proceeding — it took less time than she had spent in the farmyard waiting for it.

The tailgate came down.

Dieter swung himself up first, easy with it, a man accustomed to loading equipment. Then Hans, then Rolf. Karl picked up his kit bag and turned.

She was already moving.

She had not decided to move. Her feet were crossing the farmyard and her hand had the notebook in it — drawn from her apron pocket in the same motion, the two things together, the way she had been deciding things all autumn and probably longer than autumn: the body knowing before the thinking did, and the thinking catching up later when there was room for it. She came across the yard and stopped a few feet from him.

Lonzo had turned to look at the cab. He was looking at the cab with the complete and particular quality of a person who has decided something is not their business — so fully decided it that the looking-away was as deliberate as if he had said the words aloud, and she understood the gift he was giving without his having named it as a gift.

She had perhaps four minutes.

---

She held out the notebook.

He looked at it. She could see in his face the moment of recognition — the soft worn covers, the water stain at the lower back, the shape that had lived in her apron pocket all through the summer and now lived in her outstretched hand. He took it with both hands: one at the cover and one at the spine, the way you receive something that has been kept, that carries the weight of being kept.

He held it against his chest.

He reached into his breast pocket.

She had not expected it. But she could see immediately that it had been waiting — the folded paper came out with the ease of something placed there in advance, folded with the deliberate folds of something folded and put in the breast pocket not because there was nowhere else for it but because the breast pocket is where you keep what you mean to give. Behind the note, briefly visible, the edge of his own list: the parallel columns, the two-language record she had only glimpsed and never held. He drew the note out and held it toward her with one hand, the other still pressing the notebook to his chest.

She took the note.

She put it in her apron pocket without reading it, because reading was not what you did with four minutes, and she would read it when she had a room and a lamp and the time to hold whatever it said.

---

They stood with a foot of November air between them.

Thirteen months. The first October, the word *Seidenschwanz* coming out of his mouth in the dark and going nowhere, not knowing where to go; then her writing it in the margin of her homework at the kitchen table because if she wrote it down it would stay. January, the grain bin, *Schnee* back and forth in the cold, the word for snow from a country that had twenty kinds of need for it. The cedar waxwing landing on the water trough in the early thaw and both of them saying its name at the same moment and neither one having noticed, until that instant, that they both had it. August, the barn, the haywork smell, *Werner. Von Ansbach. Er wollte kommen.* His hands resting on the stacked bales. The tense.

His face had settled into something she found harder to read now than in the first weeks — not harder in the way of concealment, but harder in the way of depth, of something that had gone farther in. Twenty, and the year in it: the outdoor cold, the fieldwork weight, the year of being somewhere that was not home and would not become it. She had been watching this face since October of last year, across a water bucket and a fence post and a notebook open on a fence rail, and she could account for most of its particulars: the line of his jaw, the set of his eyes, the small scar at the outer edge of his right eyebrow she had first noticed in February and by March had filed alongside the rest of him. She looked at all of it.

She did not have the German for what was in his face. She did not have the English. The grammar they had built between them — the nouns and the birds and the weather words and the verbs of the farm — had been assembled around exactly this kind of thing without being adequate to name it. What was in his face was the thing the grammar circled without entering.

He said: *Hah-nah.*

The shape he had always given her name: the first syllable lifted, the *a* broader and lower than the American version, the second syllable brief and final. She had not corrected it in thirteen months and did not now.

Behind her the MP said something.

Karl looked at her for one more second.

Then he stepped up into the truck bed, sat on the bench along the wall, set the notebook on his knee. The tailgate went up.

---

She stood in the farmyard and watched the truck turn.

It was slow through the yard, finding its way through the ruts and the gate and the cattle guard. Through the slats she could see them on the bench: Dieter with his arms crossed and his eyes closed, Hans looking at the truck bed boards, Rolf with his hands on his kit bag. Karl had the notebook flat on his knee and his eyes on the farmyard. She could not tell, through the slats and the November gray, whether he could see her where she stood.

The truck went through the gate and the cattle guard slowed it again and then it straightened onto the farm road and the bare tree line swallowed it.

She turned.

Her father was on the porch.

She had not heard him come out — he had been in the barn before light, in the milking parlor, in the equipment shed before that; she had not tracked his morning and had not expected to find him here. He was standing on the top porch step in his barn coat with his hands at his sides, watching the gate where the truck had been. She stood in the farmyard. He stood on the porch. The farm was quieter already than it had been at eight o'clock — a quality in the air, an absence with a specific sound to it.

His face had the quality she had spent her life learning to read. Not empty — her father's face had not been empty since she could first remember looking at it carefully enough to know. Closed, in the way of a man who has been holding something for a long time and carries the shape of the holding in his expression the way a hand carries the shape of whatever it has gripped.

He watched the gate a moment longer.

Then he went inside.

---

*That evening.*

She sat at the kitchen table after supper and took the note from her apron pocket and unfolded it on the oilcloth.

The paper was the back of an envelope. Through the reverse she could see the faint impression of the address, canceled through once with a pen line. His handwriting: the English formed in the European way, each letter separated and upright, the letters careful with the specific care of a man working in a language not his own, each word made at the cost of making it. She understood that he had written this in English because it was for her — in German it would have been easier; in English it was exactly for her.

*Werner Grau. From Ansbach. He is dead. I am sorry.*

She read it. She read it again.

Below the four sentences, in two columns, five birds in the format she had used in the notebook: the German name on the left, the Latin on the right, the letters smaller and more careful than the sentences above.

*Seidenschwanz — Bombycilla cedrorum*
*Rotkehlchen — Turdus migratorius*
*Blaumeise — Poecile atricapillus*
*Habicht — Accipiter gentilis*
*Sperber — Falco sparverius*

The cedar waxwing at the top of the list, and the four others below it.

She looked at the list for a long time.

He had known since before August. Longer — she thought since the winter, the way his hands had stilled on the bale that morning in August before he spoke the name, the stillness of someone saying a thing they have carried through several seasons and are only now finding the occasion for. He had been carrying it in the same breast pocket as the bird list, the two things together through the months of fieldwork and the months of cold: the names of the birds they had made between them, and the name of the man.

The apology — *I am sorry* — was not for Werner's death. She understood this. It was for this: for the knowledge now in her hands, full weight, past tense, Werner Grau who had come from Ansbach and made it most of the way and the rest of which she had been holding in pieces since October of last year. Karl had kept his piece alone until August, until the barn, until the four minutes this morning, and the apology was for the landing of it — for putting her in the position of carrying the whole of what she now had.

She folded the note on its original lines.

She put it in her pocket.

---

She found her father in the sitting room with his accounts.

The ledger was open on the small table by the window, the lamp lit at the table's edge, and his pen was moving in the columns. He did not look up when she came to the doorway. The lamp made its small circle on the ledger and on his hands; the rest of the room was the dark of a November evening, the corners of the furniture going gray and soft, the rag rug at the foot of the stairs visible only as its shape.

She stood in the doorway.

The German came not because she chose it. It was the language the sentence required — it had taken its language before she thought about the choosing, the way her feet had crossed the farmyard before she thought about moving. The language of the household's keeping. The one they had been keeping it in, without naming the keeping, for over a year: in German at the grain bin in January, in German at the dinner table the night her father's hands stopped above his plate, in German in the tin box where the photograph had been waiting with its two faces and the year below them.

*Werner Grau ist tot.*

Her father did not move.

The pen was still. His other hand, flat on the open ledger, was still also. She counted without choosing to count: one, two, three, four, five. The pen above the paper. His hand flat on the page. Six, seven, eight, nine, ten.

He looked up at her.

*Ich weiß.*

Two words. The voice level, the cadence of something said that has been carried for a long time and is less heavy in the saying than in the holding. He said it simply, the way you say a thing that you have been waiting to say and have rehearsed without meaning to, and he looked at her with it in his face — not relief, exactly; not any clean word she had for it. The look of a man who has been sitting in a room with something for over a year and has just heard, from the other side of the door, the sound that tells him he is no longer sitting in it alone.

He held her eyes a moment.

Then he looked back at the ledger.

---

She did not ask what happened.

The question did not come. There was no German for it that arrived at the doorway, no English, nothing in the grammar they shared or didn't share that wanted to be the next thing said. The silence after *Ich weiß* had the quality of a silence that closes rather than opens, and she had learned the difference. This one was finished. What it covered, it covered permanently.

She nodded once.

Then she turned and went back to the kitchen.

The water in the pot was still warm from supper. She filled the basin and did the dishes — the supper plates first, then the cups, then the pot — working through them in the order she always worked through them, the warm water and the sound of it. Her hands in the basin. The dish towel. When the last cup was on the drying rack she dried her hands and stood at the window above the sink.

Through the glass she could see the farmyard.

The icehouse was dark.

Not the low settled dark of a lamp turned down for the night — the kind of light that had been visible through those windows on any night she had looked toward the icehouse since October of last year, the steady small warmth of the bunkhouse occupied. Dark in the way it had not been dark in thirteen months: the windows blank, the lamp not lit, nobody in the bunkhouse and no light to say that someone was there. The icehouse stood where it had always stood, the same gray boards and the same roofline against the November sky, and the farm was quieter than it had been before nine o'clock that morning.

The lamp was not lit.

facts: Karl Reinmar was transferred from the Pfeiffer farm by Army truck in November 1944, thirteen months after arriving in October 1943. The other three POWs transferred at the same time were Dieter Steinbach, Rolf Huber, and Hans Bauer (surnames established at transfer).
During the four-minute leave-taking before Karl boarded the truck, Lonzo Reed deliberately looked away — a complete decision, not absent-mindedness — giving Hannah and Karl an unobserved exchange.
Hannah gave Karl her bird notebook (23 entries, soft-covered, water-stained) at the transfer; he received it with both hands and carried it onto the truck.

Karl gave Hannah a note he had prepared in advance and kept in his breast pocket alongside his own private bird taxonomy list (two folded papers in the same pocket, the list briefly visible as he drew out the note).

Karl's note text (EXACT — must be quoted correctly in ch28): 'Werner Grau. From Ansbach. He is dead. I am sorry.' Below this: five bird names in two columns (German and Latin), cedar waxwing at the top — Seidenschwanz/Bombycilla cedrorum; Rotkehlchen/Turdus migratorius; Blaumeise/Poecile atricapillus; Habicht/Accipiter gentilis; Sperber/Falco sparverius.
Albrecht Pfeiffer was on the porch watching the truck's departure during part of the four-minute leave-taking. Hannah had not seen him come out.

That evening, Hannah read the note at the kitchen table. She then went to Albrecht in the sitting room (where he was working his accounts by lamplight) and said, in German: 'Werner Grau ist tot.' She said it in German not by choice but because German was the language the sentence required.

Albrecht was still for approximately ten seconds after Hannah said 'Werner Grau ist tot.' Then he looked up and said 'Ich weiß' — simply, level voice, two words only. He then looked back at his ledger. No further exchange followed. Hannah nodded and returned to the kitchen.
'Ich weiß' is the absolute limit of what Albrecht says about Werner Grau. What happened between him and Werner on the night of October 11–12, 1943 is not spoken and is not resolved.

After the Albrecht exchange, Hannah washed the dishes. Through the kitchen window above the sink she could see the icehouse — dark for the first time in thirteen months, the lamp not lit, no one in the bunkhouse.
Karl Reinmar has a small scar at the outer edge of his right eyebrow. Hannah first noticed it in February 1944 and had accounted for it by March.

Hannah's note from Karl is on the back of an envelope; the address on the front is struck through with one pen line. She folded it on its original lines and kept it in her apron pocket. This note will be shown to Marcus in ch28.

## Chapter 24 — Transfer: Draft Summary

**~2,900 words** | Hannah Pfeiffer POV | November 1944

**What the chapter does:**

The Army truck arrives at 9 AM. Hannah has been in the farmyard since 8:15, having done the milking before five — her hands occupied because they needed occupying. The four Germans come out of the icehouse with kit bags; the MP reads names; the process takes less time than Hannah expected.

Lonzo looks deliberately away — a complete decision, rendered as such — and Hannah has four minutes. She gives Karl the bird notebook (held with both hands by him); he gives her a note from his breast pocket, his private bird taxonomy briefly visible behind it. She pockets the note unread. They look at each other through thirteen months of specific accumulated moments. He says her name (*Hah-nah*). The tailgate goes up. As the truck turns, Hannah sees her father on the porch — he has been watching.

That evening she reads the note: *Werner Grau. From Ansbach. He is dead. I am sorry.* Below it: five bird names in German and Latin, cedar waxwing at the top. She understands the apology (for the landing of the knowledge, not the death). She folds the note and finds Albrecht in the sitting room.

*Werner Grau ist tot.* — said in German, the language arriving before the choice of it. Ten seconds of stillness. He looks up. *Ich weiß.* Simply. Level. The cadence of something carried for a long time. He looks back at the ledger. She nods, returns to the kitchen, washes dishes. Through the window: the icehouse dark for the first time in thirteen months.

# The Proceeding

She spread the harbor logs across the desk in order: 1935 at the left, then 1936 through the current year running right in a line, the current year's volume at the far end. Eight volumes plus the one she was still adding to. She had brought them down from the shelf above the stovepipe in two loads, the stack heavier than she usually moved them because she did not usually move more than one or two at a time. The stove was unlit; cold kept her sharp, and she had a long evening's work ahead.

The formal notice had come on Monday by the county carrier, addressed to *Acting Harbormaster, Coldwater Reach Harbor* and forwarded from the district port authority office. The language was the careful language of procedure: *notice of formal proceeding to review appointment status*, not *challenge to tenure*; *right to present the record of service before the board*, not *obligation to appear*. At the close, in the sentence that mattered most: *at the board's discretion to determine the appropriate status of the position going forward.* She had read it three times on Monday and once more on Tuesday. She had the letter in her coat pocket now, folded on its original fold, the county seal at the top left in blue ink and the county clerk's signature below it and the date: November twenty-second. Two weeks.

She knew what the proceeding was about. The record was about safe harbor management and vessel registration and fuel allocation; the proceeding was about a post, and who was understood to occupy it, and whether the occupation would be made formal. Someone at the county level had decided the occupation should change. The procedural vehicle available to them was the appointment status — she had been acting harbormaster, technically, since 1935, because the formal confirmation hearing that should have followed within eighteen months of her taking the post had never been scheduled. She had not pursued the scheduling. The harbor had not cared about her status; the work had required doing. The county board had not cared, evidently, until someone gave them a reason to care.

None of this would be said at the proceeding. The proceeding would concern itself with the record.

She opened the 1935 volume.

---

Owen's handwriting ran to November seventh.

The November sixth entry was the last full one — weather at the head in the abbreviated form, fleet positions in order, any maintenance items requiring follow-up at the bottom. He had written: partly cloudy, wind northwest twelve and building through the afternoon, barometer falling slowly. The fleet was in except for the *Selma Hatch* at the outer mooring, which he had noted was exposed with the weather developing and which he had recommended be brought to the inner before nightfall. There was a note about the bait pier fuel line, which had been difficult all October: *Will call Trowbridge in the morning. Can't have another week of this.* Three inches of handwriting. She knew its particulars — the *d* formed with the loop left open, the figure sevens cut flat, the word *barometer* abbreviated to *bar* and the word *northwest* to *NW* with the capital letter slightly larger than convention — in the way she knew any handwriting she had read beside its author for twenty-three years.

The November seventh entry was a half-line: *Storm developing. Fleet in order. Outer mooring advised clear.* Below it the date; below that, nothing.

The eighth had nothing.

Her first entry was November ninth, 1935.

She read it now for the documentation. The handwriting was not his: her loop closed, her sevens rounded, her abbreviations formed differently, her hand on the word *northwest* a shade lighter than his. The same column headings. The same abbreviated form. She had written the weather at the head — northwest fifteen moderating, sea state three at the outer head — and then the fleet positions, and then the bait pier fuel line: *Trowbridge sent a man Friday. Fitting replaced, line in operation.* Three paragraphs of ordinary harbor work, written on the first morning she had held the post. She did not remember writing them. The content was correct and the handwriting was hers.

She would bring this volume to the proceeding.

The point was not the handwriting. The point was the date. November seventh in his hand, then the gap of the eighth, then November ninth in hers — the same form, the same columns, the same attention given to the same harbor. The work had not stopped. The log showed it without requiring anyone to say so. She was not asking the board to read anything into the gap between his last entry and her first. She was asking them to see that the entries resumed, and in what condition the harbor was in when they did, and what the record showed for the eight years that followed.

She set the 1935 volume to the side and moved to 1936.

---

She went through the volumes in order.

Mooring registry first, in the systematic form she had introduced in 1937: vessel by vessel, seasonal assignment, transfer record. Forty-two registered vessels in 1936; sixty-one at present, with the additional traffic from the Navy work and the sardine carriers' increased runs to Eastport. The *Selma Hatch* condemned and laid up in 1941, her mooring freed and reassigned to the *Doris Pratt* the following spring; two new lobster boats registered in 1943 when their owners came back from the Rockland Navy contracts; the *Maud Eleanor*, which had been Owen's benchmark vessel for weather judgment, now running sardines twice a week in season, her registration current and her mooring assignment unchanged. Every transfer in the record, every assignment accounted for, every reassignment documented. The registry and the revenue ledger matched in every quarter because she checked them against each other quarterly and had done so since 1937. This was not required. She had done it because the record was either correct or it was not.

Harbor income: the comparison figures against Owen's last two full years came out eleven percent above. She had run the calculation in 1940 as part of the annual accounting and had noted the result in the supplemental ledger. She had not done it for the proceeding. She clipped the supplemental to the registry stack and set them on the left side of the desk.

The fuel ledgers she went through page by page: five columns each, every barrel from 1936 through the current volume. The supplemental allocation from the county and the USCG restrictions were in the margin for 1942 and 1943, when the allocations had dropped twice in four months — the summer of the U-boat scares, the Coast Guard running patrols out of every small harbor from Kittery to Bar Harbor and drawing fuel the way they drew fuel, the fleet modifying their running patterns to stay inside the coastal headlands, the allocation office in Portland sending revised figures on a two-week cycle. She had managed the harbor's fuel through both drops without interrupting the week's ordinary work. One error in the fuel ledgers across eight years: a posting error in October 1942, the sardine carrier's allocation entered in the wrong column in a month when she had been doing the accounting alone. Found in the same month's reconciliation. Corrected before the quarter closed. She had the correction note and the letter from the fuel authority acknowledging the correction. One error in eight years, found and corrected within the reporting period.

She had been doing the accounting alone because the assistant had been drafted in January 1942, and the county had not authorized a replacement. She had not put this in the annual reports as a complaint. She had put the assistant's line marked *vacant* and continued to do the work.

Safety inspection files: twenty-seven inspections since 1942 under the new USCG standards. One failure. The *Cecelia R.* in October of that year — port running light out, cracked exhaust elbow on the main — brought into compliance within eleven days of the written notice. She had reinspected on the twelfth day and issued the certification. The notice, the repair documentation the owner submitted, the reinspection form, and the certification were all in the file in the order the file required.

No casualty attributable to her decisions in eight years.

She put this in the summary document as the absence of an entry — the casualty log for that column was empty, and she would bring the casualty log. She had run the harbor through the worst season of 1942 with half her normal resources and no assistant and the Coast Guard treating the waterfront as their own facility whenever they wanted it, and the fleet had come in whole every November. She did not expect the board to weigh this heavily. It was in the record regardless.

---

The summary document was twelve pages of foolscap, running through the registry, the revenue comparison, the fuel record, the safety inspection record, and the casualty log. She needed three more pages to complete it: the comparative figures from Rockport and Searsport, which the county assessor had and which she had requested on Tuesday, and a final summary page. She would have the comparison numbers by Friday and the document complete before the weekend.

What the document could do was establish the record. What it could not do was address the question the proceeding was actually asking — whether the county board was prepared to confirm the post to the person who held it or to reassign it to someone they had in mind. The record was her answer to the procedural challenge. Whether the procedural answer was sufficient to meet the political one was not a calculation she had the capacity for tonight.

She reached for the county-header forms from the middle drawer.

---

She opened the middle drawer.

The Portland letter was on top.

She had placed it there in September: the Harbor Authority's reply to her registration inquiry on the stove-in dinghy, four sentences and a name. Below it the CG form, the blank space for identifying information on the body received at Coldwater Reach on October 13, 1943, still empty as it had been since she drew the form from the cabinet in October of last year.

She took both papers out.

*W. Grau, 114 Franklin Street, Portland, Maine.* The letter gave the rental record from the Commercial Street chandlery: dinghy last rented September twenty-eighth, 1943, renter's name and address as noted. She had read this in September, twice, and had not sent it to the Coast Guard because she could not use it. A rental record placed a named individual in possession of a specific dinghy on the twenty-eighth of September. By the middle of October that dinghy had been in the south cove long enough to show ten months of growth at the waterline. There was the body. There was the rental record. There was the name. She could draw the inference; she could not certify it, and the CG form's blank required what could be certified. The blank was therefore still blank.

She set the two papers on the desk corner, away from the harbor log stacks.

Not related to the proceeding. The proceeding was about the appointment status; the letter and the form were about the body on the breakwater, which was a different authority and a different column. She noted — in the reflex manner of a ledger-keeper who sees two lines from unrelated accounts showing the same discrepancy — that both were the same kind of problem. A thing waiting for its proper entry. A thing she could not close because she did not yet have what the closing required. The CG form was blank because she had not been willing to write an entry she could not verify. The proceeding existed because someone at the county level had determined that a tenure of eight years required formal confirmation before it could be made formal. Neither of these had arisen from any failure she had committed. Both were entries she was required to answer for without having done anything wrong.

She put the Portland letter and the CG form back in the drawer. The county-header forms were behind them. She took two and closed the drawer.

---

She copied the county reference number from the formal notice onto the first header sheet and set it beside the summary document. She would transcribe the summary onto the headed sheets when the draft was finished. The draft was not finished.

The oil lamp had burned low while she worked — the reservoir nearly to nothing, the flame going to nothing with it. She set the pen in the groove of the inkstand and went to the cabinet by the door for the oil tin. She had a little less than half a tin. She lifted the glass chimney carefully, filled the reservoir to the proper level, replaced the chimney, and adjusted the wick until the flame came back to its correct height: even, steady, clear.

She stood at the window before returning to the desk.

The harbor in November. The water between the pier lights was black; the inner mooring field held the laid-up shapes of most of the season's fleet, the hulls low and still in the flat water. The south headland was a dark line against a sky slightly less dark. She could hear the bell buoy at the channel entrance — faint from here, at the shed's distance from the outer pier, the slow quiet sound of the ordinary tide. No weather behind it. The outer anchorage was empty. Everything in its place.

She had been coming to this shed for nine years and had known this harbor for longer than that, and she knew what it required of whoever ran it, and she had given it that, and the record of it was on her desk.

In two weeks she would stand before the county board and present the record.

She went back to the desk. She spread the summary document in front of her and picked up her pen.

She was not done.

# Henry Crow

The boiler came on at five forty-five — not because Henry had left it that late, but because he had set the stoker timer the night before and then arrived at five-thirty to run his own check before it fired. There was a sequence to managing a firebox this size in November, and the sequence began before the fire did. He went through the pressure gauges on the main line and the secondary, tapped the return valve, opened the bypass briefly to clear the overnight sediment, and closed it again before the stoker kicked. He had been doing this for sixteen years. The building's warming from a cold night to a workable morning was entirely a function of what happened in the hour before anyone else came into it, and he would not have known by anyone's behavior whether he had done it correctly or not.

He had done it correctly for sixteen years.

The school ran the heat through radiators in the twenty-six rooms and the gymnasium and the three-floor central corridor. Each radiator had its own cycle — the ones on the north side ran slow in November and would need the secondary bleed valves opened by early December; the ones on the south side ran hot and were the first to develop the ticking in cold weather that someone reported to the principal's office at the first staff meeting of every autumn as though the tick were new. It was never new. Every October somebody sent a note down. Every October Henry adjusted the expansion valve and the ticking stopped. He had been adjusting the expansion valve for sixteen years. The boiler itself had been in the building since 1914. He had the system in his head the way he had the bus route in his head: not as a sequence he thought through, but as what was next.

His title was Chief Custodian. The children in Coldwater Reach spent their school days in warmth or in cold depending on what he did in the hour before they arrived. These facts did not appear in each other. They were not complaints. They were simply what was true.

The town had ways of knowing who did what and ways of accounting for it, and the two were not the same. Henry had understood this since 1928, which was his first year at the school, and since well before 1928, which was the rest of his life.

---

Marcus Klein had come to the Crow house in March of 1942.

Henry had known before Marcus arrived that the school board had hired a Continental educator for the German class, and that the Continental educator required lodging, and that Lillian had agreed to take him in. He had also known — because he had been in the building every day for fourteen years and had developed certain reliable capacities for reading what a man needed when he arrived somewhere new — that the Continental educator would want to know what kind of place Coldwater was, and that the understanding he developed would take the shape of whoever was first kind to him.

What Henry had watched for two and a half years was a man performing the temporary resident with very great expertise. The expertise was recognizable because Henry had seen variations of it before, though in different registers. The temporary resident kept his things organized. He held his opinions in reserve. He did not say *when I was in Vienna* except occasionally, and when he did say it he said it as evidence, not longing. He walked everywhere and said good morning to everyone on the street. He graded papers after supper and in his free hours translated things from one language into another, apparently for the exercise, filling small notebooks that he stacked on his windowsill beside whatever stone or piece of metal had caught his interest that season.

What Henry had also observed — and had not said, because it had not been asked — was that somewhere in the past year the performance had begun to wear through. Not through exhaustion. Through practice. A man who had practiced being a temporary resident for long enough had, without deciding to, become simply a man who was here.

Marcus came downstairs every morning before Lillian had the coffee finished. He sat at the table in the chair that had become his chair. He said something precise and not performed about the overnight weather, the state of the furnace in the basement (which ran low on Tuesdays), the condition of the world as reported by the radio. He had been doing this for two and a half years. A man who was planning to leave did not develop this particular quality of ordinariness. It was the quality of a man who had stopped expecting himself to need the exit.

Henry had not said any of this to Marcus. Marcus had not asked. This was a form of trust, and both of them understood it in the way they understood most things between them: without requiring it to be said.

---

The letter from James had come last Tuesday.

Henry had brought it in from the box before Lillian was up, had set it on the shelf below James's photograph, and had stood with his coat still on looking at the handwriting. James's handwriting had not changed — the same even slant, the same narrow letters, the capital J that curved a little further than it strictly needed to. The letter was shorter than the ones that had come before.

James's letters in '43 had run to two and three pages. A young man writing when he had things he was allowed to say and things he was not and was still finding the shape that held both. This one was a page and a half. Tight in the way of a letter from a man who had decided, with care, what to leave out.

*The work is hard.* That was the sentence, halfway down the first page, in the middle of a paragraph about the weather and the food and a chaplain named Delmas who had been good company on the transport ship. In James's earlier letters the equivalent sentence had been *this is a strange place* or *I am keeping busy* — the general-purpose sentences a man writes when the specific ones are not available. *The work is hard* was different. It was the precision of a man who had stopped pretending the imprecision was sufficient.

Henry had not said this to Lillian, because Lillian had read the letter and had not said anything about *the work is hard* either. They had both read it the same way. There was no use saying so.

That evening Marcus had been at the table and Henry and Lillian had talked with him about the school board meeting and a minor repair to the front steps. The letter was on the shelf, under James's photograph, in the place where the letters were kept. The photograph showed James in uniform — the studio background, the cap on straight, the same face Henry had been watching for twenty years and would know at any distance.

---

He had been thinking, lately, about October a year past.

On the twelfth — he knew it was the twelfth because it was the day after the body came in, and the body had been the talk of the building for the rest of that week and the next, and the sequence had fixed itself — he had taken the five forty-five bus as he always did, because the boilers wanted feeding before the building filled. The bus went north on the main road toward the school. He had been in it three minutes when he saw the man on the harbor road.

The man was on foot, going the other direction, toward the pier. The bus came around the curve past the Baptist church and Henry had had a clear view of ten seconds, maybe less: the man's back, then his side as the curve came around. Heavyset, not young. Square in the shoulders, a laborer's build. Wool coat with the lapels turned up, which was reasonable at five-forty in the morning in October. He was not from Coldwater. Henry had been watching the people who moved through this town for long enough to know a Coldwater walk from a coming-from-somewhere walk, and this was the second kind — deliberate, not hurried, a man who had somewhere to be and was going there without announcing it.

Henry had noted him and looked away, because the bus went on.

He had thought about it once, in the first week, when the talk in the school hallways had settled on the body and what could be known about it. He had thought: a man I didn't recognize, on foot on the harbor road, before six in the morning, going toward the pier. He had not thought it useful information, because the man had been alive at five forty-five, and the body had come in that afternoon after a three-day blow pushed the outer anchorage in. A man walking toward the harbor at five forty-five was not the same as a man found on the breakwater later. He had not gone to the Coast Guard with it, because what he had was a ten-second view from a bus window, and that was not what the Coast Guard called evidence.

He had let it sit.

And then Marcus had asked him, in the kitchen, sometime in the winter, whether he had ever heard of a man named Werner Grau. Marcus had asked it in the careful way he asked things he wasn't sure he had the right to ask. Henry had said no, because the name meant nothing to him, and this was true.

The name had stayed with him, the way names did when they arrived from a man who was usually careful about what he said and was being careful about that too.

He had put the name alongside the figure on the harbor road — the build, the coat, the direction of the walk — and he had put both of them alongside the talk of the body, which had been described in the schoolroom hallway by a seventh-grader who had gotten it from his father: a man nobody recognized, heavyset, no papers on him, probably off a vessel. Henry had not said anything in the hallway. He had listened and continued to what was next.

The three things — the figure, the body, the name Marcus had asked about — had a specific gravity when placed together. They fit in the way that things fit when they are the same thing seen from three angles.

He had not told Marcus. He had said no when Marcus asked, because the name Werner Grau had meant nothing to him then, and this remained true. What Henry had was not a name. What Henry had was a heavyset man in a turned-up coat, walking toward the harbor in the dark before the storm, who fit the description of someone Marcus was asking about a year later with the careful precision of a man who was not asking casually.

Whether that was useful to say was the same calculation he had been making for twenty years about a great many things: whether saying it changed anything, and for whom.

He had not yet decided.

---

He banked the stoker for the mid-morning cycle and checked the pressure gauge one more time. The secondary line held at its value. The north-side radiators would want their bleed valves by the first week of December, as they always did. He turned off the work lamp, took his coat from the hook, and went out into the corridor.

Upstairs the building was filling: chair legs, a door, the percussion of books dropped on the wooden stairs. The school was warm. Nobody had said anything about the warmth since October first. He did not expect them to.

James's letter was in his coat pocket. He put his hand to the pocket without taking the letter out — just to feel the paper's weight against his palm, the page and a half of James's careful leaving-out. Marcus would be at the table tonight. Lillian would have the supper on.

He had his piece of it. He held it the way he held the things he had been holding since 1928 — accurately, privately, without yet knowing whether the holding served more than the saying would.

He went up the stairs toward the light.
