# Continental Educator

The morning walk from the Crow house to the school was fifteen minutes, a calculation Marcus had verified repeatedly over nineteen months and continued to verify, partly out of habit and partly because he was a man who understood the difference between a fact that had been established and a fact that merely appeared to have been established. The one variable he had not succeeded in eliminating was the intersection at the bottom of Elm Street, where the road made its north turn and the harbor appeared briefly between two buildings — a flat gray angle of water, the breakwater's outer arm, no vessels at the south dock this morning. Some mornings he stopped. Today he did not.

Main Street at half past seven: the hardware store's windows still dark, the bakery lit, a truck outside the post office with its engine running and the driver standing beside it, watching his exhaust cloud with the peaceable attention of a man whose morning was going according to plan. Marcus nodded. The driver nodded. This exchange, which had occurred in some variation for nineteen months, had arrived at a precision of mutual acknowledgment that Marcus found, if not warm, then accurate — and in his experience accuracy was a form of warmth, or at least its structural equivalent.

The school sat back from the road behind a low iron fence and four large elms that had not yet been touched by whatever was moving through the New England elms. Three stories, dark brick, the year 1912 cut into the cornerstone — he had read it once and it had stayed, the way dates stayed, without being asked to. He went up the main steps and through the door into the smell of chalk dust and boiler heat: Henry had the building to the right temperature, as he always had it to the right temperature. Marcus hung his coat on the hook inside the teachers' entry and went upstairs.

---

His first class was Latin. This year the Latin class was three students — Cornelia Foss and two boys named Pratt and Heywood, none of whom had elected the course voluntarily but all of whom had been placed in it by the vice-principal on a theory Marcus considered neither obviously correct nor obviously wrong. He had them, and they had him, and in nineteen months of this arrangement both parties had arrived at a working understanding of what was expected.

The classroom was on the third floor, north-facing, with windows that admitted the particular flat gray light of coastal Maine in late October: not winter, not autumn, not quite either, a light without strong claims on the hour or the mood. Three desks arranged in the front half of the room, which was the correct number of desks for three students and which had the effect of making the back half of the room into a kind of reserve space — not empty, exactly, but waiting. Marcus had learned not to think about the back half of the room.

He wrote a sentence on the board. It was from Cicero's *De Amicitia*, the kind of sentence Cicero wrote when he was working at full capacity: the main clause withheld while the subordinate architecture assembled itself, so that by the time the verb arrived you had been holding the opening phrase in your mind long enough to know what weight the closing would need to carry. He underlined the subordinate clause, set the chalk in the tray, and turned.

"Don't translate it," he said.

He had been saying this in four languages, across more years and more classrooms than he intended to calculate, and what he meant by it was always the same: sit with the sentence before you reach for the English. Learn the architecture before the furniture. A translation that arrives too quickly has not understood what it has translated.

The three of them sat with it. He could read, from the quality of each student's stillness, which one was reading and which two were waiting for rescue. Cornelia Foss's stillness had a forward quality — she was inside the sentence, working. The two boys produced the carefully arranged blankness of students who have learned to display attention without generating it. The ratio — one out of three with the forward stillness — was, in Marcus's experience, approximately a constant, across Latin and German and French and any other language that required this particular quality of sitting. He found it neither discouraging nor encouraging. It was a distribution.

After a moment: "Miss Foss."

She looked up.

"Tell me what the sentence is doing."

She paused. She was the kind of mind that checked an answer before it committed to it, which Marcus had identified early and respected, it being his own habit. "It's waiting," she said. "The whole thing — it holds open until the end. You can't close it until you have all of it."

"Yes."

He did not add to this. In his experience, the correctly made observation was its own sufficient reward; adding praise introduced an economy of approval that distorted the thing being observed. He let it be. She looked back at the board, and after a moment the two boys looked back at the board, and the lesson continued.

---

The period between his Latin class and the first German section was thirty-five minutes, which Marcus divided between the staffroom on the second floor and the set of translation exercises he had marked the previous night and had comments remaining for. The staffroom coffee was, in his considered opinion, the worst he had encountered in any English-speaking institution in two continents, and he had encountered it in a number of such institutions over the past several years. He drank it.

Stillman came in. He taught geography in rooms 201 and 202, moved through the building with the slightly compressed energy of someone who had recently been somewhere else and not quite fully arrived here. He poured coffee and stood at the counter.

"Odd business down at the harbor," he said. He said most things from across a room, as though physical distance were a conversational courtesy.

Marcus set down his pen.

"What kind of business?"

"Man washed in on the breakwater after the blow last week. No papers. Nothing on him at all. CG took the body and that's the last officially."

"Town clothes, they said? Not a fisherman?"

"That's what I heard." Stillman shrugged with one shoulder. "Nobody from here. Nobody from anywhere anyone knows about. Clement Ames was down at the fish pier when the CG truck came in."

Marcus turned this over in the way he handled incomplete information: not with narrative appetite, not with the urgency that transforms the unverified into the presumed, but with the steady attention of a man who had learned over many years that the significant quality of incomplete information was its incompleteness, and that the correct response was to note it and wait. A man with no papers, washed in from a three-day storm. The verified facts were few. The range of explanations was large and at present unnarrowed. He put it in the part of his mind that held things requiring more data before they could become anything — a part that had, over the past five years, accumulated considerably.

"Has anyone put out a description?" he said.

"Not that I know of." Stillman finished his coffee. "Sailor off a convoy is what most people are saying."

Marcus nodded and returned to the translation exercises.

---

He passed the principal's open door at twenty past nine. The door stood open, as it nearly always did — the principal being the kind of administrator who managed through visibility, the open door a performance of nothing to hide. On the desk, partially in view from the hallway, was a folder with Marcus's name on the tab, and in the line below the name, in the school secretary's round and deliberate hand, the notation the town meeting had appended to his original hire: *Continental educator.*

He had seen this folder before. He had sat across from it in March of 1942, when the principal had gone through the courses Marcus would be assuming, and again the following spring, when the question of the advanced German section had required a committee meeting at which the folder had been present as a kind of documentation — a note explaining to any future questioner why the school had hired a Viennese Jewish émigré in a town of eight hundred people two years into a war. *Continental educator* accounted for him without requiring anyone to decide what they thought about it. He had found, broadly, that this was how things were explained in Coldwater Reach, and that the explanation was neither hostile nor warm, but administrative — which was also, in its way, a form of accuracy.

He kept walking.

---

The afternoon walk covered the same ground reversed. Main Street had the different character of four-thirty: a line of women outside the butcher's door with their ration books, a delivery bicycle leaned against the diner's steps, three junior-school boys occupying the hardware store's stoop until the store owner appeared in the doorway and they relocated to the next block.

The Western Union boy's bicycle was leaned against the post office wall.

Marcus noted it. He kept walking.

He had been in Coldwater ten months before he watched, from approximately this distance, a woman receive a telegram at the post office door. It had been January — clear and cold, the kind of January light that made everything look precise and final — and he had been far enough away that he saw only the shape of it: the boy, the envelope, the woman's hands, and the quality of stillness that followed the exchange. He had known what was in the envelope before it was opened. The shape was unmistakable, once you had seen it in one country, in one administrative language or another. He had kept walking that day also.

This afternoon the bicycle stood unattended. Nobody came in or out of the post office while he passed. He noted this too — the empty doorway, the bicycle, the ordinary afternoon continuing on either side of them.

He walked down Elm Street. At the corner he did not stop, and the harbor appeared briefly and was flat and gray, the south dock still empty, and he turned north.

He thought of Sherbrooke for perhaps ten seconds. Not of the camp, not of the months — the dormitory, the other men from fifteen countries assembled by their common classification as the same kind of enemy, none of them having been in a position to do much about being Austrian in 1940 — but of the specific moment of arrival: the gate intake desk, the clerk's hand lifting the document from Marcus's coat pocket and placing it on the far side of the desk, and Marcus's own hands afterward, standing in the cold with no paper in them, not knowing quite what to do with themselves. He thought of this for ten seconds. Then he was at the Crow house, and he put his hand on the gate latch and lifted it and went in.

---

The kitchen was warm. Lillian was at the stove, the iron pan over the low burner, bread already cut on the board, the tea things arranged on the counter because there was not enough counter for the tea things and anything else. She heard him come in and did not turn.

"Cold getting into it," she said.

"Yes."

She set a plate on the table without asking what he wanted. She had not asked what he wanted in approximately eighteen months, because at some point in the first season of his residence his preferences had been established and were since treated as given facts, the way Lillian treated most things she had once established to her satisfaction. This was, Marcus had come to understand, the practical form of welcome: not the performance of hospitality but its substance, which was the knowledge of another person's preferences laid down over time and expressed through a plate set at the correct height on the correct end of the table with the correct things on it. He hung his coat on the hook inside the door and sat down.

Below, Henry was in the boiler room. The sounds came up through the floor in the order Marcus had learned to follow across two winters: the knock of the pipe fitting, the steady sound of something turned, the occasional deep report of the boiler accepting what it had been given. The sounds of competent work, which Marcus had found were the same sounds regardless of the object they were applied to, and which were, in some way he had never fully articulated, reassuring — not because the boiler required reassurance, but because the sounds placed a capable person in the room below.

"How did school go?" Lillian said. She was not facing him.

"We read Cicero. More precisely, one student read Cicero and two students sat in the general area."

The sound she made was not quite a laugh but was in the same family. "German any better?"

"Somewhat."

She set the tea down and did not follow up the question. Marcus had learned, in this house, to understand the question asked and let go as a form of consideration rather than disinterest: she asked; she received; she moved on. The household had a register, and he had learned it the way he had learned every register in every house and institution he had occupied, and it was now, mostly, natural.

---

On the kitchen wall, hung from a nail above the window that looked toward the backyard: James Crow's Army photograph.

Formal. The kind taken before deployment: the uniform precise, the studio background a neutral gray, the set of his shoulders in the jacket partly the jacket's structure and partly the young man's own. He had a sergeant's formality in the way he held himself. Marcus looked at the photograph the way he looked at it each time he sat down at this table — with the attention that a face deserves and that absence makes available. He had never seen James Crow in motion. He knew the photograph, and the letters that arrived for Lillian with Pacific postmarks, and the particular adjustment in Henry's pace on the days when such a letter appeared.

He did not know James Crow. He had a static image and the outline of an absence and the sounds of a father working steadily in the room below, which was perhaps, at this distance, the truest version of a person available to him.

He ate his dinner.

Henry came up through the basement door partway through, crossed to the sink, turned on the tap.

"Fitting on the south loop's going to want replacing before December," he said.

"Will that be a difficult part to find?"

"Need to order it." Henry dried his hands on the side towel, looked at Marcus. "School all right?"

"Yes."

Henry nodded and went back downstairs.

---

His room was on the second floor, the window facing east over the yard. The curtain was heavy dark wool, the desk against the wall, the shelf holding more books than it had held in March of 1942, which was a kind of record. He sat on the edge of the bed with a book open across his knee and did not read it.

After a while came the sound of Henry closing the basement door — the sequence of steps from the back of the house forward — and then the house settled into its night disposition: the known sounds, the positioned quiet, nothing requiring response.

*Continental educator.* He had been carrying the phrase since mid-morning with the steady, absent quality he brought to things that had been said about him and that were not precisely wrong. In Vienna he had been Dr. Klein — a form of address, a specific weight in a room. In Paris he had been the Austrian, which was precisely if not unkindly meant. In London he had been the refugee, which was a category. In Sherbrooke he had been classified as the enemy alien, which was at least a position of known standing, even if the standing was wrongly arrived at. In Cambridge he had been the displaced scholar, which was accurate and was also, in its gentle way, a form of storage: a useful object held for later placement. In Coldwater he was the Continental educator, a phrase on a folder on a desk, which was all of these and was none of them.

He was, he thought, practicing something. The walk down Elm Street was a practice. The staffroom coffee was a practice. The kitchen downstairs and Lillian's plate set without asking and the sound of Henry's work coming up through the floor: all of this was practice. He was not certain — and he was, where he could be, precise about his certainties — whether what he was practicing was Coldwater or himself.

He closed the book and reached over and turned off the lamp.

# Advanced German

The bus from the Pfeiffer road dropped her at Main and Birch at seven fifty-two, and Hannah was inside the school building before the cold had finished with her collar. The building took her in: chalk and floor wax and, already, the cafeteria working at something that had been on the stove since six, a smell that had no precise name and did not require one. She hung her coat on the third hook from the left and checked the weather board at the office end of the hall — northwest, twenty, gusting thirty — before going down to the ground floor.

Third period was advanced German. Room 114, southwest corner, smallest classroom in the school. At the start of term, Marcus Klein had asked Mr. Crow to move the extra desks out, because there were three students and the gap between three students and twenty empty desks was not a ratio that served anyone. Roland Bates had told Hannah this story in the first week with some incredulity, as if the rearrangement reflected on someone. She had not said anything.

The class was Roland, who was there because his mother had arranged it and made this legible in every sentence he attempted, and Patrice Audette, who was the genuine article and knew it without making a show of the knowing, and Hannah. She had been doing German homework at the kitchen table since she was twelve, sitting across the room from a man who used the language as a country he could live inside. Whatever shape she had of the language, she'd learned it alongside that.

They were three days into the second stanza of the Rilke. *Herbsttag* — Marcus had put it on the board at the start of the week with the note written below the title: *We are working on syntax. The poem is the occasion.* Below that, the two stanzas. Below those, brackets, arrows, clause-structure notation, with the poem's actual subject — autumn, a man with no house, solitude moving in like a weather system — visible through the scaffolding but not addressed.

This morning he started from the first line of the stanza: *Wer jetzt kein Haus hat, baut sich keines mehr.*

"Roland. The subject of the second clause."

Roland looked at the page in front of him. He looked at his page with a consistency that implied something would eventually be on it if he waited long enough. "Wer."

"The same *wer* as the first clause?"

A pause. "Yes?"

"Tell me why."

Longer pause. Patrice was looking at the ceiling in the way she looked when she was waiting for something to become apparent to someone else.

"Because it carries across," Hannah said. "One subject, two predicates. The *wer* takes both."

Marcus drew an arc on the board connecting the two verb phrases. "Yes. The indefinite relative pronoun distributes without repeating. That's its purpose — it names a category once and the structure holds it." He turned. "The *keines*. Case."

Roland looked at his page again.

"Accusative," Hannah said. "Object of *baut*."

"And the *sich*?"

She thought about how to put it. "Dative. The building is for himself. Whatever he's not building, it's his own not-having."

She hadn't planned to say it that way, and she saw Marcus turn the chalk in his right hand — the small physical notation she'd come to read as satisfaction, not performed. He did this when an answer was actually right and not just close.

"Exactly. The dative makes the absence personal. He has no house, and not having a house is something he does to himself, or that does itself to him — the German leaves the direction unspecified, marks only that the self is involved." He wrote the sentence clean on the board, without brackets: *baut sich keines mehr.* "Read it beside your translation. Tell me what the English costs."

Roland produced a translation slowly, as if constructing it on the way. "'Whoever has no house now builds himself none more.'"

"The 'none more' is awkward. What is *mehr* doing?"

"Saying he won't build any."

"It's stronger than 'any.' It's 'further,' 'any longer' — the building has been decided against. The finality is already in it." He wrote on the board: *builds himself nothing further.* "That's still not right. The precision has no equivalent. You choose what to lose."

Patrice said: "'Nothing further' loses the sense that it was always going to be nothing. The *mehr* makes it retroactive."

Marcus looked at the board for a moment. "Yes. The *mehr* folds in the past. The English says it's over. The German says it was always going to be over." He set the chalk in the tray. "That's what makes it difficult. Note it."

She wrote: *retroactive finality. the German folds in the past.* She wrote it because it was worth having, even if it was too large for any exam she would ever sit.

She watched him move to the third line, chalk in hand. He wrote one word and stopped, waiting for Roland to catch up. The pause was unhurried, calculated to the minute — not impatience held back but patience given precisely. She had been watching him teach for two months and had decided that what he did with words was not skill exactly, or not only skill. It was the behavior of a man for whom the right word and the approximate word were separate categories, and the approximate one was not a valid choice. Roland couldn't see this. Patrice could see it and was not interested in it. Hannah had been watching it since September and had not said anything.

At the bell they were two lines from the end.

---

At lunch, the two girls at the table by the windows were still on the body. More than a month now and the story had grown its shape: a merchant sailor, someone had heard, come down from Eastport or up from Bath depending on who was telling it and which direction made the drowning feel more final. He'd been drinking somewhere up the coast and gone over a dock rail. Or he'd been running from something — a debt, a wife, a thing he couldn't put behind him — and the October storm had been waiting for a man in exactly that condition.

The telling was comfortable with itself. It had found its distances.

Hannah ate her sandwich. She had a piece of data that didn't fit the shape of any version on this table: her father's hands on his knife and fork at the dinner table, stopped for three seconds at the words *no papers*, the knife set down without deciding to, and then resumed. That data did not attach to the merchant sailor. It did not attach to any story being assembled here. It was not a thing she could put on this table, at this price, into this format. She ate and listened and the merchant sailor acquired one more detail she had no reason to believe.

---

After class Roland left immediately and Patrice was already gone. Hannah stayed because she had a question that was not a pretext for anything else — just a grammatical question she'd been carrying since Monday that her notes hadn't answered.

"The *es*," she said. She read the line: *Wer jetzt allein ist, wird es lange bleiben.* "I can't find what it's standing in for."

Marcus turned from the board where he'd been erasing the bracket notation. He looked at her page without appearing to need it.

"It's not standing in for anything earlier," he said. "It anticipates. It holds a place in the syntax for the predicative adjective — the aloneness — which the grammar already knows is there." He went to the board and wrote: *wird es lange bleiben.* Below: *wird … allein bleiben.* "In German—" He wrote the word: *Korrelat.* "The correlate. A placeholder the structure makes for something it already holds. The sentence knows its meaning before it has finished stating it."

She wrote *Korrelat* in the margin and put a bracket around the *es.*

"My translation has 'will long remain so,'" she said. "I wasn't sure the 'so' was right."

"It's better than 'it,'" he said. "The 'so' implies continuation — the condition already established, extending forward. That's accurate to what the German is doing." He considered it for a moment, the chalk still in his hand. "Your question was a real one."

She put the notebook in her bag. He had said *Korrelat* before he reached for the English for it — the way he always reached for the German word first and the English second, as if the German were the thing you could rely on and the English were the approximation you settled for. She had been noticing this since September. Her father's German was nothing like this. Her father's German was a retreat — a door he kept shut since the war started, something he moved into when his English wasn't safe anymore. Marcus moved toward German the way he moved toward precision; it was the direction of accuracy, the closer register. She did not have a word for the difference and she was not going to look for one in room 114.

---

The post office was two blocks from the school. She stopped before the bus to pick up the farm's mail.

The room smelled of paper and the sponge-water of the stamp pad. Two men at the far end were talking about a timber allotment; the counter clerk took a long time finding the Pfeiffer package. Hannah waited. At the counter: the OPA ration-book renewal notice, the Eastern States seed catalog — early, or she'd lost track of the month — and a letter from her cousin Marta in Portland, which she put at the bottom. She signed for the package, veterinary supplies, and was gathering the stack when the bell above the entry rang behind her.

Marcus Klein came in. He went to the window to her left.

"Hello, Miss Pfeiffer."

"Hello, Dr. Klein."

She was heading for the door and passed close enough to see what he held: one envelope, white, return address printed in the format of an institution. A department of something, a university name, the beginning of a city she caught the first letter of and then she was at the door and outside.

The cold was immediate. She walked toward the bus corner. Marcus Klein had a letter coming from a department in a city that was not Coldwater — from a place that still had him on some list, that knew where to send a thing to find him. She put the farm mail under her arm. A person with letters coming from elsewhere was a person who existed in more than one place at once. She stood at the corner and waited for the bus.

---

Dinner was salt pork and potatoes from the root cellar. She set the seed catalog at her father's place before she sat down and he reached for it as he sat, without comment, in the way he reached for anything that was properly his to reach for. He turned to the back half first — root vegetable prices, winter grain, the columns of numbers — before moving forward through the variety pages. He did this while he ate with the attentiveness he gave to anything with a practical season coming. Her mother was at her place with a straight back and ate enough that you couldn't say she wasn't. The radio was off, the way it had been for most of November.

They ate.

---

After the dishes she brought the German translation to the kitchen table. Her father moved to the sitting room with the farm accounts, the small desk by the window, and she could hear the sound of his pen through the wall — long strokes for the main columns, short ones for corrections.

She spread the Rilke page.

The *Korrelat* note in the margin, the bracket. She moved on to the last two lines: *und wird in den Alleen hin und her / unruhig wandern, wenn die Blätter treiben.* The *treiben* was where she kept stopping. To drive, to be driven, to drift, to blow — she'd tried four versions since Monday. She tried "when the leaves are driven," but "driven" in English wanted a driver, a thing pushing, and the German had no driver; it had just the fact of the motion. She tried "when the leaves run," which was wrong. "Drift" was closer but it lost the driven quality, the sense that the leaves were not choosing. She put a question mark beside "drift" and wrote both versions under the line.

She worked backward from the sense of it: the leaves were not deciding to move. They were moved. The German held both at once, the activity and the passivity in the same word. She had been working with the language for five years and still hit the words that wouldn't cross. Her father never hit these walls because the language was not a wall for him; it was the room he lived in. She was working on its ceiling.

She was finishing the fair copy when she heard the icehouse door.

---

She put the pencil down and went to the window to draw the curtain.

Karl was outside without a coat over the POW jacket, his arms at his sides, his head tilted back. The sky was the November clear that arrived after the first hard frost — stars close and particular, the cold making the air exact. He was standing still.

He said the word.

*Seidenschwanz.*

She said it at the glass, barely a breath. *Seidenschwanz.* October's word, coming back. The same quality to it — not a complaint, not addressed to anyone or asking anything of anyone, just the naming of something he knew. Saying it to the sky to keep the knowing current.

He stood a moment longer. Then he went inside. The lamp in the icehouse window was low; she watched it dim through the oil paper until it was gone.

She pulled the curtain and went back to the table.

Her father's pen moving in the accounts. The stove ticking as it cooled.

She opened the German translation to the Rilke page. Below the *Korrelat* note, below the bracket, below the question mark beside *treiben*, she wrote *Seidenschwanz* in the margin.

It had nothing to do with the poem. She drew a small circle around it to keep it from the rest.

She closed the notebook and left the lamp on, because her father was still at the accounts across the room.

# Winter Registry

The mooring roster ran to five pages for December. She laid them flat on the desk and went through them against the harbor log, one column against the other. The Ellsworth was accounted for — still on her winter run to Eastport, due back the sixteenth. Clara M. was accounted for, inner float, registration current. The Gale brothers' second boat, Ida B., was on the boatyard railway since the third of November and her entry had been updated accordingly. Ida B.'s mooring assignment would hold through the winter vacant, which was correct.

Seventeen hulls would winter in the inner harbor. She went through them one at a time.

Two of the seventeen were out of compliance on their documentation. One had let the registration lapse in October and had not responded to the September reminder; the other had moved berths without filing the change. Both were correctable by letter. She pulled paper from the center drawer and wrote both notices before she did anything else. Clean copies, dated, registered mail on the second one. She addressed the envelopes and put them in the to-mail pile at the corner of the desk.

Outside the shed window the harbor was in its December arrangement. Half the working fleet was hauled, cradles and sawhorses up in the boatyard above the high-water line, the boats sitting on their keels with a stripped and workmanlike look that was different from summer. The railway had been busy through November — she had heard it most mornings, the hauling gear running, and had noted the vessels as they came out of the water and been checked off the winter list. The cold-storage house was running on reduced hours now; Patterson had posted the December schedule on the shed door last Thursday. The inner float held what it held: Clara M., the Hartleys' double-ender, three lobster boats whose owners had calculated the winter lay-up costs and decided against it.

She went back to the roster. The outer anchorage was empty. Had been since the first week of November.

She was going through the last page when she heard boots on the fuel dock.

---

Wendell Foss ran his boat up alongside and tied the stern first. He came up the dock planks with the gas can and did not look in through the shed window or call out, because he was not a man who required an audience before he arrived. She came out to the dock.

He set the can down and reached for the pump handle.

"Heard they're putting someone from the county board to look at the harbormaster situation," he said.

He worked the pump. He had not looked at her when he said it and he did not look at her now.

"Who told you that," she said.

"Clement Ames. His cousin works for the county in some capacity." He watched the can fill. "Don't know the specifics. Just that it's under discussion."

"I'll note it."

He shut off the pump and lifted the can. He paid and went back down the dock at the same pace he'd come up. She watched him reach his boat and step aboard without looking back.

She went inside and wrote the fuel transaction in the ledger.

Then she set down the pen.

Eight years of harbor log kept to the same standard. Every vessel registration current within her authority. The mooring assignments documented and filed, the incident log accurate, the annual fuel throughput reconciled quarter by quarter. No casualty attributed to a failure in harbor management in her tenure, and no casualty that a different harbormaster's decision could have prevented either — she had run that accounting once, after the Hartley boy's accident on the outer mooring, and the conclusion was the same from every direction. The harbor income was up eleven percent over Owen's last two years. That was not a dramatic figure. It was the correct direction.

None of these numbers was what the challenge would be about.

She understood this. She went back to the roster.

---

The annual report for the county authority was a form she had filed every December since 1936. The columns did not change year to year: vessel count, fuel throughput, mooring revenue, incident log, capital expenditures, maintenance deferred and completed. She filled them in the same order she always did. The numbers went where they belonged.

But when she reached the incident log section she found herself going back over it before committing the ink. She had not done this in previous years. There had been nothing in previous years that required a second reading. She did it now.

The October 12 entry was there. She had written it exactly as it stood in the harbor log: body discovered on breakwater, 0615, CG notified 0622, arrived 0711, removed 0723. Case closed by Coast Guard, October 1943. Official determination: unidentified drowning. She had copied this to the annual report with the same words.

It was accurate. The case was closed. There was nothing in the incident log that was not in the harbor log, and nothing in the harbor log that was not accurate.

She read it through a second time and left it as it was.

She sealed the envelope, stamped it, and put it on top of the mooring notices.

---

The post office was quiet at four o'clock. Mabel Trumbull was in the back and didn't look up. Two items in the box: a registered envelope with county authority letterhead and a notice from the state harbor authority.

The registered envelope was the county authority's acknowledgment of last year's annual report. Three sentences of boilerplate. She read it, noted the date, folded it back.

The state notice concerned updated winter storm protocol requirements. New guidance on vessel notification windows and mooring inspection standards following a storm event above a specified threshold. She read it at the counter. The requirements were reasonable and not onerous. She would implement them before February.

She put both items in her coat pocket.

The Western Union boy's bicycle was not against the post office wall. She had not been looking for it; she did not have anyone she was waiting to hear from in that particular way. She noted its absence the way she noted the Ellsworth not at the fuel dock on non-delivery days. Available information, and also a form of relief. Both things at once, without contradiction.

She went out into the cold.

---

The light was almost gone when she got back to the shed. She logged the state notice — received, date, action required by February 1st — and put it in the regulatory file. She put the county acknowledgment in the correspondence folder and checked the to-mail pile one more time.

Then she put on her heavier coat and her cap and went out for the breakwater.

---

She walked the breakwater in November and December every year. In Owen's time it had been his walk; she had gone with him the first winters of their marriage, learning the habit before she learned what it was for. Now she did it the way she did the other maintenance work: from the shore end out, systematically, with the paper and pencil in her coat pocket for notes.

The granite was in its December state — damp on the upper face from the last tide, the cap stones dark. She walked the crown and checked the placement as she went, stopping where she needed to stop. Third cap stone from the shore end had a gap on the south face, probably from the October storm. The stone was seated; it wasn't going anywhere. She put it in the notes: spring assessment, south face, stone three. Tight gap, not urgent.

The chop off the outer face was four feet from the southeast, well short of the crown. The tide was running at mid-flood. She walked further, noting two more small settlements in the rubble face — both minor, both below the mean high-water line where the ice action would work on them through February and March. These went in the notes as well.

The boatyard was visible across the inner harbor, the railway track running up from the waterline, one hull still on the cradle. She thought it was Merton Galey's Penelope D. but the light was too flat now to be certain.

She walked to the elbow.

---

The elbow was where the breakwater turned. She came around it and stopped to check the inner face granite course. A fractional movement in one of the lower courses, probably the October storm as well — the capstone wasn't proud but the rubble below it had settled a small amount. She wrote it down. Spring assessment, elbow, inner face, course four. Not critical.

She straightened up.

The inner harbor was ahead of her — float lights on, the cold-storage office lamp still burning across the water. The south dock was visible from this angle, the pilings and the dock planking at the line of the harbor's south edge. Just visible. She looked at it the way she always looked at it from the elbow, without having decided to.

The night of October eleventh going into the twelfth. Past midnight. She had been at the shed's south window watching the barometer; the glass had been falling steadily since nine o'clock and she had wanted to see what it did at midnight. That was why she had been there.

Two men on the south dock.

The first: past middle age, solid in the shoulders, dark coat. Not a fisherman. She was certain of that from where she stood — certain from the coat and the way he stood on the dock planking, too deliberate, placed rather than easy, the way a man stands on a dock when he is not used to docks. He was looking toward the outer harbor. She could not see his face; the dock lamp was behind him. He turned and said something to the other man.

The second figure: wider across the back and through the shoulders. Standing further from the dock edge. His weight planted in a way she recognized — not a sailor's balance, a farmer's stillness, the kind that comes from years of standing in mud and cold and not moving much while you wait for something to finish. She had not seen his face.

The first man had walked to the shore end of the dock and gone up the ramp. The boatyard shadow had taken him. The second man had stayed another minute or two and then gone up the ramp the same way.

That was what she had. An image and a time: approximately half past midnight, October 12. The south dock, which the Gale brothers had vacated in September, not in regular use. Two men on it, neither one a sailor, in the hours before the storm peaked. And at the other end of three days of blow, a man with no papers in town clothes face-down at the elbow of the breakwater.

What she did not have: a vessel. A name. A corroboration. Anything that would make an entry in the harbor log rather than a statement that she had watched two men standing on a dock. The harbor log required specificity sufficient to establish the fact. What she had was not sufficient to establish the fact. It was sufficient to establish that she had seen something, which was a different entry.

She turned and walked back along the breakwater toward the shore.

---

The tide had come up while she walked. She stopped at the south ladder — the iron rungs set into the breakwater's shore face — and read the tide height off the granite marks. The water was at the first mark above mid, consistent with tonight's table. She had resurveyed the marks in October of 1940 and confirmed them against the Rockland gauge. They were accurate. They were what they said they were.

She went up the shore path to the shed.

Inside, she lit the lamp. The harbor was dark except for the float lights and the cold-storage lamp across the water. She stood at the south window for a moment. The south dock was barely visible, a line of pilings at the far edge of the float light's reach.

She had not written the dock figures. She had accepted this in October, when the image was new. She had accepted it again when Mercer came and she gave him technically-true answers that left the dock out of them. She accepted it now: two men on the dock, a time, a body at the elbow — not enough to establish the fact, only enough to establish that she had seen something.

For now, she had told herself in October.

For now.

She turned from the window. The desk had the Cote notice on it still, and the state harbor file, and the December mooring roster with the last page not yet filed. She sat down and pulled the roster toward her and finished it. One column, then the next. The harbor in December holding what it held — seventeen hulls, the empty outer anchorage, the water doing its work at the granite marks, accurate as always.

The entry was wrong and would stay wrong for now. For now was the part she did not examine.

# Chapter Thirteen — Displaced Scholars

The translation papers were in alphabetical order, as Marcus had trained himself to keep them, and the name at the top was Pfeiffer.

He had six students in the advanced German section. Two were seniors who had enrolled to satisfy a modern-language requirement and who wrote translations that were technically correct in the manner of things produced under mild compulsion. Three were juniors of varying ability; a boy named Graves had a natural ear for German syntax but lacked the patience for the long clause, which was a correctable problem Marcus had been correcting since September. The sixth was Hannah Pfeiffer, who was also a junior and whose work Marcus graded first not because she required more attention — she required less than any other student in the section — but because her translations tended to establish the ceiling for the evening's task, and the ceiling, once identified, made everything below it easier to assess.

Tonight's passage was from Schiller. Five lines from *Die Bürgschaft*, short and subordinate-heavy, with two dependent clauses that required the student to decide where the sentence's weight fell. The predictable failure with such constructions — the one he had spent half the autumn correcting in the intermediate section — was to flatten them: to take the weight of a dependent structure and distribute it evenly across the sentence, producing translations that were accurate and empty. In the advanced section Marcus was marking for something a Vienna professor he had once admired called *die Entscheidung der Unterordnung*, the decision of subordination — not whether the student could identify the clause but whether they understood what its dependence was doing to everything around it.

He read Hannah Pfeiffer's rendering:

*Though he who asks is master of the hour, the thing asked for lives in a different grammar.*

The original was more compressed; she had given herself room. The word *grammar* was her own interpolation, absent from Schiller's German, which had *Zeit*, time. As a rendering it was less accurate than Schiller's word. As a reading of the construction — of what the subordination was for, of why the clause held its position in the sentence rather than dissolving into the main verb — it was more precise than anything Marcus could have specified in the assignment.

He took up his pencil and wrote in the margin: *The grammar of the subordinate clause is not decoration — it is the shape of what is being withheld.* He considered the sentence for a moment, then left it. She would understand what the note was about, or she would ask him on Friday, and either would serve the instruction.

He moved through the remaining five papers in forty minutes. The classroom was empty; Henry had come through with the push broom at half past three and not returned. The afternoon light through the south-facing windows had thinned — March, longer now than February and not warm, the late light catching the dust on the glass at a low angle. The heating pipes ticked in the wall behind the blackboard. Forty minutes, and he set the graded stack to his left and uncapped his pen.

He had been composing the letter to Sondheimer in his head for nine days. The content required no composition — a name, a description, a question. What had taken nine days was the framing. In twenty years of letters written under circumstances where the wrong word could establish the wrong thing, Marcus had learned that the architecture of a request carried as much weight as its substance.

Dr. Heinrich Sondheimer's position at Columbia was nominally in the German department, but his actual function — as Marcus had understood since his own time on the Emergency Committee rolls, in the autumn of 1941 — was closer to that of an archivist of displacement. He had been on the intake end of the rescue network that the Committee had assembled as the war made rescue necessary: the person who matched names to placements, who held the files, who knew which scholars and artists had passed through the system and which had simply vanished somewhere in the gap between one country's border and another's paperwork. It was not an official position. It was a position constituted entirely by memory, by the particular willingness to keep track of people because someone ought to. In Marcus's experience, such positions were more reliable than official ones.

He wrote:

*Dear Dr. Sondheimer,*

*I hope you are well. I write on a matter of administrative record that falls, I believe, within the range of your particular knowledge. I am trying to establish the history of a Werner Grau — German national, painter or laborer by occupation, last known address Portland, Maine — specifically whether he appears on any Emergency Committee roll or affiliated rescue register, and whether his immigration status in the United States was ever formalized. I ask as a matter of private inquiry, not on behalf of any institution or authority. I have reason to believe Mr. Grau may have been in the Boston area around 1936, and that he has been in the United States since approximately that time.*

*Any record you hold, or any channel you might pursue on my behalf, would be of genuine assistance.*

He read the letter back once. The phrase *a matter of private inquiry* was accurate and included what it did not state. The phrase *any channel you might pursue* communicated that this was a question for informal handling — through the network of people who held such things in filing cabinets and memory rather than in any official record. The formality of the register established his distance from the question: an academic making a historical inquiry. Not a man with personal stakes in the answer.

This was approximately true.

He was addressing the envelope when the thought arrived, in the quiet way thoughts arrive when the hands are occupied with a mechanical task: what he had described was Marcus Klein in 1940.

A man without the correct documentation in a country not constructed for him. A man whose standing depended on a committee's willingness and a series of telephone calls between people who had been, at least, willing to make them. A man who could be required, at any moment, to demonstrate what he was doing here and whether anyone official had approved it.

He had been, in the autumn of that year and the winter that followed it, a Werner Grau.

He did not write this in the letter to Sondheimer. He did not write it anywhere. He pressed the envelope flap closed and set it on the right side of the desk where he kept things requiring the post. Then he sat for a moment in the quiet of the classroom — the graded papers on his left, the thin March light leaving the window glass, the heating pipes gone still — and held the thought in the way he had learned, at Sherbrooke, to hold thoughts that had nowhere to go. Not suppressed. Held in parallel, alongside everything else, and carried forward.

---

The road from the school to Henry and Lillian's house was three blocks toward the harbor and then one block west. He had walked it for two years in every condition this section of the Maine coast offered, and he had come to know it with the intimacy that daily repetition produces: not attachment, exactly, but familiarity so complete it had become spatial memory, each crack in the pavement belonging to its season. The spring thaw was at its worst this week — the road heaved, the edges soft, the ground giving back what it had been holding since December. He knew the smell of it. He had not expected, when he first walked this road, to come to know its smell by season as a fact of his own life, the way he knew the smell of the Ringstraße in December or the particular damp of the Paris sixth in autumn. He knew it. He walked through it.

He came in at the side door, as Lillian had told him to in his first week.

She was at the table with her cup and a length of white fabric, a piece of church sewing Marcus had seen in various states of progress for the past three weeks. Henry was across from her, and between them lay a V-Mail letter — the small photographed form, reduced by the postal process, that was what arrived when something arrived from the Pacific. The letter had the position of a thing already read and placed back with care: not put away, not left carelessly, but replaced as if putting it elsewhere had not yet been decided.

"James," Lillian said. She had not looked up.

He set his coat on the hook. "Good news?"

"He's well." She smoothed the edge of the envelope. "Somewhere he can't say."

Henry did not add anything. He drank his coffee.

Lillian read a portion of it aloud. The part she chose: James had received a meal that had given him a new and firmly held position on the subject of Army provisioning, which he had committed to paper — he noted it was the most cogent military document of the current conflict — and sent up the chain. Two weeks later, on a separate ship, a crate of canned peaches had arrived. He took this as the official reply. He asked whether the school boiler was behaving. He asked whether Mr. Marcus had been informed about the spring mud, and if not, whether someone could see to it before the term was too far gone.

Marcus said he had been informed.

Henry smiled briefly — reserving, as he always did, the full extent of it.

They sat. Lillian returned to her sewing. The kitchen was warm from the stove and from the radiator Henry had bled last week, which now ran without the complaint it had been making since January. The smell of the kitchen — coffee from the morning and something from supper that Marcus had missed, and beneath both of these the particular smell of the house itself, which Marcus had stopped noticing as foreign sometime around November — was familiar in the way the road was familiar. A fact. A specific fact belonging to a specific place.

Henry stood and rinsed his cup at the sink. He crossed to the small shelf above the kitchen radiator — the shelf that held the clock, the accumulated mail, and the one or two objects a household gathers over twenty years without deliberate selection — and placed James's letter under the clock. He had done this with every letter from James since the first one, in the spring of 1942. The clock held the paper flat. The letter did not go anywhere else.

He stood for a moment and looked at the photograph on the wall.

James in his uniform, taken at Camp Upton before he shipped — standing before some building Marcus did not recognize, shoulders squared, the expression of a man being photographed: present, composed, held slightly in reserve. The photograph had been on that wall for eighteen months.

Henry looked at it for perhaps half a minute. He did not say anything. Then he went through to the back of the house, where a pipe had been making a small complaint since the previous week.

Lillian said nothing. Marcus drank his coffee.

He thought: this is the shape of family at distance — the maintenance of the ordinary against what cannot be named. He had written letters like James's letters, from Paris, from London, from Sherbrooke in the months when letters were permitted, and the letters had been full of meals and small complaints and inquiries about things at home that were not the things he was thinking about. He knew what James's letter contained that was not in the portion Lillian had read. He did not say this. He sat with his cup and listened to the pipe being attended to in the back of the house, and when Lillian refilled his cup he said thank you and meant it precisely.

---

Sondheimer's reply came on a Friday, nine days after Marcus had posted the letter.

He found it in his school mailbox before the first class — addressed in Sondheimer's direct hand, the handwriting of someone for whom a letter is a professional instrument. Marcus read it standing at the mailboxes, then took it to his classroom and read it again at his desk, with the deliberate attention the contents required.

Sondheimer had made a telephone call to a contact in the Boston office. That contact had made another. The answer: Werner Grau, German national. Entered the United States at Boston in March 1936, on a one-year visa sponsored by the Boston Alliance for the Arts, which had brought over a small group of painters and printmakers under a cultural exchange program that ended when its funding was redirected in 1937. The visa had been renewed once, in March of 1937. It had expired in March of 1940. After that: no renewal application on record, no deportation proceeding initiated, no departure recorded.

He had been in the country without legal standing for nearly four years. From the spring of 1940 to October 1943, Werner Grau had been in the United States in the way that many men in those years had been in countries not their own: by the extension of circumstances originally intended as temporary, prolonged by a war that had made the simplest crossings impossible, sustained by the patience of whoever around him had chosen not to ask.

Marcus placed the letter beside the folder in the bottom drawer of his classroom desk: his transcription of the letter Werner had written to Albrecht Pfeiffer, set down before returning the original in January; the two pages of careful handwriting Marcus had made for himself in December, his private account of what he knew and the chain by which he had come to know it. Three documents. They occupied the space where a Latin dictionary usually rested. He looked at them briefly, then closed the drawer.

Werner Grau had been, by the classification the relevant governments applied, an enemy alien without formal standing. As had Marcus Klein, at Sherbrooke, in 1940: held for ten months under a warrant whose precise language Marcus had never been shown, released to the Committee rolls in a country that had not yet settled what to do with him. The form of Werner's situation was different. The underlying condition was the same: a man whose right to be where he was could not be demonstrated to any authority that chose to examine it.

If the body on the breakwater had been identified — if the file at Sprucehead bore a name rather than a blank — Werner Grau's four years without papers would have become the first fact of the official record. A German national, undocumented, found drowned on the Maine coast in October 1943. The sentences organized themselves cleanly. They were not false. They were simply not an account of anything that mattered about Werner Grau.

He sat with the drawer closed and the translation papers on his left, marked, ready for return in the morning. On top: Hannah Pfeiffer's Schiller, the word *grammar* in the third line, the note in his own hand in the margin. The March light had gone off the roofline of the building opposite. The heating pipes had been quiet for an hour.

He was not going to report Werner Grau's status to any authority that could act on it. He had not reasoned his way to this. His hands had made the decision when they placed the letter in the drawer, and in the seconds after his mind had confirmed it, and there was nothing further to deliberate on that count.

Whether this constituted his doing something, or his failing to do something, or simply the act of a man who understood that what mattered about Werner Grau was not the state of his papers — that question remained open, in the drawer, alongside everything else he was holding.

# Chapter Fifteen — What Grandy Soule Saw

The registration table went up at the pier head the last week of April the way it had gone up every spring Eira could remember: the clipboard, the fee box, the carbon forms weighted at the left with the big shackle she kept for this purpose, because the wind off the harbor had no patience for paperwork in April.

She had the table set before seven. The harbor lay in front of her with the particular quality of spring — the light longer now, working into the east faces of the pilings and under the boathouse eaves where the winter sun hadn't reached, the water still cold enough to raise a thin steam at the harbor entrance in the early morning air. The mud at the basin head had softened. Dark fronds of weed were coming off the south rocks. A pair of eiders worked the current beside the fish house float and did not look up.

The first boat in was the *Bertha L.* at half past, Pete Alley at the wheel with his boy in the stern. She had the hull in the card file and wrote it up while he tied off: tonnage, engine, mooring assignment. He'd put fresh paint on her over the winter and the hull had that new brightness to it that wouldn't last but was good while it lasted. She collected the fee and the signature and filed the carbon.

By noon she had seven: *Bertha L.*, *Perseverance*, *Sea Star*, *Laura K.*, *Edna C.*, and two others whose documentation was in order and whose owners had nothing more to say to her than the minimum. She wrote each entry in the column and checked it against the card file and wrote the total at the bottom of the page.

Seven. Last spring there had been nine.

*Crestview* was still in the cradle at the railway yard. Harold Oakes had gone into the Navy in January of 1942 and the boat had been on the railway since that June. She had sent two letters about the cradle fee; neither had been answered, which was not Oakes's fault. The mooring pen sat empty. *Walter D.* had been sold south to Tenants Harbor in February when the Withams made the decision they had been putting off since autumn — Lyle had taken sick and there was no one left to take the boat over. She had given that mooring pen to the *Laura K.* when Ed Croft's hip made the row from the inner float a problem for him.

Two fewer boats. The column said so.

*Sea Star* was Ray Coffin's — Fred Coffin's younger boy, who had come home from the Pacific in November with two fingers gone from the right hand and had been on the water again by April, which was not a surprise to anyone who knew the family. He signed the registration form left-handed. He wanted the mooring lines inspected before he started hauling and she made a note.

Burton Talbot on the *Edna C.* had a new inboard he was willing to explain at length. She let him explain it, asked for the documentation twice, received it the second time. New tonnage in the column. She signed the carbon.

The rest of the afternoon went the way it went: boat by boat, fee by fee, the spring talk running alongside the transactions the way it always did. Ice-out dates, trap losses from the winter, whether the herring were moving early or late, the price at the pound. Asa Parker's gear had fouled on the north ledge in January and he had things to say about it. She heard about the Gifford boy's medical discharge from Portsmouth Shipyard, about trouble with the mooring chain at the north buoy, about a rumor of striped bass in the outer bay. She listened and wrote and handed over receipts.

By two o'clock the registration table was packed and she was at the fuel dock going over the morning log when the *Maud L.* came in.

---

Grandy Soule brought her alongside the fuel dock without ceremony — no wasted motion, the boat coming against the fender the way something comes to rest in the hands of a man who has set it down in the same place for more years than he has counted. The *Maud L.* was a thirty-two-foot lobster boat with a dull red hull that had been brighter once; Soule had bought her in 1928 and she had been working this harbor since. He was perhaps seventy, perhaps past it. His age was a harbor fact she had stopped trying to fix, the same way you stop sounding every ledge you already know is there.

He paid for his fuel in exact change from his coat pocket, signed the carbon, and stood at the dock while the tank filled. The harbor went on around them: the sound of the pump, the water working the pilings, a dragger coming in from the outer harbor and taking its mooring. Soule had his eyes on the south end of the inner pier — the double-planked float at the fish house end, the one that had needed new decking since before the war and was not going to get it this spring either.

She was finishing the log entry for the *Laura K.*

He said nothing for a while and she did not expect him to.

Then, without turning: "Saw a strange dinghy at the south pier. That October night. Before your blow."

She looked up. She kept her face. "Which pier," she said.

"South end. That last float." He moved his chin toward it. "Late. After midnight. I was driving back from Owls Head."

"What night."

"Night the weather came on, or near enough. I've thought about it." He watched the harbor. "Numbers on the transom weren't Coldwater. I didn't know them."

"Could you read them?"

"Not properly. Too dark, and I didn't stop. Might have been Portland — I couldn't say for certain. Small boat, wooden tender, not large." A pause. "One man come off her. He walked up toward the main pier."

"Did you see him come back to the dinghy?"

"No." He held the mooring line, not working it yet. "I drove on. Figured whoever it was had put in because the weather was turning — thought nothing of it." He looked at the float. "Dinghy was gone when the blow cleared. I don't know when it went. Could have gone in the storm."

She looked at the fuel gauge. Her pen was in her hand. She had written nothing since he started speaking.

"One man," she said. "That's all you saw."

"One." He began working the mooring line loose. "I heard you were still asking about that October business. Thought maybe you'd want to know."

"I would," she said. "Thank you, Grandy."

He untied the *Maud L.* and backed her out with the same economy he'd brought her in with, turned toward the harbor mouth, and was gone past the outer breakwater. The wake spread into the basin and went flat. She stood at the dock end and watched the boat go.

---

She stood at the end of the fuel pier with the harbor in front of her.

She laid what she had against what she had been carrying, the way she would lay a vessel's log against the tide tables: columns together, the matches showing you what you could confirm, the gaps showing you what you hadn't accounted for yet.

Soule's column: a dinghy at the south pier, the night the storm came on or the night before. Not Coldwater registration — possibly Portland. One man came off her. He walked toward the main waterfront. He did not return to the dinghy before Soule left. The dinghy was gone when the blow cleared.

Her column: two figures on the south dock, same night, past midnight. One coming from the direction of the main pier — heavyset, town coat, moving from some distance. A second figure near the fish house end, further back, that she had taken at the time for a dock worker.

The columns met at the south pier. The man who came off the dinghy and the man she had seen from her window were the same man, or she had to explain why they weren't, and she could not.

The second figure was not in Soule's column. One man, he had said. She had seen two. Which meant the second figure had come on foot, not by water — had come separately, or had come after Soule drove on.

Two days later, with the storm in between, the body was at the breakwater elbow.

Not proof. But it had a shape.

She picked up her clipboard and walked back to the shed.

---

The harbor log was on its stand. The tide tables were pinned to the board behind the door. She hung her coat and sat at the desk. The window gave onto the inner basin — three boats still at their moorings, the outer harbor going pewter in the late-afternoon light.

She opened the middle drawer.

The letter was between the duplicate mooring assignments and the east anchorage survey notes, where she had put it in November. Coast Guard, Sprucehead station. Dated November 14, 1943. Lt. A. Mercer's signature at the bottom, the same neat hand from the October paperwork. *Should any information come to light bearing on the identity of the deceased or the circumstances of his presence in Coldwater Reach, the station would be grateful for its communication at the address above.*

She had read that sentence a dozen times since November. It said what it said.

Below it: male, fifty or older, no identifying papers, recovered at the breakwater elbow, morning of October 12, 1943. Navy wool coat with lapels, wool trousers. Probable cardiac event — no water in the lungs. No next of kin identified, no missing persons report in any register that matched. Case status: open.

She set the letter on the desk.

What the letter did not have: a dinghy at the south pier, possibly Portland registration, the night the storm came on. One man off her, walking toward the main waterfront. That was not her private information. Soule had told her at the fuel dock this afternoon in plain daylight and would confirm it if asked. She could write it in the reply, cite the source, send the letter.

What else: two figures on the south dock, past midnight, October 10 going into the eleventh. One from the direction of the main pier — heavyset, town coat. One near the fish house end, further back, a shape in the dark she had taken for a dock worker. Her own observation, from the shed window, two hundred feet of dark harbor between the glass and the south float. She had been watching the barometric trend. She had seen what she had seen.

She had held the reason for not writing it. The reason was sound: what she had seen from the window was two shapes in the dark at a distance through glass, and two shapes in the dark at a distance through glass was not what the harbor log was for. An entry that couldn't hold on its own was not an entry. She had told herself this in October and in November and in February. The column had stayed blank.

Eight years in this post and she had kept the log accurate. Every entry had something under it: a document, a witness, a measurement, a recorded time. She had not been wrong to wait for more.

What Soule had given her today changed the calculation. Not because he had seen the same things she had — he hadn't stayed long enough for that. Because he had put a transport under the man she had seen. The man coming from the direction of the main pier had not walked in from the road. He had come off a dinghy at the south float, a boat with out-of-town registration, and he had not gone back to it. The storm had come on. Two days later the body was at the elbow of the breakwater, no water in his lungs — a man who had died on land or at the dock edge, and the storm had done the rest.

Together — Soule's piece and her piece — they had a shape that neither piece had alone. A man came to Coldwater from outside, by water, at night. Someone else was on the dock the same night who had not come by water. The man from the dinghy did not return to his boat. The body was at the breakwater in the morning.

She had been holding this alone for six months.

The envelope was in the right-hand drawer. She had put it there in January when the winter had seemed like enough reason to wait.

She reached for her pen.
