# What She Told Him

The other two were out the door before *Bis Montag* had finished clearing the room — chairs pushed back, coats pulled on, gone in the organized rush they'd made automatic, the door swinging shut behind them and leaving the classroom to its own sounds: the radiator under the south window doing its work, the late January light coming sideways through the east windows, the faint noise of the school still in progress somewhere down the hall.

Hannah had both gloves on. Her coat was already buttoned. Her books were on the desk.

Marcus came down the rows with the folder, collecting the translation exercise, and when he got to her row she held out her paper. Then she said she had a question about the second paragraph. The word she'd translated as *collected*, she said — she'd looked at it again and thought *composed* might be closer.

He stopped and read the line. *Gelassen,* he said.

She nodded.

He said: the word comes from *lassen*. To let. To leave. *Gelassen* is the composure that arrives from having practiced letting go — the calm is made of the releasing, not the other way around. *Collected* is not wrong, he said, but it gets only the surface without the work that's underneath.

She wrote *composed — made of letting go* in the margin.

He took her paper with the rest and went back to his desk. She picked up her books.

She didn't go.

She stood at her desk while the school afternoon finished itself around her — footsteps going the other direction, a locker shutting twice before it caught, then quiet. Marcus was at his desk sorting papers, his back not quite to her, his pen uncapped. He had not told her she could leave; he also had not asked why she was still there.

She set her books back down.

She said: "Dr. Klein — there's something I thought you should know. Because of the German."

He set down his pen. When he looked at her it was the full attention, not the patient waiting-for-the-expected-answer, but the other kind she had learned to recognize over a year in this room: all the way in, nothing held in reserve.

She had been carrying this since November. The note was in her coat pocket. She left it there.

She said: "My parents have a tin box that lives on the top shelf of the wardrobe in their room. I found it last April — I was looking for the farm lease document, completely different errand — and I found it instead." The words came carefully, the way words came when you had been arranging them in your head a long time and were finally saying them out loud. "Inside there was a photograph. Two men standing in front of a building. On the back, in pen: *W. Grau, A. Pfeiffer, Bamberg, 1921.*"

Marcus was still.

"My father was younger in it," she said. "But the shape of him — the way he held his shoulders, I knew it." She held the image the way she'd held it since April: the photograph square and old, already browning at the corners the way photographs went after twenty-some years, the two figures in front of a stone building's façade in a city she'd never been to. The man who wasn't her father: wider, heavier in the shoulders, the build of someone who had done outdoor work for a long time, the neck thicker than his coat collar quite accommodated. His face was harder to keep — an ordinary face, the kind a photograph from 1921 wouldn't tell you much about — but the build had stayed with her. She had looked at it for maybe three minutes and then put it back. "Heavy in the shoulders," she said. "Laborer's build. I left the photograph in the box where I found it. But I saw it clearly."

Outside the east windows two crows were working the far end of the sports field, walking their methodical crow-walk through the winter-flattened grass. She watched them for a moment.

"In November," she said, "there was a transfer. One of the German prisoners assigned to our farm — the youngest one, Karl Reinmar, he'd been there since October of 1943 — he was reassigned to another work camp." She paused. "He was from Ansbach. It's about fifty kilometers from Bamberg. I measured it on the classroom map last April, after I found the photograph." She stopped herself. "I'm not going in order."

"There's no order required," Marcus said.

She put her hands on the back of the chair.

"In August," she said. "We were doing the hay. Karl and I had been talking most of the summer — as much as we could manage, given the language. He said a name: *Werner. Von Ansbach. Er wollte kommen.*" The German came easily here; this was a German room, and she had been saying the phrase to herself since August. "Werner, from Ansbach. He wanted to come. Already past tense when he said it — the wanting, and the not-arriving, the same fact." She said it the way Karl had said it, the gap between intent and outcome already folded into the grammar. "I knew the name from the photograph. I understood they meant the same person. I didn't say so to Karl. I don't know if he knew I'd recognized it."

The crows outside had moved to the far corner of the field.

She put her hand into her coat pocket and took out the note. It had been folded the same way since November, along two creases that had gone soft from handling. She held it out.

Marcus came around the desk. She placed it in his hand.

He read it. He read it a second time without any expression she could read. He handed it back.

"He gave it to you at the transfer?"

"From his breast pocket." She looked at the note. "When they were loading. He came to where I was standing."

She unfolded it on the edge of his desk and smoothed it flat with two fingers.

*Werner Grau. From Ansbach. He is dead. I am sorry.*

Below that the birds — five of them, German on the left, English or Latin on the right, Karl's careful handwriting, the letters not quite American in their shape. *Seidenschwanz / Bombycilla cedrorum* at the top.

She had read it enough times that she could hold the whole thing in her head. She read it here, in this room, and it was the same and also different — the same words, but they had somewhere to go now.

"He didn't say more than this," she said. "But he knew. And he must have known by then that I'd understand the name." She folded the note back along its creases. "I've been carrying it since November. I kept trying to think who to give it to. Or not give it to — who to show it to."

She put the note back in her pocket.

Then she told him about the kitchen.

"That evening," she said. "The same day as the transfer. My father was at the table. I came in from the barn." The German arrived in her mouth the way it did when her father's world was close and she was standing inside it: "*Werner Grau ist tot.*"

Marcus did not move.

"He didn't move either. His hands were on the table and he kept them there." She could see the kitchen: the lamp on the table, the supper things not yet cleared, her father's back and his hands and the stillness of him — not the stillness of someone who had not heard but the stillness of someone who was holding something down. "Maybe ten seconds. And then he said — " She said the two words with the weight her father had put in them, flat and definite and without give, like a door long since closed. "*Ich weiß.*"

She waited for more to come.

"Then he picked up his fork," she said.

The radiator worked its sound. Down the hall a door opened and closed. Outside, the crows had gone from the sports field — she didn't know when they'd left.

Marcus sat back in his chair. He put his hands flat on the desk and looked at them for a moment.

When he asked the first question it came precisely, without preamble: "The man in the photograph. You said middle-aged. Would you stand by that?"

She thought about it properly, giving it what it deserved. The photograph: the two men in front of the building, the formality of a picture taken in 1921, both of them arrested by the camera's demand into something more formal than they probably were. Werner Grau with his wide shoulders and the coat that didn't quite fit them and the face she couldn't hold perfectly — not young. The age her father would have been when she was very small, when she couldn't have said what middle-aged meant but knew it as a shape, a category of done-with-being-young and not-yet-old.

"Yes," she said. "Middle-aged."

He nodded once.

"And Karl — when he said Werner wanted to come. Did he give any sense of when? Which season?"

She went back to the hayfield in August, the long afternoon of it, Karl saying the name in the particular careful way he said things he'd been carrying: *Er wollte kommen*. And there was something else — a phrase from another time, months before the transfer, that she couldn't place exactly in the calendar but had in her: *vor dem großen Sturm*, before the big storm. She wasn't entirely certain it had been about Werner specifically, but it had been about that October. And there was only one October storm like the one in 1943.

"I think he meant before the storm," she said. "The October storm. 1943." She looked at Marcus. "I'm not certain — I can't give you the exact words. But that's what I understood."

Marcus said: "Thank you. You were right to tell me."

She picked up her books. The classroom was itself: the desks in their rows, the late January light going gray in the east windows, the map of central Europe above the door with its border lines belonging to a Europe that didn't exist anymore and hadn't for some time. She had been in this room enough times to know all of it without looking.

Marcus was still in his chair, watching her with the same even attention he'd had since she'd said *because of the German* — the full-attention look she had learned the shape of over a year, the one that held what it was given and didn't spill. She had known he was the right person. She had known it since August, or before.

She went to the door. At the frame she stopped, her hand on the wood.

"I thought you should know," she said. "Because of the German."

Then she went.

---

The hallway was bright and mostly empty, the afternoon session over, a few students still at lockers. She walked down it: past the lockers, past the glass case with the athletic trophies, past the front window where the service placard hung in its white border, the names in two columns. She didn't stop to read it. She kept walking.

The main door was heavy with the cold behind it. She put her shoulder to it and it gave, swinging open into the January air — the clean kind, not damp, just cold, finding the collar and the wrists and the back of the hands immediately and stating its position clearly. She went down the concrete steps.

The sky was the low white of January, not quite cloud and not quite clear, the color of the afternoon waiting to become evening. The bus stop was at the bottom of the hill. She turned toward it.

On the harbor road below she could catch the harbor on the air — salt, cold water, the stillness of things that float without going anywhere in winter. She didn't look toward it. She was walking.

Her hand went into her coat pocket. Her fingers found the note: the two soft creases, the size of it. She had been reaching for it since November the way you reach for a stone in a shoe without deciding to — the habit of a carried thing, the reflex of checking it was still there.

She took her hand out.

The bus wasn't there yet. She stood at the stop in the cold, hands at her sides, coat buttoned to the top, and the town held its January shape around her: the church, the diner windows clouded with steam, the hardware shuttered, the harbor road turning off below the rise. She stood there and didn't reach for anything.

The bus came around the lower curve, its headlights already on against the darkening afternoon, and she got on. She found a seat on the left side. The doors closed.

The town went past the windows: the church, the diner, the main road carrying on toward the south. The harbor turnoff came and went below her. She watched it without marking it, without making a column for it, and the bus went on and the afternoon went on and it carried her home.

# The Harbor Log

The county harbor authority convened at half past nine in the Rockland county building, third floor. The room had two tall windows on the east wall and a rectangular table long enough for the panel with an additional chair for the party under review. Eira arrived at nine fifteen, signed the attendance ledger in the corridor, and took her seat.

The panel filed in at nine thirty. Carver, the retired vessel inspector — white-haired, in his seventies, with the particular economy of movement that came from decades on working boats — took the rightmost chair and had read down the first two pages of her summary document before Pratt settled into the center. Pratt was the county board member who had initiated the proceeding; he set a folder on the table with the care of a man who had been waiting some months for the occasion. Haverford, from the county maritime licensing office in Camden, took the leftmost chair. She was neutral, local, harbor-familiar — there to make the proceeding formally complete.

Pratt called the proceeding to order. He read the resolution: the county board had convened a formal review of the continuity of appointment in the harbormaster's office at Coldwater Reach, to determine whether the office had been administered in compliance with the county maritime charter. Four minutes of reading. Eira followed along on her copy.

"I brought additional copies," she said when he finished, and distributed one to each seat. Her copies were tabbed with numbered flags at eight years of records: the harbor logs, the mooring registry, the fuel allocation ledger, the safety inspection reports, the annual reports filed each December.

Carver started with the logs. He asked how entries were made — contemporaneous or summarized.

"Contemporaneous," she said. "Each day's entry before midnight, dated and signed. During severe weather the entry might be written at first light the following morning covering the night's events, but it's dated to the day of occurrence."

He asked about the mooring registry — whether vessels were logged in and out or only in, whether seasonal moorings were billed differently from transient. She walked him through the September 1944 and September 1943 registries. He read them. He asked about the fuel allocation ledger. She had ledgers for all eight years; he read the September 1944 reconciliation and the quarter-end figures for three additional quarters. He asked no questions she could not answer with the open document in front of him.

Pratt asked about the October 1943 safety inspection. Who had conducted it. Whether a second party had countersigned.

She had conducted it. There was no countersignature. The harbormaster's assistant had been drafted in January 1942; no replacement had been authorized. She had conducted the inspection herself, in her capacity as acting harbormaster, and had noted one deficiency — a mooring cleat on the north face of the fuel dock with a cracked base plate — and arranged for its repair. She had the work order. Repair completed November 17, 1943.

"Your own signature on your own inspection," Pratt said.

"The charter requires the harbormaster to conduct or supervise annual safety inspections," she said. "The harbormaster conducted it. Whether the harbormaster conducts or supervises is at the harbormaster's discretion under the relevant charter section." She turned to it and put her copy on the table in front of him.

He read it. He put it aside.

Haverford had not yet asked a question. She had made two notes on her pad.

At eleven o'clock Pratt came to the matter of appointment continuity.

He read from the November 1935 county board resolution: *Eira Bowman is hereby appointed acting harbormaster of the Port of Coldwater Reach, effective December 1, 1935, pending formal review and confirmation by the county harbor authority.*

"The review," he said, "was never conducted."

"It was not," she said.

"The charter requires review and confirmation within sixty days of appointment. That review was not completed in sixty days. From the record before me, it has not been completed in eight years. The board's position is that an acting appointment without formal confirmation constitutes an unresolved appointment."

She had the 1935 letter in front of her. "The appointment letter is in the record," she said. "Signed by three board members. Issued by the authority that had the power to issue it. The authority subsequently failed to conduct the review the charter required. That failure belongs to the authority, not to the administration of the office." She kept her voice even. "The harbor has been operated without administrative irregularity for eight years. Twenty-seven safety inspections. One deficiency noted, corrected within thirty days. No incident entered in the harbormaster's casualty column." She looked at him. "If the authority would like to identify a failure in the administration of the office, I'll address it. The record is here."

Pratt looked at his folder.

Carver turned a page.

Haverford wrote a note, read it, and wrote another beneath it.

The panel recessed at eleven-thirty. Eira went to the corridor.

She stood at the window at the end of the hall. Below the county building, Rockland harbor ran out toward the breakwater — a dragger working past the head, its course straight and deliberate for the open water; a smaller boat coming in from the outer islands, sitting low and slow with traps stacked aft. She read them without effort. The dragger was heading offshore; the lobster boat had been out since before light and wanted its dock.

Coombs came down the corridor at a quarter past twelve. She had worked with him for a dozen years; he ran traps off the Caldwell Bank and landed his catch at the cold-storage house at the pier. He had his hat in one hand and a folder under his arm and was going somewhere on some other county errand. He was nearly past the window when he caught sight of her.

He stopped.

She gave him nothing to work with. He nodded — the nod that passed between two people who shared a pier, the nod that meant *you are here and this is the ordinary thing* — and she nodded back.

He went on.

She stood at the window until the clerk came to the corridor door.

---

The vote was two to one. Carver read the finding: the authority was satisfied that the harbormaster's office at Coldwater Reach had been administered in compliance with charter requirements for the duration of the appointment. Eira Bowman's appointment as harbormaster was confirmed, effective from the date of original appointment, with tenure now formally registered in the authority's records.

Pratt had voted against. He said nothing after the finding was read and left while Carver was still signing. Haverford held the certification across the table and gave her a look that was more than professional and less than warm, and that was the right amount.

Eira signed her copy. She put it in her case with the summary documents.

She walked out of the building and across to the truck.

---

The coast road went south with the sea appearing between the headlands in sections — grey water, the March light flat and white on it, patches of dirty snow on the north-facing slopes where it hadn't seen sun since December. She drove without the radio. She stopped once for gas, which took a coupon she had been saving since February. She ate the sandwich she'd packed from home outside Thomaston and watched a crow work the road verge for half a minute before the cold made staying pointless.

The harbor came into view around the south headland at half past four, the late March light going pale. The boats on the moorings had swung to face the same direction. She could have named the state of the tide before she had an angle on the water.

She parked at the top of the pier and walked down.

---

The shed was cold; she hadn't had the stove going since morning. She laid a fire and got it started and stood at the window while it caught. The south dock lay in the March dusk below — the gray water against the pilings, the boats tied and riding, the breakwater a dark horizontal line across the harbor mouth. The navigation light at the elbow would come on at five-thirty.

She sat at her desk.

She opened the middle drawer.

The Portland letter was on top, folded into thirds: the harbor authority inquiry returned, *W. Grau, 114 Franklin Street, Portland, Maine.* She had read it enough times that the address was a piece of furniture in her head. She took it out. Beneath it the CG form — blank where her signature should go, the form for reporting additional information relevant to a pending investigation, which she had picked up at the Rockland station in the spring of 1944 and brought home and put in this drawer.

She read both of them. This was not for information.

The case had been officially closed since late 1943. The CG's finding: unidentified male, probable drowning, storm-related, no identification found on person or clothing, no next of kin established. No additional reporting had come. More than a year. No letter from Portland. No inquiry at the pier, no one at the counter asking about a man from Portland who had gone missing in an October blow.

She had a name and a Portland address. She had a dinghy — stove in and beached in the south cove — registered to that name. She had her dock observation from the night of October 11, 1943, and she was about to put it where it belonged.

She did not have anything that would serve Werner Grau. The form, completed, would go to an addendum in a closed case — that was all it could accomplish. She had served the machinery of record for eight years. She knew when it served a purpose and when it did not.

She folded the CG form along its creases and put it back in the drawer.

---

The harbor logs were on the bottom shelf on the north wall: eight of hers, the first of them beginning in November 1935, and behind hers Owen's volumes going back before that — his handwriting that got faster and more abbreviated over the years as he settled into the work, the last of his stopping in November where November had taken him.

She took down the 1943 log. She carried it to the desk.

October. She turned to October.

The October 12 entry was in the middle of the page, below the October 11 night entry and above October 13. She had written it at seven in the morning, after no sleep, in the plain language that a seven-in-the-morning required: *Body discovered outer breakwater face, 0610 hours. Adult male, no identification found on person or clothing. Coast Guard notified 0620 hours. CG arrived 0740 hours, Lieutenant and two enlisted. Body transported 0820 hours. Weather at time of discovery: NW 30, gusting 38, seas 8–10 outer harbor. Vessel traffic nil.*

Below it, three lines of space before the October 13 entry.

She got her pen from the top drawer.

She wrote in the space below the October 12 entry, in her regular hand:

*0055: two men observed south dock. One unknown. One familiar by gait, farm-type. Neither vessel registered in port. Weather deteriorating.*

Nineteen words. Her handwriting matched the rest of the entry — the same pen, the same hand she'd used since the first of November 1935. The ink was the same black. It read like an entry because it was an entry: what was observed, when, under what conditions. The log took in what was given to it and held it. That was what the log was for.

She closed it.

She sat with it on the desk for a moment. Then she stood and carried it back to the north wall and slid it into its place between the volumes on either side.

---

She banked the stove, turned off the lamp, and locked the shed door behind her. She walked to the end of the pier.

The navigation light at the breakwater elbow was on. The harbor was dark except for that light and the mooring light at the pier head, and the harbor's own quiet sounds: water against the pilings, a halyard tapping somewhere on a moored boat, the low creak of the cold-storage building settling in the ebb.

The tide was going out. She could tell by the sound — the slap against the nearest piling was lower than it had been at four-thirty, the sound coming up from a different angle. She stood there long enough to be certain, and she was certain.

The harbor was hers: the water, the boats, the granite breakwater, the tide table, the fuel dock, the mooring registry, the harbor log. Formally confirmed, as of today, registered in the authority's records. The certification was in her truck. The entry was in the log.

She turned and walked back up the pier.

She went home.

# May

The route to school: three years and two months of it now, the same four blocks from Spruce Street to the post office corner and the turn north past the Congregational church to the brick building on the main road. He knew each house he passed by its season — which gardens had been turned over since the thaw and which had not, which put light in their windows at seven in the morning, which did not. The Garfield house at the corner had the kitchen garden already in motion: stakes in the ground, the earth turned dark, the row markers placed. He had learned that certain households acted in April and certain households waited, and the Garfields were a household that acted. The family next door had a cat that had established, over three years, that Marcus constituted no reasonable occasion for alarm, and confirmed this from the fence post as he passed.

The Henderson family's dog had made the same determination approximately six months into Marcus's tenure, which remained, in his estimation, among the small achievements of his residence here. It lifted its head from the step, confirmed, and set it back down.

The lilacs along the Miller fence were four or five days from opening. He had been watching them since the end of the previous week — the buds advancing through their green toward the first color, still held back by what April in this latitude permitted. He was familiar now with what spring looked like here: the crocuses first, then the mud, then the particular quality of the light, then the lilacs. He had been in Coldwater for three springs. He had thought, at the beginning of each of them, that he would be leaving before the next one. He had been wrong about this three times, and was no longer forming the thought.

He looked back once at the turn: Lillian was at the kitchen window of the Crow house, fourth from the corner. She lifted a hand; he lifted his. She had been at that window, at approximately this time, for most of three years. He did not know when this had become the texture of the ordinary.

---

Before the road turned south there was a short street that ran toward the harbor approach, and at its end the outer reach was briefly visible between the houses — perhaps a hundred yards of sight line before the angle closed. The water had the quality late April gave it: not the flat steel of November, not the heavy stillness of January, but something that held light at its surface rather than absorbing it, clear and directed. The breakwater was a gray horizontal line across the harbor mouth. He turned before it was more than registered, and it was gone.

---

He had been thinking, in recent weeks, about Werner Grau.

Not in the way he had thought about him during the first year, when each piece had required locating within the structure of what was known and what remained provisional, when the question of what to do with the assembled account was still a question in progress — but in the way he now thought about matters that had been correctly placed: without needing to disturb them.

He held what he was likely always to hold. The letter — *Lieber Albrecht* — arriving in October 1943 in his school mail because a postal clerk in the county sorting office had made a plausible guess at the address and been wrong. The plan to come to Coldwater in October; the news about the Reinmar boy at the Pfeiffer farm; the information Werner would not commit to paper and wanted to deliver in person. Marcus understood something of that restraint, or believed he did: certain things require the face across a table, the particular register of two men from the same region of Bavaria hearing each other in a language that does not require translation, in a country that belongs to neither of them. And then the face Albrecht Pfeiffer had shown when Marcus came to the farm door in January 1944: not surprise but the adjustment of a man incorporating a confirmation into something already established. Albrecht had already known Werner had come to Coldwater. This was what his face had said, precisely, without saying anything.

Karl Reinmar, from Ansbach — fifty kilometers from where Albrecht Pfeiffer had been born, from where Werner had come. The note Karl had written before the Army transport, which Hannah had read aloud on Marcus's desk in January, smoothing it flat with her hand: *Werner Grau. From Ansbach. He is dead. I am sorry.* The photograph in the Pfeiffer tin box: two men before a stone building, Bamberg, 1921 — Werner with his painter's and laborer's shoulders, the face Hannah had described as ordinary and impossible to fix in memory. And then Albrecht's reply, that autumn, to his daughter's past tense: *Ich weiß.* I know.

Werner Grau had come to Coldwater in October 1943, in deteriorating weather, in a small boat from Portland, carrying news he had been holding for months — about Karl, about the Reinmar family, about things the letter had named only as things that would not go to paper. He had been in the country without legal standing since 1940. He had come because the connection he was seeking had become more pressing than the risk: a man who has been carrying something across that long a distance will eventually put it down, in person, with the person who can receive it. Whether Werner had reached the farm that night, what had passed between him and Albrecht before the storm peaked, what brought Werner to the harbor and what he encountered there — this was not in the account and would not be. Albrecht had said *Ich weiß* and picked up his fork. That was the limit the account could reach.

Marcus was not going to report it. He had decided this in the spring of 1944, and the decision had not shifted. To complete the form and file it would be to deliver Werner Grau to the category available: undocumented alien, probable drowning, case long closed. This was accurate so far as it went. Werner's name would acquire an addendum in a file that had been closed for a year and a half, and the file would close again. Marcus knew when a form served a purpose and when it did not. The account was in the drawer, written in German, in his own hand. The holding of it was, perhaps, a form of acknowledgment: Werner Grau had existed; he had been, in specific and considerable detail, a person; his story was not entirely lost.

---

He said good morning to Mrs. Voisin at her step, and to the Kelleher boy walking his bicycle up the road with the resigned expression of someone who had concluded that the front tire was committed to its own position. He was at the school at ten past eight. The corridor: chalk dust, old wood, the compound the custodians used on the floors, which he recognized now as instinctively as he had once recognized the steam heat and old paper of his department in Vienna. Henry would have had the boiler running from six. The radiators ticked.

He passed the service placard in the main corridor without stopping. Twenty-four names: J. CROW, Army, Pacific, between Cowan J. (Navy) and Delaney T. (Marines, Confirmed Fallen August 1944). It had been there since March of 1944 — since the week after Henry had said *the principal may not have thought*, which had been the week before Marcus had taken the question to the principal's office — and it was there now, as it would continue to be, without requiring his attention each time.

His classroom, second floor, east-facing. He unlocked the door — the key's brass worn to a particular smoothness after two years of the same hand and the same pressure — and set his briefcase on the desk. The morning light lay in the windows, doing what April light did to old painted walls.

---

He had brought the stone from his room at the Crow house in January, at the beginning of the new semester, and placed it on the classroom windowsill between the latch and the corner of the frame. It was a piece of granite from the breakwater's elbow — small enough to close one hand around entirely, unremarkable in the way of coastal Maine granite: gray, close-grained, slightly heavier than its size suggested. He had picked it up on the twelfth of October, 1944, standing at the place where the body had been found a year before, and had carried it home and then brought it here, because it had seemed then like the right thing to do and had not since seemed otherwise. He picked it up now, felt its familiar weight in his palm, and set it back down. It was not a symbol. It was a piece of coastal Maine granite from a place where a man had died, that wanted to be on the windowsill, and was.

He went to the window and opened it.

The spring came in: salt from the harbor, cold mud from the south fields, and from the Bartlett property next door, the lilacs nearly open — not yet the full smell but the note that preceded it, which was its own distinct thing and not a lesser one.

The morning was quiet enough to hear the bell buoy at the channel entrance. It rang on the swell: twice, at irregular intervals, each ring distinct. He had first noticed it from his room at the Crow house in the second summer here, and it had become, over three years, one of the sounds that located him specifically: this channel, this coast, this particular water.

In approximately two weeks there would be news from Europe. He was not waiting for it with any particular impatience. It would come; the war would end; and he would be here, in this room, in this building on the main road in this town — which was where he was, and where he was going to be.

Hannah Pfeiffer's translation papers were on the desk in a stack of eleven: her working draft of the Rilke sequence Marcus had assigned to the third-year class in March, with marginal notes in both German and English. The handwriting was careful and slightly impatient, the quality of someone who is not uncertain about the word and is nonetheless holding it up to the light. She had understood, without being instructed, that what a word held in German could only be approximated in English, and that the approximation was the work itself, not a failure of it. She had been his student for nearly two years. He had something to tell her about the Rilke — about what she was doing with it, specifically — and was waiting for the translation that would show her this herself, because that was the better way.

He sat down.

Outside the open window: salt, cold mud, the lilacs at their threshold. The bell buoy, twice, in the morning quiet.

The stone on the sill.

He took out his pen and began to mark.

# The Breakwater

The outer face had taken green water.

She could see it from the headland stairs — the wrack line sitting high on the granite, a length of tarred cable draped across the top course, the iron mooring rings at the elbow gone dark with wet. She went down.

First light. Northwest wind out of Canada, fifteen knots and dropping. The blow had peaked sometime around two in the morning and then, the way storms sometimes did on this coast, had simply stopped. By four she'd been lying awake listening to the silences between gusts. By five she'd been dressed. The air coming off the water now was cleaner and colder, carrying nothing with it but temperature.

She had her clipboard.

The top course was intact along the north arm's full length — no slippage, no voids. She moved toward the elbow, checking each granite face, feeling the joint conditions where she had to. Some of the stones she knew well enough to read by looking; others needed a hand pressed to them, checking for any give. The rubble fill had held. The crown height was unchanged along the north arm.

She noted the cable. Tarred, fairly new, and it didn't belong to any vessel currently in the harbor. She'd check the boatyard, see if something in storage had lost it. She noted it for inquiry and for removal.

At the elbow, the course had shifted. An inch and a half toward the inner harbor, maybe two. She measured by eye and then by hand and noted it. The elbow always took the worst of a southeast blow, and what she was looking at was not as bad as 1939. The mortar joint at the south corner had widened. She put her finger in it: a quarter inch, three-eighths. Before the freeze, someone would need to point that joint; otherwise the ice would open it further.

The repair list for the breakwater had been three items before this morning. It was now five.

She wrote them all down.

The kelp had piled waist-high against the inner face of the elbow, black and dripping, salt-stinking. Woven into it were a coil of pot warp, a length of buoy line, the slats of a wooden crate that was stamped with something she didn't recognize — from a vessel, or perhaps from the boatyard if the storm had lifted something from the rails. A glass-ball float. A plank with a bronze fitting through it, the bolt stripped, which meant it had been working loose before the storm claimed it.

She went around the elbow, and saw the man.

---

He was face-down in the wrack, in the inner corner of the elbow where the kelp had piled deepest. The storm geometry was right for it: anything coming in from the southeast over the outer edge would have been carried into exactly this corner. He was lying with his arms at an angle — the left arm back along his body, the right arm out and slightly under him — that said he had not arranged himself there.

She stood for a moment.

The light was improving. She could see well enough.

Town clothes. A heavy wool coat, navy, with lapels that had no business on a working waterfront. Trousers, not work trousers. No boots anywhere on the breakwater that she could see, no oilskins, no gear of any kind. No vessel anywhere in the inner harbor she didn't know.

She set the clipboard on a flat section of granite and crouched down.

She checked his pockets.

Inside the coat, left breast: nothing. Right breast: nothing. Outside pockets — in the left, nothing; in the right, a folded handkerchief, and below it, grit. His trouser pockets, each in turn: nothing. Nothing. No wallet. No papers. No draft card. No ration book. No keys. Nothing with a name on it.

She stood up.

Male. The hands said fifty or older — the thickness across the knuckles, the looseness of the skin on the back of them. The hair was grey, close-cut, a working man's cut. The wool coat was good quality, that much was clear even soaked through. The trousers were wool as well. Somebody's travelling clothes, or a man's good clothes, or both.

Nothing about him said this harbor.

She picked up the clipboard. She walked back to the shed at the pier head.

---

Inside, she called Sprucehead.

The duty officer answered on the third ring. She gave him everything in order: her name, her title, the station address, the date, the time — six-twenty-two by the clock on the wall — and then the description. Male, she said. Face-down in the wrack at the elbow. Middle-aged or older. Town clothes. No papers, no identification of any kind, nothing to indicate a vessel or how he had come in. She had not touched him beyond checking his pockets. She had not moved him.

The duty officer said he would send someone. She thanked him and hung up.

She put the kettle on the single-burner plate. She checked the barometer — risen three-tenths since midnight, consistent with the storm's track, consistent with what she could see through the north window: the sky clearing fast from the northwest, the cloud deck breaking up at altitude, showing the grey beneath. She recorded the barometer reading in the tide log and noted the wind direction.

On the shelf above the telephone, seven logbooks stood in order. She'd started the current one in January, and its spine was still dark and square. The six before it went back to 1936. The one before those — thinner, its spine faded to the color of old water, Owen's handwriting on the label in the particular heavy-slanted hand he'd used for anything official — was set a little apart from the others, at the end of the shelf where the bracket met the wall. She had not moved it. It wasn't where she would have put it if she'd been setting up the shelf from scratch.

She poured a cup of tea and went back to the breakwater to wait.

---

The wind had dropped to ten knots by the time the Coast Guard truck came down off the main road onto the pier. She was standing at the breakwater's head when Lieutenant Mercer got out with his two enlisted men.

He was younger than she'd expected — mid-twenties, with the winter uniform pressed correctly and a manner that was efficient without being brisk. He introduced himself and looked at her when she gave her name.

"You're the harbormaster?" he said.

"Eight years," she said.

She walked him out to the body.

He crouched the way she had crouched, looking before he touched. He checked the pockets — the same ones she'd checked, and two more. He stood up. He asked her: when had she found it, had she moved anything, had she contacted anyone else.

No, she said. No. No.

"Any record of a vessel in difficulty? Radio calls? Report from boats that came in before the blow?"

"Nothing in the log from the past three days. No distress calls. Two draggers out to the grounds and back in before it peaked. The sardine carrier *Ellsworth* running to Eastport — she went out before the storm, due back the eighteenth."

"And no vessels you can't account for."

"Nothing in the harbor I can't account for."

He wrote in a small notebook. He was thorough rather than curious. He asked whether anyone else had access to the breakwater during the storm, and she said no one would have come out on it while the blow was on, and anyone could have come since, but she'd found no footprints in the wrack. He wrote that down as well.

She gave him the harbor log for October 9 through 12. He looked at it carefully and handed it back.

The two enlisted men brought the stretcher down from the truck. The operation was careful and correct. She watched from a few feet away and he did not ask her to step back. By the time the stretcher was going back up the breakwater, she had answered two more questions and had learned almost nothing except that the lieutenant's first name was Amos, from the nametag she'd seen when he turned his coat.

"We'll be in touch if we have questions," he said.

"I know where to reach you," she said.

The truck pulled out of the pier at seven-twenty-three.

---

She finished the breakwater survey. She walked the full length again from the shore end, checking each section now that nothing was in her way. The damage added one more item — a section of the north face's drainage where the fill had settled — and she added it to the list. She wrote the estimate for the elbow repair while she was still on the breakwater, because the light was good and she could see what she was writing about.

Back at the shed, she opened the harbor log to the day's page.

She wrote for ten minutes. The entry ran to half a page.

*October 12, 1943. Sunrise 0611. Wind NW 15kts at 0600, dropping to 10kts by 0800. Barometer 29.74 at 0600, rising. Post-storm survey, breakwater, 0615–0730: granite course displaced at elbow (est. 1.5 in. inward), mortar joint widened at south corner of elbow, iron mooring rings displaced (2), kelp and debris accumulation at elbow, drainage fill settled N. face — all noted for fall repair.*

*Vessels: all moored vessels accounted for. Sardine carrier* Ellsworth *Eastport run, ETA Oct. 18.*

*0615: Unidentified male, deceased, recovered at breakwater elbow. No papers, no identification of any kind, no associated vessel. CG Sprucehead notified 0622. CG responded, Lt. A. Mercer and two enlisted, 0711. Body removed to CG custody 0723. CG assuming jurisdiction.*

She put down the pen.

She read it once. It was accurate. Every time was correct.

She set the logbook to one side.

---

It was not yet eight-thirty. The first boats wouldn't be in from the grounds for another hour, maybe two. She stood at the shed's south window.

The south dock was empty. She could see its full length from here — the grey planking, the pilings standing in the flat water, the dock light still burning at the head of the dock, unnecessary now in the morning. The Gale brothers had moved their trap hauler to the inner float in September. The dock had not been in regular use since then.

The night before it had not been empty.

October the eleventh, going into the twelfth. Past midnight. She had been at this window watching the barometer fall. The blow was building. She had already gone out and checked the mooring chains on two of the draggers — around nine, ten o'clock — and had come back to the shed to wait. The chains were what they were. There was nothing more to do in the dark in a rising wind.

Two figures on the south dock. The dock light behind them both.

One she had not recognized. He was looking toward the outer harbor. Dark coat. The build of someone past middle age — not heavy, but solid, the kind of solid that sets into men who have worked outdoors for a long time. Standing still in the way of a man who had come somewhere specific and arrived.

The other one she had not seen clearly. Half-turned from her, the dock light cutting across from the wrong angle. The shoulders. The way of standing. Not a man whose body had been built around boats — she knew that much. Wide across the back. Feet planted like a man used to standing on flat ground, not a deck. Somebody from inland.

She had thought: two men on the dock before a storm. She had thought: their business, not mine.

Now she looked at the harbor log, open on the desk.

The entry was complete. Each time was correct.

The man on the breakwater. No papers. Wool coat. Past middle age. A working man's hands.

The man on the south dock the night before, looking out toward the outer harbor.

These were separate data points. It was possible they had nothing to do with each other, and the log entry she had written was true in every particular, and there was nothing more to do.

She picked up the pen.

She held it.

She set it down.

The south dock stood empty in the flat morning light. The harbor beyond it had gone from grey to silver as the sky cleared. The tide was going out.

# Icehouse

The water in the trough had a skim of ice — the kind that doesn't last past seven — and Hannah broke it with the heel of her hand before the first cows came in.

The barn smelled the way it smelled in October: cattle breath, wet straw, the good dense smell of old wood that had been absorbing winters longer than anyone in the family had been alive. The work lantern hung from the nail by the feed room door, yellow in the early dark. She had the feed sorted and the first three stanchions set, and the barn was, for a few minutes more, completely hers. Her father would be down from the upper hayloft soon; the four prisoners would come across the yard from the icehouse at quarter to seven; the day would become the day it was going to be. Until then she had this: the warmth coming off the cows in the cold barn air, and her hands that knew what to do without her needing to be present for it.

The cows came in the way they always came in. Bessie leading, then the two Guernseys whose names she still mixed up after two years, then the long line of them filling the central aisle without hurry, without improvisation, with the complete certainty of animals who have done this ten thousand mornings and see no reason to change on the ten thousand and first. She worked down the row: manger sections, water, the individual quirks of individual animals — the brown Guernsey that needed coaxing to the left side, the old one who liked to be spoken to. Her hands knew each of these things. Her mind went somewhere else while they worked, loose and not attached to anything, the way it went in the early mornings before it had been given a task.

She was on the sixth cow when the icehouse door opened across the yard.

She had learned, in two weeks, to read that sequence: the bar-latch lifting, the creak of the lower hinge that hadn't been fully planed when they rehung it in August, boots on the wooden step. The four of them came out in the same order they always came out — the two older ones first, then the one she thought of as the Stuttgarter because she had once caught him say that city's name in a sentence she couldn't follow the rest of, then Karl at the end, moving with a hitched, slightly too-careful gait of someone who hadn't slept flat or long enough.

Lonzo Reed was already outside the door. He was always already there — she had been trying to determine for two weeks whether he was an early riser by nature or simply wasn't sleeping much, without being able to settle it either way. He held the carbine in the crook of his arm and watched the four men cross the yard with the particular quality of attention that doesn't look like attention: his head didn't move, but nothing in the farmyard happened without him clocking it. She had seen him notice things before she did.

Her father came down from the hayloft with the pitchfork, nodded once at Lonzo — the same nod every morning, the same tilt of his chin — and spoke to the two older prisoners:

*Hier zuerst. Dann die Weide.*

Short. Pointing with his chin toward the east wall where the feed shovels were racked. The older man — the one she thought of as the Bavarian, which was maybe right and maybe half-right — picked up his bucket without being asked twice. He was a man who knew farm labor. She could tell by the way he held things.

Karl reached for the second bucket and took it by the side rim. Wrong — the bucket tilted on the way up and sloshed. The Bavarian looked at Karl's hands, not his face, and Karl shifted his grip to the bail without a word exchanged. He had been here two weeks and there were still things like this: tools picked up wrong, a gesture misread, the physical grammar of farm work not yet his. He was not incompetent. She had watched him closely enough to see that: he absorbed each correction without resentment, and before he did an unfamiliar thing he took one beat first — watched a man do it, checked his own translation before he committed to the page. Then he did the thing.

He looked up from the bucket and saw her watching him from the sixth stall.

He looked away first. He always looked away first.

She turned back to the cows. Their flanks were warm against her hands.

The four of them worked through the morning assignments. Her father moved among them in German, directing with few words, and the two older ones answered in the same economy. The Stuttgarter worked with the carefulness of a man who does not want to be corrected; Karl worked with the quickness of someone who doesn't mind it. She watched this from the edge of her attention the way she watched most things on the farm — not with the intention of understanding it, just taking it in, the way the barn takes in weather.

Her father handed her the feed tally clipboard when he passed her, not breaking stride. She took it and said "Good morning" to his profile.

*Danke,* he said, already past her, checking the stanchion locks.

She wrote the date in the upper right corner of the tally: *October 14.* She said to his back, in English: "The brown Guernsey is still off. Third morning."

He did not turn. He did not adjust.

---

She carried the milk pails across the farmyard in the early light. Lonzo Reed had come back to his post outside the icehouse door, which stood open now; through the opening she could see the interior — the two-tiered bunk frames along the walls, the small table with the lamp on it, a pair of boots set outside the lower frame at the near end. Then she went in the kitchen door.

The stove was cold; she had to go to the woodshed for kindling before she could get it going. When she came back her mother was already at the table.

Her mother's hands were around the tea cup — the white one with the thin blue ring — and the tea had gone to the temperature of the room. She was looking at a place on the table a foot beyond the cup, at nothing, with the attentiveness she sometimes brought to nothing.

Hannah broke two eggs into the pan and cut the bread and got the apple butter from the shelf. She put a plate together and set it at her mother's elbow, not directly in front of her. Directly in front felt like an instruction.

Her mother looked at the plate.

Hannah sat down in her father's empty chair. Through the kitchen window she could see the corner of the icehouse in the thin early light. Lonzo Reed was walking the farmyard perimeter — not going anywhere, just keeping himself to a shape. His breath came in small clouds.

Her mother's cup made a sound against the table.

After a while Hannah got up and put her own eggs on her own plate and stood at the counter and ate them, looking out the window.

---

She had to run the last stretch to the Route 1 stop, her coat half-buttoned and mud still on her boots from the barn. She got on the bus out of breath and slid into the middle section where the seats were more intact.

Ruthanne Gorey and June Pullen were two rows ahead, talking since the Gorey stop, and what they were talking about got into the bus around Hannah the way cold gets into a building — not through any one opening but through all the small ones at once.

A body on the breakwater. Ruthanne's father had heard it from Clement Ames, who'd been at the fish pier on Tuesday morning when the Coast Guard truck came down. A man from nowhere anyone knew, and no papers at all, nothing on him. Probably a sailor off a convoy, Ruthanne said — those men never carried papers on them, the papers stayed with the ship, that was what her father said. June thought maybe a fisherman swept overboard, some boat no one had reported yet. Her brother had heard something about a U-boat in the Penobscot. Ruthanne said that was last October and everyone was always saying that. They went back and forth with it, not unkindly, the way you discuss something terrible that has happened to no one you know.

Hannah listened.

*No papers.* She turned the phrase and looked at its underside. What she was thinking about was not the body — she had no image for it, had not been near the harbor — but the condition itself. To arrive somewhere carrying nothing that said your name, your nationality, where you had come from or where you were going. To be, in the official sense, unattached to the record of yourself.

The bus was cold. She tucked her hands into her sleeves.

She sat through history and algebra and English and watched, during fourth period, as the birches at the edge of the playing field let go of their leaves in ones and twos.

---

Dinner was late. Her father had been out to the north pasture fence — a section down from the storm, needing restringing before the cows found the opening — and came in with mud to both knees. Her mother had already reset the table with the everyday dishes.

They sat.

The lamp was the brass one that had been her grandmother's. Under it her father's face looked older than it did in the barn, the lines deeper, settled into angles she recognized without being able to name. He cut his meat. Her mother worked the bread at the edge of her plate, pulling it into smaller pieces without eating it.

"I heard there was a body on the breakwater," Hannah said.

"A man nobody knows. No papers."

Her father's knife and fork stopped.

Both, together, on the plate. Three seconds — she counted. Then he cut the meat and put the piece in his mouth and chewed it and swallowed. He reached for his water glass and set it down. He looked at his plate.

He said nothing.

He did not look at her.

Her mother had not looked up from the bread.

Hannah finished her dinner. She washed the plates in the order she always washed them, hung the dish towel on the stove bar, went upstairs.

---

Her room was on the east side of the house, the window looking over the farmyard — past the barn's near corner to the icehouse beyond, its low roofline, its single window, the wooden step. Since the first night in October when the lamp appeared there, she had looked at it last thing before she slept. It had seemed wrong to her at first, that rectangle of light in the wrong place. Then less wrong. Then simply part of what the farmyard was at night.

She lay on top of the quilt with her boots still on and looked at the ceiling. The house was quiet. Her parents' door was shut. Through the east pine the wind moved in long passes, a sound she had fallen asleep under her whole life.

She was still carrying the day. Her father's knife and fork stopped for three seconds on the plate. Her mother's hands around the cold cup in the same position as when she'd left for the barn. *No papers* — the phrase turning and turning without the right question to stop it. Karl's bucket shifted from rim to bail before anyone said a word.

After a while she turned over and looked out the window.

Karl was standing outside the icehouse door.

He had on the jacket with the stenciling on the back, collar turned up against the cold. He was looking at the sky with his whole head tipped back — the stars were out tonight, more than usual, the clear dry October dark you got when the fog lifted and the cold came in from inland. He held a cigarette between two fingers, its ember small and reddish, burning down on its own.

He said something.

One word, maybe two. She had the window shut and couldn't hear it, but she could see his lips move and his breath make a small cloud and the word go out of him into the night air. Not to anyone.

He said it again, the same one.

She pressed her fingertips against the glass. His breath made another cloud. He said it a third time, and this time, in the stillness of the yard, she caught it through the cold glass: *Seidenschwanz.* She held the sound. She did not know what it meant. She had German enough to follow her father's directives and the vocabulary Dr. Klein put on the board, and this was neither of those things. It was Karl's word, and the night's word, and whatever it was naming she could not say.

He stood outside a while longer. He finished the cigarette and dropped it on the step and put his boot on it with the careful deliberateness of someone told to be careful about that. He looked up at the sky one last time, his face tilted back and still. Then he went inside.

The lamp in the icehouse window dimmed — not all at once, but down, turned low, to almost nothing.

She watched the dark rectangle.

Through the window's edge, where the seal had never been right since she'd known this room: turned earth, the October cold that comes from inland fields without any salt in it, and underneath that the faint warmth of the barn.

She reached up and pulled the window shut.

The icehouse was dark.

# Continental Educator

The morning walk from the Crow house to the school was fifteen minutes, a calculation Marcus had verified repeatedly over nineteen months and continued to verify, partly out of habit and partly because he was a man who understood the difference between a fact that had been established and a fact that merely appeared to have been established. The one variable he had not succeeded in eliminating was the intersection at the bottom of Elm Street, where the road made its north turn and the harbor appeared briefly between two buildings — a flat gray angle of water, the breakwater's outer arm, no vessels at the south dock this morning. Some mornings he stopped. Today he did not.

Main Street at half past seven: the hardware store's windows still dark, the bakery lit, a truck outside the post office with its engine running and the driver standing beside it, watching his exhaust cloud with the peaceable attention of a man whose morning was going according to plan. Marcus nodded. The driver nodded. This exchange, which had occurred in some variation for nineteen months, had arrived at a precision of mutual acknowledgment that Marcus found, if not warm, then accurate — and in his experience accuracy was a form of warmth, or at least its structural equivalent.

The school sat back from the road behind a low iron fence and four large elms that had not yet been touched by whatever was moving through the New England elms. Three stories, dark brick, the year 1912 cut into the cornerstone — he had read it once and it had stayed, the way dates stayed, without being asked to. He went up the main steps and through the door into the smell of chalk dust and boiler heat: Henry had the building to the right temperature, as he always had it to the right temperature. Marcus hung his coat on the hook inside the teachers' entry and went upstairs.

---

His first class was Latin. This year the Latin class was three students — Cornelia Foss and two boys named Pratt and Heywood, none of whom had elected the course voluntarily but all of whom had been placed in it by the vice-principal on a theory Marcus considered neither obviously correct nor obviously wrong. He had them, and they had him, and in nineteen months of this arrangement both parties had arrived at a working understanding of what was expected.

The classroom was on the third floor, north-facing, with windows that admitted the particular flat gray light of coastal Maine in late October: not winter, not autumn, not quite either, a light without strong claims on the hour or the mood. Three desks arranged in the front half of the room, which was the correct number of desks for three students and which had the effect of making the back half of the room into a kind of reserve space — not empty, exactly, but waiting. Marcus had learned not to think about the back half of the room.

He wrote a sentence on the board. It was from Cicero's *De Amicitia*, the kind of sentence Cicero wrote when he was working at full capacity: the main clause withheld while the subordinate architecture assembled itself, so that by the time the verb arrived you had been holding the opening phrase in your mind long enough to know what weight the closing would need to carry. He underlined the subordinate clause, set the chalk in the tray, and turned.

"Don't translate it," he said.

He had been saying this in four languages, across more years and more classrooms than he intended to calculate, and what he meant by it was always the same: sit with the sentence before you reach for the English. Learn the architecture before the furniture. A translation that arrives too quickly has not understood what it has translated.

The three of them sat with it. He could read, from the quality of each student's stillness, which one was reading and which two were waiting for rescue. Cornelia Foss's stillness had a forward quality — she was inside the sentence, working. The two boys produced the carefully arranged blankness of students who have learned to display attention without generating it. The ratio — one out of three with the forward stillness — was, in Marcus's experience, approximately a constant, across Latin and German and French and any other language that required this particular quality of sitting. He found it neither discouraging nor encouraging. It was a distribution.

After a moment: "Miss Foss."

She looked up.

"Tell me what the sentence is doing."

She paused. She was the kind of mind that checked an answer before it committed to it, which Marcus had identified early and respected, it being his own habit. "It's waiting," she said. "The whole thing — it holds open until the end. You can't close it until you have all of it."

"Yes."

He did not add to this. In his experience, the correctly made observation was its own sufficient reward; adding praise introduced an economy of approval that distorted the thing being observed. He let it be. She looked back at the board, and after a moment the two boys looked back at the board, and the lesson continued.

---

The period between his Latin class and the first German section was thirty-five minutes, which Marcus divided between the staffroom on the second floor and the set of translation exercises he had marked the previous night and had comments remaining for. The staffroom coffee was, in his considered opinion, the worst he had encountered in any English-speaking institution in two continents, and he had encountered it in a number of such institutions over the past several years. He drank it.

Stillman came in. He taught geography in rooms 201 and 202, moved through the building with the slightly compressed energy of someone who had recently been somewhere else and not quite fully arrived here. He poured coffee and stood at the counter.

"Odd business down at the harbor," he said. He said most things from across a room, as though physical distance were a conversational courtesy.

Marcus set down his pen.

"What kind of business?"

"Man washed in on the breakwater after the blow last week. No papers. Nothing on him at all. CG took the body and that's the last officially."

"Town clothes, they said? Not a fisherman?"

"That's what I heard." Stillman shrugged with one shoulder. "Nobody from here. Nobody from anywhere anyone knows about. Clement Ames was down at the fish pier when the CG truck came in."

Marcus turned this over in the way he handled incomplete information: not with narrative appetite, not with the urgency that transforms the unverified into the presumed, but with the steady attention of a man who had learned over many years that the significant quality of incomplete information was its incompleteness, and that the correct response was to note it and wait. A man with no papers, washed in from a three-day storm. The verified facts were few. The range of explanations was large and at present unnarrowed. He put it in the part of his mind that held things requiring more data before they could become anything — a part that had, over the past five years, accumulated considerably.

"Has anyone put out a description?" he said.

"Not that I know of." Stillman finished his coffee. "Sailor off a convoy is what most people are saying."

Marcus nodded and returned to the translation exercises.

---

He passed the principal's open door at twenty past nine. The door stood open, as it nearly always did — the principal being the kind of administrator who managed through visibility, the open door a performance of nothing to hide. On the desk, partially in view from the hallway, was a folder with Marcus's name on the tab, and in the line below the name, in the school secretary's round and deliberate hand, the notation the town meeting had appended to his original hire: *Continental educator.*

He had seen this folder before. He had sat across from it in March of 1942, when the principal had gone through the courses Marcus would be assuming, and again the following spring, when the question of the advanced German section had required a committee meeting at which the folder had been present as a kind of documentation — a note explaining to any future questioner why the school had hired a Viennese Jewish émigré in a town of eight hundred people two years into a war. *Continental educator* accounted for him without requiring anyone to decide what they thought about it. He had found, broadly, that this was how things were explained in Coldwater Reach, and that the explanation was neither hostile nor warm, but administrative — which was also, in its way, a form of accuracy.

He kept walking.

---

The afternoon walk covered the same ground reversed. Main Street had the different character of four-thirty: a line of women outside the butcher's door with their ration books, a delivery bicycle leaned against the diner's steps, three junior-school boys occupying the hardware store's stoop until the store owner appeared in the doorway and they relocated to the next block.

The Western Union boy's bicycle was leaned against the post office wall.

He kept walking.

He had been in Coldwater ten months before he watched, from approximately this distance, a woman receive a telegram at the post office door. It had been January — clear and cold, the kind of January light that made everything look precise and final — and he had been far enough away that he saw only the shape of it: the boy, the envelope, the woman's hands, and the quality of stillness that followed the exchange. He had known what was in the envelope before it was opened. The shape was unmistakable, once you had seen it in one country, in one administrative language or another. He had kept walking that day also.

This afternoon the bicycle stood unattended. Nobody came in or out of the post office while he passed. The empty doorway, the bicycle, the ordinary afternoon continuing on either side of them.

He walked down Elm Street. At the corner he did not stop, and the harbor appeared briefly and was flat and gray, the south dock still empty, and he turned north.

He thought of Sherbrooke for perhaps ten seconds. Not of the camp, not of the months — the dormitory, the other men from fifteen countries assembled by their common classification as the same kind of enemy, none of them having been in a position to do much about being Austrian in 1940 — but of the specific moment of arrival: the gate intake desk, the clerk's hand lifting the document from Marcus's coat pocket and placing it on the far side of the desk, and Marcus's own hands afterward, standing in the cold with no paper in them, not knowing quite what to do with themselves. He thought of this for ten seconds. Then he was at the Crow house, and he put his hand on the gate latch and lifted it and went in.

---

The kitchen was warm. Lillian was at the stove, the iron pan over the low burner, bread already cut on the board, the tea things arranged on the counter because there was not enough counter for the tea things and anything else. She heard him come in and did not turn.

"Cold getting into it," she said.

"Yes."

She set a plate on the table without asking what he wanted. She had not asked what he wanted in approximately eighteen months, because at some point in the first season of his residence his preferences had been established and were since treated as given facts, the way Lillian treated most things she had once established to her satisfaction. He hung his coat on the hook inside the door and sat down.

Below, Henry was in the boiler room. The sounds came up through the floor in the order Marcus had learned to follow across two winters: the knock of the pipe fitting, the steady sound of something turned, the occasional deep report of the boiler accepting what it had been given. The sounds of competent work, which Marcus had found were the same sounds regardless of the object they were applied to, and which were, in some way he had never fully articulated, reassuring — not because the boiler required reassurance, but because the sounds placed a capable person in the room below.

"How did school go?" Lillian said. She was not facing him.

"We read Cicero. More precisely, one student read Cicero and two students sat in the general area."

The sound she made was not quite a laugh but was in the same family. "German any better?"

"Somewhat."

She set the tea down and did not follow up the question. Marcus had learned, in this house, to understand the question asked and let go as a form of consideration rather than disinterest: she asked; she received; she moved on. The household had a register, and he had learned it the way he had learned every register in every house and institution he had occupied, and it was now, mostly, natural.

---

On the kitchen wall, hung from a nail above the window that looked toward the backyard: James Crow's Army photograph.

Formal. The kind taken before deployment: the uniform precise, the studio background a neutral gray, the set of his shoulders in the jacket partly the jacket's structure and partly the young man's own. He had a sergeant's formality in the way he held himself. Marcus looked at the photograph the way he looked at it each time he sat down at this table — with the attention that a face deserves and that absence makes available. He had never seen James Crow in motion. He knew the photograph, and the letters that arrived for Lillian with Pacific postmarks, and the particular adjustment in Henry's pace on the days when such a letter appeared.

He did not know James Crow. He had a static image and the outline of an absence and the sounds of a father working steadily in the room below, which was perhaps, at this distance, the truest version of a person available to him.

He ate his dinner.

Henry came up through the basement door partway through, crossed to the sink, turned on the tap.

"Fitting on the south loop's going to want replacing before December," he said.

"Will that be a difficult part to find?"

"Need to order it." Henry dried his hands on the side towel, looked at Marcus. "School all right?"

"Yes."

Henry nodded and went back downstairs.

---

His room was on the second floor, the window facing east over the yard. The curtain was heavy dark wool, the desk against the wall, the shelf holding more books than it had held in March of 1942, which was a kind of record. He sat on the edge of the bed with a book open across his knee and did not read it.

After a while came the sound of Henry closing the basement door — the sequence of steps from the back of the house forward — and then the house settled into its night disposition: the known sounds, the positioned quiet, nothing requiring response.

*Continental educator.* He had been carrying the phrase since mid-morning with the steady, absent quality he brought to things that had been said about him and that were not precisely wrong. In Vienna he had been Dr. Klein — a form of address, a specific weight in a room. In Paris he had been the Austrian, which was precisely if not unkindly meant. In London he had been the refugee, which was a category. In Sherbrooke he had been classified as the enemy alien, which was at least a position of known standing, even if the standing was wrongly arrived at. In Cambridge he had been the displaced scholar, which was accurate and was also, in its gentle way, a form of storage: a useful object held for later placement. In Coldwater he was the Continental educator, a phrase on a folder on a desk, which was all of these and was none of them.

He was, he thought, practicing something. The walk down Elm Street was a practice. The staffroom coffee was a practice. The kitchen downstairs and Lillian's plate set without asking and the sound of Henry's work coming up through the floor: all of this was practice. He was not certain — and he was, where he could be, precise about his certainties — whether what he was practicing was Coldwater or himself.

He closed the book and reached over and turned off the lamp.
