# The Visit

The letter had been in his desk drawer since November — center drawer, under the Latin dictionary, which was where he had put it and where it had remained while he decided, over the course of six weeks, what to do. That morning he had taken it out before the first class, held it in both hands for a moment, and placed it in his coat pocket. The act of placing it in his coat was the decision itself; the walking would settle what remained.

Henry had offered the truck the previous evening. Marcus had said it was no trouble, he would walk, and Henry had received this with the quiet attention he gave to information that did not quite add up and had chosen not to press it. He was not wrong not to press it. The reason Marcus had for declining was difficult to explain without sounding like a man who made things more effortful than they needed to be, which, in this instance, was essentially accurate. Movement was how he prepared for difficult things. It had been this in Vienna — he had walked the Ringstrasse before faculty meetings that required a particular positioning of himself — and it remained so in Coldwater, a town whose geography was flat enough to accommodate the habit without much planning.

He went out the back gate at quarter past eight, between the first class and the second, through a morning that was cold with a particular Maine January coldness: still air, temperatures well below freezing but without the sharp edge that wind would have given it, the sky an even dull white from the horizon up. He walked the harbor road to the bridge and then north on Route 1, where the town gave out within half a mile — the last storefront, a gap, a fence row, and then only the land.

He had three miles.

What he knew: Werner Grau had written from Portland in late September 1943, planning to travel up the coast to Coldwater in October, carrying news of a family in Ansbach that he would not commit to paper. What he knew less certainly, from secondhand accounts filtered through the staffroom and one conversation with Stillman: a man in town clothes had come in on the breakwater after the October storm, no papers, and the Coast Guard had classified it as an unidentified drowning and closed the case. What he had assembled, and kept assembled, over the weeks since November: the plausible connection between these two facts. Plausible was not proof. He had been careful, in his private accounting, to keep the distinction exact.

He knew also what he did not intend to say. He was not going to Albrecht Pfeiffer's farm to investigate. He had no standing for investigation and would not have known what to do with standing if it had been offered. He was going because the letter in his coat pocket was Albrecht Pfeiffer's letter — had always been Albrecht Pfeiffer's letter — and had come to Marcus only through a postal error and a school secretary's pragmatic decision, and it was not his to hold indefinitely. The misdelivery could be corrected. He was correcting it. If Albrecht Pfeiffer's response to receiving his letter told Marcus something he had not known before, Marcus would receive that information in whatever form it arrived and decide then what to do with it.

He would not, under any circumstances, mention Werner Grau's name or the body on the breakwater unless Albrecht opened that door. It was not his door.

The land past the last woodlots was drumlin country — long grass-covered hills left by the glaciers, lying in parallel ridges under their January white, the hay fields flat between them. He had walked this road once before, in his first spring, when the walking had been a kind of inventory of the place he had landed in, and he had found the agricultural plainness of it after coastal terrain surprising and then not surprising. Inland land looked like what it was for. There was a satisfaction in that.

The road bent west at a line of cedar fence posts. He found the farm road, which was dirt and hard and showed no tire tracks from the last few days, and turned onto it.

---

The farm materialized from behind a stand of red maples — leafless, the trunks dark with recent moisture, the lower branches still holding some snow. Then the barn came into view: gray board siding weathered to the particular silver of very old wood, the gambrel roof carrying a good eighteen inches of packed white on its south-facing pitch, the whole structure giving the impression — familiar to Marcus from a different part of the world, from the villages northeast of Vienna where his maternal grandmother had had relations — of something built with the expectation of lasting several lifetimes and now well along in delivering on that expectation.

He read the cornerstone as he entered the farmyard. 1763, half-covered in ice, the numerals carved in the flat-ended strokes of the period. Pre-Revolutionary. Built before the choices the Revolution required, by people who had not yet had to make them.

In the dooryard between the barn and the farmhouse, dry stalks stood through the snow at waist height, stripped by autumn to their skeletons, each branching terminal forked and bearing the dried ruin of seed heads — burred, compact, architecturally complete in their stripped state. *Arctium.* He had the Latin name before he had the English. He always did; it was an inconvenience of his training and he had long since stopped apologizing for it to himself.

The icehouse bunkhouse was visible past the barn's north corner — a small structure with a new wooden step and a bar-latch door, currently closed. As Marcus came across the frozen farmyard a POW emerged from the barn carrying a metal bucket, moving at the measured unhurried pace of a man who has found the exact ratio of effort to temperature and holds to it without thinking. He was one of the older ones — not Karl Reinmar; this man was in his mid-thirties or beyond, with the build of a man grown by agricultural work over many years, broad through the back and settled in his movement. He stopped when he saw Marcus. The stop was brief — two seconds at most — and it was the stop of a man conducting an assessment, which Marcus recognized because it was the stop of a man who has learned to assess strangers as a matter of course and to do it without display. Having completed the assessment, the POW went on with the bucket, neither hurried nor slow, without looking back.

He had been assessed this way in more than one country by men in a range of circumstances, and he knew its grammar. He nodded, once, at the POW's back, and continued toward the barn door.

---

Albrecht Pfeiffer was crouching at the wheel of a manure spreader — or rather at the axle housing, which he was examining with the close attentiveness of a man who has identified a problem and is deciding its complexity before deciding his response to it. He heard Marcus's footfall at approximately ten feet and straightened and turned.

He was in his middle fifties, thick through the shoulders, his face weathered by outdoor work beyond what his age alone would account for — not aged but used, in the way that outdoor faces in cold climates were used, the lines reading as information about the weather rather than as complaint. He looked at Marcus with a direct, unhurried attention that Marcus had encountered before in this part of the world: the attention of a man who was ready to hear a thing and had not yet decided whether the particular thing now arriving was the one he had been readying himself for.

Marcus introduced himself carefully. He taught at the school — German and Latin. He knew Hannah, who was a student in his advanced German section. In the fall, a piece of correspondence had been misdelivered to the school — addressed to Albrecht, in German — and the school secretary had passed it to Marcus on the grounds that it was in German and he would be best placed to handle it. He had been meaning to see it properly delivered. He reached into his coat and produced the envelope.

He watched Albrecht look at the envelope.

There was a small tightening around the eyes — something that moved quickly, a contraction and release, less than a second. Albrecht took the envelope from Marcus's hand with a steadiness that required, Marcus thought, a small effort to sustain. He looked at the return address. He looked at the postmark. He turned the envelope over, examined the back, and then opened it, drawing the letter out by its fold.

He read.

Marcus stood and did not look away. He had made a study, across the course of a life spent among many languages, of the face reading. A person receiving something they did not know had a particular quality of attention: the eyes moved carefully from line to line, the face open in the way of a container being filled, something held in readiness to adjust. A person receiving something they already knew had a different quality entirely. The attention was concentrated but abbreviated; the face still, and still in the way of a closed room rather than an open one. The pace of the eyes was quicker, not because the words were simpler but because the words were confirming rather than informing, and confirmation moved faster than discovery.

Albrecht Pfeiffer's face, reading Werner Grau's letter, was moving at the second rate.

There was a moment — midway through the first side, Marcus thought; Werner had used his full name in the middle of a sentence, not merely at the close — where something crossed Albrecht's face that Marcus found he could name precisely only after it had passed. It was not surprise. It was not grief, though grief was in the neighborhood of it. It was the expression of a man receiving what he had expected to receive and finding, as one always found, that the expectation had not been sufficient preparation for the arrival. Recognition of a specific kind: the kind that says *I knew this was coming*, and the confirmation says *yes*, and the *yes* requires something from the person hearing it that the waiting had not yet required.

Marcus had seen this face before. He had seen it in Vienna in 1938, on people reading the news, when the thing that could not happen had happened and their faces had shifted from the look of a person watching a storm gather to the look of a person on whom the storm had broken. He had worn some version of it himself — in Sherbrooke, when the intake clerk had placed his document on the far side of the desk and he had understood what the gesture meant before anyone had used words. Albrecht Pfeiffer was not reading news about a political catastrophe. He was reading a letter from a man who had planned to come to Coldwater in October, in a January that was three months past that October, and the letter was not information. It was Werner's voice, arriving after Werner.

Albrecht folded the letter. He held it across its center, both hands, and was still for a moment. Then he looked at Marcus.

"When did this come to you?" His English was careful — chosen, unhurried, the English of a man who was selecting a language rather than falling into it. Slightly formal without being stilted. Not the English of his household; the English of an occasion.

"November," Marcus said.

Albrecht nodded once. It was a slow nod, a full acknowledgment, not a mere receipt of information.

"Thank you," he said.

The two words were complete. They had in them a quality that Marcus recognized from other languages and other contexts: the quality of a door being closed from the inside. Not locked, not unfriendly — the hostility of a door slammed was entirely absent — but latched. The conversation was over. The question of whether there was anything further to say had been decided, quietly, without Marcus being consulted, and the decision had been reached before the question was raised, probably before Albrecht Pfeiffer had finished the letter's second side. *Thank you.* A full sentence. The space after it was not a pause; it was a close.

Marcus said it was no trouble. He did not say anything else. He did not say the things he was holding — the questions arranged behind the letter, the sequence he had assembled in six weeks of carrying the connection from November's discovery to this January morning. He had come with a letter. The letter was now Albrecht Pfeiffer's. What stood behind the letter was not Marcus's to present.

He turned and walked back down the farm road.

---

He did not look back. The red maples thinned and fell away behind him and the road ran straight between the drumlin fields under the white sky.

He ran the sequence.

Werner Grau had written to Albrecht Pfeiffer on September 28, 1943. He had planned to come to Coldwater in October. The body on the breakwater had arrived after the October storm: a man in town clothes, no papers, no vessel missing a man, the Portland finding a probable cardiac event, the Coast Guard case closed. The connection between these two facts was plausible; he had held it as plausible since November.

Albrecht Pfeiffer had read Werner Grau's letter and had not been surprised.

He had not been surprised by the name. He had not been surprised by the date or the contents or the fact of the letter's existence. He had read it with the face of a man receiving a confirmation rather than a discovery, and the confirmation he had received was not the contents of the letter — which were Werner's plans for a visit in October, plans now three months past — but the existence of the letter itself: Werner had written. Werner had planned to come. Werner had been Werner, three months ago and twenty years before that, Werner enough to write to Albrecht after however many years of American silence and to sign himself *Ihr alter Freund.*

Which meant — Marcus slowed on the iced rut without noticing he had slowed, the cold exact on his face, Route 1's utility poles visible now ahead in the distance — which meant that Albrecht Pfeiffer knew, had known since October, that Werner Grau had come to Coldwater and had not come back. He had been sitting with this knowledge through the fall and through December and into January, with no one to give it to and no apparent intention of giving it to anyone. The letter arriving was not news to him. It was Werner's voice, which he already knew had gone silent, speaking once more from the month before it went silent.

Marcus could not prove this. He had inference and a face, and the face was not courtroom evidence and would not be. But he had been reading faces and language for most of a lifetime, and the reading he had done at the barn door was the reading of a man who knows what he has seen.

Albrecht Pfeiffer had known Werner Grau had come to Coldwater.

Which meant he had seen Werner — or received word that Werner had come — before the storm.

He had been carrying this since October.

Marcus walked north. Route 1 came up and he turned onto it without deciding to. The cold was steady in his coat. He thought about the letter's weight — its actual physical weight, which had been slight, two pages written on a single sheet — and about the different weight he had been holding since November, the inferential weight, and about the way Albrecht Pfeiffer had folded the letter across its center and held it with both hands. There was a way a person held something when they had been waiting for it. The hands did not know how to be casual about it, whatever the face had decided.

He did not know what had happened on the night Werner Grau had died. He knew what was plausible; he knew, now, that Albrecht Pfeiffer knew more than was plausible. He did not know whether Werner had reached the farm that night or not. He did not know what Albrecht knew about the hours between Werner's arrival in Coldwater and the storm. He did not know and had no way to know, and had made no move, at the barn door, to ask — because he had not been offered the right to ask and would not have received an answer if he had taken the right uninvited.

He held what he had. It was not nothing. It was not enough to do anything with, and he was not at all certain what *do* would mean here, in any case.

The town came back around him gradually: the first outbuildings, then the fence rows tightening, then the first storefront with its wooden sign. He walked up Main Street and turned onto Elm and went up the hill toward the house.

---

Henry's truck was not in the yard. The front of the house was dark, the curtains in the parlor where Marcus never went drawn against the afternoon cold. He came around through the back gate, which was his entrance, and up the back step.

Lillian was at the stove, the lid of the soup pot sitting slightly ajar, the smell of it beginning to reach the room. She looked up when the door opened and looked back at the pot. This was her form of greeting, which Marcus had received nearly every evening for almost two years: *you are in, the meal is going, you are accounted for.* He had learned to receive it as what it was — not a performance of welcome but welcome itself, in the practical form it took in this household.

He took off his coat and hung it on the hook by the door.

The pocket, empty now, had the shape of its former contents — or he was giving it that shape, which amounted to the same thing. Three months the letter had been in his desk drawer. Three months he had been holding a plausible connection that was nobody else's business and that he had no authorized use for. He had carried it this morning from the drawer to his coat and down the farm road and into the farmyard and across the conversation that had consisted of an introduction, a delivery, and two short sentences, and he had left the letter in Albrecht Pfeiffer's hands, where it had always belonged. He had given the one thing over that he'd had any standing to give.

He stood at the hook.

What Marcus held now was not the letter. He held the inference — the sequence, the face, the folded paper held across its center — and these were not a thing he could put in a desk drawer, and he understood, standing at the coat hook with Lillian at the stove and the winter afternoon going dark outside the kitchen window, that he had known this before he'd started walking.

Lillian set two plates on the table.

He sat down.

# What She Didn't Ask

The homework was not going anywhere. Hannah had the German notebook open to the conditional letter — *Ich hoffe, wir werden uns bald sehen* — and the margin question she'd made on Thursday and meant to ask Marcus on Friday, except she had not asked on Friday, and now it was the following week and the notebook was open on the kitchen table and she was looking at the question mark instead of the sentence when she looked up.

A figure on the farm road. Far end, near the cedar fence posts, walking toward the barn.

She knew it in a moment, the way you know a person's approach before you have seen their face — the particular walk, the uprightness of it, the coat that was not a farm coat. Her German teacher walked everywhere; she knew this from school, from the post office line in November, from the way the town spoke about him with a residual mild puzzlement at a man who did not own a car. He walked, and this was him walking, three miles up the Pfeiffer farm road in January.

She stayed at the table. Her mother was in the window chair — the other window, south-facing, toward the crabapple and the stone wall where the cedar waxwings came — and had not looked up. Her mother rarely looked up at anything from the road. She sat with her cup and the gray outside and whatever she was watching that was not the yard.

Hannah watched.

---

Her father came out of the barn as Marcus reached the farmyard. She couldn't hear what passed — the kitchen was closed up against the cold, storm windows on, and even in summer she would have needed the door open to catch more than a sentence from across the yard. What she had was the window, and the window gave her: her father straightening from whatever he had been doing at the barn door, turning; Marcus stopping at a distance that was polite for outdoors, the way you stopped when you did not know a place well; her father's face, turned just enough toward the house that she could see the left side of it.

Marcus was speaking. She could see the small cloud of breath, and she knew from the slow regular pace of it that it was not a long speech, not an emergency. He reached into his coat.

Her father looked at what Marcus had produced. From the size and the flatness of what passed between them she thought: an envelope. Her father took it without looking at Marcus's face, the way you look at the thing itself when the thing itself is what you have been waiting for.

He opened it. He read.

She watched him read from the kitchen window, and what she saw was this: his head still, his shoulders still, his eyes moving down the page with the careful unhurried pace of a man who already knows the shape of what he is reading and is confirming the details rather than taking in the substance. She had never seen her father read a letter before. She did not know she had thought about how he read until she saw him doing it and found she had expected something different — expected his face to open the way her own did with a letter, taking in each line as if the line were a gift or a small surprise. His face did not open. It was still in the way of a room with the door closed, and the stillness was not blankness.

She had seen this stillness in him before. It was the stillness from the first week of October — his hands stopping on the knife and fork when she had said *a man nobody knows, no papers* — and then resuming, and him eating, and saying nothing, and her filing it without knowing what column it went in. She had carried that image for three months without a place to put it. Here it was again, the same stillness, and she still did not have a column.

Her father folded the paper. He said something to Marcus. One sentence, she thought; brief enough that she could watch Marcus take it in without his face changing. Marcus said something back. Her father nodded once, the slow confirming nod he used when something was settled. Marcus turned and walked back down the farm road without lingering.

Her father stood at the barn door for a long moment with the folded paper in his hands. He looked at it once more — not reading, just looking at the thing — and then went inside. Not the barn. The house.

Hannah looked down at her notebook. *Ich hoffe.* The question mark in the margin was still there.

---

He came through the kitchen door without looking up from what he was doing, which was putting the folded paper into the inside pocket of his coat — the deeper pocket, the one he used for things he meant to keep. He went to the basin and washed his hands in the way he always washed his hands after barn work: deliberate, thorough, the same number of strokes she had watched since she could remember watching anything. He dried on the towel behind the basin and turned toward the table and then he saw her.

His face settled. It went from wherever it had been into the face he used for looking at her — not cold, not unkind, but arranged.

She stood and put the kettle on. She cut bread. Her hands did them without instruction while her attention was still partly at the window.

He sat. She put the bread and the coffee cup before him. He put both hands around the cup without pouring.

She sat across from him. Through the south window she could see the edge of her mother's chair — Magda's shoulder, the dark cardigan, the angle of her head toward the crabapple. Whether her mother was watching the birds or resting her eyes on nothing was a thing Hannah had stopped trying to determine. The silence in this kitchen had two shapes. Her father's was the kind with something arranged behind it, pressed against an interior wall. Her mother's had let go of whatever it had once been pressing against. Right now the kitchen had both.

Her father's hands were around the cup.

The folded paper was in his coat pocket.

There were things she could ask. She sorted through them while she sat with her German notebook still open in front of her, the conditional letter she had been translating before the figure appeared on the road. She could ask who that man was on the farm road — she knew who it was, her German teacher, Dr. Klein, three miles in January on foot, which was not an accident of proximity and which meant something she didn't know. She could ask what he had brought, what was in the envelope. She could ask whether her father had known anything, since October, about the man on the breakwater, the man in town clothes with no papers that the school and the diner and the post office had turned into a drunk sailor with a debt and a wife, which she had never believed, because of the hands stopping on the fork.

These questions were all available to her. She held them and did not ask them. She had been doing it for months with her mother's silence and her father's German and Karl in the farmyard and the lamp in the icehouse at night; she was practiced at it.

She asked: had the herd count been off this week, or had she miscounted on Tuesday. She had thought the number came up short by one but she might have gone too fast through the east stalls.

Her father looked at her. He was still for a moment. Then:

"No," he said. "The count is right. You miscounted."

She nodded. She had thought so.

She was beginning to frame the next thing — something about the manure spreader and the axle, which she had noticed him working on — when she stopped. Because he had answered her in English. He had said *no* and *the count is right* and *you miscounted* in his careful chosen English, the English she had not heard from him at the kitchen table since sometime in the spring, the English of a man who selected a language rather than fell into it. She had been waiting for that English for months without knowing she was waiting for it, and now it had arrived to answer a question about cows and she was so surprised she did not say anything at all.

He poured his coffee. He looked at the window.

She did not ask about the manure spreader. She did not ask anything else.

---

After supper she washed the dishes while her father sat in his chair by the lamp with the farm accounts ledger open on his knee. Magda had gone to bed early. The kitchen was quiet — the stove settling, the January wind off the bay in the eaves, a higher more even register than the October wind, sustained and without the gusts.

Hannah washed each bowl and cup and set it in the rack. The dish water was hot; her hands went pink in it. Outside the window the farmyard was dark — the icehouse, the shapes of the burdock stalks in the field beyond, the black line of the cedar fence posts along the road. No lamp in the icehouse window. The four Germans would be asleep by now or quiet, their voices settling for the night the way the barn settled after the evening feeding.

Her father's coat was on the hook by the door. The folded paper was in it; she knew it was there because she had watched him put it there and had watched him at supper make no move to take it out again, not once through the meal, just sitting with it in the coat on the hook behind him as though the coat were an ordinary coat and the paper were an ordinary paper and neither required any particular attention or explanation.

It was six feet from her hands to the hook.

She did not cross the six feet. She had thought about it once, briefly, when she was setting the table and her father was still in the barn for the evening check — the thought arrived clean and factual: *you could look at it.* She had thought: yes. And then she had set the plates and that had been that.

When the dishes were done she dried her hands, said good night, took the lamp upstairs.

---

The bedroom was cold the way it was always cold in January until the lamp had been burning for a while. She got into bed with her socks on and pulled the quilt up and lay on her back and looked at the ceiling.

She thought about who wrote to her father in German. There had always been letters in German — she had seen them going back as far as she had any memory of the mail, European handwriting on envelopes that arrived and went somewhere, she'd never asked where, the same way she had never asked a great number of things that were simply part of the texture of this household, the way *danke* was part of the texture, the way his silence at supper had become part of the texture, the way *Ich weiß nicht* from across the barn meant the decision was not made yet.

She thought about Dr. Klein walking three miles in January, declining whatever easier arrangement might have existed, because the thing in the envelope required a person and not the mail. She had seen enough of him at school — the way he came at grammar from the Latin side first, the way he carried the German word in front of the English word as if the German were the precision and the English the approximation — to understand that he was not a man who made gestures without considering what the gesture cost.

She thought about her father's English. *The count is right. You miscounted.* Both sentences precise and plain, the careful careful English that belonged to the occasions he had decided required exactness. She tried to count forward from the last time she had heard it at this table. She could not reach the beginning. The months since spring had accumulated into one long German winter without landmarks, and the English she had stopped expecting had arrived today to answer a question about cows.

Why that question. Why today.

There was something in it she could almost reach, a shape she could see the edge of without being able to see the whole. As if the paper in his coat had loosened something that had been held very still for a long time, and the only thing that had leaked through was one sentence in the country's language — not an explanation, not a name, not anything she could fit against the things she did not know. Just *you miscounted*, in English, and the cup held between his hands without being poured.

She had the questions. She just did not know how to ask them of a man who had closed himself so thoroughly for so long that a sentence about cows felt like something she might break if she pressed on it.

The lamp guttered; she turned it down before the oil was gone.

In the dark the questions arranged themselves in the order she had been turning them, and went on arranging themselves, and she held them with no place to put them — a letter in an inside pocket, the stillness on her father's face, the English like a door opened half an inch — and eventually she slept.

## 10-what-she-didnt-ask

### Meta-commentary on cognition

1. **Cut:** `— and that was a strange thing to think, and she noted it and did not say it`
   From: `…the way you look at the thing itself when the thing itself is what you have been waiting for — and that was a strange thing to think, and she noted it and did not say it.`
   The image of Albrecht taking the envelope "the way you look at the thing itself when the thing itself is what you have been waiting for" already lands. The tail annotates her noticing the thought ("she noted it"), which is the style guide's exact example. Cut; sentence now ends at "for."

2. **Cut:** `She had learned to tell the difference.`
   From the two-shapes-of-silence passage. The immediately prior two sentences demonstrate the distinction precisely; the label states what the reader has just seen demonstrated.

3. **Cut:** `— the thought arrived and she held it and examined it —`
   Parenthetical inside "She could ask — the thought arrived and she held it and examined it — whether her father had known anything…" Labels the arrival and examination of a thought the narrative is already enacting. Removal makes "She could ask whether her father…" direct.

4. **Cut:** `and was aware she was holding them, which was different from not noticing.`
   From "She held them and did not ask them and was aware she was holding them, which was different from not noticing." The action (held, did not ask) is the point; adding meta-awareness of the holding explains what the prose already does.

5. **Cut:** `She turned this over.`
   Precedes "There was something in it she could almost reach…" — labels the act of reflection that the following sentence performs. Dead weight.

### Thesis restatement

6. **Cut:** `Noticing and not asking was the thing she did.`
   Follows the "was aware she was holding them" cut (same sentence cluster). States the chapter's governing theme in abstract terms. The chapter title and every scene demonstrate this; no announcement needed.

### Emotional structural analysis

7. **Cut:** `The face of a man who has decided that what he is carrying is his own and has made that decision so thoroughly that it holds even when he doesn't know he's being watched.`
   After "His face settled. It went from wherever it had been into the face he used for looking at her — not cold, not unkind, but arranged." The dramatization is complete at "arranged." The following sentence explains the architecture of "arranged."

8. **Cut:** `These were the things you did in January when someone came in from outside;`
   From the sentence `These were the things you did in January when someone came in from outside; her hands did them without instruction while her attention was still partly at the window.` The actions (kettle, bread) are self-evident; the clause explains their seasonal logic. Remainder, "Her hands did them without instruction while her attention was still partly at the window," kept as it carries real information about her distraction.

9. **Cut:** `; it was a form of skill that felt, this afternoon, more like a weight than a skill.`
   End of "She had been doing it for months with her mother's silence and her father's German and Karl in the farmyard and the lamp in the icehouse at night; she was practiced at it; it was a form of skill that felt, this afternoon, more like a weight than a skill." After the earned enumeration and "she was practiced at it," the appended emotional label diagrams what the list already conveys.

### Post-scene subtext naming

10. **Cut:** `Three miles in January was a considered gesture.`
    Final sentence of the Dr. Klein paragraph in Hannah's bedtime reflection. The prior two sentences — "declining whatever easier arrangement might have existed, because the thing in the envelope required a person and not the mail" and "he was not a man who made gestures without considering what the gesture cost" — already name the deliberateness. The closing sentence repeats the same point as a caption.

# Chapter Eleven — Load Calculations

She was three entries into the December fuel receipts when the door opened. The man said his name — Tarbell, Amos Tarbell — and the county harbor authority, and that he was here for the routine inspection.

Eira put down her pen. "Harbormaster Bowman," she said. "I've been expecting someone from the county."

He had a clipboard with a county authority form already clipped to the board and a brown wool overcoat that had been brushed clean. Mid-thirties. His politeness had the quality of a specific instruction carefully followed.

"How long have you held this position?" he asked.

"Eight years."

"Prior experience in harbor operations?"

"Assistant harbormaster. Under the previous harbormaster." She let him write. "Owen Bowman. My husband."

He looked up once. Then he looked back at his clipboard.

"How long as assistant?"

"Four years."

"You currently have no assistant of your own."

"Since January 1942. He enlisted." She kept her voice even. "The county authority hasn't authorized a replacement. I've managed without one."

He wrote something on his form. She could not read it from across the desk.

She had laid the winter documents out on the table before he came: the mooring registry open to the current page, the fuel allocation ledger beside it, the vessel registration file beneath. The safety inspection folder was on the shelf; she would take it down when they reached it.

She walked him through the mooring registry. Each vessel currently on a winter mooring in the inner harbor: the lobster boats Ida May, Sadie H., and Clara B., and three others on the west float; the dragger East Wind; the cold storage skiff; the Ellsworth against the east float on her winter berth. Seventeen vessels in total. She named each one, its registration status, its current mooring position. He checked them against his form. He did not find a discrepancy, because there was not one.

The fuel allocation ledger was next. Wartime supplemental allocation for harbor operations: every vessel drawing against the harbor's quarterly allotment from the Department of the Interior was entered by vessel name, date, and quantity in gallons, each entry initialed. The column balanced to the gallon.

"The authorization document?" Tarbell asked.

She took it from the folder beneath the ledger. He read through it. He handed it back without comment.

They went outside.

February cold, flat gray sky, the harbor on an ebbing tide. The dragger that worked the offshore grounds had gone out at first light and would not be back until afternoon. The Ellsworth sat against the east float with her forward lines gone slack in the ebb. The compressor at the cold storage house ran in a steady cycle. The inner harbor water was undisturbed except where the tide drew over the submerged ledge at the harbor mouth.

Tarbell walked the length of the pier to the breakwater end. She walked beside him. He asked about the depth at the elbow at mean low water, the height of the inner float at mean high water, the fuel storage configuration. He asked whether the tank was inside the hundred-foot setback from the waterline.

"Inside," she said. "By eight feet. The wartime exception was filed in June of 1942."

"Section four."

"Subsection B."

He wrote it down. At the pier head he stopped and looked at the harbor for a moment without writing anything. She stood beside him and looked at the same water. The sky was low and the gray ran without break from the cloud to the harbor surface.

"Everything here appears to be in order," he said.

"Yes," she said.

They went back inside.

The vessel registration file came next, then the safety inspection folder. Forty-two active vessel registrations, all current, no lapses, no outstanding renewals. The safety inspections for the winter-berthed vessels complete; the summer boats scheduled for spring before the season opened, the schedule printed on the folder's back page. He read the schedule. He made a note. His form was nearly full.

Tarbell sat down across the desk. He set his pencil on the clipboard.

"I want to ask you about the formal basis of your appointment," he said. "The — transitional nature of it."

She opened the bottom drawer and took out a folder she had kept there since 1935. Inside was a single typed letter on county authority letterhead. She set it on the table in front of him.

"November 21, 1935," she said. "Signed by Director Pearce. It appoints me harbormaster of Coldwater Reach pending formal review by the county harbor authority board."

Tarbell picked up the letter. He read it. He had the look of a man reading something he had already been briefed on — the eyes moving at the speed of confirmation.

"This review," he said. "It was scheduled?"

"December 1935. Then rescheduled. Then not rescheduled again."

"You never pressed for it."

"I did the work," she said. "The review would have confirmed what the work showed. I took it to be the board's matter to pursue."

He turned the letter over. The back was blank. He set it face up.

"You might have requested formal appointment on your own initiative," he said.

"I might have," she said. "What I did instead was manage the harbor."

She let that sit. Outside, the compressor cycled off and ran. The last of the ebb moved through the pilings.

"There is one more thing I'd like to show you," she said.

She went to the north shelf and took down the harbor log for 1935. Green board cover, the year inked on the spine in Owen's hand — a forward-leaning cursive with compressed vowels and the particular t-crossings that ran slightly below the stalk. The log she had opened more times than she had ever counted, for reasons she did not examine. She set it on the desk and opened it to November.

November 7. *Barometer 29.4, NE backing N, Beaufort 5 outer harbor. Doubled all moorings afternoon watch. Advised small craft haul 1600. E. Anderson dory on A-ring 1645. Harbor secure 1800.* Owen's entries were that way: terse, accurate, complete. She had been reading them for eight years and could still hear his attention in the abbreviations — the way a man writes when he is doing the actual work and the writing is the record of the work, not a separate act.

November 8 was blank.

November 9 was hers. *Barometer 29.2, NW 8, seas 4–6 outer harbor, abating. O. Bowman, harbormaster, missing evening 7 November. Search conducted CG Sprucehead and harbor tender. Body not yet recovered. Harbor open. All moorings secure.* Her own hand, smaller and more vertical than his.

"A continuity of record," she said. "Unbroken."

Tarbell looked at both entries for longer than he had looked at anything else in the shed. He read November 7 and then November 9. He looked at the blank November 8 in between them. He set his pencil down flat on the clipboard.

"November 7 to November 9," he said.

"Forty hours."

He picked up the pencil and wrote something on his form. It was the longest entry he had made all morning. She did not try to read it.

There was a pause. The cold storage compressor ran outside. The harbor was quiet the way it was always quiet in February — the boats that were left had already found their winter arrangement; the pier held only the sounds of the tide.

"I want to tell you," Tarbell said, "that there are some parties on the county board who have expressed concerns. About the long-term stability of the arrangement."

"Stability," she said.

"The formal basis of your appointment." He stopped. He started again. "They believe the matter of formal confirmation should be addressed."

"What would constitute a satisfactory confirmation?" she asked. "In the board's view."

He turned the pencil between his fingers. He was choosing words. He chose them and they did not constitute a direct answer.

"The board's preference," he said, "is that the appointment be placed on a formally established footing."

"What process would satisfy the board?"

He looked at the county authority letter on the desk. He looked at his clipboard. He looked at the window.

He did not answer.

She gave him one more moment. He did not fill it.

"I see," she said.

Tarbell gathered his clipboard and reached for the county authority letter. He asked whether he could take it to copy for his file; she said yes, and asked him to return it when he was done. He put it in his briefcase. He stood. He said he would file his report with the county authority office by the end of the week. He thanked her for her time.

"Thank you for coming," she said.

She walked him to the door. She stood in the doorway and watched him cross the pier and turn up the road toward town. The tide had turned; the Ellsworth's forward lines had gone taut again. She noted the time: twenty past eleven.

Inside, she put the 1935 harbor log back on the north shelf. She returned the fuel ledger and the vessel registration file and the safety inspection folder to their places. She straightened the table.

Then she put the kettle on.

The harbor lay in February quiet: the dragger out, the Ellsworth cold at the east float, the lobster boats on their moorings with their bow lines leading east into the turned current. Ice on the float cleats, thin enough to break with a boot. The cold storage house ran steady. The sky was flat and would not change before dark.

She looked at the north shelf. The harbor logs ran left to right across it — the years in Owen's hand, then the 1935 volume with both their hands in it, then hers from 1936 on. Eight spines in a row, identical green board. The column ran unbroken.

The water came to the boil. She poured her cup and went back to the December fuel receipts.

# Chapter Twelve — Ansbach

The fourth cow on his row was the old one, the one that would kick if you came at her from the left. He came from the right, settled on the three-legged stool, and began. The milk came down in the rhythm he had learned. This had surprised him — that his hands could learn a new herd. His father kept Simmental on the farm in Ansbach, brown and cream, and these were Holstein, black and white, and the cold here was a different cold, harder at its edge, without the softness the Franconian hills put into winter. But the hands had learned without needing to be told.

Four months. He held the number the way you hold a stone: not warm yet, not simply part of the weight you carry, but manageable.

He did not count toward an end. There was no end to count toward. The war would end when it ended. Until then there was this row of cows and the pail going heavier and the barn smelling of hay and dung and animal-warm, which smelled the same in Maine as in Bavaria. This sameness was not comfort.

The bakery on Karolinenstraße opened at five. By six the smell reached the kitchen window — the sweetness of *Hefegebäck* in morning cold — and his mother would call from the back of the house. Not urgently. Just the daily calling of his name from a known direction, which meant: you are here, it is morning, this is still the place.

He held this for a moment. Then he set it down.

Not buried. Set down at his side.

---

Through the barn door he could see across the farmyard. The sky had begun to lighten at its far edge — not sunrise yet, but what comes before it: the sky deciding. Hannah Pfeiffer crossed from the henhouse toward the feed shed, her coat buttoned to the collar, her breath a white cloud, a pail in each hand.

He watched.

She did not look through him. Fischer and Bauer and Hentschel were present — men in the same difficulty, which was a kind of presence — and Reed the guard was present as a watcher: noting him, accounting for him, not seeing him. Old Pfeiffer moved between barn and house with the quality of a man who had placed himself somewhere by accident and had found no procedure for revising it. The Army men who came each month with the supply truck were a form, a function, a category.

Hannah looked at him like a person at a specific person.

There had been the bird — *Seidenschwanz* — and she had said the English back, and after that she had said his name. *Karl.* He had been called many things. That word, said that way, was not common.

He did not have German or English for what this was. He knew it was not nothing.

---

The waxwing arrived at the fence post at the barn door without any announcement, the way they always arrived: already there when you looked. Black mask, yellow tail-tip, the small red wax of the secondary feathers.

"*Seidenschwanz*," he said. Quietly, so as not to startle it.

He kept a count. Forty-one birds since October, each given its German name and held in some interior list he had not meant to start keeping. It had begun with this one — the waxwing in the autumn, the first bird he had recognized at a distance in a country where none of the field-names matched anything he carried. And then the others, one by one: *Meisen* for the chickadees, black cap and white cheek, the same birds you found in any German woodlot; *Graureiher* for the great blue heron that came to the drainage ditch at the low end of the east field; *Bussard* for the red-tailed hawk that worked the north stone wall in the afternoon light. The small brown ones that moved through the meadow in January flocks he had not been able to name with certainty — he thought *Ammern*, something in the bunting family, but he was not sure.

It was not nostalgia.

The waxwing turned its head and looked at nothing in particular.

---

Fischer had said it last Tuesday, quietly, in the icehouse after supper. Not to Karl specifically — Fischer's way was to make announcements to the air and leave the air to distribute them. He had been a *Feldwebel*, a sergeant, and he kept his accounts.

*"Der Mann, der dich besuchen sollte. Er ist nicht gekommen."*

The man who was supposed to visit you. He didn't come.

Karl had known this already. He had known it since November, though in November he had been calling it something else — delay, the slowness of wartime mail. By December he had stopped calling it anything. It had become a shape: a gap in a fence line where the rail is missing. You know the gap when you reach it.

In September, a scrap of paper had come folded inside his mother's monthly letter. Three sentences in German, no name signed. Werner Grau, who had known Karl's father from the years on Karolinenstraße, was now in America. Werner hoped, if circumstances allowed, to arrange some contact. If it was possible.

He had read those three sentences until he could say them in his sleep.

October: nothing. November: nothing. December: nothing. January, and Fischer's voice in the icehouse, making the accounting that Fischer always made.

Karl had nodded at the air and returned to his bread. There was nothing to say in return. Fischer had not known Werner or Karl's father and had only heard something through whatever channel Fischer used for such things.

---

What he turned in his mind now — he moved to the next cow in the row and sat and set his hands to the work and let the thought run alongside it — was not the absence of contact itself. Men in wartime did not keep appointments. Men in wartime died or were arrested or crossed a border at the wrong moment and went into some process that had no window in it. He had been away long enough to know this; he had seen the gap in the fence from both sides.

The thing he kept turning was this: Werner Grau had come all this way. *Amerika.* Not by accident. He had made a plan and the plan had included Maine and had been close enough to completion that the three sentences could be sent, that the unsigned note could travel inside his mother's letter to this barn, to this farm, to a boy milking cows who was also from Karolinenstraße and would understand who Werner Grau was.

And then the October storm. Karl had watched it from the icehouse window: three days of wind and rain from the northeast, beginning the night of the eleventh or the twelfth, the lower field going to mud, the hay bent flat along the ground. He had watched it and not thought anything particular about it at the time — it had been weather, the weather of this place, harder than what he knew.

He did not think Werner had simply been lost in it. He thought Werner had found something, or come close to finding it, and that the storm had been the last thing in a sequence Karl could not see from inside the icehouse. He thought the gap in the fence was Werner — Werner who had crossed the Atlantic when crossing the Atlantic was not a small thing, who had found his way to Maine, who had known where the farm was and who was on it, and who had not come.

Karl did not know what had happened. He knew the shape. He knew the shape and he knew he was not going to learn the rest of it from here, in this barn, in a language of twelve words.

He set the pail down and moved to the last cow on his row.

---

The waxwing lifted from the fence post. It crossed the farmyard in a low arc, unhurried, and disappeared into the woodlot at the far edge of the field.

He watched the treeline for a moment. The woodlot held the bird — inside and invisible, already become a sound among sounds.

The barn was warm with the bodies of cows. Not the warmth a stove makes, arriving from one direction and weakening with distance, but the warmth of animals: patient, surrounding, the same in any country. His breath still showed. Outside the cold had not changed. But inside the warmth the work continued and the cold was only a fact about the air beyond the door, and he could hold that.

He heard Hannah cross the farmyard again. The empty pail swung from her hand and caught the fence post with a small sound. She did not look toward the barn.

*Seidenschwanz.* Gone.

He set his hands back to the work.

# Chapter Thirteen — Displaced Scholars

The translation papers were in alphabetical order, as Marcus had trained himself to keep them, and the name at the top was Pfeiffer.

He had six students in the advanced German section. Two were seniors who had enrolled to satisfy a modern-language requirement and who wrote translations that were technically correct in the manner of things produced under mild compulsion. Three were juniors of varying ability; a boy named Graves had a natural ear for German syntax but lacked the patience for the long clause, which was a correctable problem Marcus had been correcting since September. The sixth was Hannah Pfeiffer, who was also a junior and whose work Marcus graded first not because she required more attention — she required less than any other student in the section — but because her translations tended to establish the ceiling for the evening's task, and the ceiling, once identified, made everything below it easier to assess.

Tonight's passage was from Schiller. Five lines from *Die Bürgschaft*, short and subordinate-heavy, with two dependent clauses that required the student to decide where the sentence's weight fell. The predictable failure with such constructions — the one he had spent half the autumn correcting in the intermediate section — was to flatten them: to take the weight of a dependent structure and distribute it evenly across the sentence, producing translations that were accurate and empty. In the advanced section Marcus was marking for something a Vienna professor he had once admired called *die Entscheidung der Unterordnung*, the decision of subordination — not whether the student could identify the clause but whether they understood what its dependence was doing to everything around it.

He read Hannah Pfeiffer's rendering:

*Though he who asks is master of the hour, the thing asked for lives in a different grammar.*

The original was more compressed; she had given herself room. The word *grammar* was her own interpolation, absent from Schiller's German, which had *Zeit*, time. As a rendering it was less accurate than Schiller's word. As a reading of the construction — of what the subordination was for, of why the clause held its position in the sentence rather than dissolving into the main verb — it was more precise than anything Marcus could have specified in the assignment.

He took up his pencil and wrote in the margin: *The grammar of the subordinate clause is not decoration — it is the shape of what is being withheld.* He considered the sentence for a moment, then left it. She would understand what the note was about, or she would ask him on Friday, and either would serve the instruction.

He moved through the remaining five papers in forty minutes. The classroom was empty; Henry had come through with the push broom at half past three and not returned. The afternoon light through the south-facing windows had thinned — March, longer now than February and not warm, the late light catching the dust on the glass at a low angle. The heating pipes ticked in the wall behind the blackboard. Forty minutes, and he set the graded stack to his left and uncapped his pen.

He had been composing the letter to Sondheimer in his head for nine days. The content required no composition — a name, a description, a question. What had taken nine days was the framing. In twenty years of letters written under circumstances where the wrong word could establish the wrong thing, Marcus had learned that the architecture of a request carried as much weight as its substance.

Dr. Heinrich Sondheimer's position at Columbia was nominally in the German department, but his actual function — as Marcus had understood since his own time on the Emergency Committee rolls, in the autumn of 1941 — was closer to that of an archivist of displacement. He had been on the intake end of the rescue network that the Committee had assembled as the war made rescue necessary: the person who matched names to placements, who held the files, who knew which scholars and artists had passed through the system and which had simply vanished somewhere in the gap between one country's border and another's paperwork. It was not an official position. It was a position constituted entirely by memory, by the particular willingness to keep track of people because someone ought to. In Marcus's experience, such positions were more reliable than official ones.

He wrote:

*Dear Dr. Sondheimer,*

*I hope you are well. I write on a matter of administrative record that falls, I believe, within the range of your particular knowledge. I am trying to establish the history of a Werner Grau — German national, painter or laborer by occupation, last known address Portland, Maine — specifically whether he appears on any Emergency Committee roll or affiliated rescue register, and whether his immigration status in the United States was ever formalized. I ask as a matter of private inquiry, not on behalf of any institution or authority. I have reason to believe Mr. Grau may have been in the Boston area around 1936, and that he has been in the United States since approximately that time.*

*Any record you hold, or any channel you might pursue on my behalf, would be of genuine assistance.*

He read the letter back once. The phrase *a matter of private inquiry* was accurate and included what it did not state. The phrase *any channel you might pursue* communicated that this was a question for informal handling — through the network of people who held such things in filing cabinets and memory rather than in any official record.

This was approximately true.

He was addressing the envelope when the thought arrived: what he had described was Marcus Klein in 1940.

A man without the correct documentation in a country not constructed for him. A man whose standing depended on a committee's willingness and a series of telephone calls between people who had been, at least, willing to make them. A man who could be required, at any moment, to demonstrate what he was doing here and whether anyone official had approved it.

He had been, in the autumn of that year and the winter that followed it, a Werner Grau.

He did not write this in the letter to Sondheimer. He did not write it anywhere. He pressed the envelope flap closed and set it on the right side of the desk where he kept things requiring the post. Then he sat for a moment in the quiet of the classroom — the graded papers on his left, the thin March light leaving the window glass, the heating pipes gone still — and held the thought in the way he had learned, at Sherbrooke, to hold thoughts that had nowhere to go.

---

The road from the school to Henry and Lillian's house was three blocks toward the harbor and then one block west. He had walked it for two years in every condition this section of the Maine coast offered, and he had come to know it with the intimacy that daily repetition produces: not attachment, exactly, but familiarity so complete it had become spatial memory, each crack in the pavement belonging to its season. The spring thaw was at its worst this week — the road heaved, the edges soft, the ground giving back what it had been holding since December. He knew the smell of it. He had not expected, when he first walked this road, to come to know its smell by season as a fact of his own life, the way he knew the smell of the Ringstraße in December or the particular damp of the Paris sixth in autumn. He knew it. He walked through it.

He came in at the side door, as Lillian had told him to in his first week.

She was at the table with her cup and a length of white fabric, a piece of church sewing Marcus had seen in various states of progress for the past three weeks. Henry was across from her, and between them lay a V-Mail letter — the small photographed form, reduced by the postal process, that was what arrived when something arrived from the Pacific. The letter had the position of a thing already read and placed back with care: not put away, not left carelessly, but replaced as if putting it elsewhere had not yet been decided.

"James," Lillian said. She had not looked up.

He set his coat on the hook. "Good news?"

"He's well." She smoothed the edge of the envelope. "Somewhere he can't say."

Henry did not add anything. He drank his coffee.

Lillian read a portion of it aloud. The part she chose: James had received a meal that had given him a new and firmly held position on the subject of Army provisioning, which he had committed to paper — he noted it was the most cogent military document of the current conflict — and sent up the chain. Two weeks later, on a separate ship, a crate of canned peaches had arrived. He took this as the official reply. He asked whether the school boiler was behaving. He asked whether Mr. Marcus had been informed about the spring mud, and if not, whether someone could see to it before the term was too far gone.

Marcus said he had been informed.

Henry smiled briefly — reserving, as he always did, the full extent of it.

They sat. Lillian returned to her sewing. The kitchen was warm from the stove and from the radiator Henry had bled last week, which now ran without the complaint it had been making since January. The smell of the kitchen — coffee from the morning and something from supper that Marcus had missed, and beneath both of these the particular smell of the house itself, which Marcus had stopped noticing as foreign sometime around November — was familiar in the way the road was familiar.

Henry stood and rinsed his cup at the sink. He crossed to the small shelf above the kitchen radiator — the shelf that held the clock, the accumulated mail, and the one or two objects a household gathers over twenty years without deliberate selection — and placed James's letter under the clock. He had done this with every letter from James since the first one, in the spring of 1942. The clock held the paper flat. The letter did not go anywhere else.

He stood for a moment and looked at the photograph on the wall.

James in his uniform, taken at Camp Upton before he shipped — standing before some building Marcus did not recognize, shoulders squared, the expression of a man being photographed: present, composed, held slightly in reserve. The photograph had been on that wall for eighteen months.

Henry looked at it for perhaps half a minute. He did not say anything. Then he went through to the back of the house, where a pipe had been making a small complaint since the previous week.

Lillian said nothing. Marcus drank his coffee.

He had written letters like James's letters, from Paris, from London, from Sherbrooke in the months when letters were permitted, and the letters had been full of meals and small complaints and inquiries about things at home that were not the things he was thinking about. He knew what James's letter contained that was not in the portion Lillian had read. He did not say this. He sat with his cup and listened to the pipe being attended to in the back of the house, and when Lillian refilled his cup he said thank you and meant it precisely.

---

Sondheimer's reply came on a Friday, nine days after Marcus had posted the letter.

He found it in his school mailbox before the first class — addressed in Sondheimer's direct hand, the handwriting of someone for whom a letter is a professional instrument. Marcus read it standing at the mailboxes, then took it to his classroom and read it again at his desk, with the deliberate attention the contents required.

Sondheimer had made a telephone call to a contact in the Boston office. That contact had made another. The answer: Werner Grau, German national. Entered the United States at Boston in March 1936, on a one-year visa sponsored by the Boston Alliance for the Arts, which had brought over a small group of painters and printmakers under a cultural exchange program that ended when its funding was redirected in 1937. The visa had been renewed once, in March of 1937. It had expired in March of 1940. After that: no renewal application on record, no deportation proceeding initiated, no departure recorded.

He had been in the country without legal standing for nearly four years. From the spring of 1940 to October 1943, Werner Grau had been in the United States in the way that many men in those years had been in countries not their own: by the extension of circumstances originally intended as temporary, prolonged by a war that had made the simplest crossings impossible, sustained by the patience of whoever around him had chosen not to ask.

Marcus placed the letter beside the folder in the bottom drawer of his classroom desk: his transcription of the letter Werner had written to Albrecht Pfeiffer, set down before returning the original in January; the two pages of careful handwriting Marcus had made for himself in December, his private account of what he knew and the chain by which he had come to know it. Three documents. They occupied the space where a Latin dictionary usually rested. He looked at them briefly, then closed the drawer.

Werner Grau had been, by the classification the relevant governments applied, an enemy alien without formal standing. As had Marcus Klein, at Sherbrooke, in 1940: held for ten months under a warrant whose precise language Marcus had never been shown, released to the Committee rolls in a country that had not yet settled what to do with him. The form of Werner's situation was different. The underlying condition was the same: a man whose right to be where he was could not be demonstrated to any authority that chose to examine it.

If the body on the breakwater had been identified — if the file at Sprucehead bore a name rather than a blank — Werner Grau's four years without papers would have become the first fact of the official record. A German national, undocumented, found drowned on the Maine coast in October 1943. The sentences organized themselves cleanly. They were not false. They were simply not an account of anything that mattered about Werner Grau.

He sat with the drawer closed and the translation papers on his left, marked, ready for return in the morning. On top: Hannah Pfeiffer's Schiller, the word *grammar* in the third line, the note in his own hand in the margin. The March light had gone off the roofline of the building opposite. The heating pipes had been quiet for an hour.

He was not going to report Werner Grau's status to any authority that could act on it.

Whether this constituted his doing something, or his failing to do something, or simply the act of a man who understood that what mattered about Werner Grau was not the state of his papers — that question remained open, in the drawer, alongside everything else he was holding.
