# The Breakwater

The outer face had taken green water.

She could see it from the headland stairs — the wrack line sitting high on the granite, a length of tarred cable draped across the top course, the iron mooring rings at the elbow gone dark with wet. She went down.

First light. Northwest wind out of Canada, fifteen knots and dropping. The blow had peaked sometime around two in the morning and then, the way storms sometimes did on this coast, had simply stopped. By four she'd been lying awake listening to the silences between gusts. By five she'd been dressed. The air coming off the water now was cleaner and colder, carrying nothing with it but temperature.

She had her clipboard.

The top course was intact along the north arm's full length — no slippage, no voids. She moved toward the elbow, checking each granite face, feeling the joint conditions where she had to. Some of the stones she knew well enough to read by looking; others needed a hand pressed to them, checking for any give. The rubble fill had held. The crown height was unchanged along the north arm.

She noted the cable. Tarred, fairly new, and it didn't belong to any vessel currently in the harbor. She'd check the boatyard, see if something in storage had lost it. She noted it for inquiry and for removal.

At the elbow, the course had shifted. An inch and a half toward the inner harbor, maybe two. She measured by eye and then by hand and noted it. The elbow always took the worst of a southeast blow, and what she was looking at was not as bad as 1939. The mortar joint at the south corner had widened. She put her finger in it: a quarter inch, three-eighths. Before the freeze, someone would need to point that joint; otherwise the ice would open it further.

The repair list for the breakwater had been three items before this morning. It was now five.

She wrote them all down.

The kelp had piled waist-high against the inner face of the elbow, black and dripping, salt-stinking. Woven into it were a coil of pot warp, a length of buoy line, the slats of a wooden crate that was stamped with something she didn't recognize — from a vessel, or perhaps from the boatyard if the storm had lifted something from the rails. A glass-ball float. A plank with a bronze fitting through it, the bolt stripped, which meant it had been working loose before the storm claimed it.

She went around the elbow, and saw the man.

---

He was face-down in the wrack, in the inner corner of the elbow where the kelp had piled deepest. The storm geometry was right for it: anything coming in from the southeast over the outer edge would have been carried into exactly this corner. He was lying with his arms at an angle — the left arm back along his body, the right arm out and slightly under him — that said he had not arranged himself there.

She stood for a moment.

The light was improving. She could see well enough.

Town clothes. A heavy wool coat, navy, with lapels that had no business on a working waterfront. Trousers, not work trousers. No boots anywhere on the breakwater that she could see, no oilskins, no gear of any kind. No vessel anywhere in the inner harbor she didn't know.

She set the clipboard on a flat section of granite and crouched down.

She checked his pockets.

Inside the coat, left breast: nothing. Right breast: nothing. Outside pockets — in the left, nothing; in the right, a folded handkerchief, and below it, grit. His trouser pockets, each in turn: nothing. Nothing. No wallet. No papers. No draft card. No ration book. No keys. Nothing with a name on it.

She stood up.

Male. The hands said fifty or older — the thickness across the knuckles, the looseness of the skin on the back of them. The hair was grey, close-cut, a working man's cut. The wool coat was good quality, that much was clear even soaked through. The trousers were wool as well. Somebody's travelling clothes, or a man's good clothes, or both.

Nothing about him said this harbor.

She picked up the clipboard. She walked back to the shed at the pier head.

---

Inside, she called Sprucehead.

The duty officer answered on the third ring. She gave him everything in order: her name, her title, the station address, the date, the time — six-twenty-two by the clock on the wall — and then the description. Male, she said. Face-down in the wrack at the elbow. Middle-aged or older. Town clothes. No papers, no identification of any kind, nothing to indicate a vessel or how he had come in. She had not touched him beyond checking his pockets. She had not moved him.

The duty officer said he would send someone. She thanked him and hung up.

She put the kettle on the single-burner plate. She checked the barometer — risen three-tenths since midnight, consistent with the storm's track, consistent with what she could see through the north window: the sky clearing fast from the northwest, the cloud deck breaking up at altitude, showing the grey beneath. She recorded the barometer reading in the tide log and noted the wind direction.

On the shelf above the telephone, seven logbooks stood in order. She'd started the current one in January, and its spine was still dark and square. The six before it went back to 1936. The one before those — thinner, its spine faded to the color of old water, Owen's handwriting on the label in the particular heavy-slanted hand he'd used for anything official — was set a little apart from the others, at the end of the shelf where the bracket met the wall. She had not moved it. It wasn't where she would have put it if she'd been setting up the shelf from scratch.

She poured a cup of tea and went back to the breakwater to wait.

---

The wind had dropped to ten knots by the time the Coast Guard truck came down off the main road onto the pier. She was standing at the breakwater's head when Lieutenant Mercer got out with his two enlisted men.

He was younger than she'd expected — mid-twenties, with the winter uniform pressed correctly and a manner that was efficient without being brisk. He introduced himself and looked at her when she gave her name.

"You're the harbormaster?" he said.

"Eight years," she said.

She walked him out to the body.

He crouched the way she had crouched, looking before he touched. He checked the pockets — the same ones she'd checked, and two more. He stood up. He asked her: when had she found it, had she moved anything, had she contacted anyone else.

No, she said. No. No.

"Any record of a vessel in difficulty? Radio calls? Report from boats that came in before the blow?"

"Nothing in the log from the past three days. No distress calls. Two draggers out to the grounds and back in before it peaked. The sardine carrier *Ellsworth* running to Eastport — she went out before the storm, due back the eighteenth."

"And no vessels you can't account for."

"Nothing in the harbor I can't account for."

He wrote in a small notebook. He was thorough rather than curious. He asked whether anyone else had access to the breakwater during the storm, and she said no one would have come out on it while the blow was on, and anyone could have come since, but she'd found no footprints in the wrack. He wrote that down as well.

She gave him the harbor log for October 9 through 12. He looked at it carefully and handed it back.

The two enlisted men brought the stretcher down from the truck. The operation was careful and correct. She watched from a few feet away and he did not ask her to step back. By the time the stretcher was going back up the breakwater, she had answered two more questions and had learned almost nothing except that the lieutenant's first name was Amos, from the nametag she'd seen when he turned his coat.

"We'll be in touch if we have questions," he said.

"I know where to reach you," she said.

The truck pulled out of the pier at seven-twenty-three.

---

She finished the breakwater survey. She walked the full length again from the shore end, checking each section now that nothing was in her way. The damage added one more item — a section of the north face's drainage where the fill had settled — and she added it to the list. She wrote the estimate for the elbow repair while she was still on the breakwater, because the light was good and she could see what she was writing about.

Back at the shed, she opened the harbor log to the day's page.

She wrote for ten minutes. The entry ran to half a page.

*October 12, 1943. Sunrise 0611. Wind NW 15kts at 0600, dropping to 10kts by 0800. Barometer 29.74 at 0600, rising. Post-storm survey, breakwater, 0615–0730: granite course displaced at elbow (est. 1.5 in. inward), mortar joint widened at south corner of elbow, iron mooring rings displaced (2), kelp and debris accumulation at elbow, drainage fill settled N. face — all noted for fall repair.*

*Vessels: all moored vessels accounted for. Sardine carrier* Ellsworth *Eastport run, ETA Oct. 18.*

*0615: Unidentified male, deceased, recovered at breakwater elbow. No papers, no identification of any kind, no associated vessel. CG Sprucehead notified 0622. CG responded, Lt. A. Mercer and two enlisted, 0711. Body removed to CG custody 0723. CG assuming jurisdiction.*

She put down the pen.

She read it once. It was accurate. Every time was correct.

She set the logbook to one side.

---

It was not yet eight-thirty. The first boats wouldn't be in from the grounds for another hour, maybe two. She stood at the shed's south window.

The south dock was empty. She could see its full length from here — the grey planking, the pilings standing in the flat water, the dock light still burning at the head of the dock, unnecessary now in the morning. The Gale brothers had moved their trap hauler to the inner float in September. The dock had not been in regular use since then.

The night before it had not been empty.

October the eleventh, going into the twelfth. Past midnight. She had been at this window watching the barometer fall. The blow was building. She had already gone out and checked the mooring chains on two of the draggers — around nine, ten o'clock — and had come back to the shed to wait. The chains were what they were. There was nothing more to do in the dark in a rising wind.

Two figures on the south dock. The dock light behind them both.

One she had not recognized. He was looking toward the outer harbor. Dark coat. The build of someone past middle age — not heavy, but solid, the kind of solid that sets into men who have worked outdoors for a long time. Standing still in the way of a man who had come somewhere specific and arrived.

The other one she had not seen clearly. Half-turned from her, the dock light cutting across from the wrong angle. The shoulders. The way of standing. Not a man whose body had been built around boats — she knew that much. Wide across the back. Feet planted like a man used to standing on flat ground, not a deck. Somebody from inland.

She had thought: two men on the dock before a storm. She had thought: their business, not mine.

Now she looked at the harbor log, open on the desk.

The entry was complete. Each time was correct.

These were separate data points. It was possible they had nothing to do with each other, and the log entry she had written was true in every particular, and there was nothing more to do.

She picked up the pen.

She held it.

She set it down.

The south dock stood empty in the flat morning light. The harbor beyond it had gone from grey to silver as the sky cleared. The tide was going out.

# Continental Educator

The morning walk from the Crow house to the school was fifteen minutes, a calculation Marcus had verified repeatedly over nineteen months and continued to verify, partly out of habit and partly because he was a man who understood the difference between a fact that had been established and a fact that merely appeared to have been established. The one variable he had not succeeded in eliminating was the intersection at the bottom of Elm Street, where the road made its north turn and the harbor appeared briefly between two buildings — a flat gray angle of water, the breakwater's outer arm, no vessels at the south dock this morning. Some mornings he stopped. Today he did not.

Main Street at half past seven: the hardware store's windows still dark, the bakery lit, a truck outside the post office with its engine running and the driver standing beside it, watching his exhaust cloud with the peaceable attention of a man whose morning was going according to plan. Marcus nodded. The driver nodded. This exchange, which had occurred in some variation for nineteen months, had arrived at a precision of mutual acknowledgment that Marcus found, if not warm, then accurate — and in his experience accuracy was a form of warmth, or at least its structural equivalent.

The school sat back from the road behind a low iron fence and four large elms that had not yet been touched by whatever was moving through the New England elms. Three stories, dark brick, the year 1912 cut into the cornerstone — he had read it once and it had stayed, the way dates stayed, without being asked to. He went up the main steps and through the door into the smell of chalk dust and boiler heat: Henry had the building to the right temperature, as he always had it to the right temperature. Marcus hung his coat on the hook inside the teachers' entry and went upstairs.

---

His first class was Latin. This year the Latin class was three students — Cornelia Foss and two boys named Pratt and Heywood, none of whom had elected the course voluntarily but all of whom had been placed in it by the vice-principal on a theory Marcus considered neither obviously correct nor obviously wrong. He had them, and they had him, and in nineteen months of this arrangement both parties had arrived at a working understanding of what was expected.

The classroom was on the third floor, north-facing, with windows that admitted the particular flat gray light of coastal Maine in late October: not winter, not autumn, not quite either, a light without strong claims on the hour or the mood. Three desks arranged in the front half of the room, which was the correct number of desks for three students and which had the effect of making the back half of the room into a kind of reserve space — not empty, exactly, but waiting. Marcus had learned not to think about the back half of the room.

He wrote a sentence on the board. It was from Cicero's *De Amicitia*, the kind of sentence Cicero wrote when he was working at full capacity: the main clause withheld while the subordinate architecture assembled itself, so that by the time the verb arrived you had been holding the opening phrase in your mind long enough to know what weight the closing would need to carry. He underlined the subordinate clause, set the chalk in the tray, and turned.

"Don't translate it," he said.

He had been saying this in four languages, across more years and more classrooms than he intended to calculate, and what he meant by it was always the same: sit with the sentence before you reach for the English. Learn the architecture before the furniture. A translation that arrives too quickly has not understood what it has translated.

The three of them sat with it. He could read, from the quality of each student's stillness, which one was reading and which two were waiting for rescue. Cornelia Foss's stillness had a forward quality — she was inside the sentence, working. The two boys produced the carefully arranged blankness of students who have learned to display attention without generating it. The ratio — one out of three with the forward stillness — was, in Marcus's experience, approximately a constant, across Latin and German and French and any other language that required this particular quality of sitting. He found it neither discouraging nor encouraging. It was a distribution.

After a moment: "Miss Foss."

She looked up.

"Tell me what the sentence is doing."

She paused. She was the kind of mind that checked an answer before it committed to it, which Marcus had identified early and respected, it being his own habit. "It's waiting," she said. "The whole thing — it holds open until the end. You can't close it until you have all of it."

"Yes."

He did not add to this. In his experience, the correctly made observation was its own sufficient reward; adding praise introduced an economy of approval that distorted the thing being observed. He let it be. She looked back at the board, and after a moment the two boys looked back at the board, and the lesson continued.

---

The period between his Latin class and the first German section was thirty-five minutes, which Marcus divided between the staffroom on the second floor and the set of translation exercises he had marked the previous night and had comments remaining for. The staffroom coffee was, in his considered opinion, the worst he had encountered in any English-speaking institution in two continents, and he had encountered it in a number of such institutions over the past several years. He drank it.

Stillman came in. He taught geography in rooms 201 and 202, moved through the building with the slightly compressed energy of someone who had recently been somewhere else and not quite fully arrived here. He poured coffee and stood at the counter.

"Odd business down at the harbor," he said. He said most things from across a room, as though physical distance were a conversational courtesy.

Marcus set down his pen.

"What kind of business?"

"Man washed in on the breakwater after the blow last week. No papers. Nothing on him at all. CG took the body and that's the last officially."

"Town clothes, they said? Not a fisherman?"

"That's what I heard." Stillman shrugged with one shoulder. "Nobody from here. Nobody from anywhere anyone knows about. Clement Ames was down at the fish pier when the CG truck came in."

Marcus turned this over in the way he handled incomplete information: not with narrative appetite, not with the urgency that transforms the unverified into the presumed, but with the steady attention of a man who had learned over many years that the significant quality of incomplete information was its incompleteness, and that the correct response was to note it and wait. A man with no papers, washed in from a three-day storm. The verified facts were few. The range of explanations was large and at present unnarrowed. He put it in the part of his mind that held things requiring more data before they could become anything — a part that had, over the past five years, accumulated considerably.

"Has anyone put out a description?" he said.

"Not that I know of." Stillman finished his coffee. "Sailor off a convoy is what most people are saying."

Marcus nodded and returned to the translation exercises.

---

He passed the principal's open door at twenty past nine. The door stood open, as it nearly always did — the principal being the kind of administrator who managed through visibility, the open door a performance of nothing to hide. On the desk, partially in view from the hallway, was a folder with Marcus's name on the tab, and in the line below the name, in the school secretary's round and deliberate hand, the notation the town meeting had appended to his original hire: *Continental educator.*

He had seen this folder before. He had sat across from it in March of 1942, when the principal had gone through the courses Marcus would be assuming, and again the following spring, when the question of the advanced German section had required a committee meeting at which the folder had been present as a kind of documentation — a note explaining to any future questioner why the school had hired a Viennese Jewish émigré in a town of eight hundred people two years into a war. *Continental educator* accounted for him without requiring anyone to decide what they thought about it. He had found, broadly, that this was how things were explained in Coldwater Reach, and that the explanation was neither hostile nor warm, but administrative — which was also, in its way, a form of accuracy.

He kept walking.

---

The afternoon walk covered the same ground reversed. Main Street had the different character of four-thirty: a line of women outside the butcher's door with their ration books, a delivery bicycle leaned against the diner's steps, three junior-school boys occupying the hardware store's stoop until the store owner appeared in the doorway and they relocated to the next block.

The Western Union boy's bicycle was leaned against the post office wall.

He kept walking.

He had been in Coldwater ten months before he watched, from approximately this distance, a woman receive a telegram at the post office door. It had been January — clear and cold, the kind of January light that made everything look precise and final — and he had been far enough away that he saw only the shape of it: the boy, the envelope, the woman's hands, and the quality of stillness that followed the exchange. He had known what was in the envelope before it was opened. The shape was unmistakable, once you had seen it in one country, in one administrative language or another. He had kept walking that day also.

This afternoon the bicycle stood unattended. Nobody came in or out of the post office while he passed. The empty doorway, the bicycle, the ordinary afternoon continuing on either side of them.

He walked down Elm Street. At the corner he did not stop, and the harbor appeared briefly and was flat and gray, the south dock still empty, and he turned north.

He thought of Sherbrooke for perhaps ten seconds. Not of the camp, not of the months — the dormitory, the other men from fifteen countries assembled by their common classification as the same kind of enemy, none of them having been in a position to do much about being Austrian in 1940 — but of the specific moment of arrival: the gate intake desk, the clerk's hand lifting the document from Marcus's coat pocket and placing it on the far side of the desk, and Marcus's own hands afterward, standing in the cold with no paper in them, not knowing quite what to do with themselves. He thought of this for ten seconds. Then he was at the Crow house, and he put his hand on the gate latch and lifted it and went in.

---

The kitchen was warm. Lillian was at the stove, the iron pan over the low burner, bread already cut on the board, the tea things arranged on the counter because there was not enough counter for the tea things and anything else. She heard him come in and did not turn.

"Cold getting into it," she said.

"Yes."

She set a plate on the table without asking what he wanted. She had not asked what he wanted in approximately eighteen months, because at some point in the first season of his residence his preferences had been established and were since treated as given facts, the way Lillian treated most things she had once established to her satisfaction. He hung his coat on the hook inside the door and sat down.

Below, Henry was in the boiler room. The sounds came up through the floor in the order Marcus had learned to follow across two winters: the knock of the pipe fitting, the steady sound of something turned, the occasional deep report of the boiler accepting what it had been given. The sounds of competent work, which Marcus had found were the same sounds regardless of the object they were applied to, and which were, in some way he had never fully articulated, reassuring — not because the boiler required reassurance, but because the sounds placed a capable person in the room below.

"How did school go?" Lillian said. She was not facing him.

"We read Cicero. More precisely, one student read Cicero and two students sat in the general area."

The sound she made was not quite a laugh but was in the same family. "German any better?"

"Somewhat."

She set the tea down and did not follow up the question. Marcus had learned, in this house, to understand the question asked and let go as a form of consideration rather than disinterest: she asked; she received; she moved on. The household had a register, and he had learned it the way he had learned every register in every house and institution he had occupied, and it was now, mostly, natural.

---

On the kitchen wall, hung from a nail above the window that looked toward the backyard: James Crow's Army photograph.

Formal. The kind taken before deployment: the uniform precise, the studio background a neutral gray, the set of his shoulders in the jacket partly the jacket's structure and partly the young man's own. He had a sergeant's formality in the way he held himself. Marcus looked at the photograph the way he looked at it each time he sat down at this table — with the attention that a face deserves and that absence makes available. He had never seen James Crow in motion. He knew the photograph, and the letters that arrived for Lillian with Pacific postmarks, and the particular adjustment in Henry's pace on the days when such a letter appeared.

He did not know James Crow. He had a static image and the outline of an absence and the sounds of a father working steadily in the room below, which was perhaps, at this distance, the truest version of a person available to him.

Henry came up through the basement door partway through, crossed to the sink, turned on the tap.

"Fitting on the south loop's going to want replacing before December," he said.

"Will that be a difficult part to find?"

"Need to order it." Henry dried his hands on the side towel, looked at Marcus. "School all right?"

"Yes."

Henry nodded and went back downstairs.

---

His room was on the second floor, the window facing east over the yard. The curtain was heavy dark wool, the desk against the wall, the shelf holding more books than it had held in March of 1942, which was a kind of record. He sat on the edge of the bed with a book open across his knee and did not read it.

After a while came the sound of Henry closing the basement door — the sequence of steps from the back of the house forward — and then the house settled into its night disposition: the known sounds, the positioned quiet, nothing requiring response.

*Continental educator.* He had been carrying the phrase since mid-morning with the steady, absent quality he brought to things that had been said about him and that were not precisely wrong. In Vienna he had been Dr. Klein — a form of address, a specific weight in a room. In Paris he had been the Austrian, which was precisely if not unkindly meant. In London he had been the refugee, which was a category. In Sherbrooke he had been classified as the enemy alien, which was at least a position of known standing, even if the standing was wrongly arrived at. In Cambridge he had been the displaced scholar, which was accurate and was also, in its gentle way, a form of storage: a useful object held for later placement. In Coldwater he was the Continental educator, a phrase on a folder on a desk, which was all of these and was none of them.

He was, he thought, practicing something. The walk down Elm Street was a practice. The staffroom coffee was a practice. The kitchen downstairs and Lillian's plate set without asking and the sound of Henry's work coming up through the floor: all of this was practice. He was not certain — and he was, where he could be, precise about his certainties — whether what he was practicing was Coldwater or himself.

He closed the book and reached over and turned off the lamp.

# Advanced German

The bus from the Pfeiffer road dropped her at Main and Birch at seven fifty-two, and Hannah was inside the school building before the cold had finished with her collar. The building took her in: chalk and floor wax and, already, the cafeteria working at something that had been on the stove since six, a smell that had no precise name and did not require one. She hung her coat on the third hook from the left and checked the weather board at the office end of the hall — northwest, twenty, gusting thirty — before going down to the ground floor.

Third period was advanced German. Room 114, southwest corner, smallest classroom in the school. At the start of term, Marcus Klein had asked Mr. Crow to move the extra desks out, because there were three students and the gap between three students and twenty empty desks was not a ratio that served anyone. Roland Bates had told Hannah this story in the first week with some incredulity, as if the rearrangement reflected on someone. She had not said anything.

The class was Roland, who was there because his mother had arranged it and made this legible in every sentence he attempted, and Patrice Audette, who was the genuine article and knew it without making a show of the knowing, and Hannah. She had been doing German homework at the kitchen table since she was twelve, sitting across the room from a man who used the language as a country he could live inside. Whatever shape she had of the language, she'd learned it alongside that.

They were three days into the second stanza of the Rilke. *Herbsttag* — Marcus had put it on the board at the start of the week with the note written below the title: *We are working on syntax. The poem is the occasion.* Below that, the two stanzas. Below those, brackets, arrows, clause-structure notation, with the poem's actual subject — autumn, a man with no house, solitude moving in like a weather system — visible through the scaffolding but not addressed.

This morning he started from the first line of the stanza: *Wer jetzt kein Haus hat, baut sich keines mehr.*

"Roland. The subject of the second clause."

Roland looked at the page in front of him. He looked at his page with a consistency that implied something would eventually be on it if he waited long enough. "Wer."

"The same *wer* as the first clause?"

A pause. "Yes?"

"Tell me why."

Longer pause. Patrice was looking at the ceiling in the way she looked when she was waiting for something to become apparent to someone else.

"Because it carries across," Hannah said. "One subject, two predicates. The *wer* takes both."

Marcus drew an arc on the board connecting the two verb phrases. "Yes. The indefinite relative pronoun distributes without repeating. That's its purpose — it names a category once and the structure holds it." He turned. "The *keines*. Case."

Roland looked at his page again.

"Accusative," Hannah said. "Object of *baut*."

"And the *sich*?"

She thought about how to put it. "Dative. The building is for himself. Whatever he's not building, it's his own not-having."

She hadn't planned to say it that way, and she saw Marcus turn the chalk in his right hand — the small physical notation she'd come to read as satisfaction, not performed.

"Exactly. The dative makes the absence personal. He has no house, and not having a house is something he does to himself, or that does itself to him — the German leaves the direction unspecified, marks only that the self is involved." He wrote the sentence clean on the board, without brackets: *baut sich keines mehr.* "Read it beside your translation. Tell me what the English costs."

Roland produced a translation slowly, as if constructing it on the way. "'Whoever has no house now builds himself none more.'"

"The 'none more' is awkward. What is *mehr* doing?"

"Saying he won't build any."

"It's stronger than 'any.' It's 'further,' 'any longer' — the building has been decided against. The finality is already in it." He wrote on the board: *builds himself nothing further.* "That's still not right. The precision has no equivalent. You choose what to lose."

Patrice said: "'Nothing further' loses the sense that it was always going to be nothing. The *mehr* makes it retroactive."

Marcus looked at the board for a moment. "Yes. The *mehr* folds in the past. The English says it's over. The German says it was always going to be over." He set the chalk in the tray. "That's what makes it difficult. Note it."

She wrote: *retroactive finality. the German folds in the past.* She wrote it because it was worth having, even if it was too large for any exam she would ever sit.

She watched him move to the third line, chalk in hand. He wrote one word and stopped, waiting for Roland to catch up. The pause was unhurried, calculated to the minute — not impatience held back but patience given precisely. Hannah had been watching it since September and had not said anything.

At the bell they were two lines from the end.

---

At lunch, the two girls at the table by the windows were still on the body. More than a month now and the story had grown its shape: a merchant sailor, someone had heard, come down from Eastport or up from Bath depending on who was telling it and which direction made the drowning feel more final. He'd been drinking somewhere up the coast and gone over a dock rail. Or he'd been running from something — a debt, a wife, a thing he couldn't put behind him — and the October storm had been waiting for a man in exactly that condition.

Hannah ate her sandwich. She had a piece of data that didn't fit the shape of any version on this table: her father's hands on his knife and fork at the dinner table, stopped for three seconds at the words *no papers*, the knife set down without deciding to, and then resumed. That data did not attach to the merchant sailor. It did not attach to any story being assembled here. It was not a thing she could put on this table, at this price, into this format. She ate and listened and the merchant sailor acquired one more detail she had no reason to believe.

---

After class Roland left immediately and Patrice was already gone. Hannah stayed because she had a question that was not a pretext for anything else — just a grammatical question she'd been carrying since Monday that her notes hadn't answered.

"The *es*," she said. She read the line: *Wer jetzt allein ist, wird es lange bleiben.* "I can't find what it's standing in for."

Marcus turned from the board where he'd been erasing the bracket notation. He looked at her page without appearing to need it.

"It's not standing in for anything earlier," he said. "It anticipates. It holds a place in the syntax for the predicative adjective — the aloneness — which the grammar already knows is there." He went to the board and wrote: *wird es lange bleiben.* Below: *wird … allein bleiben.* "In German—" He wrote the word: *Korrelat.* "The correlate. A placeholder the structure makes for something it already holds. The sentence knows its meaning before it has finished stating it."

She wrote *Korrelat* in the margin and put a bracket around the *es.*

"My translation has 'will long remain so,'" she said. "I wasn't sure the 'so' was right."

"It's better than 'it,'" he said. "The 'so' implies continuation — the condition already established, extending forward. That's accurate to what the German is doing." He considered it for a moment, the chalk still in his hand. "Your question was a real one."

She put the notebook in her bag. He had said *Korrelat* before he reached for the English for it — the way he always reached for the German word first and the English second, as if the German were the thing you could rely on and the English were the approximation you settled for. Her father's German was nothing like this. Her father's German was a retreat — a door he kept shut since the war started, something he moved into when his English wasn't safe anymore. Marcus moved toward German the way he moved toward precision; it was the direction of accuracy, the closer register. She did not have a word for the difference and she was not going to look for one in room 114.

---

Dinner was salt pork and potatoes from the root cellar. She set the seed catalog at her father's place before she sat down and he reached for it as he sat, without comment, in the way he reached for anything that was properly his to reach for. He turned to the back half first — root vegetable prices, winter grain, the columns of numbers — before moving forward through the variety pages. He did this while he ate with the attentiveness he gave to anything with a practical season coming. Her mother was at her place with a straight back and ate enough that you couldn't say she wasn't. The radio was off, the way it had been for most of November.

They ate.

---

After the dishes she brought the German translation to the kitchen table. Her father moved to the sitting room with the farm accounts, the small desk by the window, and she could hear the sound of his pen through the wall — long strokes for the main columns, short ones for corrections.

She spread the Rilke page.

The *Korrelat* note in the margin, the bracket. She moved on to the last two lines: *und wird in den Alleen hin und her / unruhig wandern, wenn die Blätter treiben.* The *treiben* was where she kept stopping. To drive, to be driven, to drift, to blow — she'd tried four versions since Monday. She tried "when the leaves are driven," but "driven" in English wanted a driver, a thing pushing, and the German had no driver; it had just the fact of the motion. She tried "when the leaves run," which was wrong. "Drift" was closer but it lost the driven quality, the sense that the leaves were not choosing. She put a question mark beside "drift" and wrote both versions under the line.

She had been working with the language for five years and still hit the words that wouldn't cross. Her father never hit these walls because the language was not a wall for him; it was the room he lived in. She was working on its ceiling.

She was finishing the fair copy when she heard the icehouse door.

---

She put the pencil down and went to the window to draw the curtain.

Karl was outside without a coat over the POW jacket, his arms at his sides, his head tilted back. The sky was the November clear that arrived after the first hard frost — stars close and particular, the cold making the air exact. He was standing still.

He said the word.

*Seidenschwanz.*

She said it at the glass, barely a breath. *Seidenschwanz.* October's word, coming back. The same quality to it — not a complaint, not addressed to anyone or asking anything of anyone, just the naming of something he knew. Saying it to the sky to keep the knowing current.

He stood a moment longer. Then he went inside. The lamp in the icehouse window was low; she watched it dim through the oil paper until it was gone.

She pulled the curtain and went back to the table.

Her father's pen moving in the accounts. The stove ticking as it cooled.

She opened the German translation to the Rilke page. Below the *Korrelat* note, below the bracket, below the question mark beside *treiben*, she wrote *Seidenschwanz* in the margin.

It had nothing to do with the poem. She drew a small circle around it to keep it from the rest.

She closed the notebook and left the lamp on, because her father was still at the accounts across the room.

# Winter Registry

The mooring roster ran to five pages for December. She laid them flat on the desk and went through them against the harbor log, one column against the other. The Ellsworth was accounted for — still on her winter run to Eastport, due back the sixteenth. Clara M. was accounted for, inner float, registration current. The Gale brothers' second boat, Ida B., was on the boatyard railway since the third of November and her entry had been updated accordingly. Ida B.'s mooring assignment would hold through the winter vacant, which was correct.

Seventeen hulls would winter in the inner harbor. She went through them one at a time.

Two of the seventeen were out of compliance on their documentation. One had let the registration lapse in October and had not responded to the September reminder; the other had moved berths without filing the change. Both were correctable by letter. She pulled paper from the center drawer and wrote both notices before she did anything else. Clean copies, dated, registered mail on the second one. She addressed the envelopes and put them in the to-mail pile at the corner of the desk.

Outside the shed window the harbor was in its December arrangement. Half the working fleet was hauled, cradles and sawhorses up in the boatyard above the high-water line, the boats sitting on their keels with a stripped and workmanlike look that was different from summer. The railway had been busy through November — she had heard it most mornings, the hauling gear running, and had noted the vessels as they came out of the water and been checked off the winter list. The cold-storage house was running on reduced hours now; Patterson had posted the December schedule on the shed door last Thursday. The inner float held what it held: Clara M., the Hartleys' double-ender, three lobster boats whose owners had calculated the winter lay-up costs and decided against it.

She went back to the roster. The outer anchorage was empty. Had been since the first week of November.

She was going through the last page when she heard boots on the fuel dock.

---

Wendell Foss ran his boat up alongside and tied the stern first. He came up the dock planks with the gas can and did not look in through the shed window or call out, because he was not a man who required an audience before he arrived. She came out to the dock.

He set the can down and reached for the pump handle.

"Heard they're putting someone from the county board to look at the harbormaster situation," he said.

He worked the pump. He had not looked at her when he said it and he did not look at her now.

"Who told you that," she said.

"Clement Ames. His cousin works for the county in some capacity." He watched the can fill. "Don't know the specifics. Just that it's under discussion."

"I'll note it."

He shut off the pump and lifted the can. He paid and went back down the dock at the same pace he'd come up. She watched him reach his boat and step aboard without looking back.

She went inside and wrote the fuel transaction in the ledger.

Then she set down the pen.

Eight years of harbor log kept to the same standard. Every vessel registration current within her authority. The mooring assignments documented and filed, the incident log accurate, the annual fuel throughput reconciled quarter by quarter. No casualty attributed to a failure in harbor management in her tenure, and no casualty that a different harbormaster's decision could have prevented either — she had run that accounting once, after the Hartley boy's accident on the outer mooring, and the conclusion was the same from every direction. The harbor income was up eleven percent over Owen's last two years. That was not a dramatic figure. It was the correct direction.

She went back to the roster.

---

The annual report for the county authority was a form she had filed every December since 1936. The columns did not change year to year: vessel count, fuel throughput, mooring revenue, incident log, capital expenditures, maintenance deferred and completed. She filled them in the same order she always did. The numbers went where they belonged.

But when she reached the incident log section she found herself going back over it before committing the ink.

The October 12 entry was there. She had written it exactly as it stood in the harbor log: body discovered on breakwater, 0615, CG notified 0622, arrived 0711, removed 0723. Case closed by Coast Guard, October 1943. Official determination: unidentified drowning. She had copied this to the annual report with the same words.

It was accurate. The case was closed. There was nothing in the incident log that was not in the harbor log, and nothing in the harbor log that was not accurate.

She read it through a second time and left it as it was.

She sealed the envelope, stamped it, and put it on top of the mooring notices.

---

The post office was quiet at four o'clock. Two items in the box — county boilerplate and a state winter storm protocol notice she would implement before February. She added both to her coat pocket. The Western Union boy's bicycle was not against the wall. Available information, and also a form of relief.

She went out into the cold.

---

The light was almost gone when she got back to the shed. She logged the state notice and checked the to-mail pile one more time.

Then she put on her heavier coat and her cap and went out for the breakwater.

---

She walked the breakwater in November and December every year. In Owen's time it had been his walk; she had gone with him the first winters of their marriage, learning the habit before she learned what it was for. Now she did it the way she did the other maintenance work: from the shore end out, systematically, with the paper and pencil in her coat pocket for notes.

The granite was in its December state — damp on the upper face from the last tide, the cap stones dark. She walked the crown and checked the placement as she went, stopping where she needed to stop. Third cap stone from the shore end had a gap on the south face, probably from the October storm. The stone was seated; it wasn't going anywhere. She put it in the notes: spring assessment, south face, stone three. Tight gap, not urgent.

The chop off the outer face was four feet from the southeast, well short of the crown. The tide was running at mid-flood. She walked further, noting two more small settlements in the rubble face — both minor, both below the mean high-water line where the ice action would work on them through February and March. These went in the notes as well.

The boatyard was visible across the inner harbor, the railway track running up from the waterline, one hull still on the cradle. She thought it was Merton Galey's Penelope D. but the light was too flat now to be certain.

She walked to the elbow.

---

The elbow was where the breakwater turned. She came around it and stopped to check the inner face granite course. A fractional movement in one of the lower courses, probably the October storm as well — the capstone wasn't proud but the rubble below it had settled a small amount. She wrote it down. Spring assessment, elbow, inner face, course four. Not critical.

She straightened up.

The inner harbor was ahead of her — float lights on, the cold-storage office lamp still burning across the water. The south dock was visible from this angle, the pilings and the dock planking at the line of the harbor's south edge. Just visible. She looked at it the way she always looked at it from the elbow, without having decided to.

The night of October eleventh going into the twelfth. Past midnight. She had been at the shed's south window watching the barometer; the glass had been falling steadily since nine o'clock and she had wanted to see what it did at midnight. That was why she had been there.

Two men on the south dock.

The first: past middle age, solid in the shoulders, dark coat. Not a fisherman. She was certain of that from where she stood — certain from the coat and the way he stood on the dock planking, too deliberate, placed rather than easy, the way a man stands on a dock when he is not used to docks. He was looking toward the outer harbor. She could not see his face; the dock lamp was behind him. He turned and said something to the other man.

The second figure: wider across the back and through the shoulders. Standing further from the dock edge. His weight planted in a way she recognized — not a sailor's balance, a farmer's stillness, the kind that comes from years of standing in mud and cold and not moving much while you wait for something to finish. She had not seen his face.

The first man had walked to the shore end of the dock and gone up the ramp. The boatyard shadow had taken him. The second man had stayed another minute or two and then gone up the ramp the same way.

That was what she had. An image and a time: approximately half past midnight, October 12. The south dock, which the Gale brothers had vacated in September, not in regular use. Two men on it, neither one a sailor, in the hours before the storm peaked. And at the other end of three days of blow, a man with no papers in town clothes face-down at the elbow of the breakwater.

What she did not have: a vessel. A name. A corroboration. Anything that would make an entry in the harbor log rather than a statement that she had watched two men standing on a dock. The harbor log required specificity sufficient to establish the fact. It was sufficient to establish that she had seen something, which was a different entry.

She turned and walked back along the breakwater toward the shore.

---

The tide had come up while she walked. She stopped at the south ladder — the iron rungs set into the breakwater's shore face — and read the tide height off the granite marks. The water was at the first mark above mid, consistent with tonight's table. She had resurveyed the marks in October of 1940 and confirmed them against the Rockland gauge. They were accurate. They were what they said they were.

She went up the shore path to the shed.

Inside, she lit the lamp. The harbor was dark except for the float lights and the cold-storage lamp across the water. She stood at the south window for a moment. The south dock was barely visible, a line of pilings at the far edge of the float light's reach.

She had not written the dock figures. She had accepted this in October, when the image was new. She had accepted it again when Mercer came and she gave him technically-true answers that left the dock out of them. She accepted it now: two men on the dock, a time, a body at the elbow.

For now, she had told herself in October.

For now.

She turned from the window. The desk had the Cote notice on it still, and the state harbor file, and the December mooring roster with the last page not yet filed. She sat down and pulled the roster toward her and finished it. One column, then the next. The harbor in December holding what it held — seventeen hulls, the empty outer anchorage, the water doing its work at the granite marks.

The entry was wrong and would stay wrong for now.

# Cedar Waxwing

She broke the ice on the water trough first, the way she did every January morning — striking the base of the pail against the surface until it cracked and came away in one curved gray sheet. She pushed the pieces aside and set the pail underneath the pump. The water came up cold enough that the pail immediately fogged in the barn air.

Her father was already in the stanchion row. She could hear his voice from the far end — short sentences in German to the Stuttgarter about the feed count, *morgen, genug, nein* — and she caught the words without trying to catch them, the way she had been catching her father's German her whole life: not translation, just the sounds arriving and meaning washing in behind them.

The cold came through the board gaps on the north wall and lay along the floor in a way that was different from yard cold. Barn cold was thick with the animals, warmed and weighted by sixteen cows in their stanchions, and it carried the particular smell of January in a working barn — the bedding packed down now, worked through three months of winter use, the hay older and darker than it had been in October, the floor settled and compacted into itself. She had stopped noticing the smell the way you stop noticing a sound that doesn't change. She noticed it now because she'd been away two days at her cousin Marta's in Portland for Christmas and had come back into the smell as something new for a few minutes before it closed around her again.

The four Germans were already on the morning routine. She went to her row.

Karl was at the far end with the difficult cow, and he was not having difficulty. She caught this in the periphery. He moved through the milking lane without choosing his feet. He knew the cow: knew she went easily if you came from the left and didn't come from the right, knew the particular patience she required at the start of the morning, knew when to wait and when to push. This had taken him until December to learn. It was January now and he had it the way you have anything that's become the body's knowledge and stopped being the mind's.

She had learned to count to twelve in German from the morning counts: *eins, zwei, drei* — heard often enough that it had simply moved in without asking. Karl had twelve English words, by her count, and she had thirty German ones, and neither of them counted, and both of them had stopped noticing the asymmetry because the asymmetry was not the point.

---

She was filling the trough for the second time when the bird landed on the rim.

Cedar waxwing — the crest raised, the black mask tight across the eyes, the small yellow bracket at the tail's edge. It sat on the trough rim and looked at the water with the alert composure waxwings have, as if they have made a formal evaluation and decided to stay. She had been watching them in the old crabapple by the stone wall all December, working whatever the frozen berries still held.

Karl had come up to fill his pail. He stopped.

*Seidenschwanz,* he said. To the bird, or to himself — quietly.

She had known the word for two months. She'd found it in November in her father's bird guide — had run her finger down the *S* column until the entry was there, and had stood at the bookshelf until she understood the parts: *Seide* for silk, *Schwanz* for tail. Silk-tail. Cedar waxwing. The sound settling into the shape, finally, two months after she'd first heard it.

She said, "Cedar waxwing."

Karl looked at her. Then at the bird. Then back at her.

"Ce-dar," he said. "Wax-wing." He said it the way he said all new English — with the German vowels sitting inside the English syllables, the weight coming down a half-beat off from where American weight came down. It wasn't wrong. It was exact in its way, the way of someone learning a new material and handling each piece carefully before putting it down. He sounded each syllable as if he were measuring it, and in the measuring it became his.

She said *Seidenschwanz* back to him. The *ei* closing the way it should, or near enough. The *schw* she had been practicing privately — the German *sch* was not in English anywhere and you had to find the place in your mouth that made it.

He nodded once.

The bird sat on the trough rim for another two seconds and then was gone — up into the cold air and away toward the stone wall, a shape against the white sky, gone.

This was the form the thirty words took. They had built the vocabulary the way you build a fence: one piece at a time, where the need was, with whatever material was on hand. *Kuh, Eimer, kalt, morgen, Zaun, Tor.* Cow, bucket, cold, tomorrow, fence, gate. And now *Seidenschwanz* and cedar waxwing.

Her name in his mouth was *Hah-nah* — not the flat American version, both syllables equal and done with, but something with a shape to it, a slight lift at the first syllable as if it required a breath before it, as if a name were something worth arriving at properly. She had not corrected this. She was not going to correct it.

---

Her father came in for the grain check.

She heard the barn door and then his boots on the swept planks and she stayed at the trough, doing the work of topping off the second stall's water, not watching. He went to the bin, checked it by weight of the door, then by eye, and said something to Karl. Short sentences, the practical register, a grain count and a timeline for the afternoon: the German her father used for farm directives, which was not his full German, just the working face of it.

Karl answered. She heard the answer — the level of the grain, the afternoon plan, the correct present and future tense.

Her father did not respond immediately.

She looked up from the trough.

He was standing at the grain bin with his back to her. Not doing anything, not checking anything, just standing. The lamp threw his shadow long on the back wall. She watched the angle of his shoulders, the stillness in them — the specific stillness that was not waiting but the pause before something settled.

She had learned: fifty kilometers from Ansbach, her father had told her once, years before, in the matter-of-fact way of a person naming something factual that did not yet have weight to it. The farms, the particular look of that land in autumn. She had not done much with it at the time. It was doing something now, standing in her head while she watched the angle of her father's back, because Karl's German was not just German — it was the German of that region, those fifty kilometers, those particular vowels and the weight they were given, the sound of the place where her father had been a boy.

He had heard something in Karl's German.

Her father finished with the bin. He turned and walked back toward the door, passing her, and his face when he passed was closed in the way it had been closed for two years now, the expression stored somewhere past her reach. He did not look at her. He went out. The door swung shut.

She stood at the trough with the empty pail and listened to his boots crossing the farmyard.

Then she went back to her row.

---

At noon she brought her mother's tray upstairs — broth, bread, a dish of the stored applesauce — and set it on the table beside the window chair. Her mother looked at the tray. She picked up the spoon.

Hannah sat on the edge of the bed.

She had stopped talking at noon. It had taken most of the fall — she had been bringing the day's small reports along with the tray, offering them the way you offer something to fill a silence, and had understood eventually that the offering was for herself as much as her mother, and that her mother did not need it. She had stopped sometime in November. It hadn't been a decision. She had arrived one noon with nothing ready to say and had sat down, and it had been right in a way the talking hadn't been.

Her mother ate slowly. The window held the January afternoon — pale and flat, the kind of light that gave no warmth and asked no questions. The barn was visible, the icehouse was visible, the stone wall with the old crabapple. The bare top of it moved slightly in the wind.

Hannah had been trying to figure out for weeks whether her mother watched the farmyard or whether her eyes, when they were at the window, rested on nothing at all. She could not tell. Her mother's face when it was like this was closed the way certain skies were closed — weather in them, or not, and no way to know from outside.

Her father's silence was under pressure. It held something arranged against an interior wall, something that moved if you watched long enough. Her mother's silence was different. It had let go of something, or something had let go of it, and what was left was not waiting and was not grieving — it was simply what it was, settled at the bottom of itself. She had learned to sit inside it without trying to pull it toward her.

Her mother set the spoon down. Hannah picked up the tray.

---

The German homework was a translation exercise — two pages, a fictional letter, two people arranging a meeting. Marcus had written the assignment on the board in his careful hand: *Future and conditional: what the sentence commits to before the event. We are working on grammar. The letter is the occasion.*

She worked through the first page at the kitchen table with the stove going at her back. The words went cleanly. She could hear the grammar working — the verb held at the end of the clause, the sentence suspending all of its weight until the last piece arrived and everything resolved. She had liked this about German from the beginning: the sentence's patience with itself, the way it waited. Her father's German was like this. Karl's German was like this. Even the German she couldn't follow had this quality of holding back until the moment arrived.

Halfway through the second page she stopped.

She read back through it. The meeting was being arranged. Both people wanted to meet. The sentences were grammatically correct from beginning to end. And yet the conditional kept appearing where it didn't have to: *wenn es möglich ist, sofern die Umstände erlauben* — if it is possible, circumstances permitting. Both people used it. Both of them chose the construction that held the uncertainty open when they could have chosen the one that closed it.

She sat with this for a minute.

Marcus had given them a letter between two people who were not saying what they meant. She wasn't sure if he had done this on purpose or incidentally — if the grammar was the point and the content was just along for the grammar, or if he had chosen a sentence that meant something. She worked past it. She finished the translation and wrote her version in the exercise notebook and looked at what she had: two people arranging a meeting in the grammar of people who do not know whether they will see each other again.

She laid down the pencil. The kitchen window looked out at the farmyard, where nothing was moving except the crabapple top working slightly in the wind — the branches stripped now, nothing left on them, the movement small and reflexive, the tree going through the motion of wind without any leaves to show for it.

She closed the notebook. She would finish the last line Thursday. She would ask Marcus about the conditional if there was time after class.

---

The last barn check was after supper. She went through quickly in the cold — stove banked, water level at the second mark, latch secured against the wind. The cows were settled. She went out and latched the outer door.

Crossing the farmyard back toward the house, she passed the icehouse.

The lamp was on inside. It showed through the small oilpaper window, amber and steady, the warm color that the oilpaper gave to any light. She could hear voices through the plank wall — four of them, the low run of men talking at the end of the day. She couldn't hear the words. It was only the texture of it, four different registers going at once, the sound of men inside a room saying whatever you say when the work is finished and you have nowhere else to be.

She knew one of the voices by its position among the others. She kept walking.

---

In her room she stood at the curtain for a moment. Across the farmyard the icehouse lamp still showed — the oilpaper square holding its amber in the dark, steady, the way a lamp holds when there's no draft to move it.

The wind was in the eaves. It had been there since the December blow, the same low note running through the house frame every night, the eaves going with it and settling and going again. She had made peace with it during the daylight hours. At night it came back.

She set the exercise notebook on the dresser. Picked it up. Set it back down. She was not going to finish the last line tonight.

She got into bed.

*Seidenschwanz.* The *ei* closing in the mouth, the sound folding back on itself the way it didn't in English anywhere. She had tried it again today and been almost right — the *schw* nearly exact, the diphthong nearly closing the way his did. He had said *ce-dar wax-wing* with the German vowels inside the syllables, carrying their origin into the new language the way you carry anything long enough to become aware of the carrying.

The translation notebook was on the dresser. The last line had a question mark in the margin where she hadn't found the English equivalent that kept the right grammar and still felt like something a person would say. She would ask Thursday.

The wind went in the eaves. The lamp across the yard burned through the curtain, the amber she could feel at the edge of her vision without looking directly at it. She lay still and held the word — *Seidenschwanz*, cedar waxwing, *Seidenschwanz* — and the lamp kept its amber and the eaves kept their note, and she fell asleep with both of them going, the word and the wind and the light across the yard still burning.
