# Werner Grau

He laid the papers in order before he sat down.

The letter first: W. Grau to A. Pfeiffer, September 28, 1943, in the original envelope — the delivery error penciled at the upper left in a postal clerk's hand, not his. He positioned it at the left of the available space, which was how he organized working materials, and smoothed the crease with his thumb. Beside it, to the right: Sondheimer's reply — one page, typed, the Columbia letterhead at the top, dated February 28, returned here in the second week of March. And in the center, the sheet of school composition paper he had been adding to since December: five items written out in ink at different times, the last dated March 6, and below the fifth item a space he had been leaving for the concluding sentence.

He sat. The rain had been coming down since before he woke — the steady, considered rain of Maine in May, not February's cold driving kind but something more deliberate, as though the season had decided to be thorough about it. Henry had brought the porch rocker inside the night before. Lillian was in the kitchen, two floors below, the sound of her muffled and occasional. Otherwise the house was quiet. It was Sunday.

He read the letter again, though he did not need to. Werner Grau had written it on lined notepaper in the vertical German hand that Marcus recognized as belonging to men of a certain education and a certain generation — the same penmanship taught at the gymnasium in Vienna, though Werner's was slightly looser, less attended to, the hand of a man who wrote for communication rather than for record. *Lieber Albrecht.* The salutation of an old friendship, long enough that ceremony would have been an insult. He had written from Portland, and the return address was a street number and nothing else — no district, no institution. He had been planning to come to Coldwater in October. There were things he could not commit to paper, which was why he was making the journey in person. He had news of the Reinmars, whom he had been carrying for months and would deliver himself. *Ihr alter Freund, Werner Grau.*

The Sondheimer reply began with what the records confirmed: entry at Boston, March 1936, arts-organization visa sponsored by the Boston Alliance for the Arts, a cultural exchange program for painters and printmakers whose funding had redirected the following year. Renewed once, in March 1937. Expired March 1940. After the expiry, the record had three fields where information might exist — renewal, deportation proceeding, departure — and in each field the same notation: *no record.* Sondheimer had added, at the close, that the records were incomplete, which was a professional courtesy and also a precise observation.

Marcus looked at his own sheet.

The five items had been written at different times; the ink varied from entry to entry because he had not used the same pen. Item one: *W. Grau — German national, born approximately 1890–1900 (inference: letter's tone; A. Pfeiffer's approximate age as peer; quality of handwriting — a man in his middle years, educated).* Item two: *In the United States, March 1936 to October 1943. Legal standing: valid through March 1940. After: no record of any kind. Duration without standing: approximately three and a half years.* Item three: *Occupation: painter and printmaker (Boston Alliance for the Arts, cultural exchange program, 1936). Last known address: Portland, Maine — street number only, no institution.* Item four: *Known associations: A. Pfeiffer, Bamberg, before 1922; Reinmar family, Ansbach (reference in letter to 'Reinmars Junge' — Karl Reinmar, nineteen, currently at Pfeiffer farm under the federal POW labor program, Camp Houlton satellite).* Item five, added March 6: *No legal standing from spring 1940 onward. No record thereafter of any kind.*

And below: the blank space.

---

He had decided that morning, when he woke, that he would write the concluding paragraph — not because new evidence had arrived, but because the evidence he held was not going to change, and the space had been waiting long enough to have become itself a kind of position. He had learned at the university that an unfinished argument was worse than a precisely imprecise one, provided the imprecision was named. He would name it.

He wrote at the top of the remaining space: *Plausible account:* He wrote it as a heading, because what followed was an inference, not a finding, and the distinction mattered to him.

*W. Grau rented or borrowed a vessel in Portland — a small boat, capable of coastal travel in fair conditions. He traveled north along the coast to Coldwater Reach, arriving on the night of October 11–12, 1943. He was on the south waterfront at some point during that night. He attempted to locate A. Pfeiffer, or located him. Before the storm's peak on the morning of October 12, he died — by drowning, by cardiac event, by the storm, by some combination of these things.*

He stopped. He read what he had written. Then he drew a careful circle around *by some combination of these things* — not to mark it for revision but because it was the account's honest center, the claim the evidence would not close over. The medical finding he had heard in October, second-hand through two conversations at the school: no water in the lungs. Which meant the storm had been the occasion but not necessarily the cause. What had preceded the storm — what Werner Grau had been doing on the south waterfront, whom he had met or not met, what physical condition he had been in when the weather came on — was not in any document Marcus held. What Albrecht Pfeiffer's face had shown him, across a cold farmyard in January, was recognition without surprise — which meant Albrecht had known Werner came to Coldwater, had perhaps seen him, had perhaps been the last person to see him. What had passed between them on the night of October 11, if anything passed between them, Marcus did not have.

He circled *by some combination of these things* and left it.

---

Werner Grau in 1940 had been, by the law of the country in which he was living, what Marcus Klein had been in 1940 by the law of a different one: a German-category national without valid status in a country that considered itself at war, or shortly would, with the country named on his papers. The category had been applied to both of them on the same grounds — not the politics of either man, not his conduct or his intentions, but the accident of the nation in which he had been born and the timing of his departure from it. Whether the man had left under duress; what he had left behind; what he thought about what the nation on his papers was doing in his name — these had not been the relevant questions. The category was the category.

In Canada, the category had produced an internment camp at Sherbrooke, Quebec: approximately ten months, the administration correct in the main, the library inadequate, the company of approximately thirty other men in similar circumstances, the Emergency Committee placement in Cambridge that had come through in 1941 as it might not have come through in 1942. He had lost a year. He had lost access to his books, his correspondence, his professional record, and the ordinary continuity of a working life. He had come out with those losses and a particular watchfulness about paperwork that had not entirely left him.

In Portland, the same category had apparently produced something different. Werner had been painting, or working, or doing whatever a man without legal standing does in a port city large enough for a marginal economy to absorb him — painting, renting a room, keeping an address on a street with no institutional affiliation. He had not been found, or he had been found and tolerated, or he had been, for three and a half years, invisible in the specific way such economies make people invisible. He had been alive and planning a journey in September 1943.

The difference between them was not character. Not capacity, not intention, not the content of any file any authority had ever compiled on either of them.

It was, partly, the country. Canada had interned; America — or this corner of America — had looked away. And it was, more than partly, luck, a category Marcus had spent a number of years trying to name accurately: without the false comfort of fate and without the false precision of something that could have been otherwise if he had simply been more careful.

He knew this, and had known it since March. He held it at that.

---

The account required things of him that he could not do.

He could not bring it to the Coast Guard station at Sprucehead. The CG's record on the body was, as far as he knew, still open — no papers, no identification, no next of kin, case status unresolved. A man arriving at Sprucehead with a name to attach to that record would also be arriving, necessarily, with an immigration status: no legal standing for three and a half years at the time of death. This would not remain confined to Werner Grau. Albrecht Pfeiffer had been on the south waterfront the same night, or Marcus had strong grounds for believing so; any inquiry beginning with Werner Grau's name would not stop at Werner Grau. Karl Reinmar was at the Pfeiffer farm under an arrangement that depended on the smooth administration of federal programs that did not benefit from additional scrutiny.

He could not bring it to anyone official. He was not, himself, fully official — his appointment had been authorized under wartime provisions and renewed twice by the school board; his own papers were in order; but *official,* as a designation for the kind of standing that would give such a delivery any weight, was a word he had learned to apply to himself with care.

He would not suppress it. This was also a fact about his situation, though of a different kind — a constraint of a different order than the ones above, which were practical, and this one was not. Suppression required performing, for some imagined audience, a version of himself who had not assembled these five items and their plausible conclusion, who did not hold the account he held. That performance was not available to him. He held the account; the account was accurate; he would hold it accurately. That was the verb he had.

Whether this constituted doing something — whether it constituted not doing something — whether the distinction had operational meaning from inside his particular position — this was a question he had been sitting with since January, and he had concluded, provisionally, that it was not a question he could answer from where he stood. He left it circled, alongside the cause of Werner Grau's death, marked present and unclosed.

---

He stacked the documents: letter, Sondheimer's reply, the sheet of school paper. He folded the Sondheimer reply in thirds, as it had arrived. He folded the sheet in half on the horizontal axis and then once more, so it came to roughly the letter's dimensions, and tucked it inside the envelope with the reply. The letter to Albrecht Pfeiffer he returned to its original envelope, which he resealed with a strip of paper and paste — not because he expected anyone to open the drawer, but because the envelope was the document's proper housing and the document deserved its proper housing.

He opened the bottom drawer. The Latin dictionary had been resting on top of the folder since October, when he had placed it there because the dictionary's weight kept the papers flat and because the Latin dictionary was the thing most like a private object he owned in this room; it had seemed correct that it should be the one to lie over the rest. He put the new envelope alongside the earlier materials, arranged everything so it lay flat, and set the Latin dictionary back on top.

He locked the drawer and put the key in the pocket of his coat, which was on the hook by the door.

---

Outside, the rain was unchanged. He put on his coat and hat and went down through the back hall and out past the entrance to Henry's boiler room, where the mop handle Henry had propped against the wall three days ago still leaned, apparently permanent now. Around the side of the house to the street.

The street was quiet with the Sunday-morning quiet that a small town in rain takes on — traffic in, doors closed, the surface of things reduced to its own sound. The maple at the Gifford corner had leafed out in the early way of May, the green still light and tentative, not yet committed to summer. He had been walking this street three or four times a day since March 1942; he knew it in every weather now, knew the way the gravel at the road edge shifted after frost, the way the Gifford daffodils came and went in the second week of April.

He walked to the north end where the street met the road that went inland, toward the drumlins and the hay fields, the direction of the Pfeiffer farm. He stood where the pavement gave onto the dirt section and looked at the road going out into the flat country. The rain darkened its surface evenly. After a moment he turned and walked back, the full length of the street, past the house and past the maple, to the south end where the road bent toward the main road and from there down to the waterfront. Nine minutes from Henry's front door to the pier head — he had measured it in the first week, as he measured all distances in a new place. He could hear the harbor from here: a mooring chain, something working the outer basin, the particular patience of water against wood.

He stood at the bend.

Then he walked back.

Upstairs, he sat at the desk with the papers gone. The window gave onto the back of the house, not the harbor, but the harbor smell came through regardless — three streets off, window closed, the salt and diesel that was the specific smell of this air, in this place, on a Sunday in May. He had been aware of it since his first week here, when it had seemed one foreign element among a landscape composed entirely of foreign elements. He was aware of it now in a different register: not foreign, not local exactly, but as the smell this air had, here, with the rain coming down and the drawer locked and Werner Grau in it.

# The Sixth of June

The radio was on downstairs.

She heard it before she heard him — the sound coming up through the boards as a man's voice, steady and formal, saying something she couldn't separate into words from the top of the stairs. Then underneath it her father's voice, low, not calling her.

She came down in her socks, holding the banister in the dark.

The kitchen was lit only by the orange of the radio dial and the first gray beginning at the window above the sink. The clock on the shelf read ten past four. Her father was standing at the table with his barn coat over the chair behind him, hands at his sides. He had been there for some time. She could tell by the particular settled quality of his stillness — the way a person stands when they have already done the hard work of arriving at a thing and are now simply inside it.

She stood by the cold stove and listened.

*—Allied forces have landed on the coast of northern France, in the region known as Normandy—*

Her father did not look at her. The voice on the radio was deliberate, each sentence placed as if placement were a form of accuracy. She tried to find Normandy on the wall map Mr. Klein kept in the classroom — a physical geography map of Europe, mountain ranges rendered as hatch marks — and she could find France in her mind generally but could not find the northern coast of it, could not locate the region.

*—General Eisenhower has confirmed that operations are continuing and that Allied forces have established positions along multiple beach approaches—*

The signal dropped for a moment and came back at a different pitch. Another voice, lower, reading something that sounded like an official statement. *Beachhead. Sustained operations. Allied forces.* She was hearing the shapes of words rather than their meaning.

He had not made coffee. She looked at his hands on the table and did not ask.

---

Her mother came down at twenty past four. Hannah heard the careful step on the stairs — her mother's way of walking when she was tired or deliberate — and then Magda was in the doorway, in her robe, hair loose over her shoulders. She stood looking at the radio.

She did not come into the kitchen.

The signal had shifted; it was speaking from London now, someone said. It came in slightly cleaner before full dawn, the way foreign signals sometimes did at that hour.

Hannah made coffee. She knew where they stood with the ration book; she had checked two days before. She decided it was worth it. The match smell, the soft sound of the gas, the small flame finding itself. She stood by the stove and waited and looked at her mother in the doorway. Her mother was watching the radio itself, not her father — the cabinet, as if the signal were visible inside it.

When the coffee was ready she poured two cups. She set one at her father's place. He looked at it for a moment and then picked it up with both hands. She brought the second to the doorway and her mother took it, both hands around the cup, and held it without drinking.

They listened.

The voice named towns. It named a number of ships in a tone that meant the number was very large. The word *paratroopers.* The phrase *naval bombardment* said in the same even register as everything else. She listened for her father's face to change and it did not change in any way she could name. He had shifted his hands; they were flat on the table now, weight forward. He knows where Normandy is. He can hear those town names and put them on the coast. She watched his face for the look of a person tracking something through space and she thought she could see it in the set of his jaw, the forward lean.

The clock moved from four-thirty to five. The June light came in fast — the barn materialized out of the dark, then the fence posts along the east field, then the hay fields themselves in the early flat gray. Birds started outside, a few at first and then more of them, and by five minutes before five it was a full sound with the radio running underneath it.

She made herself useful. She set the oatmeal to soak for when they would want it. She straightened the dish towels that did not need straightening. Her mother had not moved from her chair; her father had not moved from the table. The radio continued — a fourth voice now, a correspondent somewhere, saying something about the men who had gone in before dawn, the ones who had gone by parachute into the dark.

She tried to make the distance real and could not. The voice was coming out of the BC-1206 the same way it always came out, filling the kitchen the same way the weather report filled it, and somewhere behind the voice there were men coming off boats onto a beach in France and she could not picture the beach.

Her father said, in English: "It will be over soon."

He said it to the room. Not to her, not to her mother — to the kitchen, to the radio, to the window where the June morning was showing itself. She had not heard a full English sentence from him since — she searched backward, through months — since January. Maybe longer. His English had not gone away; she had never believed it had. It was still in him the way a radio signal was always traveling even when the set was off.

Not relief exactly. She was watching his face and there was nothing in it that looked like the American kind, the easy kind, the kind that made you exhale loudly or put your hand over your eyes. Something else: the look of a man who has been watching for a specific thing to begin, and believes it has begun.

Her mother moved from the doorway.

One step onto the linoleum. Then another. She crossed to the table in three steps and she pulled out the chair and she sat. She folded both hands around the cup. She looked at the tabletop.

She did not speak. She was in the kitchen. She was at the table, which was not the doorway, and Hannah did not look at it too long.

*Erleichterung.* She had the German and not the English for it, because German was the language she had been made in, and the German word held the shape of what it named. Not relief — that word was too clean, too finished at its edges. More like: a weight becoming less heavy. Something that has been pressing, without stopping, for a very long time — longer than she had understood the full shape of it — beginning, on this specific morning in June, to ease by one small degree.

She did not say the word.

The radio went on.

An hour later her father put on his barn coat and boots and went out. The screen door. Hannah washed the cups. Her mother stayed at the table, hands folded, not sleeping, not reading, just there in the new morning light. After a while Magda reached over and turned the radio down one notch — not off, just quieter — and Hannah left her there.

She milked. She fed. She hauled water and swept the milking parlor and split a quarter-cord of kindling from the pile behind the barn that had been waiting two weeks for someone to get to it. The work went the way the work always went: the weight of the pails, the patience of the cows, the rhythm of the axe in the June morning. Somewhere in the middle of it, there were kitchens all up the road where people were having the versions of these hours that belonged to them — people with sons on those beaches, people who could follow the town names on the coast. She didn't have any of that. She had her father's hands flat on the table and the sentence he had said into the kitchen with no one in particular to hear it.

---

That afternoon the radio was everywhere in town. She heard it from the diner when she stopped the truck at the intersection for the feed run — someone had turned the set up high and the voice came through the screen door and across the sidewalk. At the post office two women stood in the open doorway with their arms folded against their chests, listening to the set inside. Three men on the sidewalk in front of the hardware store, standing in the June sun, not talking to each other.

She loaded the feed and drove back on the south road. The afternoon had come in with the first real summer warmth — the kind that settles in the open fields and won't move until after supper, the kind that means the season has made up its mind. The fields on the south side of the road were deep green and tall. She was thinking about their hay. The south field had been ready for two weeks; her father would cut it this week if the weather held.

At the farm, Lonzo had his portable radio on the icehouse step — a small set with a black handle, volume turned up enough to carry inside. She could hear it as she crossed the yard with the first water bucket, the afternoon broadcast, the same careful voices. The door was propped open. She heard Lonzo's chair shift inside.

She put the bucket down and went back for the second.

---

Karl was on the step.

He had come outside while she was in the barn. He was sitting with his elbows on his knees, looking at the fence line and the hay field beyond it. The hay was at its full summer height — she had been watching it get tall for two weeks — silver-green in the afternoon light, moving sometimes in the way tall grass moves when there is no particular wind, the stalks making small adjustments to their own weight. His forearms were tanned from three weeks of fieldwork. He was not looking at her.

She had been going to walk past to the pump.

She stopped.

Four or five yards from the step. Lonzo was inside; she could hear the radio still going, hear his chair. Her father's sentence had been in her head since five that morning. It had ridden with her through the barn work and the drive to town and through the afternoon, and it was there now in the June heat in this specific piece of yard where she was not supposed to stop.

She said it before she had decided what she was doing.

"It will be over soon."

She said it quietly, looking at the fence past his shoulder. The way her father had said it — not to anyone in the room in particular, just the sentence released into the air.

Karl looked at her.

He looked at her for a moment and then he nodded. Once, slow. Not yes, not agreement. The nod she had seen him give Lonzo when Lonzo explained something Karl had already worked out for himself. *I hear you.* He looked back at the fields.

She stayed where she was with the pail.

He said, in English: "My home."

Not a question. The two words and then quiet, his hands loose between his knees, his eyes on the fields.

She did not ask what he thought he would find there.

She stood one moment longer. Then she picked up the pail and turned and walked toward the pump.

---

She heard him say something behind her. She was already several steps away — the radio going in the icehouse, the heat and the distance — and she caught only the shape of the words, not the words themselves.

*Es wird bald vorbei sein.*

The hay field beyond the fence held its full summer height. The smell of turned earth came across from the south field where her father had been working since before dawn, before the radio, before the sentence he had said into the kitchen. She kept walking. The pump handle at the corner of the barn would be warm from sitting in the afternoon sun.

# Harbor Traffic

The *Edna C.* came in off the grounds at two-fifty-eight, heavier than she looked. Talbot brought her in clean through the afternoon chop, which was running south-southeast at two feet and building. Eira logged the time and estimated the catch from the boxes on deck — Talbot would want to correct the tonnage entry against the scale once he'd offloaded, but there was enough in the hold to see from the pier head and she put down a working number. She could revise it in the morning.

Four more vessels to account for before dark. She turned back to the fuel log.

The Navy tender at the outer anchorage had run its weekly fueling at nine that morning, and the allocation she'd authorized — drawn against the defense supplemental, not the commercial reserve — had taken a larger bite out of the shared dock supply than she'd anticipated. Pete Alley had come to her before noon wanting to know whether his allotment was going to cover his run to the outer grounds. She'd checked the figures and it wouldn't, not without an adjustment. She made the adjustment: signed the form, moved the amount from the supplemental line, wrote her authorization in the margin. She did not ask anyone's approval because the handbook did not require it. Alley took the form and filled his tank and went.

In the summer of 1942, this same move would have required a county sign-off and three days. She did not think about it often. When she did, it was as a log entry: what the column shows this year against what it showed before.

---

The afternoon was full. June kept long hours, the light staying good until past seven, which meant the traffic did not thin before six and on some evenings she was still logging at dusk. She did not object to this. The harbor in summer was the harbor at its most itself: boats on the water, fuel in the tanks, money moving, the cold-storage house working around the clock. The harbor in December was harder to manage and quieter, which was not the same as easier.

Grandy Soule had the *Maud L.* at the east float on account of a sports boat from Portland tying in his usual slip without permission. She'd had him at her elbow at noon, not saying much but standing in a way that said plenty. She'd walked down the ramp and told the man in the sports boat's cockpit that the slip was not available. He had a dock hand's tan and a new sportsman's jacket and the particular patience of a man who expected his arrangements to be accommodated. He looked at her for the length of time it took to understand that she had said what she meant. Then he cast off his lines and moved to slip fourteen, which she had indicated.

Soule, when she came back up the ramp, said nothing. She said nothing. She went back to the log.

The second dispute of the afternoon was between Burton Talbot and Ray Coffin's boy over a question of priority at the fuel dock — both had radioed at the same hour, and Coffin had gotten there first. She looked at the log and told them the order of the log was the order of the dock. Coffin fueled. Talbot waited. Both left without arguing. The argument had lasted four minutes and she had used twelve words, which seemed like the right ratio.

She was making a note about the outer berth allotment when Talbot came back up from the dock.

He had his hat in his hand. Talbot did not take his hat off on the dock as a rule.

"My sister's boy is in it," he said. He meant Normandy. It had been three weeks.

"How old is he."

"Nineteen."

She put the pen down and looked at him. She had known Burton Talbot for eight years.

"All right," she said.

He put his hat back on and went up the pier.

She wrote the tonnage entry and the time.

---

That was the quality of the harbor since the sixth of June — the particular way the men spoke now. Before June the waiting had been accumulative: each week adding to the prior week, the not-yet getting larger. Since June there was still waiting, but at a fixed position. The thing had been identified; it had a location and a direction. You could track it now. This was not the same as better. Osgood's boy had been missing in Normandy since the fourteenth and his mother came to the post office every morning. The telegrams had not stopped. But the quality of what people were waiting with had changed, and she could feel it in the way they stood at the fuel dock and in the number of words they used.

She could not write any of this in the harbor log. She kept track of it elsewhere, in the same place she kept track of other things she couldn't put in the official record.

---

The afternoon turned still around four. This happened in late June on certain days: the wind dropped off and the harbor went flat, the water the color of pewter, the pilings showing their reflections straight down. The cold-storage house was quiet between runs. The three lobstermen still out on the grounds would be thinking about coming in.

She checked the clock on the shed wall and checked her watch against it. Four-forty-three, which was accurate.

She made a note in the weather log: flat calm at 1643, channel at slack. She had been making these notes for eight years, in the same format, with the same shorthand. The notes would not change the weather. They were the record.

---

Marcus Klein came along the harbor road at five minutes past five.

She had seen him on this road at this hour for two years going on three — the same walk, the same pace, the same slight forward lean that was his particular posture, as if he were attending to something at chest height that the rest of the road was not showing. He was not a large man and he dressed for the season: a good hat in winter, shirtsleeves in June. She had seen him in all weathers. He walked the way someone walked who had no car and had decided not to mind it, which was to say at a deliberate pace and without any appearance of hurry.

Most days he came even with the pier entrance, nodded in her direction — she may or may not have been visible; it made no difference to the nod — and continued south toward the Crow house on the hill. She had come to expect this the way she expected the position of the channel markers: a regular fixed point in the afternoon's accounting.

Today he stopped.

He came a few steps through the gate. "Good afternoon," he said.

"Afternoon."

He looked at the pier and then at her. "Are the Pfeiffer family managing all right, do you think?"

The phrasing was assembled — not casual, not a question asked in passing to fill a silence, but a question whose specific terms had been chosen before it was asked. *The Pfeiffer family,* not the Pfeiffers. *Managing all right,* not *how are they* or *any trouble out there.* It was a question designed to be answerable without requiring her to say what she actually knew, which gave her a good deal of information about what he thought she might know.

"As far as I know," she said.

Which was accurate. The farm was running; the county had raised no complaint about the work arrangement; the daughter came to the post office like any other family in town; Albrecht Pfeiffer had been in for his feed run three weeks ago. She knew nothing more specific than this. She said what she knew.

He nodded once. "Thank you," he said.

He went on down the road.

---

She watched him walk the harbor road to the south bend and go around it, out of sight.

The exchange had taken perhaps forty seconds. She went back to the pier head and picked up her pen.

The *Sea Star* would be in by six. She had the form ready.

She did not write anything about Marcus Klein. There was nothing to write — a man had asked a question and she had answered it.

She held it in the back of the afternoon's accounting the way she held any piece of information that did not have a column yet.

He had been walking this road for going on three years. In that time he had said perhaps twenty words to her. She had always read him as someone who chose his words with attention — the particular precision of a man who had learned to be careful with language. He was not a man who stopped at pier gates to ask after inland farm families without a reason for it.

He was the German teacher. The Pfeiffer daughter was in his advanced German class; she knew that much from conversation at the post office. Whether he had any other connection to the farm she did not know.

She turned the question over. No obvious answer presented itself. If he had asked the question behind the question, it would have been: *is anything wrong out there.* She could not account for what had put that question in him. She did not have enough to build a theory.

There was one other piece she was carrying that she had no column for. The dock figures from the October night — the two shapes on the south float before the blow, one with something under his arm, the pale coat. She had been keeping that entry for eight months without a label, because she still did not have enough to classify it. Soule's account in April had come part of the way, had corroborated the dinghy and one figure, and she had reached for the pen and then set it down again. She knew what she'd seen and she knew what Soule had seen and she knew the two accounts met at the south float, and she still did not have a label for what that column was.

The column now had two entries in it.

She put the pen down and did not invent a label. The column was there; she knew it was there; both entries were in it correctly and were going to stay there until she had enough to name what the column was. Not longer. Not shorter.

---

The *Sea Star* came in at six-twelve. Coffin's boy ran her through the channel entrance with economy, and she logged the time and the catch and wrote the weather note for the outer grounds. He said four words about the chop past Seal Island and she wrote that too, because the chop past Seal Island in late June could matter to the morning forecast.

She transferred the afternoon to the permanent record: fuel allotments, berth assignments, arrival times, departures, tonnages. Alley's supplemental form and her authorization. Talbot's working tonnage figure and the notation to revise in the morning. The two berth disputes resolved. Everything in its column, every column labeled correctly.

She put the pen down and put the log on its shelf.

The last light was running at a long angle off the channel, making the water look shallow even where it wasn't. The outer anchorage tender was riding easy and dark. The lobster boats were resting at their lines, hulls knocking gently against the fenders, the particular sound the harbor made in the slack after a working day.

She turned off the shed light and went out.

The harbor would manage the night without her. It was good at that.

# Another Year

The hardware store had put out its summer display — aluminum pails, a coil of garden hose in a shade of green that seemed to belong somewhere less austere — and Marcus stopped to regard it before walking on. The diner's screen door was propped with a brick, as it had been propped since May, when the evenings finally warranted it. He had lived in Coldwater for two years and four months. He knew the brick. He knew the diner owner's habit of playing the radio at a volume that seemed to assume the building was empty, and he knew, having verified it over the course of two summers, that this was simply her volume — not a statement about the building, not an invitation, simply the way the sound occupied the space she was in. He knew which three houses on the north block had dogs and in which order they would announce his passage. He knew the bakery's exhaust vent, open in summer, which emitted a smell of something with sugar in it that he had spent several weeks identifying before he thought to simply look at the building's south wall. He knew the cat in the upper right window of the gray house at the far end, which watched him daily without sound, with a consistency that was, he had come to understand, its form of acknowledgment.

He extended his walk tonight past the usual turning point at the harbor road's south bend, continuing down to the pier end and along the last quarter mile toward the south headland, where the road ended at the boatyard's locked gate. The boatyard was closed for the evening, its equipment organized in the particular way of a yard whose foreman considered the arrangement to be its own kind of order. The Ellsworth was in her summer berth. The lobster boats from the outer grounds had come in and the men were gone. The harbor in July was a different harbor from the harbor in October or in February: more traffic, longer light, but no urgency in it — the work was the same work, but the weather was forgiving enough that it had stopped being the kind of work that could make errors fatal, and this gave the working waterfront a different quality, almost relaxed, which was a word he would not have used for it in November.

He had been thinking about the letter for five weeks.

It was not, precisely, from Sondheimer. Sondheimer was at Columbia and had been at Columbia since 1942, answering his telephone before it finished ringing and placing scholars with the efficiency of a man running a clearing operation under deadline. The letter was from a colleague of Sondheimer's — a man named Althaus, affiliated with the Emergency Committee in some ancillary capacity — who had a position to fill at a small college outside Boston. German literature, beginning September 1944. The letter was professional, appropriately cordial, and had been composed by someone who was confident the offer would be received as welcome. The library would be better than whatever Marcus had access to in coastal Maine. The salary was better. The department had two other members, both scholars of some reputation; there was the prospect of colleagues, in the professional sense, rather than a schoolroom he shared with the supply closet and a staffroom whose only other daily occupant was the trigonometry teacher. The letter noted, with some care, that there was a German émigré community of substance in the Cambridge area. It did not say *you must be lonely*, but it arranged its facts in a manner that made the inference available.

He had been considering it at one remove, with the discipline of a man who had learned to examine choices from a slight distance rather than from within their force field. When he tried to imagine Boston — the apartment he would need to locate, the departmental room with the other two faculty, the particular October quality of a college library's reading room in the afternoon — the image that came was not quite Boston. It was a composite assembled from memory of other institutions: reading rooms in Vienna, in Paris, the brief unhappy months in London. An accurate image of the category and a generic image of the particular. The Boston apartment had no street address. The departmental room had no windows he could place. He had tried for five weeks to make the image specific and he could not do it.

When he tried to imagine Coldwater in September — the boiler starting in the school's basement, the harbor road going its autumn gray, Hannah Pfeiffer's translation papers on his desk with their marginalia in two languages, Henry's coffee at six in the morning, the sound of Henry's footstep on the stair distinguishable from any other footstep in the building — the image was specific without requiring effort. He could render it in accurate detail. The boiler's particular sound when it came on was different from any boiler he had known before, and he knew it. The distinction between the two qualities of imagination — the generic and the specific, the category and the particular — seemed to him like data of some kind, though he had not yet decided what it was evidence for.

The breakwater was visible from the south end of the road, its lower arm running out toward the elbow in the evening light. He looked at it for a moment, as he looked at it most evenings when he was at this end of the street. Then he looked away and turned back toward Henry's house.

Through the kitchen window, as he came up the street, he could see Lillian setting the table. She moved through the kitchen with the particular efficiency of a person in their own space — adjusting for the cabinet door she knew without looking, setting the plates down in a way he recognized from three hundred evenings in this house. He had a room here; he had a key; he paid his rent on the first of each month and had been doing so since the spring of 1942. He had always understood this relationship correctly, in his own accounting: he was a tenant, occupying a room in a house that belonged to Henry and Lillian in the way that only a house thirty years lived in belongs to people. He had, for two years and four months, thought of it as Henry's house, in the same way he had thought of every room he had rented since 1938 as belonging to whoever owned or kept it — a form of precision that was also, he recognized, a form of self-protection, since a room that belongs to someone else is a room you can leave without leaving something that is yours.

Coming up the street toward it now, the summer evening very long and the kitchen light very certain in the dimming July light, he found that he was not walking toward a room he was occupying. He was going back to a place.

He did not examine this in the middle of the street. He filed it and walked on.

---

*That evening.*

He sat at the desk in his room and wrote the reply to Althaus. It was shorter than the original. He thanked Althaus, noted that the position was well suited to his qualifications and that he had no doubt the college would find an excellent candidate for it, and stated that he was committed to his current position in Coldwater and found it — here he chose the word *suited* with care, the way he chose all his words in professional correspondence, for precision rather than warmth — suited to his capacities in the ways that currently mattered. He offered to recommend colleagues from the Emergency Committee rolls who might be available for the September start. He closed with appropriate formality.

He did not write *at least one further academic year*, though that was the phrase in his own mind, the honest accounting of a man who did not wish to make claims that exceeded his current state of resolution. What the letter said was *committed* to Coldwater. He was clear about the distinction. The "at least" was in his own mind, where he could keep it accurate and revisit it as conditions required, without having communicated a hedged commitment to a professional contact who had no means of interpreting the hedge and no reason to receive it charitably. He was not lying to Althaus. He was simply not exporting the hedge. This seemed to him defensible.

He sealed the envelope and wrote the address in his usual hand and put it in the inside pocket of his coat, which was on the chair, for the morning mail.

He stayed at the desk. The window was open. Henry and Lillian had gone upstairs an hour ago, and the house had the quality of a house in which two people were already settled for the night — a particular sense of an occupied building at rest, familiar to him now in a way it had not been in the first winter, when the settling sounds of the structure had woken him more than once.

Then, from outside, carried on the harbor breeze that was moving in from the southeast, he heard the bell buoy.

---

He had heard it before, at intervals, on other quiet nights from this window. It was the bell buoy at the channel entrance, placed by the Coast Guard to mark the deep line of the approach, and it rang on the swell in the rhythm of the water rather than the rhythm of a clock — neither metronomic nor erratic, but in the particular irregular pattern of a float responding to what was actually there. He had heard it as he heard most of the harbor's ongoing sounds: as acoustic texture, as part of the category of harbor sounds that occupied the audible background of this street, along with the diesel engines at five in the morning and the gulls over the fish pier and the occasional sound of a dragger coming in off the outer grounds after dark. He had heard it and not distinguished it.

He distinguished it now because the night was quiet and because he was at his desk with the window open and a coat on the chair with a letter in the pocket, and the buoy's sound was not the sound of harbor-in-general but the sound of the bell buoy at the entrance to the channel at Coldwater Reach — a specific sound in a specific place, which was this place. It could not be heard from Althaus's small college outside Boston. It could not be heard from Cambridge or London or Sherbrooke or Paris or Vienna. It could be heard from this room, with this window open at this angle to the southeast, on nights when the harbor breeze came from the right direction and the town was quiet enough to let it through.

He was not persuaded by this observation. He was aware that sentiment could be constructed from almost any available material, and that the sentiment of *this specific sound* was available to any man who had spent sufficient time in proximity to a harbor with a bell buoy in it.

The grammar interested him more.

The difference between *I am staying* and *I have stopped leaving* was a matter of aspect: the first located the action in the present, ongoing, as though staying were an activity requiring continuous effort of will; the second registered a prior event whose effects persisted into the present without requiring continuous maintenance. Both produced the same present-tense situation — a man in a room in Coldwater in July 1944. What they differed on was what each attributed the situation to. *I am staying* implied a decision being renewed. *I have stopped leaving* implied a decision already made, no longer under active reconsideration.

He was not certain which was accurate. He suspected that neither was, exactly — that the distinction between choice and inertia, when applied to the accumulation of two years in a specific place, was not as clean as the grammar required. He had made no formal decision to leave Coldwater and had accordingly never formally stopped leaving. He had, on several occasions, been presented with the option of leaving — first after his first winter, when Sondheimer had written about a high school position in Hartford; then in the spring of 1943, when there had been a brief inquiry about translation work in Washington that had come to nothing; and now this, from Althaus, which was the most substantial of the three. He had declined each one without, so far as he could identify, a sense of sacrifice. The question was whether a pattern of not-leaving, accumulated over three iterations, constituted a form of staying. He thought it might, observed from a sufficient distance. He was not certain he was in a position to observe it from a sufficient distance yet.

The buoy rang three times in close succession, then twice more, then the interval extended.

He was not going anywhere — not this September, and, he thought, not the September after. He had not decided this. He had written a letter and addressed it and put it in his coat for the morning mail, and the letter said *committed* with no hedge in it, and the hedge in his own mind was the honest ledger of a man who knew himself well enough to know that the present moment's resolution was provisional in the way all present-moment resolutions were provisional. But the provisionalness of the resolution was not the same as the resolution being absent. The letter was in the coat. He would mail it in the morning.

The harbor outside went on with its business without requiring any acknowledgment from him. The bell buoy rang at the entrance to the channel in the rhythm of the water and not of any clock. The summer night in Coldwater continued in the usual way of summer nights in Coldwater, which was to say: it went on past the time when most of the houses were dark, steady and unhurried.

# Field Birds

By noon she had made seven trips from the pump to the field.

The south field was down: her father had started the mowing before the light was up, and by the time she came out to milk at six the windrows were already lying in their long parallel lines across the field, the green going pale in the August morning. The baler was running before breakfast. She knew the sound of it from every August of her life — the engine's steady knock, the thump and clank of the bale chamber, the sharp clicking of the knotters that meant the machine was working right — and she had long since stopped hearing it as sound. It was what August was. The field going from windrow to bale to stacked wagon in passes and passes until the south field was bare and the hay was in.

The heat was complete by ten.

She walked the fence line with the water bucket. The cut-grass smell was everywhere — the sweet fermenting smell of hay in the August sun, the dusty smell of it when the baler shook it down. She had her sleeves rolled and her hair under the old straw hat she kept on the back porch for fieldwork. The back of her neck was damp. Ahead of her the tractor crawled through its next pass and her father's silhouette was small against the far end of the field, the exhaust coming up straight into the dead August air.

She gave him water first. He drank without looking at her, used his handkerchief, put the machine in gear. She watched him go and then went down the fence line toward the near wagon.

Dieter took the dipper and said something she couldn't hear over the baler. She nodded. He handed it back. Rolf and Hans in sequence, coming off the wagon for thirty seconds and returning to the work. Then the baler rounded the north end of the field and the noise changed quality and she could hear what was under it — the insects in the uncut grass along the fence, the dry clicking sound the heat made in the cut windrows, a crow somewhere on the far side of the treeline calling once and not again.

Karl came last.

He took the dipper and drank and stood looking at the fence for a moment before handing it back. She reached into her apron pocket.

---

She had picked up the notebook from the windowsill that morning when she went past it, without deciding to. Now she held it out.

It was a composition notebook in its second summer of use — the covers gone soft from handling, the corners worn through to the cardboard, a water stain low on the back from a September she had been getting ahead of herself. Twenty-three entries now, two columns across each page: German on the left, English on the right, the scientific names above in her best handwriting. In the margins were her drawings — pencil, done from life where she could and from memory where she couldn't, accurate in species and imprecise in anatomy. The kingfisher looked like a hammer. The hermit thrush had too much neck. The cedar waxwing, drawn twice, was the best.

He took the notebook from her carefully — more carefully than the notebook required, or exactly as carefully as it required; she wasn't sure which. He turned each page from the bottom corner. He was reading both columns.

She watched his face.

*Rotkehlchen / Robin* — he stopped on that one. *Krickente / Green-winged Teal* — he looked at the sketch. *Blaumeise / Black-capped Chickadee* — she could see him placing the English, his lips moving the faintest fraction.

The baler went past on a return pass and the noise was everything for thirty seconds.

When it moved away Karl was on the first page.

*Seidenschwanz / Cedar Waxwing.*

The drawing was the best one: a fat-bodied bird with a crest and the yellow tip of the tail, the red on the secondary feathers done in the only colored pencil she owned — a stub of red from the kitchen drawer. She had looked at the drawing a dozen times since October and each time she had decided it was close enough. The bird was recognizable. The color was slightly off.

He stood with the notebook open to that entry for long enough that she counted the seconds without meaning to.

He said: "October."

He said it looking at the page, quietly, not quite to her.

"October," she said.

He looked up. She didn't have the German or the English for what she saw in his face — she had the shape of it, the shape without the name.

He looked at the entry once more. He closed the notebook and handed it back.

---

She put it in her pocket and thought of something to give him.

"Hawk," she said. She held her arms out in the flat spread and slight angle she had worked out over the summer — the motion for soaring birds, good enough to be understood if not quite accurate.

He watched her hands. He said: *Habicht.*

She repeated it. He shook his head — not wrong, but not the right bird. He made the gesture back at her with a different angle at the wrist: the motion of a bird that came in direct and low rather than wheeling overhead. That hawk. Then he made another gesture, smaller, quicker — the rapid flutter above the fence line, the hovering she knew.

*Sperber,* he said.

She knew this one. She had been watching it all summer over the south fence — the sparrow hawk, the small one that held its position above the grass before it dropped. She had had the English and not the German until now.

She wrote both in the notebook, standing there: *Habicht / Goshawk. Sperber / Sparrow Hawk.* She would draw them both later. She would probably get one wrong.

The dipper dripped onto the dry grass.

*Kommen,* he said. Then in English: "Come."

She said it back: *kommen.* He said "come." They had been adding verbs to the nouns all summer, one piece at a time — *kommen* and "come," *bleiben* and "stay," the words needed for what the day required. By her count they had perhaps eighty words between them now. A grammar of necessity, from what the farm asked. It was not a language. It had the bones of one: birds and tools and the weather words, the farm-labor nouns, and now some of the basic verbs in two forms, the direction and the tense.

She said: *Morgen.* Tomorrow.

He said: "Tomorrow."

She said: "Morning."

He considered. Then he held up one finger: *Morgen,* pointing forward. And then *Morgen* again, spreading his hands to indicate the pale light, the hour before the baler started. The word going two directions at once. She had known this but had not thought about it as something he would be carrying — the German word that meant both at the same time, tomorrow and morning.

She nodded. He looked at the field.

The baler came around again and the noise filled everything.

---

The last load came off the field at half past four.

The light had gone from white to long gold and the heat had settled into something different — still full but changed, lying quiet and dense on the cut stubble. The wagon came in with the final bales piled high, swaying slightly on the ruts of the farm lane, and her father steered the tractor through the gate and into the far bay of the barn. The four prisoners off-loaded in twenty minutes: the steady rhythm of lifted bales and stacked rows, bodies that had been at this all afternoon and knew the count without being told.

Her father unhooked the baler and drove the tractor around to the equipment shed.

Lonzo came to the barn door. He spoke to Dieter. Dieter and Rolf and Hans filed out the south gate and headed toward the icehouse, Lonzo following. At the fence corner he stopped and took his cap off and fanned his face with it, put it back on, stood with his arms folded, looking out at the cut stubble field.

Twenty yards. A little more.

Hannah had not left the far bay.

Karl was still there, stacking the last bales from the second wagon against the back wall. She worked from the other side — four bales wide, two high, the satisfying thunk of each bale placed. The barn smelled the way it always smelled after a hayload: the sweet dry smell of this summer's cut grass over the older smell of every summer the barn had been receiving hay, the accumulated smell of all those Augusts stacked against the back wall and the one before that and the one before that. She had been breathing this smell her whole life. She could not have said what it was called.

She thought of nothing in particular. She worked.

---

He set the last bale in the rack.

He stood with both hands resting on the top bale, not moving. She had stopped too, and they were at opposite ends of the finished work.

He was looking at the fence. Not at Lonzo — past him, at the post where the top rail ran into the corner brace. She had watched Karl Reinmar through ten months of fieldwork and water rounds and the pidgin they had built between them, and she had learned his different kinds of looking. The looking that was rest. The looking that was waiting for the next instruction. The looking that was the field and nothing in it.

This one she did not have a name for.

She waited.

"Werner," he said.

Quietly, looking at the post. Not to her. The name released in the way he released things sometimes — not offered, not explained, put into the air and left there.

A pause long enough that she thought he had finished.

"Von Ansbach."

---

*W. Grau. A. Pfeiffer. Bamberg, 1921.*

She had looked at that photograph perhaps twenty times since April. The young man standing in outdoor light — twenties probably, city clothes, a street behind him she didn't know — standing beside her father who was not yet her father, who was twenty or twenty-five in some other country, whose face she could find in her father's face only if she looked for the bones of it. *W. Grau.* She had been holding the initial for four months. A door with no handle.

Werner.

From Ansbach. Near Bamberg. The same low Bavarian hills, the same fifty kilometers that was not far in that country — not far if you grew up in it, not far if you had grown up knowing the roads between those towns. She had measured it on the classroom map in April, after she found the photograph. She had used her thumb and converted.

Werner Grau. From near where her father was born.

---

*Er wollte kommen,* Karl said.

He wanted to come.

Not: he wants. Not: he is coming. He wanted: past. The tense of a thing that was already finished before it arrived at where it was going.

She understood the past tense. She had understood it in October at the dinner table — her father's fork stopped between plate and mouth, the brief stillness, the resumed eating that was not the same eating as before. She had understood it again in April, the photograph face-up on the oilcloth, his hands going still again for the same reason.

Karl had not turned from the fence.

She said: *Du weißt.*

Both hands on the top bale.

Karl had not turned from the fence.

He turned. He looked at her across the stacked hay, the afternoon light crossing the barn floor in angled stripes. Then he nodded, once, and turned back to the fence.

---

A meadowlark landed on the post where Karl had been looking.

It stood for a moment — yellow-chested, upright, indifferent to the barn and to them and to the whole August evening. Neither of them said its name.

It lifted and was gone into the cut field and the long light.

---

She picked up the bucket from beside the wagon wheel.

She walked out of the barn and across the yard. The sun was at the west hillside now, the long shadows running flat across the stubble field. The south field was pale and open in the low light — the hay off, the cut stubble clean and even, the way a field looks in the first hours after: not yet itself.

The notebook was in her apron pocket. She felt the weight of it — the soft-covered composition notebook, its twenty-three entries, first October to now. Light, and specific.

She was thinking of her father's hands stopped above the plate. She was thinking of the name coming from two directions — an initial from a tin box, a given name from a fence post in an August barn — and landing in the same place.

She went up the back step and into the kitchen. She did not look back at the barn.

# Lonzo Reed

The chair was a wooden kitchen chair he had brought from the supply room in the icehouse's second week, when he understood that standing post was going to mean sitting post. The carbine lay across his thighs with the barrel pointed east. He was not going to need the carbine. He had not needed it in ten months and he was not going to need it today. He kept it across his thighs because the Army said to keep it across his thighs, and Lonzo Reed had, at sixty-two, arrived at a useful understanding of which rules were weight-bearing and which were decoration. This one was decoration. He kept it anyway.

The chair sat on packed dirt in front of the icehouse door. The afternoon light came long across the farmyard from the west, and behind him he could hear Dieter and Rolf working the near stall — the steady rhythm of their work, which was unhurried and efficient in the way of men who have decided to get through the day and no more. He had understood this about them in the first month.

He knew this piece of ground the way he knew certain things: by having stood in it long enough that the knowing had become its own kind of muscle. The layout of the farmyard. The sound the barn door made when the crossbar was not set. The way the shadow fell off the icehouse roof by the hour. The pattern of the Pfeiffer family's movements through the day — the father up before light, the mother appearing at the kitchen window at intervals, the girl out to the field or the barn at whatever the day required. He knew the names of the cows and the rhythm of their milking. He knew the smell of the late-season pasture and the cut-grass smell still carrying from last week and underneath both the standing smell of a dairy farm that had been a dairy farm longer than anyone on it could say.

He had been watching all his life. There were good reasons for it, and the watching had been its own education.

---

He had read the four Germans in the first month.

Dieter and Rolf and Hans: older men, all past forty, who had come to this war through years of a certain kind of obedience and understood the obedience required of them here in exactly the same way. Not dangerous. Not interested in making trouble. Interested in getting through the day and eventually through the war, which was all most men wanted from a war when they had any sense. He had managed them without incident by being exactly what he was: a sixty-two-year-old man with a carbine who was not going to do anything stupid and expected the same. The arrangement had held through ten months without a problem that required anything beyond a look and, once, a word.

Karl was different only in the way that nineteen was different from forty-three.

He had started calling the boy the waxwing boy sometime in the winter, after he spent an afternoon watching Karl watch the field above the fence. Not doing nothing — watching. Cataloguing. Lonzo had watched birds himself, in the way of a man who spent long hours in a chair and learned what to do with his eyes. He knew the cedar waxwing: the yellow tip of the tail, the crest, the red wax-colored spots on the wing that gave the bird its name. He had watched Karl standing at the pasture fence for the length of an afternoon and seen what the boy was doing and filed it.

He watched the girl too. He watched her write in the notebook the first time she brought it out, and he watched the notebook reappear through the winter and the spring and this summer. He watched the two of them build their back-and-forth of names for things in the way of people building something and not stopping until it was built.

He watched them the way he had watched most things: without announcing himself, without pretending not to watch. The kind of attention the girl had — the kind that knew it was paying attention — he had recognized that in October and tracked it through ten months. The regulations said no fraternizing, and what they had assembled between them — the notebook and the bird names and the words they had built from what the farm asked of them — was something those regulations had not been written to see.

He was not approving. He was not alarmed. He was watching to make sure it stayed inside the range of what he could permit.

It had stayed there.

---

His sister's boy Desmond was in the Army. Had been since March 1943. The Pacific.

The letters came to Desmond's mother, not to Lonzo, because Lonzo was not the kind of family that went on the letter list. He was the uncle. The one who had moved up from Georgia in '29 when the bottom fell out, who had wired money back when he had it, who had shown up in three different towns in fifteen years before landing here. He did not have a household. He had people, and Desmond was one of them.

The letters were getting shorter.

He didn't dwell on it. He noted it the way he noted other things: as a fact that had to be held somewhere, and that he was the holder of. The Pacific was a long way from a farmyard in Maine. He was sixty-two years old and there was no version of this where he was not standing in a farmyard in Maine while his sister's boy got shorter in a letter.

---

In October, in the post's first week, he had been driving back from the post office in town later than his usual time. A personal matter — a letter from Desmond's mother, shorter than the one before it, and then the time it took him to write a reply and find the right envelope. By the time he was on the road it was near eleven.

The farm road off Route 1 was not lit. He drove it twice a day and knew it at night by memory. The two bends. The low place where water stood after rain. The spot where the fence came close enough to the shoulder that he had to swing wide with the truck.

He was about a quarter mile from the front gate when the headlights picked up a man walking on the shoulder.

He slowed.

The man was heavyset, not young. Town clothes, not farm clothes — a coat with lapels, substantial cloth. He was moving toward the farm at a deliberate pace, not hurrying, not looking behind him, the pace of a man who had come a long way and was not going to stop short of where he was going.

By the time Lonzo pulled even with where the man had been, he was off the shoulder. He had turned onto the field track that ran alongside the east pasture fence — the track that went behind the hayfield, not the farm's proper entrance road. Lonzo could see the shape of him moving away into the dark, past the reach of the headlights, following the fence line.

Lonzo did not stop. It was a public road. The man was not on the farm property. His post was the icehouse and the four prisoners inside it. He drove on through the gate and parked the truck and went to the icehouse and found them all asleep.

He had thought about it more than once since.

He made the connection in February or March, when the body story was still going around town. A man found on the breakwater in October, heavyset, middle-aged, no papers. Nobody local. Nobody claiming him. He had heard it in the feed store and then at the post office. The Coast Guard had closed it without a name.

He could not be certain — not from what he had. A man on this road on that night, moving toward this farm. That was all of it. It was enough to put in front of someone.

He had been deciding who someone was for going on six months.

He knew how the conversation went. He had been in that room before, or rooms close enough to it that the difference didn't matter. The explaining of who he was. The questions that started before he finished. The weight put on one part of what he said and not the rest. He was not naive about what a sixty-two-year-old Coastal Patrol private's account of a man on a road in the dark at eleven o'clock would look like in an official record.

He had the piece. He was deciding what a piece was worth doing with.

---

The shadows were coming long across the farmyard when Karl came out of the icehouse.

He sat on the step the way he sometimes did in the late afternoon, his forearms on his knees, and looked up at the sky.

The sky was clear. The late-August light had that quality of the far end of the season — not the white-hot light of July but something going long and gold and slant, like a day that was still full but had started to understand itself. Karl was doing the thing he did: looking up with the particular quality of attention he used when he was looking for something to name.

A bird crossed the far edge of the field. Small, quick. Gone before Lonzo had fixed it.

Karl watched the air where it had been.

Lonzo watched Karl.

He thought about the man on the farm road. Heavyset, not young, moving toward the farm in the October dark at the pace of a man carrying something that mattered to him. He thought about what the man had found when he got to wherever the field track took him, and whether any of it had come to anything before the storm.

He did not know.

Karl looked at the sky a moment more. Then he went back through the icehouse door.

Lonzo watched the door.

The waxwing boy at his post. The man on the farm road heading toward it in October. One inside the icehouse; one on the breakwater by morning. He didn't know what was between those two facts. He was not certain there was anything.

He had not decided.
