# The Cove

The survey ran north to south: Heron Point first, then Seal Neck, then the two unnamed pockets between the outer heads, then the south cove behind the headland. She did this every September before the season closed. The work was not difficult. She had run the same route for eight years and the harbor launch knew the shape of it.

She went out at the morning ebb. The ebb pulled the water off the rock and showed what the season had deposited — pots and hawsers and storm-blown floats, the gear that accumulated where the harbor's circulation said it would accumulate. The pattern was reliable. Drifted things moved in a direction that could be predicted given the prevailing set of the tides and the shape of the headlands. She had mapped the pattern in her first years by noting what turned up where, and the map had held.

Heron Point: two lobster pots with the surface buoys worn blank. She logged the positions and the condition and went on. The gannet working the tide rip off the point was nothing to log; she logged it anyway, a habit from her early years when she was still learning what went into the record and what did not, a habit she had since decided to keep.

Seal Neck: a length of commercial hawser above the tide line, fifty feet or better, flagged for the boatyard to collect at their convenience. The small pocket east of Seal Neck: a mooring float she had been carrying in the spring records since the line parted in April. She hooked it with the boat hook and brought it aboard and wrote the return in the log. The second unnamed pocket: a section of fish net from some farm operation, three seasons old if she was reading the growth right, too far gone to save.

The light in September was flat and honest. Not the glare of August that showed the water's surface and pressed everything into a shimmer, and not the November light that compressed the whole harbor into gray distance. September put things at their actual size. She could see what was there.

She came around the south headland at half-ebb.

---

The cove behind the south headland was a hundred yards end to end. Its entrance faced east, which set it across the prevailing swell; what came in on the northeast blow came in, and what drifted on the tidal circulation from around the headland came in and stayed. She had learned the cove's habits in her second year and added it to the survey route in her third. In eight years she had found in it, among other things, a salmon net from a farm forty miles up the bay, a fuel drum still three-quarters full, and two sections of the old outer marker that the Navy had replaced and apparently lost track of. She expected gear.

The dinghy was not gear.

She saw it before she was within fifty yards: a white hull, discolored, the shape unfamiliar. She brought the launch down to drift and worked in toward the cove's north end. The dinghy had come to rest bow-on to the granite, the bow caught on a ledge a foot above the current waterline with the stern swung around on the ebb. Its freeboard on the port side was low — the hull was down amidships where something had gone wrong with it. She put the launch alongside the rock and looked.

Twelve feet, twelve and a half at most. A pulling boat with a flat bottom, the kind built for a sheltered harbor and nothing past the heads. The damage was to the port side amidships: planking crushed inward, the frames behind it broken, the seam at the garboard open on both sides of the break. The hull had taken a hard blow or had been ground hard against something with weight behind it. Below the damaged section, the boat had shipped water enough to settle it. Above the damage, the hull cleared the surface, held up by the bow on its ledge.

She put her hand on the rock and steadied the launch against it and looked at the waterline.

The weed was the record. It grew at a predictable rate on a hull left in one place; it stopped at the surface; it did not lie about the time elapsed. The line of growth on this hull ran six inches above the cove's present waterline, which meant the hull had come to rest here when the tide was running six inches higher than today's ebb — a normal tidal variation, nothing unusual. The barnacle growth started below the weed line and went down into the murk. She estimated ten months. Maybe eleven. Late autumn or early winter, which put the arrival somewhere in the months after the October blow.

She shipped the oars and stepped onto the rock.

---

The bow ring was brass, tarnished to near-black, but solid. She got both hands through it and pulled back, working her grip down toward the waterline, bracing her feet against a lower ledge. The hull was heavy — waterlogged through and through, the planking saturated, the broken section adding to the weight by holding water in the bilge. She set her weight against it and worked it up the rock in stages until the transom lifted clear of the water.

She held it there and looked at the transom.

The paint was gone. Where it had been heaviest it had left a primer stain on the wood; where it had been thin it was down to bare grain. There had been a name painted on the board, centered, in large letters and a dark color. Most of it was unreadable. The middle section — the heart of the letters, where the wood had worked most through the wetting and drying of eleven months — had come down to bare board. What remained was at the right end of the painted surface: four characters at the edge of where the name had ended. *STEN,* in the trace of a pigment that had held on a little better than the rest.

That was all the name had left.

She held the bow up with one hand and got the log out of her coat pocket with the other. Below the remnant of the name, set into the lower edge of the transom on a rectangular plate, was the registration. The bronze had gone green at the edges but the center was still readable: the Portland Harbor Authority's district and vessel number, stamped in standard format, the registration year clear at the right. She wrote the number in the log against the date and the position.

She let the bow down. The dinghy swung back on its ledge.

She spent another minute on the hull: looking at the damage, reading the angles of the broken frames. A rock in the cove could have done it, or a dock edge, or a piling in a blow. She could not say what had made the wound or when, except that it was at least as old as the growth on the waterline, which meant it had happened before the hull came to rest here or at the same time. She could not say more than that.

She stepped back to the launch and rowed out of the cove.

---

She wrote up the outer cove survey in the afternoon. Six items: the two Heron Point pots, the Seal Neck hawser, the recovered mooring float, the old fish net, and the dinghy. For the dinghy she noted the position, the condition, the estimated time the hull had been in place, and the registration number, and flagged the entry for a Portland inquiry.

The inquiry form was standard. She had submitted three in eight years, all for vessels that had come adrift and ended up where they did not belong. Registration number, found position, condition on discovery, date. She was the reporting officer; she signed her name. She addressed the envelope to the Portland Harbor Authority, Commercial Street, and put it in the outgoing tray.

Portland kept good records. She would have a reply within the week.

---

She did not think much about the dinghy in the three days between sending the letter and receiving the reply. The survey's other items wanted attention: the mooring float needed a return notation against the spring record; the boatyard needed the authorization for the autumn railway haul-out, which she had been building since August and could finalize now that the season's last draggers had scheduled their maintenance dates; the winter mooring allocation list wanted revision now that two of the summer vessels had declared they were laying up in Portland rather than Coldwater. The harbor did not stop.

The reply came Thursday. One page, the Portland Harbor Authority heading, a brief paragraph below it.

She read it.

The registration number submitted belonged to a chandlery on Commercial Street, Portland, operating a rental service for small harbor craft — dinghies and similar vessels, civilian use. The registered vessel had last been carried in the active rental fleet as of late September 1943. At that time it had been rented and not returned. The chandlery's record listed the matter as unresolved. The last rental entry showed the vessel released on the twenty-eighth of September, 1943.

The customer at time of rental had provided a name and an address.

*W. Grau, 114 Franklin Street, Portland, Maine.*

---

She read it twice.

W. Grau. She turned the paper over as if the back would offer something, which it did not. The initial was nothing by itself. The last name was nothing she recognized: not a Coldwater name, not a harbor name, not a name from any registration or manifest she had handled in eight years at this post. Portland was sixty miles south. Portland men worked the outer grounds; they had business everywhere on the coast.

But a rental dinghy out of Portland on the twenty-eighth of September, 1943.

She did not need to calculate. The sequence was there: the dinghy goes out from Portland at the end of September; the three-day blow runs the ninth through the eleventh of October; the body arrives on the breakwater on the morning of the twelfth; the dinghy comes to rest in the south cove in the months after. The middle was not visible. The two ends were visible and they pointed toward each other.

She did not write any of this in the log.

She opened the middle desk drawer.

The CG form was as she had left it: Mercer's case number at the top, the date October 1943, the blank for identifying information still blank, the blank for additional observations below her final logged entry still empty.

She set the Portland letter on top of the CG form and looked at them together.

W. Grau, 114 Franklin Street, Portland. The name on the rental form was not necessarily the name of the man who had used the boat; a man could give any name at a chandler's counter, and a man with a reason for one name had a reason for another. But a man with a reason gave the name he gave, and the name he gave went into the record, and the record was in her desk drawer now alongside the unanswered form.

The column without a label had more in it now.

---

She closed the drawer.

The harbor was quiet in September. The offshore fleet had been coming in since the first of the month — the season declaring itself over in the way it always did, gradually and then at once. The boatyard was on maintenance schedule. The cold-storage house was running reduced hours. The summer traffic was done and the winter's rhythm had not yet started, and between those two states the harbor had its annual brief stillness, a week or two when the pier held fewer boats than at any other time of year and the water in the channel was flat and clear.

She looked at the desk: the open log, the fuel ledger, the stacked forms in the outgoing tray for the mail boat. The middle drawer was closed.

She had a name. The name had an address. The address was in Portland, which was a city with a post office and a record of residents, and a harbormaster who knew what a harbormaster knew. She was not certain it made anything possible except what she was already doing, which was holding pieces and waiting for them to accumulate into something that could be entered in the correct column.

She turned back to the log.

The channel held the September light. The mooring chains ran straight down to their blocks with no motion in them — full slack at this hour, the fleet riding easy. The two outer buoys were in their positions at the harbor mouth, the red to port and the green to starboard, visible from the pier head window where she had watched them through eight years of whatever the harbor had brought.

She wrote the afternoon's log. She wrote it correctly.

The drawer stayed closed.

# One Year

He took the harbor road from the foot of Schoolhouse Hill, as he had taken it on most afternoons in two and a half years. The road ran three-quarters of a mile to the pier head, crushed stone with the grass coming through the middle where the wheels did not run; the smell of the harbor moved against him as he came down — cold salt water and diesel, and under both the smell of wet granite that he had absorbed, over the course of his time here, into what he thought of as the working inventory of the place.

It was the twelfth of October.

One year since the harbormaster's log had carried its first entry on the matter. Two and a half years since he had set his suitcase on the floor of the spare room at the top of Henry Crow's stairs. Six years since Vienna. He held these intervals as he held all precise dates: accurately, as a matter of discipline, not to be confused with what the accumulation of them was for.

The harbor came into view past the cold-storage house.

---

The cold in October had a different quality than the summer cold, which was still a marine cold, the cold of fog and damp and the offshore breeze moderated by the season's remaining warmth. October had given up on moderation. The air off the harbor at the foot of the hill was the air of what was coming rather than what had been, and it carried, mixed with the salt and the diesel, the low-tide smell of October flats: cold mud and rockweed, the harbor floor exposed an extra foot by the autumn tidal range. He had added this smell to the inventory in his second October here, filed under the heading of *this place in this particular week of autumn*, which was as specific as any entry in the inventory was required to be.

Most of the offshore fleet was hauled or preparing to haul. Three draggers were already up on the boatyard railway, their hulls in the pale wood of fresh bottom paint, their shapes oddly elevated without the sea to hold them level. The sardine carrier at the fish pier was loading its last run of the season. The lobster boats were down from their summer counts — he had been counting the mooring buoys in the inner harbor since his first October here without having decided to count them, in the way you come to know the dimensions of a room by crossing it often enough before you think to measure its walls.

The inner harbor was quiet in the way of the brief interval between the end of the season's work and the beginning of what winter made of the harbor — a week or two of stillness, the mooring chains running straight down in the slack water without motion. The water in the channel moved between what was still there without urgency. The cold was steady and without argument.

He turned at the boatyard fence toward the pier head.

---

The breakwater extended from the south headland in an L, the outer arm turning at its elbow toward open water. He had looked at it many times — from the pier head, from the harbor road in its various weathers, from the harbormaster's shed window as he passed on his afternoon walks. He had not walked it.

There was no reason he could have stated precisely for walking it today. The afternoon's marking was done; the stack of translation exercises on his desk was not going anywhere. The light was still adequate. He walked toward the breakwater's landward end and went over the low seawall step and onto the granite without having told himself he was going to.

The surface was irregular — rubble construction, the stones fitted without mortar, the faces worn smooth between the courses. His shoes found the flat planes between the higher stones and moved along them with some care. To his left the outer face dropped to the October sea: twelve or fifteen feet of granite to the water, which was the gray-green here of deep water without a bottom to lighten it. The swell was working in on a long period, lifting and falling against the outer face without violence, the sound at the base of the rock a low continuous suck and drain that was not the sound of the inner harbor but the sound of open water doing what it did against fixed stone, without particular regard for what the stone was there for.

He walked to the elbow.

---

At the elbow the cap widened where the construction doubled back, and there was a section of flat stone large enough to stand on without having to pick between the irregular courses. He stood on it.

The wind from the east had no land behind it, coming off open water without the headland's modification. It carried the cold of unobstructed distance, which was a different quality than the harbor cold — less interested in compromise. The bell buoy at the channel entrance was audible from here in a different way than from the pier head or from his room at night: not muffled by the headland's bulk, closer to its actual sound on the water, which was a lower note and longer interval than the version that arrived through walls and granite.

He looked at the October water.

He had been carrying Werner Grau for a year in the way one carries an assembled account: as a set of documented and plausible facts, each uncertainty marked, the limits of the account defined. He had put everything on a sheet of school paper in May of 1944, had drawn a circle around the phrase *by some combination*, and had locked it in the bottom desk drawer, where it had remained since.

For a year Werner Grau had existed in that drawer. The classified account. The provisional conclusions.

What Marcus had not done — what the year had apparently required without his noticing that it was requiring it — was consider Werner in the other way. Not as a set of established facts with their limits marked, but as a person who had made a set of choices.

A man from Ansbach, in Bavaria, which was a market town in a region Marcus could place precisely on any map and had no personal experience of. A man who had left Germany in 1938 or 1939, when leaving had still been possible for a person who moved with some decisiveness, and who had then managed five years in a country not his own on papers whose legitimacy had become, by 1943, a matter of administrative interpretation. Who had managed this for five years and had then decided — for reasons the letter had given Marcus only obliquely, the Pfeiffer name and the Reinmar name and the implication of a message that had waited long enough — that the time had come to come to Maine.

Marcus had made a version of this calculation himself, in Paris in the autumn of 1939, standing at his desk with a newspaper that clarified what the summer had still held in suspension. The calculation was not complicated. It had a correct answer and an incorrect answer, and the correct answer required leaving. He had the address of a colleague in London; he had money enough; he had the competence of a man who had left one country already and knew the mechanics of leaving a second. He had left in October and been in London by November.

Werner had made the same calculation. Werner had made it with less institutional support and onto a harbor dinghy on the coast of Maine at the end of September with the blow coming on. These were the variables of Werner's version, not Marcus's, and Marcus had stopped, at some point in the past year, placing them in the same column.

He had been carrying — according to what the letter implied, between the lines of a letter composed by a man who had learned to say only what needed saying and trusted the recipient to supply the rest — something in the category of message. Here is where Karl Reinmar is; here is what you should know. More than twenty years since Bamberg, where a photograph had been taken and two young men had been in the same place at the same time without any knowledge of what the next twenty years would require of either of them. Werner had come from wherever five years of managed displacement had taken him to put something directly into another man's hands, because some things could not be trusted to a letter.

He had made it to Maine. He had made it most of the way.

Marcus stood at the elbow of the breakwater for some time. The October water moved below him without hurry. The bell buoy rang its interval at the channel entrance, and then rang again.

---

He looked down.

One of the breakwater stones had broken from its course — roughly fist-sized, the fracture face still comparatively sharp, the outer surface worn smooth to the same gray-green as the cap stone around it. It had settled into the joint between two larger stones, held in place by its neighbors on three sides.

He picked it up.

Cold, in the way of granite that has been sitting in October air near October water. Heavier than its size suggested — the specific density of granite, which was what made it the material of choice for anything meant to hold its position against what the sea brought. He turned it once in his palm, looked at the rough fracture face and the worn outer surface, the gray-green that was the color of this harbor in this season.

He put it in his coat pocket.

He had the stone. He would carry it home.

---

He walked back along the breakwater.

The inner harbor opened ahead of him as he came toward the landward end: the anchorage, the boatyard with the hauled hulls on their jack stands, the cold-storage house, the pier head with the harbormaster's shed at its end and the window lit against the October dusk. Above the roofline the town held its standard configuration — the Congregational steeple the highest point, the school chimney beginning to smoke now that Henry had the boiler running again this week.

At the seawall step he paused. The bell buoy rang from the channel entrance — the same sound that came to his room on certain nights with the wind out of the east, the sound that had been part of the specific air of that room since his first week here, already filed in the inventory under the heading of *this place, this particular channel entrance, this buoy*. He heard it now without modification, from its actual position, with nothing between.

He went over the seawall step and walked back along the harbor road.

---

Henry was at the kitchen table when Marcus came in the back. A boiler fitting lay in a rag in front of him, two wrenches beside it; his hands were moving with the unhurried attention of a man who has understood the problem fully and is in no hurry about the solution. He looked up at Marcus in the way he always looked up — taking note, not requiring commentary — and then looked back at the fitting.

Marcus hung his coat on the peg by the door — the coat with the stone in its pocket, which he would carry upstairs after supper — and washed his hands at the kitchen sink. Lillian had left a covered plate in the warming oven, as she did on evenings when the household schedules did not align in time for a shared meal. He poured coffee from the pot on the stove and sat at the kitchen table, not in Henry's way, and Henry went on working the fitting.

After supper he went upstairs.

The room was as he had left it: the window over the back garden, the desk with the exercise papers stacked and waiting, the bookshelf with its two rows of German and Latin and the three English titles he had bought in Cambridge and never returned. The chair by the window where he read on Sunday mornings when the light came in at the right angle. He took the stone from his coat pocket.

He set it on the windowsill.

It sat there as granite sits — its weight absorbed into the surface below it without demonstration or comment, without either offering or withholding. Gray-green, fist-sized, one face rough where it had broken from the course and the rest worn smooth by whatever number of years it had spent at the breakwater's elbow before this afternoon. A piece of the breakwater in the room where he slept, which was a fact of the same kind as the other facts in the room: accurate, present, making no claim about what it meant. He looked at it for a moment.

He went downstairs.

---

Through the dining room window the October dark was completing itself over the town. The streetlight at the corner came on — one of the town's fixed intervals, reliable and without reference to whether anyone was watching. The Congregational steeple held its position against what remained of the western light, which was diminishing in the way of October evenings, steadily and without drama.

Lillian passed the bread.

He took a piece. Henry was explaining the boiler fitting — whether the thread wanted redressing or whether a new washer would resolve it, a practical question with a knowable answer, the kind the evening ran on. Marcus ate. Outside the window the October dark settled over the street in the way it had settled over it in every October he had watched it from this table.

# The Proceeding

She spread the harbor logs across the desk in order: 1935 at the left, then 1936 through the current year running right in a line, the current year's volume at the far end. Eight volumes plus the one she was still adding to. She had brought them down from the shelf above the stovepipe in two loads, the stack heavier than she usually moved them because she did not usually move more than one or two at a time. The stove was unlit; cold kept her sharp, and she had a long evening's work ahead.

The formal notice had come on Monday by the county carrier, addressed to *Acting Harbormaster, Coldwater Reach Harbor* and forwarded from the district port authority office. The language was the careful language of procedure: *notice of formal proceeding to review appointment status*, not *challenge to tenure*; *right to present the record of service before the board*, not *obligation to appear*. At the close, in the sentence that mattered most: *at the board's discretion to determine the appropriate status of the position going forward.* She had read it three times on Monday and once more on Tuesday. She had the letter in her coat pocket now, folded on its original fold, the county seal at the top left in blue ink and the county clerk's signature below it and the date: November twenty-second. Two weeks.

The record was about safe harbor management and vessel registration and fuel allocation; the proceeding was about a post, and who was understood to occupy it, and whether the occupation would be made formal. Someone at the county level had decided the occupation should change. The procedural vehicle available to them was the appointment status — she had been acting harbormaster, technically, since 1935, because the formal confirmation hearing that should have followed within eighteen months of her taking the post had never been scheduled. She had not pursued the scheduling. The harbor had not cared about her status; the work had required doing. The county board had not cared, evidently, until someone gave them a reason to care.

None of this would be said at the proceeding. The proceeding would concern itself with the record.

She opened the 1935 volume.

---

Owen's handwriting ran to November seventh.

The November sixth entry was the last full one — weather at the head in the abbreviated form, fleet positions in order, any maintenance items requiring follow-up at the bottom. He had written: partly cloudy, wind northwest twelve and building through the afternoon, barometer falling slowly. The fleet was in except for the *Selma Hatch* at the outer mooring, which he had noted was exposed with the weather developing and which he had recommended be brought to the inner before nightfall. There was a note about the bait pier fuel line, which had been difficult all October: *Will call Trowbridge in the morning. Can't have another week of this.* Three inches of handwriting. She knew its particulars — the *d* formed with the loop left open, the figure sevens cut flat, the word *barometer* abbreviated to *bar* and the word *northwest* to *NW* with the capital letter slightly larger than convention — in the way she knew any handwriting she had read beside its author for twenty-three years.

The November seventh entry was a half-line: *Storm developing. Fleet in order. Outer mooring advised clear.* Below it the date; below that, nothing.

The eighth had nothing.

Her first entry was November ninth, 1935.

She read it now for the documentation. The handwriting was not his: her loop closed, her sevens rounded, her abbreviations formed differently, her hand on the word *northwest* a shade lighter than his. The same column headings. The same abbreviated form. She had written the weather at the head — northwest fifteen moderating, sea state three at the outer head — and then the fleet positions, and then the bait pier fuel line: *Trowbridge sent a man Friday. Fitting replaced, line in operation.* Three paragraphs of ordinary harbor work, written on the first morning she had held the post. She did not remember writing them. The content was correct and the handwriting was hers.

She would bring this volume to the proceeding.

The point was not the handwriting. The point was the date. November seventh in his hand, then the gap of the eighth, then November ninth in hers — the same form, the same columns, the same attention given to the same harbor. The work had not stopped. The log showed it without requiring anyone to say so. She was not asking the board to read anything into the gap between his last entry and her first. She was asking them to see that the entries resumed, and in what condition the harbor was in when they did, and what the record showed for the eight years that followed.

She set the 1935 volume to the side and moved to 1936.

---

She went through the volumes in order.

Mooring registry first, in the systematic form she had introduced in 1937: vessel by vessel, seasonal assignment, transfer record. Forty-two registered vessels in 1936; sixty-one at present, with the additional traffic from the Navy work and the sardine carriers' increased runs to Eastport. The *Maud Eleanor*, which had been Owen's benchmark vessel for weather judgment, now running sardines twice a week in season. Every transfer in the record, every assignment accounted for, every reassignment documented. The registry and the revenue ledger matched in every quarter because she checked them against each other quarterly and had done so since 1937. This was not required. She had done it because the record was either correct or it was not.

Harbor income: the comparison figures against Owen's last two full years came out eleven percent above. She had run the calculation in 1940 as part of the annual accounting and had noted the result in the supplemental ledger. She had not done it for the proceeding. She clipped the supplemental to the registry stack and set them on the left side of the desk.

The fuel ledgers she went through page by page: five columns each, every barrel from 1936 through the current volume. The supplemental allocation from the county and the USCG restrictions were in the margin for 1942 and 1943, when the allocations had dropped twice in four months. She had managed the harbor's fuel through both drops without interrupting the week's ordinary work. One error in the fuel ledgers across eight years: a posting error in October 1942, the sardine carrier's allocation entered in the wrong column in a month when she had been doing the accounting alone. Found in the same month's reconciliation. Corrected before the quarter closed. She had the correction note and the letter from the fuel authority acknowledging the correction. One error in eight years, found and corrected within the reporting period.

She had been doing the accounting alone because the assistant had been drafted in January 1942, and the county had not authorized a replacement. She had not put this in the annual reports as a complaint. She had put the assistant's line marked *vacant* and continued to do the work.

Safety inspection files: twenty-seven inspections since 1942 under the new USCG standards. One failure. The *Cecelia R.* in October of that year — port running light out, cracked exhaust elbow on the main — brought into compliance within eleven days of the written notice. She had reinspected on the twelfth day and issued the certification. The notice, the repair documentation the owner submitted, the reinspection form, and the certification were all in the file in the order the file required.

No casualty attributable to her decisions in eight years.

She put this in the summary document as the absence of an entry — the casualty log for that column was empty, and she would bring the casualty log. She had run the harbor through the worst season of 1942 with half her normal resources and no assistant and the Coast Guard treating the waterfront as their own facility whenever they wanted it, and the fleet had come in whole every November. She did not expect the board to weigh this heavily. It was in the record regardless.

---

The summary document was twelve pages of foolscap, running through the registry, the revenue comparison, the fuel record, the safety inspection record, and the casualty log. She needed three more pages to complete it: the comparative figures from Rockport and Searsport, which the county assessor had and which she had requested on Tuesday, and a final summary page. She would have the comparison numbers by Friday and the document complete before the weekend.

What the document could do was establish the record. What it could not do was address the question the proceeding was actually asking — whether the county board was prepared to confirm the post to the person who held it or to reassign it to someone they had in mind. The record was her answer to the procedural challenge. Whether the procedural answer was sufficient to meet the political one was not a calculation she had the capacity for tonight.

---

She opened the middle drawer.

The Portland letter was on top.

She had placed it there in September: the Harbor Authority's reply to her registration inquiry on the stove-in dinghy, four sentences and a name. Below it the CG form, the blank space for identifying information on the body received at Coldwater Reach on October 13, 1943, still empty as it had been since she drew the form from the cabinet in October of last year.

She took both papers out.

*W. Grau, 114 Franklin Street, Portland, Maine.* The letter gave the rental record from the Commercial Street chandlery: dinghy last rented September twenty-eighth, 1943, renter's name and address as noted. She had read this in September, twice, and had not sent it to the Coast Guard because she could not use it. A rental record placed a named individual in possession of a specific dinghy on the twenty-eighth of September. By the middle of October that dinghy had been in the south cove long enough to show ten months of growth at the waterline. There was the body. There was the rental record. There was the name. She could draw the inference; she could not certify it, and the CG form's blank required what could be certified. The blank was therefore still blank.

She set the two papers on the desk corner, away from the harbor log stacks.

Not related to the proceeding. The proceeding was about the appointment status; the letter and the form were about the body on the breakwater, which was a different authority and a different column. A thing waiting for its proper entry. A thing she could not close because she did not yet have what the closing required. The CG form was blank because she had not been willing to write an entry she could not verify. The proceeding existed because someone at the county level had determined that a tenure of eight years required formal confirmation before it could be made formal.

She put the Portland letter and the CG form back in the drawer. The county-header forms were behind them. She took two and closed the drawer.

---

She copied the county reference number from the formal notice onto the first header sheet and set it beside the summary document. She would transcribe the summary onto the headed sheets when the draft was finished. The draft was not finished.

The oil lamp had burned low while she worked — the reservoir nearly to nothing, the flame going to nothing with it. She set the pen in the groove of the inkstand and went to the cabinet by the door for the oil tin. She had a little less than half a tin. She lifted the glass chimney carefully, filled the reservoir to the proper level, replaced the chimney, and adjusted the wick until the flame came back to its correct height: even, steady, clear.

She stood at the window before returning to the desk.

The harbor in November. The water between the pier lights was black; the inner mooring field held the laid-up shapes of most of the season's fleet, the hulls low and still in the flat water. The south headland was a dark line against a sky slightly less dark. She could hear the bell buoy at the channel entrance — faint from here, at the shed's distance from the outer pier, the slow quiet sound of the ordinary tide. No weather behind it. The outer anchorage was empty. Everything in its place.

She had been coming to this shed for nine years and had known this harbor for longer than that, and she knew what it required of whoever ran it, and she had given it that, and the record of it was on her desk.

In two weeks she would stand before the county board and present the record.

She went back to the desk. She spread the summary document in front of her and picked up her pen.

She was not done.

# Permanent Resident

The board convenes at seven, in the room above the post office that also serves the Selectmen when the Selectmen require a room, and the consequence of this double occupancy is a layered residue of both functions: the faint staleness of cigar smoke belonging to no one present, the particular quality of air that accumulates in spaces where civic obligation is discharged by men who would generally prefer to be elsewhere, and a row of windows along the east wall looking out on the main road below, which offers at least the evidence that the world is conducting its ordinary business regardless of what is transpiring on the second floor.

Marcus arrives at six fifty-three. He has walked from the Crow house in ten minutes, the December cold of the direct variety — not damp but capable, and interested in finding the gaps in one's coat — arriving at the stair below the meeting room while his hands were still finding the temperature of the night. He has been before this board three times: the original appointment review in the spring of 1942, the first annual renewal in the spring of 1943, and tonight. He knows four of the five members well enough to read their positions from their posture before a word is spoken.

Mrs. Vance, who chairs, is the kind of administrator that mid-coast Maine produces at intervals: direct, efficient, possessed of clear opinions that she communicates without theater and pursues without cruelty. Keller and Ames are both fishing-family men who sit on the board by civic obligation and who vote, in Marcus's experience, as Mrs. Vance votes unless given a specific reason to do otherwise, which no one has yet provided them. Stowe, the pharmacist, is a well-meaning man for whom conflict functions as a form of expenditure he finds difficult to justify; he has a genuine interest in the school and a genuine incapacity for contention, which produces a reliable combination of good intentions and two-second pauses before votes. The fifth member is Holcomb, who runs the hardware store on the south end of the main road and who has been, across two and a half years of contract meetings and school board sessions, the most consistent practitioner of what Marcus has come to think of as managed indefiniteness: a form of objection carefully maintained at a temperature below the threshold at which it would require naming.

The second reading of the contract renewal is the formal item. It occupies four minutes, or would have; the contract is unchanged from the first reading, no amendments are pending, and there is no procedural basis for any delay. Mrs. Vance moves through the evening's prefatory matters — a budget item, a question about the gymnasium roof that Henry has raised through proper channels — and arrives at the renewal.

Holcomb says: "I think the board would like to understand something about the long-term intentions of the candidate regarding his place in the community."

*The candidate.* Marcus allows this to rest where it has been placed.

The room does the thing rooms do when a thing long circling has finally been said: it steadies, slightly, as though the low-grade vibration that has attended Holcomb's presence across twenty-six months has resolved into a single audible frequency and can now dissipate.

Several questions are embedded in what Holcomb has said. Some of them are the board's legitimate business: whether Marcus intends to remain in Coldwater, which is a reasonable administrative concern. Some of them are something else, a question about category and belonging that is not this board's jurisdiction and never was. Marcus answers the answerable question.

"I filed the initial declaration of intent for naturalization in November," he says. "At the federal district court in Rockland. These are the first papers — the beginning of the formal process, not the conclusion of it. I mention it because it seems relevant to the question of long-term intentions."

Holcomb's pen, which has been in his hand, descends to the table.

Mrs. Vance looks at Holcomb. She waits three seconds, which is longer than she generally waits for anything, which is its own form of statement. Then she calls the vote.

Keller: in favor. Ames: in favor. Stowe, after his characteristic pause: in favor. Holcomb: opposed. Mrs. Vance: in favor, noting same in the minutes. Renewed.

There is a minor quality of interest, Marcus thinks, in Holcomb's having voted opposed rather than abstaining — it is the first specific position the man has committed to paper across twenty-six months of board service relative to Marcus's employment, which means the first papers have had the secondary effect of finally making Holcomb legible, a function Marcus had not considered when he filed them and does not consider a loss.

The meeting adjourns at seven twenty-one. Mrs. Vance extends her hand; Marcus takes it; she releases it and turns to the minutes.

---

He does not leave by the side door. His usual entrance and exit is the side, which puts him directly on the street he walks home; tonight he takes the main corridor, which runs the length of the building and exits past the front window.

The placard has been there since November 1942. It is white-bordered, approximately twenty by thirty inches, with the heading COLDWATER REACH MEN IN SERVICE, and below it a list alphabetical by surname, two columns: name on the left, branch and theater on the right. He has read it many times without looking at it closely. Tonight he is looking for a specific entry.

In March — the tenth, a Thursday, which he can date because it was the day after the first decent break in the winter weather, when the temperature had climbed above freezing for the first time since January and the road outside the Crow house had smelled of it — Henry had come to the kitchen table before Marcus's second cup of coffee. He said, without preface, whether Marcus thought James should be on the window list at the school.

The principal may not have thought, Henry said. Not *overlooked*; not *chose not to include*; the principal *may not have thought*. It was the most precisely accurate description of what had most likely occurred — an omission produced by a form of inattention that is not hostile, merely incomplete.

He had gone to the principal the next morning. He had said: "I notice that James Crow's name is not on the service list in the front window." The principal looked at him. "He serves in the United States Army, Pacific theater," Marcus said. The principal said he would look into it. The name appeared the following week. That was in March; it has been there nine months.

He finds it now: J. CROW, Army, Pacific. Between Cowan, J. — Navy — and Delaney, T. — Marines, Confirmed Fallen, August 1944, which is new; Delaney was missing the last time Marcus read the placard closely.

Twenty-four names. He counts.

Outside, the main road is empty in the December cold, the far streetlamp putting a yellow circle on the pavement below.

He goes out the side.

---

The town hall is on his route home — the corner of Main and the harbor road — and he passes it at seven thirty-five. The second-floor windows are dark; the building has a particular solidity that comes from the conviction, in the men who built it in 1904, that civic buildings should not be easily moved.

He had been here at four forty in the afternoon, before the evening meeting, to deliver a letter to the county clerk's office counter. The errand had taken twelve minutes.

The relief administration had been sending correspondence to the Crow household since the previous April concerning the tax status of the property assessment — correspondence that correctly identified the applicable regulation and incorrectly identified which subsection of it applied, generating a determination that was consequently wrong by a margin that had been costing Lillian Crow a specific assessable amount each quarter. The error was not large. It was not small. It had been producing further correspondence in response since April and had not resolved.

Marcus had located the applicable authority in October: Section 4(b) of the federal relief circular, read against a 1941 district court decision out of Portland that was directly on point and that Rideout's office had not cited, possibly because it had not located it, possibly for other reasons. He had drafted the letter in the first week of December. He had corrected one imprecision of phrasing in the second reading — a matter of the precise scope of the 1941 decision's holding — and then let it stand.

He had not told Henry or Lillian he was doing it. There was no reason to tell them before it was done; once it was done, they would know from the outcome.

Rideout, when Marcus presented the envelope, read the return address and then opened it and read the letter while Marcus waited at the counter. He set it on the desk to his right. He did not ask any questions. He said he would see to it. This was, in Marcus's considered assessment, an accurate statement about what would happen, given what the letter contained.

---

Past the town hall the route goes by the chandler's, which is shuttered at this hour, and the diner, whose front windows fog with steam from the coffee urns and through which Marcus can make out the shapes of three or four people at the counter. Then Holcomb's hardware, which is dark, a fact he notes without slowing. Then the Baptist church, where someone has put a cedar wreath on the door in the last day or two — it is still the bright green of recently cut cedar, which by Christmas will be the gray-green that cedar goes and then the dry brown that it stays until someone takes it down in February or leaves it for a March blow to manage.

The sidewalk has a raised seam at the quarter-block past the church. He has known this for two years and nine months.

Three things, in the span of some weeks: the name in the C's on the school window, the letter on Rideout's desk, the receipt in the drawer. They are of different scales and different orders of consequence.

He had taken the seven-fifteen bus to Rockland on a Thursday in November. The clerk's name at the filing window was Moreau, a woman in her early thirties who processed the declaration with the precision of someone for whom it is a familiar procedure. She had asked whether he intended in good faith to become a citizen of the United States. He had said yes. She date-stamped the declaration, recorded the filing number, gave him a receipt.

The receipt is in the right-hand drawer of his desk, beneath the Latin dictionary, where it has been since November.

He walks. The cold is direct. He is walking at his usual pace, which is the pace of a man who knows where the sidewalk is uneven.

He turns onto the street that the town calls Spruce Street — not its formal name, but the name it is known by, on account of two old spruce trees at the corner that have survived all the road work by the apparent fact of being too large for anyone to move. The Crow house is the fourth from the corner, with the kitchen light on.

---

The back entry is narrow — boots on the mat, extra wood stacked against the wall, the smell of cold air and pine sap caught between the outside cold and the warmth of the kitchen. He gets his coat off and his scarf and the wool hat that Lillian pressed on him in November, which is wool and dark and does not pretend to be anything other than a hat.

Lillian is at the range.

She says: "Thank you for the letter."

"You're welcome," Marcus says.

She does not turn from the stove. He goes to the cabinet where the cups live and takes one down. The coffee is on; the pot is warm. He pours and carries the cup to the table and sits.

Henry comes in from the hallway a few minutes later — from the sitting room, where he is on Tuesday evenings; Marcus can hear, faintly, that the radio has been left on. Henry takes a cup from the cabinet, pours, and sits at the table across from Marcus without speaking. The stove makes its particular sound: the low tick of the metal contracting around the fire in the way it does at this hour, when the evening has been burning down for several hours and the kitchen has reached whatever equilibrium it will hold for the night.

Lillian brings the pot to the table. She fills her cup and sits at her end — the near corner, which is hers by the accumulation of evenings rather than by assignment.

Three cups on the table. The coffee is thin — the ration book being what it has been all fall, and what they call coffee in December being forty percent coffee and the rest being chicory and good intentions — but it is hot and it is in a cup and the cup is on the table and there is no reason to be anywhere else.

Outside the window the yard is dark and still. The woodpile is a shape against the fence. The apple tree at the far corner, which Marcus has been watching since October, is bare.

The stove ticks.

He is not going anywhere.

# What She Told Him

The other two were out the door before *Bis Montag* had finished clearing the room — chairs pushed back, coats pulled on, gone in the organized rush they'd made automatic, the door swinging shut behind them and leaving the classroom to its own sounds: the radiator under the south window doing its work, the late January light coming sideways through the east windows, the faint noise of the school still in progress somewhere down the hall.

Hannah had both gloves on. Her coat was already buttoned. Her books were on the desk.

Marcus came down the rows with the folder, collecting the translation exercise, and when he got to her row she held out her paper. Then she said she had a question about the second paragraph. The word she'd translated as *collected*, she said — she'd looked at it again and thought *composed* might be closer.

He stopped and read the line. *Gelassen,* he said.

She nodded.

He said: the word comes from *lassen*. To let. To leave. *Gelassen* is the composure that arrives from having practiced letting go — the calm is made of the releasing, not the other way around. *Collected* is not wrong, he said, but it gets only the surface without the work that's underneath.

She wrote *composed — made of letting go* in the margin.

He took her paper with the rest and went back to his desk. She picked up her books.

She didn't go.

She stood at her desk while the school afternoon finished itself around her — footsteps going the other direction, a locker shutting twice before it caught, then quiet. Marcus was at his desk sorting papers, his back not quite to her, his pen uncapped. He had not told her she could leave; he also had not asked why she was still there.

She set her books back down.

She said: "Dr. Klein — there's something I thought you should know. Because of the German."

He set down his pen. When he looked at her it was the full attention, not the patient waiting-for-the-expected-answer, but the other kind she had learned to recognize over a year in this room: all the way in, nothing held in reserve.

She had been carrying this since November. The note was in her coat pocket. She left it there.

She said: "My parents have a tin box that lives on the top shelf of the wardrobe in their room. I found it last April — I was looking for the farm lease document, completely different errand — and I found it instead." The words came carefully, the way words came when you had been arranging them in your head a long time and were finally saying them out loud. "Inside there was a photograph. Two men standing in front of a building. On the back, in pen: *W. Grau, A. Pfeiffer, Bamberg, 1921.*"

Marcus was still.

"My father was younger in it," she said. "But the shape of him — the way he held his shoulders, I knew it." She held the image the way she'd held it since April: the photograph square and old, already browning at the corners the way photographs went after twenty-some years, the two figures in front of a stone building's façade in a city she'd never been to. The man who wasn't her father: wider, heavier in the shoulders, the build of someone who had done outdoor work for a long time, the neck thicker than his coat collar quite accommodated. His face was harder to keep — an ordinary face, the kind a photograph from 1921 wouldn't tell you much about — but the build had stayed with her. She had looked at it for maybe three minutes and then put it back. "Heavy in the shoulders," she said. "Laborer's build. I left the photograph in the box where I found it. But I saw it clearly."

Outside the east windows two crows were working the far end of the sports field, walking their methodical crow-walk through the winter-flattened grass. She watched them for a moment.

"In November," she said, "there was a transfer. One of the German prisoners assigned to our farm — the youngest one, Karl Reinmar, he'd been there since October of 1943 — he was reassigned to another work camp." She paused. "He was from Ansbach. It's about fifty kilometers from Bamberg. I measured it on the classroom map last April, after I found the photograph." She stopped herself. "I'm not going in order."

"There's no order required," Marcus said.

She put her hands on the back of the chair.

"In August," she said. "We were doing the hay. Karl and I had been talking most of the summer — as much as we could manage, given the language. He said a name: *Werner. Von Ansbach. Er wollte kommen.*" The German came easily here; this was a German room, and she had been saying the phrase to herself since August. "Werner, from Ansbach. He wanted to come. Already past tense when he said it — the wanting, and the not-arriving, the same fact." "I knew the name from the photograph. I understood they meant the same person. I didn't say so to Karl. I don't know if he knew I'd recognized it."

The crows outside had moved to the far corner of the field.

She put her hand into her coat pocket and took out the note. It had been folded the same way since November, along two creases that had gone soft from handling. She held it out.

Marcus came around the desk. She placed it in his hand.

He read it. He read it a second time without any expression she could read. He handed it back.

"He gave it to you at the transfer?"

"From his breast pocket." She looked at the note. "When they were loading. He came to where I was standing."

She unfolded it on the edge of his desk and smoothed it flat with two fingers.

*Werner Grau. From Ansbach. He is dead. I am sorry.*

Below that the birds — five of them, German on the left, English or Latin on the right, Karl's careful handwriting, the letters not quite American in their shape. *Seidenschwanz / Bombycilla cedrorum* at the top.

She had read it enough times that she could hold the whole thing in her head.

"He didn't say more than this," she said. "But he knew. And he must have known by then that I'd understand the name." She folded the note back along its creases. "I've been carrying it since November. I kept trying to think who to give it to. Or not give it to — who to show it to."

She put the note back in her pocket.

Then she told him about the kitchen.

"That evening," she said. "The same day as the transfer. My father was at the table. I came in from the barn." The German arrived in her mouth the way it did when her father's world was close and she was standing inside it: "*Werner Grau ist tot.*"

Marcus did not move.

"He didn't move either. His hands were on the table and he kept them there." She could see the kitchen: the lamp on the table, the supper things not yet cleared, her father's back and his hands and the stillness of him — not the stillness of someone who had not heard but the stillness of someone who was holding something down. "Maybe ten seconds. And then he said — " She said the two words with the weight her father had put in them, flat and definite and without give, like a door long since closed. "*Ich weiß.*"

She waited for more to come.

"Then he picked up his fork," she said.

The radiator worked its sound. Down the hall a door opened and closed. Outside, the crows had gone from the sports field — she didn't know when they'd left.

Marcus sat back in his chair. He put his hands flat on the desk and looked at them for a moment.

When he asked the first question it came precisely, without preamble: "The man in the photograph. You said middle-aged. Would you stand by that?"

She thought about it properly, giving it what it deserved. The photograph: the two men in front of the building, the formality of a picture taken in 1921, both of them arrested by the camera's demand into something more formal than they probably were. Werner Grau with his wide shoulders and the coat that didn't quite fit them and the face she couldn't hold perfectly — not young. The age her father would have been when she was very small, when she couldn't have said what middle-aged meant but knew it as a shape, a category of done-with-being-young and not-yet-old.

"Yes," she said. "Middle-aged."

He nodded once.

"And Karl — when he said Werner wanted to come. Did he give any sense of when? Which season?"

She went back to the hayfield in August, the long afternoon of it, Karl saying the name in the particular careful way he said things he'd been carrying: *Er wollte kommen*. And there was something else — a phrase from another time, months before the transfer, that she couldn't place exactly in the calendar but had in her: *vor dem großen Sturm*, before the big storm. She wasn't entirely certain it had been about Werner specifically, but it had been about that October. And there was only one October storm like the one in 1943.

"I think he meant before the storm," she said. "The October storm. 1943." She looked at Marcus. "I'm not certain — I can't give you the exact words. But that's what I understood."

Marcus said: "Thank you. You were right to tell me."

She picked up her books. The classroom was itself: the desks in their rows, the late January light going gray in the east windows, the map of central Europe above the door with its border lines belonging to a Europe that didn't exist anymore and hadn't for some time. She had been in this room enough times to know all of it without looking.

Marcus was still in his chair, watching her with the same even attention he'd had since she'd said *because of the German* — the full-attention look she had learned the shape of over a year, the one that held what it was given and didn't spill.

She went to the door. At the frame she stopped, her hand on the wood.

"I thought you should know," she said. "Because of the German."

Then she went.

---

The hallway was bright and mostly empty, the afternoon session over, a few students still at lockers. She walked down it: past the lockers, past the glass case with the athletic trophies, past the front window where the service placard hung in its white border, the names in two columns. She didn't stop to read it. She kept walking.

The main door was heavy with the cold behind it. She put her shoulder to it and it gave, swinging open into the January air — the clean kind, not damp, just cold, finding the collar and the wrists and the back of the hands immediately and stating its position clearly. She went down the concrete steps.

The sky was the low white of January, not quite cloud and not quite clear, the color of the afternoon waiting to become evening. The bus stop was at the bottom of the hill. She turned toward it.

On the harbor road below she could catch the harbor on the air — salt, cold water, the stillness of things that float without going anywhere in winter. She didn't look toward it. She was walking.

Her hand went into her coat pocket. Her fingers found the note: the two soft creases, the size of it. She had been reaching for it since November the way you reach for a stone in a shoe without deciding to.

She took her hand out.

The bus wasn't there yet. She stood at the stop in the cold, hands at her sides, coat buttoned to the top, and the town held its January shape around her: the church, the diner windows clouded with steam, the hardware shuttered, the harbor road turning off below the rise. She stood there and didn't reach for anything.

The bus came around the lower curve, its headlights already on against the darkening afternoon, and she got on. She found a seat on the left side. The doors closed.

The town went past the windows: the church, the diner, the main road carrying on toward the south. The harbor turnoff came and went below her. She watched it without marking it, without making a column for it, and the bus went on and the afternoon went on and it carried her home.

# The Breakwater

The outer face had taken green water.

She could see it from the headland stairs — the wrack line sitting high on the granite, a length of tarred cable draped across the top course, the iron mooring rings at the elbow gone dark with wet. She went down.

First light. Northwest wind out of Canada, fifteen knots and dropping. The blow had peaked sometime around two in the morning and then, the way storms sometimes did on this coast, had simply stopped. By four she'd been lying awake listening to the silences between gusts. By five she'd been dressed. The air coming off the water now was cleaner and colder, carrying nothing with it but temperature.

She had her clipboard.

The top course was intact along the north arm's full length — no slippage, no voids. She moved toward the elbow, checking each granite face, feeling the joint conditions where she had to. Some of the stones she knew well enough to read by looking; others needed a hand pressed to them, checking for any give. The rubble fill had held. The crown height was unchanged along the north arm.

She noted the cable. Tarred, fairly new, and it didn't belong to any vessel currently in the harbor. She'd check the boatyard, see if something in storage had lost it. She noted it for inquiry and for removal.

At the elbow, the course had shifted. An inch and a half toward the inner harbor, maybe two. She measured by eye and then by hand and noted it. The elbow always took the worst of a southeast blow, and what she was looking at was not as bad as 1939. The mortar joint at the south corner had widened. She put her finger in it: a quarter inch, three-eighths. Before the freeze, someone would need to point that joint; otherwise the ice would open it further.

The repair list for the breakwater had been three items before this morning. It was now five.

She wrote them all down.

The kelp had piled waist-high against the inner face of the elbow, black and dripping, salt-stinking. Woven into it were a coil of pot warp, a length of buoy line, the slats of a wooden crate that was stamped with something she didn't recognize — from a vessel, or perhaps from the boatyard if the storm had lifted something from the rails. A glass-ball float. A plank with a bronze fitting through it, the bolt stripped, which meant it had been working loose before the storm claimed it.

She went around the elbow, and saw the man.

---

He was face-down in the wrack, in the inner corner of the elbow where the kelp had piled deepest. The storm geometry was right for it: anything coming in from the southeast over the outer edge would have been carried into exactly this corner. He was lying with his arms at an angle — the left arm back along his body, the right arm out and slightly under him — that said he had not arranged himself there.

She stood for a moment.

The light was improving. She could see well enough.

Town clothes. A heavy wool coat, navy, with lapels that had no business on a working waterfront. Trousers, not work trousers. No boots anywhere on the breakwater that she could see, no oilskins, no gear of any kind. No vessel anywhere in the inner harbor she didn't know.

She set the clipboard on a flat section of granite and crouched down.

She checked his pockets.

Inside the coat, left breast: nothing. Right breast: nothing. Outside pockets — in the left, nothing; in the right, a folded handkerchief, and below it, grit. His trouser pockets, each in turn: nothing. Nothing. No wallet. No papers. No draft card. No ration book. No keys. Nothing with a name on it.

She stood up.

Male. The hands said fifty or older — the thickness across the knuckles, the looseness of the skin on the back of them. The hair was grey, close-cut, a working man's cut. The wool coat was good quality, that much was clear even soaked through. The trousers were wool as well. Somebody's travelling clothes, or a man's good clothes, or both.

Nothing about him said this harbor.

She picked up the clipboard. She walked back to the shed at the pier head.

---

Inside, she called Sprucehead.

The duty officer answered on the third ring. She gave him everything in order: her name, her title, the station address, the date, the time — six-twenty-two by the clock on the wall — and then the description. Male, she said. Face-down in the wrack at the elbow. Middle-aged or older. Town clothes. No papers, no identification of any kind, nothing to indicate a vessel or how he had come in. She had not touched him beyond checking his pockets. She had not moved him.

The duty officer said he would send someone. She thanked him and hung up.

She put the kettle on the single-burner plate. She checked the barometer — risen three-tenths since midnight, consistent with the storm's track, consistent with what she could see through the north window: the sky clearing fast from the northwest, the cloud deck breaking up at altitude, showing the grey beneath. She recorded the barometer reading in the tide log and noted the wind direction.

On the shelf above the telephone, seven logbooks stood in order. She'd started the current one in January, and its spine was still dark and square. The six before it went back to 1936. The one before those — thinner, its spine faded to the color of old water, Owen's handwriting on the label in the particular heavy-slanted hand he'd used for anything official — was set a little apart from the others, at the end of the shelf where the bracket met the wall. She had not moved it. It wasn't where she would have put it if she'd been setting up the shelf from scratch.

She poured a cup of tea and went back to the breakwater to wait.

---

The wind had dropped to ten knots by the time the Coast Guard truck came down off the main road onto the pier. She was standing at the breakwater's head when Lieutenant Mercer got out with his two enlisted men.

He was younger than she'd expected — mid-twenties, with the winter uniform pressed correctly and a manner that was efficient without being brisk. He introduced himself and looked at her when she gave her name.

"You're the harbormaster?" he said.

"Eight years," she said.

She walked him out to the body.

He crouched the way she had crouched, looking before he touched. He checked the pockets — the same ones she'd checked, and two more. He stood up. He asked her: when had she found it, had she moved anything, had she contacted anyone else.

No, she said. No. No.

"Any record of a vessel in difficulty? Radio calls? Report from boats that came in before the blow?"

"Nothing in the log from the past three days. No distress calls. Two draggers out to the grounds and back in before it peaked. The sardine carrier *Ellsworth* running to Eastport — she went out before the storm, due back the eighteenth."

"And no vessels you can't account for."

"Nothing in the harbor I can't account for."

He wrote in a small notebook. He was thorough rather than curious. He asked whether anyone else had access to the breakwater during the storm, and she said no one would have come out on it while the blow was on, and anyone could have come since, but she'd found no footprints in the wrack. He wrote that down as well.

She gave him the harbor log for October 9 through 12. He looked at it carefully and handed it back.

The two enlisted men brought the stretcher down from the truck. The operation was careful and correct. She watched from a few feet away and he did not ask her to step back. By the time the stretcher was going back up the breakwater, she had answered two more questions and had learned almost nothing except that the lieutenant's first name was Amos, from the nametag she'd seen when he turned his coat.

"We'll be in touch if we have questions," he said.

"I know where to reach you," she said.

The truck pulled out of the pier at seven-twenty-three.

---

She finished the breakwater survey. She walked the full length again from the shore end, checking each section now that nothing was in her way. The damage added one more item — a section of the north face's drainage where the fill had settled — and she added it to the list. She wrote the estimate for the elbow repair while she was still on the breakwater, because the light was good and she could see what she was writing about.

Back at the shed, she opened the harbor log to the day's page.

She wrote for ten minutes. The entry ran to half a page.

*October 12, 1943. Sunrise 0611. Wind NW 15kts at 0600, dropping to 10kts by 0800. Barometer 29.74 at 0600, rising. Post-storm survey, breakwater, 0615–0730: granite course displaced at elbow (est. 1.5 in. inward), mortar joint widened at south corner of elbow, iron mooring rings displaced (2), kelp and debris accumulation at elbow, drainage fill settled N. face — all noted for fall repair.*

*Vessels: all moored vessels accounted for. Sardine carrier* Ellsworth *Eastport run, ETA Oct. 18.*

*0615: Unidentified male, deceased, recovered at breakwater elbow. No papers, no identification of any kind, no associated vessel. CG Sprucehead notified 0622. CG responded, Lt. A. Mercer and two enlisted, 0711. Body removed to CG custody 0723. CG assuming jurisdiction.*

She put down the pen.

She read it once. It was accurate. Every time was correct.

She set the logbook to one side.

---

It was not yet eight-thirty. The first boats wouldn't be in from the grounds for another hour, maybe two. She stood at the shed's south window.

The south dock was empty. She could see its full length from here — the grey planking, the pilings standing in the flat water, the dock light still burning at the head of the dock, unnecessary now in the morning. The Gale brothers had moved their trap hauler to the inner float in September. The dock had not been in regular use since then.

The night before it had not been empty.

October the eleventh, going into the twelfth. Past midnight. She had been at this window watching the barometer fall. The blow was building. She had already gone out and checked the mooring chains on two of the draggers — around nine, ten o'clock — and had come back to the shed to wait. The chains were what they were. There was nothing more to do in the dark in a rising wind.

Two figures on the south dock. The dock light behind them both.

One she had not recognized. He was looking toward the outer harbor. Dark coat. The build of someone past middle age — not heavy, but solid, the kind of solid that sets into men who have worked outdoors for a long time. Standing still in the way of a man who had come somewhere specific and arrived.

The other one she had not seen clearly. Half-turned from her, the dock light cutting across from the wrong angle. The shoulders. The way of standing. Not a man whose body had been built around boats — she knew that much. Wide across the back. Feet planted like a man used to standing on flat ground, not a deck. Somebody from inland.

She had thought: two men on the dock before a storm. She had thought: their business, not mine.

Now she looked at the harbor log, open on the desk.

The entry was complete. Each time was correct.

These were separate facts. It was possible they had nothing to do with each other, and the log entry she had written was true in every particular, and there was nothing more to do.

She picked up the pen.

She held it.

She set it down.

The south dock stood empty in the flat morning light. The harbor beyond it had gone from grey to silver as the sky cleared. The tide was going out.
