# The Visit

The letter had been in his desk drawer since November — center drawer, under the Latin dictionary, which was where he had put it and where it had remained while he decided, over the course of six weeks, what to do. That morning he had taken it out before the first class, held it in both hands for a moment, and placed it in his coat pocket. The act of placing it in his coat was the decision itself; the walking would settle what remained.

Henry had offered the truck the previous evening. Marcus had said it was no trouble, he would walk, and Henry had received this with the quiet attention he gave to information that did not quite add up and had chosen not to press it. He was not wrong not to press it. The reason Marcus had for declining was difficult to explain without sounding like a man who made things more effortful than they needed to be, which, in this instance, was essentially accurate. Movement was how he prepared for difficult things. It had been this in Vienna — he had walked the Ringstrasse before faculty meetings that required a particular positioning of himself — and it remained so in Coldwater, a town whose geography was flat enough to accommodate the habit without much planning.

He went out the back gate at quarter past eight, between the first class and the second, through a morning that was cold with a particular Maine January coldness: still air, temperatures well below freezing but without the sharp edge that wind would have given it, the sky an even dull white from the horizon up. He walked the harbor road to the bridge and then north on Route 1, where the town gave out within half a mile — the last storefront, a gap, a fence row, and then only the land.

He had three miles.

What he knew: Werner Grau had written from Portland in late September 1943, planning to travel up the coast to Coldwater in October, carrying news of a family in Ansbach that he would not commit to paper. What he knew less certainly, from secondhand accounts filtered through the staffroom and one conversation with Stillman: a man in town clothes had come in on the breakwater after the October storm, no papers, and the Coast Guard had classified it as an unidentified drowning and closed the case. What he had assembled, and kept assembled, over the weeks since November: the plausible connection between these two facts. Plausible was not proof. He had been careful, in his private accounting, to keep the distinction exact.

He knew also what he did not intend to say. He was not going to Albrecht Pfeiffer's farm to investigate. He had no standing for investigation and would not have known what to do with standing if it had been offered. He was going because the letter in his coat pocket was Albrecht Pfeiffer's letter — had always been Albrecht Pfeiffer's letter — and had come to Marcus only through a postal error and a school secretary's pragmatic decision, and it was not his to hold indefinitely. The misdelivery could be corrected. He was correcting it. If Albrecht Pfeiffer's response to receiving his letter told Marcus something he had not known before, Marcus would receive that information in whatever form it arrived and decide then what to do with it.

He would not, under any circumstances, mention Werner Grau's name or the body on the breakwater unless Albrecht opened that door. It was not his door.

The land past the last woodlots was drumlin country — long grass-covered hills left by the glaciers, lying in parallel ridges under their January white, the hay fields flat between them. He had walked this road once before, in his first spring, when the walking had been a kind of inventory of the place he had landed in, and he had found the agricultural plainness of it after coastal terrain surprising and then not surprising. Inland land looked like what it was for. There was a satisfaction in that.

The road bent west at a line of cedar fence posts. He found the farm road, which was dirt and hard and showed no tire tracks from the last few days, and turned onto it.

---

The farm materialized from behind a stand of red maples — leafless, the trunks dark with recent moisture, the lower branches still holding some snow. Then the barn came into view: gray board siding weathered to the particular silver of very old wood, the gambrel roof carrying a good eighteen inches of packed white on its south-facing pitch, the whole structure giving the impression — familiar to Marcus from a different part of the world, from the villages northeast of Vienna where his maternal grandmother had had relations — of something built with the expectation of lasting several lifetimes and now well along in delivering on that expectation.

He read the cornerstone as he entered the farmyard. 1763, half-covered in ice, the numerals carved in the flat-ended strokes of the period. Pre-Revolutionary. Built before the choices the Revolution required, by people who had not yet had to make them.

In the dooryard between the barn and the farmhouse, dry stalks stood through the snow at waist height, stripped by autumn to their skeletons, each branching terminal forked and bearing the dried ruin of seed heads — burred, compact, architecturally complete in their stripped state. *Arctium.* He had the Latin name before he had the English. He always did; it was an inconvenience of his training and he had long since stopped apologizing for it to himself.

The icehouse bunkhouse was visible past the barn's north corner — a small structure with a new wooden step and a bar-latch door, currently closed. As Marcus came across the frozen farmyard a POW emerged from the barn carrying a metal bucket, moving at the measured unhurried pace of a man who has found the exact ratio of effort to temperature and holds to it without thinking. He was one of the older ones — not Karl Reinmar; this man was in his mid-thirties or beyond, with the build of a man grown by agricultural work over many years, broad through the back and settled in his movement. He stopped when he saw Marcus. The stop was brief — two seconds at most — and it was the stop of a man conducting an assessment, which Marcus recognized because it was the stop of a man who has learned to assess strangers as a matter of course and to do it without display. Having completed the assessment, the POW went on with the bucket, neither hurried nor slow, without looking back.

He had been assessed this way in more than one country by men in a range of circumstances, and he knew its grammar. He nodded, once, at the POW's back, and continued toward the barn door.

---

Albrecht Pfeiffer was crouching at the wheel of a manure spreader — or rather at the axle housing, which he was examining with the close attentiveness of a man who has identified a problem and is deciding its complexity before deciding his response to it. He heard Marcus's footfall at approximately ten feet and straightened and turned.

He was in his middle fifties, thick through the shoulders, his face weathered by outdoor work beyond what his age alone would account for — not aged but used, in the way that outdoor faces in cold climates were used, the lines reading as information about the weather rather than as complaint. He looked at Marcus with a direct, unhurried attention that Marcus had encountered before in this part of the world: the attention of a man who was ready to hear a thing and had not yet decided whether the particular thing now arriving was the one he had been readying himself for.

Marcus introduced himself carefully. He taught at the school — German and Latin. He knew Hannah, who was a student in his advanced German section. In the fall, a piece of correspondence had been misdelivered to the school — addressed to Albrecht, in German — and the school secretary had passed it to Marcus on the grounds that it was in German and he would be best placed to handle it. He had been meaning to see it properly delivered. He reached into his coat and produced the envelope.

He watched Albrecht look at the envelope.

There was a small tightening around the eyes — something that moved quickly, a contraction and release, less than a second. Albrecht took the envelope from Marcus's hand with a steadiness that required, Marcus thought, a small effort to sustain. He looked at the return address. He looked at the postmark. He turned the envelope over, examined the back, and then opened it, drawing the letter out by its fold.

He read.

Marcus stood and did not look away. He had made a study, across the course of a life spent among many languages, of reading faces. A person receiving something they did not know had a particular quality of attention: the eyes moved carefully from line to line, the face open in the way of a container being filled, something held in readiness to adjust. A person receiving something they already knew had a different quality entirely. The attention was concentrated but abbreviated; the face still, and still in the way of a closed room rather than an open one. The pace of the eyes was quicker, not because the words were simpler but because the words were confirming rather than informing, and confirmation moved faster than discovery.

Albrecht Pfeiffer's face, reading Werner Grau's letter, was moving at the second rate.

There was a moment — midway through the first side, Marcus thought; Werner had used his full name in the middle of a sentence, not merely at the close — where something crossed Albrecht's face that Marcus found he could name precisely only after it had passed. It was not surprise. It was not grief, though grief was in the neighborhood of it. It was the expression of a man receiving what he had expected to receive and finding, as one always found, that the expectation had not been sufficient preparation for the arrival. Recognition of a specific kind: the kind that says *I knew this was coming*, and the confirmation says *yes*, and the *yes* requires something from the person hearing it that the waiting had not yet required.

Marcus had seen this face before. He had seen it in Vienna in 1938, on people reading the news, when the thing that could not happen had happened and their faces had shifted from the look of a person watching a storm gather to the look of a person on whom the storm had broken. He had worn some version of it himself — in Sherbrooke, when the intake clerk had placed his document on the far side of the desk and he had understood what the gesture meant before anyone had used words. Albrecht Pfeiffer was not reading news about a political catastrophe. He was reading a letter from a man who had planned to come to Coldwater in October, in a January that was three months past that October, and the letter was not information. It was Werner's voice, arriving after Werner.

Albrecht folded the letter. He held it across its center, both hands, and was still for a moment. Then he looked at Marcus.

"When did this come to you?" His English was careful — chosen, unhurried, the English of a man who was selecting a language rather than falling into it. Slightly formal, slightly stilted. Not the English of his household; the English of an occasion.

"November," Marcus said.

Albrecht nodded once. It was a slow nod, a full acknowledgment, not a mere receipt of information.

"Thank you," he said.

The two words were complete. They had in them a quality that Marcus recognized from other languages and other contexts: the quality of a door being closed from the inside. Not locked, not unfriendly — the hostility of a door slammed was entirely absent — but latched. The conversation was over. The question of whether there was anything further to say had been decided, quietly, without Marcus being consulted, and the decision had been reached before the question was raised, probably before Albrecht Pfeiffer had finished the letter's second side. *Thank you.* A full sentence. The space after it was not a pause; it was a close.

Marcus said it was no trouble. He did not say anything else. He did not say the things he was holding — the questions arranged behind the letter, the sequence he had assembled in six weeks of carrying the connection from November's discovery to this January morning. He had come with a letter. The letter was now Albrecht Pfeiffer's. What stood behind the letter was not Marcus's to present.

He turned and walked back down the farm road.

---

He did not look back. The red maples thinned and fell away behind him and the road ran straight between the drumlin fields under the white sky.

He ran the sequence.

Albrecht Pfeiffer had read Werner Grau's letter and had not been surprised.

He had not been surprised by the name. He had not been surprised by the date or the contents or the fact of the letter's existence. He had read it with the face of a man receiving a confirmation rather than a discovery, and the confirmation he had received was not the contents of the letter — which were Werner's plans for a visit in October, plans now three months past — but the existence of the letter itself: Werner had written. Werner had planned to come. Werner had been Werner, three months ago and twenty years before that, Werner enough to write to Albrecht after however many years of American silence and to sign himself *Ihr alter Freund.*

Which meant — Marcus slowed on the iced rut without noticing he had slowed, the cold exact on his face, Route 1's utility poles visible now ahead in the distance — which meant that Albrecht Pfeiffer knew, had known since October, that Werner Grau had come to Coldwater and had not come back. He had been sitting with this knowledge through the fall and through December and into January, with no one to give it to and no apparent intention of giving it to anyone. The letter arriving was not news to him. It was Werner's voice, which he already knew had gone silent, speaking once more from the month before it went silent.

Marcus could not prove this. He had inference and a face, and the face was not courtroom evidence and would not be. But he had been reading faces and language for most of a lifetime, and the reading he had done at the barn door was the reading of a man who knows what he has seen.

Albrecht Pfeiffer had known Werner Grau had come to Coldwater.

Which meant he had seen Werner — or received word that Werner had come — before the storm.

He had been carrying this since October.

Marcus walked north. Route 1 came up and he turned onto it without deciding to. The cold was steady in his coat. He thought about the letter's weight — its actual physical weight, which had been slight, two pages written on a single sheet — and about the different weight he had been holding since November, the inferential weight, and about the way Albrecht Pfeiffer had folded the letter across its center and held it with both hands. There was a way a person held something when they had been waiting for it. The hands did not know how to be casual about it, whatever the face had decided.

He did not know what had happened on the night Werner Grau had died. He knew what was plausible; he knew, now, that Albrecht Pfeiffer knew more than was plausible. He did not know whether Werner had reached the farm that night or not. He did not know what Albrecht knew about the hours between Werner's arrival in Coldwater and the storm. He did not know and had no way to know, and had made no move, at the barn door, to ask — because he had not been offered the right to ask and would not have received an answer if he had taken the right uninvited.

He held what he had. It was not nothing. It was not enough to do anything with, and he was not at all certain what *do* would mean here, in any case.

The town came back around him gradually: the first outbuildings, then the fence rows tightening, then the first storefront with its wooden sign. He walked up Main Street and turned onto Elm and went up the hill toward the house.

---

Henry's truck was not in the yard. The front of the house was dark, the curtains in the parlor where Marcus never went drawn against the afternoon cold. He came around through the back gate, which was his entrance, and up the back step.

Lillian was at the stove, the lid of the soup pot sitting slightly ajar, the smell of it beginning to reach the room. She looked up when the door opened and looked back at the pot. This was her form of greeting, which Marcus had received nearly every evening for almost two years: *you are in, the meal is going, you are accounted for.* He had learned to receive it as what it was — not a performance of welcome but welcome itself, in the practical form it took in this household.

He took off his coat and hung it on the hook by the door.

The pocket, empty now, had the shape of its former contents — or he was giving it that shape, which amounted to the same thing. Three months the letter had been in his desk drawer. Three months he had been holding a plausible connection that was nobody else's business and that he had no authorized use for. He had carried it this morning from the drawer to his coat and down the farm road and into the farmyard and across the conversation that had consisted of an introduction, a delivery, and two short sentences, and he had left the letter in Albrecht Pfeiffer's hands, where it had always belonged. He had given the one thing over that he had had any standing to give.

He stood at the hook.

What Marcus held now was not the letter. He held the inference — the sequence, the face, the folded paper held across its center — and these were not a thing he could put in a desk drawer, and he understood, standing at the coat hook with Lillian at the stove and the winter afternoon going dark outside the kitchen window, that he had known this before he had started walking.

Lillian set two plates on the table.

He sat down.

# Chapter Eleven — Load Calculations

She was three entries into the December fuel receipts when the door opened. The man said his name — Tarbell, Amos Tarbell — and the county harbor authority, and that he was here for the routine inspection.

Eira put down her pen. "Harbormaster Bowman," she said. "I've been expecting someone from the county."

He had a clipboard with a county authority form already clipped to the board and a brown wool overcoat that had been brushed clean. Mid-thirties. His politeness had the quality of a specific instruction carefully followed.

"How long have you held this position?" he asked.

"Eight years."

"Prior experience in harbor operations?"

"Assistant harbormaster. Under the previous harbormaster." She let him write. "Owen Bowman. My husband."

He looked up once. Then he looked back at his clipboard.

"How long as assistant?"

"Four years."

"You currently have no assistant of your own."

"Since January 1942. He enlisted." She kept her voice even. "The county authority hasn't authorized a replacement. I've managed without one."

He wrote something on his form. She could not read it from across the desk.

She had laid the winter documents out on the table before he came: the mooring registry open to the current page, the fuel allocation ledger beside it, the vessel registration file beneath. The safety inspection folder was on the shelf; she would take it down when they reached it.

She walked him through the mooring registry. Each vessel currently on a winter mooring in the inner harbor: the lobster boats Ida May, Sadie H., and Clara B., and three others on the west float; the dragger East Wind; the cold storage skiff; the Ellsworth against the east float on her winter berth. Seventeen vessels in total. She named each one, its registration status, its current mooring position. He checked them against his form. He did not find a discrepancy, because there was not one.

The fuel allocation ledger was next. Wartime supplemental allocation for harbor operations: every vessel drawing against the harbor's quarterly allotment from the Department of the Interior was entered by vessel name, date, and quantity in gallons, each entry initialed. The column balanced to the gallon.

"The authorization document?" Tarbell asked.

She took it from the folder beneath the ledger. He read through it. He handed it back without comment.

They went outside.

February cold, flat gray sky, the harbor on an ebbing tide. The dragger that worked the offshore grounds had gone out at first light and would not be back until afternoon. The Ellsworth sat against the east float with her forward lines gone slack in the ebb. The compressor at the cold storage house ran in a steady cycle. The inner harbor water was undisturbed except where the tide drew over the submerged ledge at the harbor mouth.

Tarbell walked the length of the pier to the breakwater end. She walked beside him. He asked about the depth at the elbow at mean low water, the height of the inner float at mean high water, the fuel storage configuration. He asked whether the tank was inside the hundred-foot setback from the waterline.

"Inside," she said. "By eight feet. The wartime exception was filed in June of 1942."

"Section four."

"Subsection B."

He wrote it down. At the pier head he stopped and looked at the harbor for a moment without writing anything. She stood beside him and looked at the same water. The sky was low and the gray ran without break from the cloud to the harbor surface.

"Everything here appears to be in order," he said.

"Yes," she said.

They went back inside.

The vessel registration file came next, then the safety inspection folder. Forty-two active vessel registrations, all current, no lapses, no outstanding renewals. The safety inspections for the winter-berthed vessels complete; the summer boats scheduled for spring before the season opened, the schedule printed on the folder's back page. He read the schedule. He made a note. His form was nearly full.

Tarbell sat down across the desk. He set his pencil on the clipboard.

"I want to ask you about the formal basis of your appointment," he said. "The — transitional nature of it."

She opened the bottom drawer and took out a folder she had kept there since 1935. Inside was a single typed letter on county authority letterhead. She set it on the table in front of him.

"November 21, 1935," she said. "Signed by Director Pearce. It appoints me harbormaster of Coldwater Reach pending formal review by the county harbor authority board."

Tarbell picked up the letter. He read it. He had the look of a man reading something he had already been briefed on — the eyes moving at the speed of confirmation.

"This review," he said. "It was scheduled?"

"December 1935. Then rescheduled. Then not rescheduled again."

"You never pressed for it."

"I did the work," she said. "The review would have confirmed what the work showed. I took it to be the board's matter to pursue."

He turned the letter over. The back was blank. He set it face up.

"You might have requested formal appointment on your own initiative," he said.

"I might have," she said. "What I did instead was manage the harbor."

She let that sit. Outside, the compressor cycled off and ran. The last of the ebb moved through the pilings.

"There is one more thing I'd like to show you," she said.

She went to the north shelf and took down the harbor log for 1935. Green board cover, the year inked on the spine in Owen's hand — a forward-leaning cursive with compressed vowels and the particular t-crossings that ran slightly below the stalk. The log she had opened more times than she had ever counted, for reasons she did not examine. She set it on the desk and opened it to November.

November 7. *Barometer 29.4, NE backing N, Beaufort 5 outer harbor. Doubled all moorings afternoon watch. Advised small craft haul 1600. E. Anderson dory on A-ring 1645. Harbor secure 1800.* Owen's entries were that way: terse, accurate, complete. She had been reading them for eight years and could still hear his attention in the abbreviations — the way a man writes when he is doing the actual work and the writing is the record of the work, not a separate act.

November 8 was blank.

November 9 was hers. *Barometer 29.2, NW 8, seas 4–6 outer harbor, abating. O. Bowman, harbormaster, missing evening 7 November. Search conducted CG Sprucehead and harbor tender. Body not yet recovered. Harbor open. All moorings secure.* Her own hand, smaller and more vertical than his.

"A continuity of record," she said. "Unbroken."

Tarbell looked at both entries for longer than he had looked at anything else in the shed. He read November 7 and then November 9. He looked at the blank November 8 in between them. He set his pencil down flat on the clipboard.

"November 7 to November 9," he said.

"Forty hours."

He picked up the pencil and wrote something on his form. It was the longest entry he had made all morning. She did not try to read it.

There was a pause. The cold storage compressor ran outside. The harbor was quiet the way it was always quiet in February — the boats that were left had already found their winter arrangement; the pier held only the sounds of the tide.

"I want to tell you," Tarbell said, "that there are some parties on the county board who have expressed concerns. About the long-term stability of the arrangement."

"Stability," she said.

"The formal basis of your appointment." He stopped. He started again. "They believe the matter of formal confirmation should be addressed."

"What would constitute a satisfactory confirmation?" she asked. "In the board's view."

He turned the pencil between his fingers. He was choosing words. He chose them and they did not constitute a direct answer.

"The board's preference," he said, "is that the appointment be placed on a formally established footing."

"What process would satisfy the board?"

He looked at the county authority letter on the desk. He looked at his clipboard. He looked at the window.

He did not answer.

She gave him one more moment. He did not fill it.

"I see," she said.

Tarbell gathered his clipboard and reached for the county authority letter. He asked whether he could take it to copy for his file; she said yes, and asked him to return it when he was done. He put it in his briefcase. He stood. He said he would file his report with the county authority office by the end of the week. He thanked her for her time.

"Thank you for coming," she said.

She walked him to the door. She stood in the doorway and watched him cross the pier and turn up the road toward town. The tide had turned; the Ellsworth's forward lines had gone taut again. Twenty past eleven.

Inside, she put the 1935 harbor log back on the north shelf. She returned the fuel ledger and the vessel registration file and the safety inspection folder to their places. She straightened the table.

Then she put the kettle on.

The harbor lay in February quiet: the dragger out, the Ellsworth cold at the east float, the lobster boats on their moorings with their bow lines leading east into the turned current. Ice on the float cleats, thin enough to break with a boot. The cold storage house ran steady. The sky was flat and would not change before dark.

She looked at the north shelf. The harbor logs ran left to right across it — the years in Owen's hand, then the 1935 volume with both their hands in it, then hers from 1936 on. Eight spines in a row, identical green board.

The water came to the boil. She poured her cup and went back to the December fuel receipts.

# Chapter Fourteen — The Photograph

The tin box lived on the shelf in her parents' room, above the folded shirts — had lived there, as far as Hannah could trace, since before she was old enough to notice things on shelves. Small and dark, the paint worn through at the corners to bright metal, a small dent near the clasp that she had pressed her thumbnail into many times without ever asking how it got there. She had moved the box dozens of times to reach the shirts. She had never opened it.

Her mother was downstairs. The room had the particular cold of upstairs rooms in April, heated only by what rose from the kitchen below, which in April was not much. The smell: cedar from the blocks Magda kept in the bottom drawer with the wool things, and beneath that something fainter — her father's shaving soap, or the wood of the floor still releasing winter, or simply the close particular smell of a room where two people have slept for twenty years. The bureau along the north wall had a painted border she had traced with her finger since she was four. The quilt on the bed was one her mother had made the winter before Hannah was born, eighteen years old and not looking it.

She set the laundry basket on the bed and began to sort.

Her mother's room, her mother's order. She moved with the particular care of a person who has learned to take up only the space she has been given. Her mother's blouses, her father's good shirts, the household linens. When she lifted the stack of folded shirts to place them on the shelf, the tin box came forward against her hands.

She set it on the bedspread.

The same as it had always been. The bright corners, the dent near the clasp. She held it a moment, the weight of it in both hands — lighter than it looked — and then she lifted the clasp and opened it.

Letters, folded to fit the box. She could see without reading them that they were in German — her father's hand, the cramped vertical script, the particular way he formed his capital *S* that she had known before she learned to write herself. She didn't unfold them. They were her parents' letters; that was enough. There were papers beneath, creased many times over, that might have been documents; she touched the edge of one and let it go. At the bottom, held together with a rubber band that had gone dry and left a faint brown mark on the photograph on top, a small stack of pictures.

She looked.

The first was a woman she didn't know — older, perhaps a grandmother, seated before a painted studio backdrop wearing the expression of someone enduring a long exposure. No name on the back. The second was a group of men outside a building she couldn't place, European, with a low-pitched slate roof. Nobody she recognized.

She came to the third photograph and stopped.

Two men before a stone doorway. A carved lintel above them, heavy and deliberate — civic, she thought, or a church entrance, the kind of archwork that had been standing for two or three centuries and didn't expect to stop. Both men in their thirties. Wool coats, hats held in their hands: they had taken the hats off for the photograph, which was what men did when they wanted the photograph to count. Both squinting. The shadows on the paving were short, the light full and direct, a summer afternoon or early autumn with the summer still in it. A quality to the light she couldn't name exactly, except that it was not the light here — not the flat particular grey of coastal Maine but something more direct, more central, a light that knew where it was from.

One of the men was her father.

She knew him by the jaw and the set of his shoulders and the way he held the hat brim, which hadn't changed. He looked younger than she had ever seen him — not happy exactly, but present. Unguarded. His face was simply a face, open to the bright day, not yet arranged into whatever it had since become arranged into.

The other man she looked at for a long time.

Heavy in the shoulders. A laborer's build, the neck thicker than her father's, the coat a little tight across the chest. She guessed he was her father's age in the photograph, early thirties. His face was ordinary — she looked at it and found nothing to catch on. Not unkind, not cold, not worried or proud or marked by any particular feeling. Just the face of a man who happened to be standing in front of a stone doorway on a bright day. The kind of face that comes up ahead of you in a line somewhere and by the time he's gone you couldn't say whether his eyes were light or dark. She kept looking, trying to fix it in memory, and the harder she looked the more it seemed to come apart, until what she was seeing was features in a rough vicinity of each other rather than a person. The squinting might have been concentration. It might have been the sun.

She turned the photograph over.

Her father's pencil. His vertical German hand.

*A. Pfeiffer. W. Grau. Bamberg, 1921.*

She stood at the edge of the bed and held the photograph and thought about Bamberg. Bavaria — she was fairly sure. Somewhere in the middle of the country, north of Munich. Not where her father's family was from; they had been from south of there, nearer the Austrian border. But not far from Ansbach either, she thought, and the thought came and went before she decided whether to catch it. The photograph was from 1921. The year before her parents came to Maine.

*W. Grau.* She had never heard the name. *Grau*: in German, grey. A man named Grey, standing beside her father in the afternoon light of a stone doorway, twenty-three years ago.

She put the photograph back with the others. Replaced the rubber band. Closed the box and latched it. Set it on the shelf above the shirts where it had always been.

She picked up the laundry basket and went back to her work.

---

The afternoon was farm work, which it had been every April of her life.

She filled the near trough and opened the gate to the far pasture, which had been closed since November. The mud on the track between the barn and the gate was deep and cold and smelled of the earth beginning to come back — different from summer mud, more mineral than animal, with something green underneath it. Two cows came out and stood in the new grass looking at it with their usual expression, which was the expression they had for everything. She worked the pump handle and let the water run. In the north field she could hear the four Germans — the sound of tools in turned ground, a word or two carried on the wind, Lonzo Reed's voice in its usual even tone and then quiet. She didn't look that way.

She split kindling. The axe came down and the cedar split clean, the smell sharp in the cold air. She stacked it under the overhang and worked until her shoulders told her to stop.

*W. Grau.*

The name was there through all of it, not urgently. The way a half-heard phrase stays with you during repetitive work — you think about something else and there it is again, unchanged. She tried to hold the face from the photograph and it kept going. Her father's face stayed because her father was here and she saw the same face every day. But the man beside him dissolved each time she turned her attention away, until what came back was only the shape of the shoulders and the squinting and the stone archway behind them, and not the face itself.

He had written both names on the back in pencil — in his own vertical German hand, a name for each face so neither would slip without the other. He had wanted to remember.

October arrived in her, the way it kept arriving: dinner, three weeks or so after the storm, her saying *they found a body on the breakwater* in the same tone she carried any news home from school, and her father's hands going still on his utensils. She had said something about the milking instead, because not asking had seemed the right thing, the careful thing, the choice that maintained the particular equilibrium of silence her household ran on.

She wasn't sure anymore that it had been.

She went inside.

Her mother was at the kitchen window, standing with her arms at her sides, looking out at the east field. Hannah had learned, over the better part of a year, not to try to read those stillnesses. She measured flour. She put the kettle on. Magda moved to the table and sat down, and neither of them spoke, which was the usual arrangement and worked well enough.

She kneaded the dough longer than she needed to and covered it with a cloth and sat at the table with her library book and read two pages three times without them settling into anything.

The letters in the tin box were in German; she hadn't read them. The papers she hadn't unfolded. Whatever her parents had kept from before — before Maine, before she was born, before whatever the before was that had become this household — it was in that box on the shelf in their room, and she had opened it today for the first time, and she was seventeen years old and had found a name she had never heard.

She took the loaves out when the kitchen smelled right and went to set the table.

---

Her father came in from the fields at half past five, which was when he always came in. His boots on the porch step, the pump, the towel on its nail. He sat down. Magda brought the soup. Hannah set the bread on the board, the pickles, the salt.

The lamp was on the table between them. The ceiling wiring had been unreliable since the spring rain two nights ago and her father didn't trust it after wet weather, so the oil lamp, which made the kitchen smaller and closer, the corners going to warm shadow, the window above the sink dark and reflecting the room back at itself.

Her father bowed his head.

*Komm, Herr Jesu, sei unser Gast.* The same four lines he had always said, always in German, at every meal, since before she was old enough to know what grace was. She moved her lips with the words without making sound — habit, and also she didn't want to forget them entirely. Her mother was still. Then her father raised his head and picked up his spoon.

The soup: potatoes, the last of the winter's dried beans, a hamhock stretched to its limit. There was bread. The lamp flame shifted in a brief draft from the hallway and stilled. Her father broke bread. Her mother moved her spoon through the broth.

She set her spoon down.

"Papa." Not carefully, not carelessly. A normal tone of voice, the tone she would use to ask about the fields or the feed. "Who is W. Grau?"

Her father's hands stopped.

She watched them. His fork was raised, and the piece of bread he had broken in his other hand, and both stopped where they were — two or three inches above the plate, suspended. The lamp flame moved again in the same draft. One second. Two. The flame stilled. Three. Then her father's hands came down. He set the bread on the side of his plate and picked up his spoon.

He said nothing.

She looked at her mother.

Magda had looked up.

Magda, who for months had kept her eyes to the table or the window or the interior distance she had been moving toward since the start of the war — Magda had looked up. Quickly. Her eyes found Hannah's across the lamp and the table.

What was in them was not alarm. Not the particular flatness of the depression that had been Magda's face for the better part of a year. Something older than that, something worn smooth by being held a long time — not bitterness, not grief exactly, though grief was somewhere underneath it. The look of a woman who has been sitting beside a door for a long time without knowing when it will open, and has now heard the latch.

Two seconds. Then Magda's eyes went back to her bowl.

Her father said nothing. He ate. He drank from his water glass. He broke the bread and ate the bread and did not look at Hannah and did not answer.

---

Hannah washed the dishes. Magda dried, her hands moving from bowl to towel to shelf with the efficiency of someone for whom the task has long since stopped requiring thought. Through the window above the sink the farmyard had gone dark. The barn roof flat against the sky. At the base of the icehouse door, a thin line of yellow light showed, steady and faint.

She handed the last plate to her mother and dried her own hands.

Her father had moved to the accounts book. The table was as it always was at this hour: book open to the usual page, his pen in his hand, the bread plate at the side, the salt beside it, the lamp moved to give him light on the columns. His pen made its small sounds. He did not look up when she passed.

She went upstairs.

Her room was dark. She sat on the edge of the bed without lighting the lamp and listened to the house — the pen, faintly; her mother's chair; outside, the April wind working at the window frame, still with winter in it at this hour. Down the hall, through the wall, the shelf above the shirts.

She tried once more to hold the face from the photograph. The shoulders, the squinting, the ordinary arrangement of features she had looked at and looked at and couldn't keep. She held it for a moment. Then it was gone, the same as it had gone every time.

But her father's hands had stopped.

She lay down in her coat. Downstairs, the pen moved in its columns. Outside the window, the wind worked at the frame.

# Chapter Fifteen — What Grandy Soule Saw

The registration table went up at the pier head the last week of April the way it had gone up every spring Eira could remember: the clipboard, the fee box, the carbon forms weighted at the left with the big shackle she kept for this purpose, because the wind off the harbor had no patience for paperwork in April.

She had the table set before seven. The harbor lay in front of her the way it lay every spring — the light longer now, working into the east faces of the pilings and under the boathouse eaves where the winter sun hadn't reached, the water still cold enough to raise a thin steam at the harbor entrance in the early morning air. The mud at the basin head had softened. Dark fronds of weed were coming off the south rocks. A pair of eiders worked the current beside the fish house float and did not look up.

The first boat in was the *Bertha L.* at half past, Pete Alley at the wheel with his boy in the stern. She had the hull in the card file and wrote it up while he tied off: tonnage, engine, mooring assignment. He'd put fresh paint on her over the winter and the hull had that new brightness to it that wouldn't last but was good while it lasted. She collected the fee and the signature and filed the carbon.

By noon she had seven: *Bertha L.*, *Perseverance*, *Sea Star*, *Laura K.*, *Edna C.*, and two others whose documentation was in order and whose owners had nothing more to say to her than the minimum. She wrote each entry in the column and checked it against the card file and wrote the total at the bottom of the page.

Seven. Last spring there had been nine.

*Crestview* was still in the cradle at the railway yard. Harold Oakes had gone into the Navy in January of 1942 and the boat had been on the railway since that June. She had sent two letters about the cradle fee; neither had been answered, which was not Oakes's fault. The mooring pen sat empty. *Walter D.* had been sold south to Tenants Harbor in February when the Withams made the decision they had been putting off since autumn — Lyle had taken sick and there was no one left to take the boat over. She had given that mooring pen to the *Laura K.* when Ed Croft's hip made the row from the inner float a problem for him.

Two fewer boats. The column said so.

*Sea Star* was Ray Coffin's — Fred Coffin's younger boy, who had come home from the Pacific in November with two fingers gone from the right hand and had been on the water again by April, which was not a surprise to anyone who knew the family. He signed the registration form left-handed. He wanted the mooring lines inspected before he started hauling and she made a note.

Burton Talbot on the *Edna C.* had a new inboard he was willing to explain at length. She let him explain it, asked for the documentation twice, received it the second time. New tonnage in the column. She signed the carbon.

The rest of the afternoon went the way it went: boat by boat, fee by fee, the spring talk running alongside the transactions the way it always did. She listened and wrote and handed over receipts.

By two o'clock the registration table was packed and she was at the fuel dock going over the morning log when the *Maud L.* came in.

---

Grandy Soule brought her alongside the fuel dock without ceremony — no wasted motion, the boat coming against the fender the way something comes to rest in the hands of a man who has set it down in the same place for more years than he has counted. The *Maud L.* was a thirty-two-foot lobster boat with a dull red hull that had been brighter once; Soule had bought her in 1928 and she had been working this harbor since. He was perhaps seventy, perhaps past it. His age was a harbor fact she had stopped trying to fix, the same way you stop sounding every ledge you already know is there.

He paid for his fuel in exact change from his coat pocket, signed the carbon, and stood at the dock while the tank filled. The harbor went on around them: the sound of the pump, the water working the pilings, a dragger coming in from the outer harbor and taking its mooring. Soule had his eyes on the south end of the inner pier — the double-planked float at the fish house end, the one that had needed new decking since before the war and was not going to get it this spring either.

She was finishing the log entry for the *Laura K.*

He said nothing for a while and she did not expect him to.

Then, without turning: "Saw a strange dinghy at the south pier. That October night. Before your blow."

She looked up. She kept her face. "Which pier," she said.

"South end. That last float." He moved his chin toward it. "Late. After midnight. I was driving back from Owls Head."

"What night."

"Night the weather came on, or near enough. I've thought about it." He watched the harbor. "Numbers on the transom weren't Coldwater. I didn't know them."

"Could you read them?"

"Not properly. Too dark, and I didn't stop. Might have been Portland — I couldn't say for certain. Small boat, wooden tender, not large." A pause. "One man come off her. He walked up toward the main pier."

"Did you see him come back to the dinghy?"

"No." He held the mooring line, not working it yet. "I drove on. Figured whoever it was had put in because the weather was turning — thought nothing of it." He looked at the float. "Dinghy was gone when the blow cleared. I don't know when it went. Could have gone in the storm."

She looked at the fuel gauge. Her pen was in her hand. She had written nothing since he started speaking.

"One man," she said. "That's all you saw."

"One." He began working the mooring line loose. "I heard you were still asking about that October business. Thought maybe you'd want to know."

"I would," she said. "Thank you, Grandy."

He untied the *Maud L.* and backed her out with the same economy he'd brought her in with, turned toward the harbor mouth, and was gone past the outer breakwater. The wake spread into the basin and went flat. She stood at the dock end and watched the boat go.

---

She laid what she had against what she had been carrying, the way she would lay a vessel's log against the tide tables: columns together, the matches showing you what you could confirm, the gaps showing you what you hadn't accounted for yet.

Her column: two figures on the south dock, same night, past midnight. One coming from the direction of the main pier — heavyset, town coat, moving from some distance. A second figure near the fish house end, further back, that she had taken at the time for a dock worker.

The columns met at the south pier. The man who came off the dinghy and the man she had seen from her window were the same man, or she had to explain why they weren't, and she could not.

The second figure was not in Soule's column. One man, he had said. She had seen two. Which meant the second figure had come on foot, not by water — had come separately, or had come after Soule drove on.

Two days later, with the storm in between, the body was at the breakwater elbow.

Not proof. But it had a shape.

She picked up her clipboard and walked back to the shed.

---

The harbor log was on its stand. The tide tables were pinned to the board behind the door. She hung her coat and sat at the desk. The window gave onto the inner basin — three boats still at their moorings, the outer harbor going pewter in the late-afternoon light.

She opened the middle drawer.

The letter was between the duplicate mooring assignments and the east anchorage survey notes, where she had put it in November. Coast Guard, Sprucehead station. Dated November 14, 1943. Lt. A. Mercer's signature at the bottom, the same neat hand from the October paperwork. *Should any information come to light bearing on the identity of the deceased or the circumstances of his presence in Coldwater Reach, the station would be grateful for its communication at the address above.*

She had read that sentence a dozen times since November. It said what it said.

Below it: male, fifty or older, no identifying papers, recovered at the breakwater elbow, morning of October 12, 1943. Navy wool coat with lapels, wool trousers. Probable cardiac event — no water in the lungs. No next of kin identified, no missing persons report in any register that matched. Case status: open.

She set the letter on the desk.

What the letter did not have: a dinghy at the south pier, possibly Portland registration, the night the storm came on. One man off her, walking toward the main waterfront. That was not her private information. Soule had told her at the fuel dock this afternoon in plain daylight and would confirm it if asked.

What else: two figures on the south dock, past midnight, October 10 going into the eleventh. One from the direction of the main pier — heavyset, town coat. One near the fish house end, further back, a shape in the dark she had taken for a dock worker. Her own observation, from the shed window, two hundred feet of dark harbor between the glass and the south float. She had been watching the barometric trend. She had seen what she had seen.

She had held the reason for not writing it. The reason was sound: what she had seen from the window was two shapes in the dark at a distance through glass, and two shapes in the dark at a distance through glass was not what the harbor log was for. The column had stayed blank.

Eight years in this post and she had kept the log accurate. Every entry had something under it: a document, a witness, a measurement, a recorded time.

What Soule had given her today changed the calculation. Not because he had seen the same things she had — he hadn't stayed long enough for that. Because he had put a transport under the man she had seen.

The envelope was in the right-hand drawer. She had put it there in January when the winter had seemed like enough reason to wait.

She reached for her pen.

# The Sixth of June

The radio was on downstairs.

She heard it before she heard him — the sound coming up through the boards as a man's voice, steady and formal, saying something she couldn't separate into words from the top of the stairs. Then underneath it her father's voice, low, not calling her.

She came down in her socks, holding the banister in the dark.

The kitchen was lit only by the orange of the radio dial and the first gray beginning at the window above the sink. The clock on the shelf read ten past four. Her father was standing at the table with his barn coat over the chair behind him, hands at his sides. He had been there for some time. She could tell by the particular settled quality of his stillness — the way a person stands when they have already done the hard work of arriving at a thing and are now simply inside it.

She stood by the cold stove and listened.

*—Allied forces have landed on the coast of northern France, in the region known as Normandy—*

Her father did not look at her. The voice on the radio was deliberate, each sentence placed as if placement were a form of accuracy. She tried to find Normandy on the wall map Mr. Klein kept in the classroom — a physical geography map of Europe, mountain ranges rendered as hatch marks — and she could find France in her mind generally but could not find the northern coast of it, could not locate the region.

*—General Eisenhower has confirmed that operations are continuing and that Allied forces have established positions along multiple beach approaches—*

The signal dropped for a moment and came back at a different pitch. Another voice, lower, reading something that sounded like an official statement. *Beachhead. Sustained operations. Allied forces.* She was hearing the shapes of words rather than their meaning.

He had not made coffee. She looked at his hands on the table and did not ask.

---

Her mother came down at twenty past four. Hannah heard the careful step on the stairs — her mother's way of walking when she was tired or deliberate — and then Magda was in the doorway, in her robe, hair loose over her shoulders. She stood looking at the radio.

She did not come into the kitchen.

The signal had shifted; it was speaking from London now, someone said. It came in slightly cleaner before full dawn, the way foreign signals sometimes did at that hour.

Hannah made coffee. She knew where they stood with the ration book; she had checked two days before. She decided it was worth it. The match smell, the soft sound of the gas, the small flame catching. She stood by the stove and waited and looked at her mother in the doorway. Her mother was watching the radio itself, not her father — the cabinet, as if the signal were visible inside it.

When the coffee was ready she poured two cups. She set one at her father's place. He looked at it for a moment and then picked it up with both hands. She brought the second to the doorway and her mother took it, both hands around the cup, and held it without drinking.

They listened.

The voice named towns. It named a number of ships in a tone that meant the number was very large. The word *paratroopers.* The phrase *naval bombardment* said in the same even register as everything else. She listened for her father's face to change and it did not change in any way she could name. He had shifted his hands; they were flat on the table now, weight forward. He knows where Normandy is. He can hear those town names and put them on the coast. She watched his face for the look of a person tracking something through space and she thought she could see it in the set of his jaw, the forward lean.

The clock moved from four-thirty to five. The June light came in fast — the barn materialized out of the dark, then the fence posts along the east field, then the hay fields themselves in the early flat gray. Birds started outside, a few at first and then more of them, and by five minutes before five it was a full sound with the radio running underneath it.

She made herself useful. She set the oatmeal to soak for when they would want it. She straightened the dish towels that did not need straightening. Her mother had not moved from her chair; her father had not moved from the table. The radio continued — a fourth voice now, a correspondent somewhere, saying something about the men who had gone in before dawn, the ones who had gone by parachute into the dark.

She tried to make the distance real and could not. The voice was coming out of the BC-1206 the same way it always came out, filling the kitchen the same way the weather report filled it, and somewhere behind the voice there were men coming off boats onto a beach in France and she could not picture the beach.

Her father said, in English: "It will be over soon."

He said it to the room. Not to her, not to her mother — to the kitchen, to the radio, to the window where the June morning was showing itself. She had not heard a full English sentence from him since — she searched backward, through months — since January. Maybe longer. His English had not gone away; she had never believed it had. It was still in him the way a radio signal was always traveling even when the set was off.

Not relief exactly. She was watching his face and there was nothing in it that looked like the American kind, the easy kind, the kind that made you exhale loudly or put your hand over your eyes. Something else: the look of a man who has been watching for a specific thing to begin, and believes it has begun.

Her mother moved from the doorway.

One step onto the linoleum. Then another. She crossed to the table in three steps and she pulled out the chair and she sat. She folded both hands around the cup. She looked at the tabletop.

She did not speak. She was in the kitchen. She was at the table, which was not the doorway, and Hannah did not look at it too long.

*Erleichterung.* She had the German and not the English for it, because German was the language she had been made in, and the German word held the shape of what it named. Not relief — that word was too clean, too finished at its edges. More like: a weight becoming less heavy. Something that has been pressing, without stopping, for a very long time — longer than she had understood the full shape of it — beginning, on this specific morning in June, to ease by one small degree.

She did not say the word.

The radio went on.

An hour later her father put on his barn coat and boots and went out. The screen door. Hannah washed the cups. Her mother stayed at the table, hands folded, not sleeping, not reading, just there in the new morning light. After a while Magda reached over and turned the radio down one notch — not off, just quieter — and Hannah left her there.

She milked. She fed. She hauled water and swept the milking parlor and split a quarter-cord of kindling from the pile behind the barn that had been waiting two weeks for someone to get to it. The work went the way the work always went: the weight of the pails, the patience of the cows, the rhythm of the axe in the June morning. Somewhere in the middle of it, there were kitchens all up the road where people were having the versions of these hours that belonged to them — people with sons on those beaches, people who could follow the town names on the coast. She didn't have any of that. She had her father's hands flat on the table and the sentence he had said into the kitchen with no one in particular to hear it.

---

That afternoon the radio was everywhere in town. She heard it from the diner when she stopped the truck at the intersection for the feed run — someone had turned the set up high and the voice came through the screen door and across the sidewalk. At the post office two women stood in the open doorway with their arms folded against their chests, listening to the set inside. Three men on the sidewalk in front of the hardware store, standing in the June sun, not talking to each other.

She loaded the feed and drove back on the south road. The afternoon had come in with the first real summer warmth — the kind that settles in the open fields and won't move until after supper, the kind that means the season has made up its mind. The fields on the south side of the road were deep green and tall. She was thinking about their hay. The south field had been ready for two weeks; her father would cut it this week if the weather held.

At the farm, Lonzo had his portable radio on the icehouse step — a small set with a black handle, volume turned up enough to carry inside. She could hear it as she crossed the yard with the first water bucket, the afternoon broadcast, the same careful voices. The door was propped open. She heard Lonzo's chair shift inside.

She put the bucket down and went back for the second.

---

Karl was on the step.

He had come outside while she was in the barn. He was sitting with his elbows on his knees, looking at the fence line and the hay field beyond it. The hay was at its full summer height — she had been watching it get tall for two weeks — silver-green in the afternoon light, moving sometimes in the way tall grass moves when there is no particular wind, the stalks making small adjustments to their own weight. His forearms were tanned from three weeks of fieldwork. He was not looking at her.

She had been going to walk past to the pump.

She stopped.

Four or five yards from the step. Lonzo was inside; she could hear the radio still going, hear his chair. Her father's sentence had been in her head since five that morning. It had ridden with her through the barn work and the drive to town and through the afternoon, and it was there now in the June heat in this specific piece of yard where she was not supposed to stop.

She said it before she had decided what she was doing.

"It will be over soon."

She said it quietly, looking at the fence past his shoulder. The way her father had said it — not to anyone in the room in particular, just the sentence released into the air.

Karl looked at her.

He looked at her for a moment and then he nodded. Once, slow. Not yes, not agreement. The nod she had seen him give Lonzo when Lonzo explained something Karl had already worked out for himself. *I hear you.* He looked back at the fields.

She stayed where she was with the pail.

He said, in English: "My home."

Not a question. The two words and then quiet, his hands loose between his knees, his eyes on the fields.

She did not ask what he thought he would find there.

She stood one moment longer. Then she picked up the pail and turned and walked toward the pump.

---

She heard him say something behind her. She was already several steps away — the radio going in the icehouse, the heat and the distance — and she caught only the shape of the words, not the words themselves.

*Es wird bald vorbei sein.*

The hay field beyond the fence held its full summer height. The smell of turned earth came across from the south field where her father had been working since before dawn, before the radio, before the sentence he had said into the kitchen. She kept walking. The pump handle at the corner of the barn would be warm from sitting in the afternoon sun.

# Harbor Traffic

The *Edna C.* came in off the grounds at two-fifty-eight, heavier than she looked. Talbot brought her in clean through the afternoon chop, which was running south-southeast at two feet and building. Eira logged the time and estimated the catch from the boxes on deck — Talbot would want to correct the tonnage entry against the scale once he'd offloaded, but there was enough in the hold to see from the pier head and she put down a working number. She could revise it in the morning.

Four more vessels to account for before dark. She turned back to the fuel log.

The Navy tender at the outer anchorage had run its weekly fueling at nine that morning, and the allocation she'd authorized — drawn against the defense supplemental, not the commercial reserve — had taken a larger bite out of the shared dock supply than she'd anticipated. Pete Alley had come to her before noon wanting to know whether his allotment was going to cover his run to the outer grounds. She'd checked the figures and it wouldn't, not without an adjustment. She made the adjustment: signed the form, moved the amount from the supplemental line, wrote her authorization in the margin. She did not ask anyone's approval because the handbook did not require it. Alley took the form and filled his tank and went.

In the summer of 1942, this same move would have required a county sign-off and three days. She did not think about it often. When she did, it was as a log entry: what the column shows this year against what it showed before.

---

The afternoon was full. June kept long hours, the light staying good until past seven, which meant the traffic did not thin before six and on some evenings she was still logging at dusk. She did not object to this. The harbor in summer was the harbor at its most itself: boats on the water, fuel in the tanks, money moving, the cold-storage house working around the clock. The harbor in December was harder to manage and quieter, which was not the same as easier.

Grandy Soule had the *Maud L.* at the east float on account of a sports boat from Portland tying in his usual slip without permission. She'd had him at her elbow at noon, not saying much but standing in a way that said plenty. She'd walked down the ramp and told the man in the sports boat's cockpit that the slip was not available. He had a dock hand's tan and a new sportsman's jacket and the particular patience of a man who expected his arrangements to be accommodated. He looked at her for the length of time it took to understand that she had said what she meant. Then he cast off his lines and moved to slip fourteen, which she had indicated.

Soule, when she came back up the ramp, said nothing. She said nothing. She went back to the log.

The second dispute of the afternoon was between Burton Talbot and Ray Coffin's boy over a question of priority at the fuel dock — both had radioed at the same hour, and Coffin had gotten there first. She looked at the log and told them the order of the log was the order of the dock. Coffin fueled. Talbot waited. Both left without arguing. The argument had lasted four minutes and she had used twelve words, which seemed like the right ratio.

She was making a note about the outer berth allotment when Talbot came back up from the dock.

He had his hat in his hand. Talbot did not take his hat off on the dock as a rule.

"My sister's boy is in it," he said. He meant Normandy. It had been three weeks.

"How old is he."

"Nineteen."

She put the pen down and looked at him. She had known Burton Talbot for eight years.

"All right," she said.

He put his hat back on and went up the pier.

She wrote the tonnage entry and the time.

---

That was the quality of the harbor since the sixth of June — the particular way the men spoke now. Before June the waiting had been accumulative: each week adding to the prior week, the not-yet getting larger. Since June there was still waiting, but at a fixed position. The thing had been identified; it had a location and a direction. You could track it now. This was not the same as better. Osgood's boy had been missing in Normandy since the fourteenth and his mother came to the post office every morning. The telegrams had not stopped. But the quality of what people were waiting with had changed, and she could feel it in the way they stood at the fuel dock and in the number of words they used.

She could not write any of this in the harbor log. She kept track of it elsewhere, in the same place she kept track of other things she couldn't put in the official record.

---

The afternoon turned still around four. This happened in late June on certain days: the wind dropped off and the harbor went flat, the water the color of pewter, the pilings showing their reflections straight down. The cold-storage house was quiet between runs. The three lobstermen still out on the grounds would be thinking about coming in.

She checked the clock on the shed wall and checked her watch against it. Four-forty-three, which was accurate.

She made a note in the weather log: flat calm at 1643, channel at slack. She had been making these notes for eight years, in the same format, with the same shorthand. The notes would not change the weather. They were the record.

---

Marcus Klein came along the harbor road at five minutes past five.

She had seen him on this road at this hour for two years going on three — the same walk, the same pace, the same slight forward lean that was his particular posture, as if he were attending to something at chest height that the rest of the road was not showing. He was not a large man and he dressed for the season: a good hat in winter, shirtsleeves in June. She had seen him in all weathers. He walked the way someone walked who had no car and had decided not to mind it, which was to say at a deliberate pace and without any appearance of hurry.

Most days he came even with the pier entrance, nodded in her direction — she may or may not have been visible; it made no difference to the nod — and continued south toward the Crow house on the hill. She had come to expect this the way she expected the position of the channel markers: a regular fixed point in the afternoon's accounting.

Today he stopped.

He came a few steps through the gate. "Good afternoon," he said.

"Afternoon."

He looked at the pier and then at her. "Are the Pfeiffer family managing all right, do you think?"

The phrasing was assembled — not casual, not a question asked in passing to fill a silence, but a question whose specific terms had been chosen before it was asked. *The Pfeiffer family,* not the Pfeiffers. *Managing all right,* not *how are they* or *any trouble out there.* It was a question designed to be answerable without requiring her to say what she actually knew, which told her enough.

"As far as I know," she said.

Which was accurate. The farm was running; the county had raised no complaint about the work arrangement; the daughter came to the post office like any other family in town; Albrecht Pfeiffer had been in for his feed run three weeks ago. She knew nothing more specific than this. She said what she knew.

He nodded once. "Thank you," he said.

He went on down the road.

---

She watched him walk the harbor road to the south bend and go around it, out of sight.

The exchange had taken perhaps forty seconds. She went back to the pier head and picked up her pen.

The *Sea Star* would be in by six. She had the form ready.

She did not write anything about Marcus Klein. There was nothing to write — a man had asked a question and she had answered it.

She held it in the back of the afternoon's accounting the way she held any piece of information that did not have a column yet.

He had been walking this road for going on three years. In that time he had said perhaps twenty words to her. She had always read him as someone who chose his words with attention — the particular precision of a man who had learned to be careful with language. He was not a man who stopped at pier gates to ask after inland farm families without a reason for it.

He was the German teacher. The Pfeiffer daughter was in his advanced German class; she knew that much from conversation at the post office. Whether he had any other connection to the farm she did not know.

She turned the question over. No obvious answer presented itself. If he had asked the question behind the question, it would have been: *is anything wrong out there.* She could not account for what had put that question in him. She did not have enough to build a theory.

There was one other piece she was carrying that she had no column for. The dock figures from the October night — the two shapes on the south float before the blow, one with something under his arm, the pale coat. She had been keeping that entry for eight months without a label, because she still did not have enough to classify it. Soule's account in April had come part of the way, had corroborated the dinghy and one figure, and she had reached for the pen and then set it down again. She knew what she'd seen and she knew what Soule had seen and she knew the two accounts met at the south float, and she still did not have a label for what that column was.

The column now had two entries in it.

She put the pen down and did not invent a label. The column was there; she knew it was there; both entries were in it correctly and were going to stay there until she had enough to name what the column was. Not longer. Not shorter.

---

The *Sea Star* came in at six-twelve. Coffin's boy ran her through the channel entrance with economy, and she logged the time and the catch and wrote the weather note for the outer grounds. He said four words about the chop past Seal Island and she wrote that too, because the chop past Seal Island in late June could matter to the morning forecast.

She transferred the afternoon to the permanent record: fuel allotments, berth assignments, arrival times, departures, tonnages. Alley's supplemental form and her authorization. Talbot's working tonnage figure and the notation to revise in the morning. The two berth disputes resolved. Everything in its column, every column labeled correctly.

She put the pen down and put the log on its shelf.

The last light was running at a long angle off the channel, making the water look shallow even where it wasn't. The outer anchorage tender was riding easy and dark. The lobster boats were resting at their lines, hulls knocking gently against the fenders, the particular sound the harbor made in the slack after a working day.

She turned off the shed light and went out.

The harbor would manage the night without her. It was good at that.
